2.7.6 Dipoles Planar; Dipoles sobre Juntas de Circuito Impreso

Los dipoles se implementan rutinariamente en tableros de circuito impreso (PCB); un ejemplo se muestra en la Figura 2.13. Esto es obviamente conveniente cuando sea posible, ya que normalmente la mayoría o todos los electrónicos en una radio también se implementan en un PCB. Sin embargo, un dipolo PCB tiene dos características no consideradas previamente: Primero, la proximidad del material dieléctrico. Mientras la dielectricidad sea eléctricamente delgada (por ejemplo comparable a a) y no hay plano de tierra en el lado opuesto, el efecto de la dieléctrica es típicamente muy pequeño. Segundo, la dipole es necesariamente planar, en lugar de cilíndrico, en la sección transversal.

Mientras la dimensión máxima de la sección transversal sea muy pequeña en comparación con L y λ, un dipolo plano que tiene anchura w es aproximadamente equivalente a un dipole cilíndrico que tiene radio a = w/4 [9]. En todos los demás aspectos, los dipoles PCB se comportan de forma similar a los dipolos cilíndricos en espacio libre.
Por supuesto es posible crear dipoles planarios de “libre standing” independientes de la implementación de PCB, en cuyo caso se aplica también el estado de antípodo anterior.
2.7.7 Otras antenas tipo Dipole

Las antenas prácticas de tipo dipolo existen en un número asombroso de variantes – algunas apenas reconocibles como dipoles. Aunque el alcance de este libro impide una discusión detallada, la Figura 2.14 muestra algunas variantes que son demasiado populares por no mencionar:

• Un dipolo de manga (Figura 2.14(a)) es un HWD formado por cable coaxial: El conductor central forma un brazo del dipole, y el escudo se vuelve a formar el otro brazo del dipóle. Cuando está diseñado correctamente, la sección de doble escudo también sirve como un balun de cuarto de onda que mitiga adecuadamente la diferencia entre el modo de corriente no balanceado y el modo HWD

• Dipolo plegado (Figura) 2.14b) se forma a partir de dos secciones de longitud de onda: una es una tradicional más o menos HWD, mientras que el otro es esencialmente un cortocircuito HWD. Las secciones están conectadas en los extremos. ≪λ, por lo que hay una fuerte interacción entre las secciones. El resultado es la longitud efectiva y el patrón similar a un HWD, pero con mayor ancho de banda y ZA que se trata de 4 tiempos más grandes que el de un HWD; es decir, aproximadamente 292 + j168 Ω. Esta mayor impedancia es más conveniente para ciertos tipos de línea de transmisión; en particular la línea de “conductor paralelo” que tiene una impedancia característica nominal 300 Ω. El dipolo plegado también es conveniente para 4-element arrays porque 4 dipoles plegados alimentados en paralelo tienen una impedancia combinada que está cerca de la impedancia de los tipos de líneas de transmisión comunes (es decir, 50 Ωand 75 Ω); más sobre esto en la sección 2.11.

• La pajarita (Figura 2.14(c))) y las antenas comparables son ejemplos de “dipoles en grasa”: dipoles con L/a muy pequeña “eficacia” pero no necesariamente exhibiendo la sección transversal cilíndrica presumida hasta este punto. La ventaja principal de esta topología es el ancho de banda aumentado, que puede ser hasta alrededor de 25% dependiendo del particular

El patrón y la impedancia de estas antenas se determinan típicamente por experiencia, mediciones o por métodos numéricos como el método de momentos o FDTD, especialmente cuando se requiere respuesta sobre una gama de frecuencias. Detalles adicionales sobre estas y varias otras variantes útiles de dipolo está bien cubierto en varios libros de texto y manuales de antena incluyendo [10, 78].

2.7.1 General Characteristics

To begin, a convenient generalization of the current distribution for L/a ≫1 (reminder: a is the radius) in response to a terminal current IT is

Also note that this expression yields the expected nearly-triangular distribution for the ESD (L ≪λ, Equation 2.12, and Figure 2.3). Although Equation 2.49 is presented here as an “educated guess”, the validity of this approximation is easily confirmed using rigorous theoretical and/or numerical methods. Figure 2.9 shows current distributions computed using Equation 2.49 for a variety of dipole lengths.

Electrically-thin straight dipoles of arbitrary length can be analyzed using the methods of Sections 2.2.2–2.2.3. Results for the dipoles shown in Figure 2.9 (as well as for the ESD) are shown in Table 2.1. (For Rrad, only the “at center” column is relevant for the moment). In all cases the patterns are omnidirectional and very similar to those of the ESD (Figure 2.7); the primary difference is a reduction in angular extent of the E-plane pattern. This is quantified in terms of the half-power beamwidth (HPBW) in Table 2.1. HPBW is defined as the angle over which power density is at least one-half the maximum power density.

Note that dipoles longer than L = 5λ/4 are not shown in Table 2.1, as these suffer from bifurcation of the main lobe and are therefore generally less useful in radio applications.

2.7.2 Electrically-Thin Half-Wave Dipole

For the metals typically used in the construction of HWDs, Rloss ≪Rrad, and therefore ǫrad ∼= 1 is typically a good approximation for HWDs in free space.

2.7.3 Electrically-Thin Dipoles with λ/2 < L ≤λ; Off-Center-Fed Dipoles

As length increases beyond λ/2, directivity and radiation resistance continue to increase and HPBW continues to decrease, as indicated in Table 2.1. However the current distribution changes such that the center of the dipole is no longer a current maximum, as is evident in Figure 2.9. This reaches an extreme condition when L = λ, for which the current at the center of the dipole goes to zero. This is a full-wave dipole (FWD). Since the terminal current of a FWD is zero, the radiation resistance of a FWD is infinite. At first glance, this would seem to preclude the use of a FWD in any practical application, since there appears to be no possibility of power transfer to or from the antenna. Furthermore, examination of Figure 2.10 seems to indicate that dipoles throughout the range 0.7λ < L < 1.2λ have Rrad and XA so large as to make impedance matching intractable.

A simple modification that makes these dipoles useable is to simply move the terminals from the center of the dipole to the position of a current maximum. This is shown for the FWD in Figure 2.11. With this modification the impedance of a FWD is much easier to accommodate, and there is no change in the current distribution or characteristics other than the impedance. The impedance for terminals located at the current maximum is indicated in Table 2.1 and Figure 2.10. Such dipoles are commonly-referred to as being off-center-fed.

In principle dipoles of any length can be off-center-fed. In general, moving the terminals to a position of lower current increases the radiation resistance. Thus, shifting the position of the terminals may be used to assist in matching the dipole to its associated electronics.4

2.7.4 Electrically-Thin 5/4-λ Dipole

As L increases beyond 5λ/4, the main lobe of the dipole bifurcates into two lobes and a null emerges in the broadside direction. This pattern has diminished applications in most radio applications. However L = 5λ/4 – i.e., just before pattern bifurcation – is of great interest because this dipole achieves the greatest broadside directivity and minimum HPBW of any straight dipole, and is relatively easy to match even when center-fed. This dipole finds applications in base station applications in the UHF range and above, where the length (2.5 times that of a HWD) is of little consequence.

4One might consider using this trick to increase the radiation resistance of an ESD. The limitation in practice is that the gap associated with the separation between the terminals becomes significant compared to the length of the dipole, so the results are typically disappointing.

2.7.5 Equivalent Circuits and Numerical Methods for Straight Dipoles of Arbitrary Length and Radius

It is often convenient to have an equivalent circuit model for the dipole impedance ZA, consisting of discrete resistors, capacitors, and inductors. Such a model has the advantage that ZA = Rrad + jXA can then be computed as a single quantity using simple circuit theory methods, as opposed to having separate procedures for determining Rrad and XA from relatively complex electromagnetic theory. Equivalent circuits also provide a relatively simple means to account for a variety of dipole thicknesses L/a.

A variety of solutions to this problem exist; here we present two. The equivalent circuit proposed by Tang, Tieng & Gunn (1993) [79] is shown in Figure 2.12.5 The component values are given below in terms of the length L in meters and the thickness parameter b ≡L/a:

This method yields Rrad which is accurate to within about 1% and XA which is accurate to within about 15% for L < 0.6λ and L/a > 300.

For dipoles longer than about 0.6λ, a different equivalent circuit model is needed. One possibility among many is the model of Hamid & Hamid (1997) [25], which models the impedance of dipoles having L > λ/2 using circuits of increasing numbers of components with increasing length. The center-fed impedance is determined, which must subsequently be adjusted if the dipole is intended to be off-center-fed as described in Section 2.7.3.

When the dipole is very thick (e.g., L/a less than about 100) or consists of less-good conductors (such as brass), or when accurate pattern or directivity data are also required, it is somewhat more common to use a computational electromagnetics technique such as the moment method or FDTD. This approach is typically required when the dipole is located close (e.g., within a few wavelengths) to other antennas or structures.

2.7.6 Planar Dipoles; Dipoles on Printed Circuit Boards

Dipoles are routinely implemented on printed circuit boards (PCBs); an example is shown in Figure 2.13. This is obviously convenient when possible, since typically most or all of the electronics in a radio are also implemented on a PCB. However a PCB dipole has two features not previously considered: First, the proximity of dielectric material. As long as the dielectric is electrically thin (e.g. comparable to a) and there is no ground plane on the opposite side, the effect of the dielectric is typically very small. Second, the dipole is necessarily planar, as opposed to cylindrical, in cross-section.

As long as the maximum dimension of the cross-section is very small compared to both L and λ, a planar dipole having width w is approximately equivalent to a cylindrical dipole having radius a = w/4 [9]. In all other respects, PCB dipoles behave similarly to cylindrical dipoles in free space.

Of course it is possible to create “free standing” planar dipoles independent of PCB implementation, in which case the above rule-of-thumb also applies.

2.7.7 Other Dipole-Type Antennas

Practical dipole-type antennas exist in an astounding number of variants – some barely recognizable as dipoles. Although the scope of this book precludes a detailed discussion, Figure 2.14 shows a few variants that are too popular not to mention:

• A sleeve dipole (Figure 2.14(a)) is a HWD formed from coaxial cable: The center conductor forms one arm of the dipole, and the shield is turned back on itself to form the other arm of the dipole. When properly designed, the doubled-back shield section also serves as a quarter-wave balun which properly mitigates the difference between the unbalanced current mode of the coaxial cable and the balanced mode of the HWD.

• A folded dipole (Figure 2.14(b)) is formed from two half-wavelength sections: One is a more-or-less traditional HWD, whereas the other is essentially a short-circuited HWD. The sections are connected at the ends. The spacing between sections is ≪λ, so there is strong interaction between the sections. The result is effective length and pattern similar to a HWD, but with increased bandwidth and ZA which is about 4 times greater than that of a HWD; i.e. roughly 292 + j168 Ω. This higher impedance is more convenient for certain types of transmission line; in particular “parallel conductor” line which has a nominal characteristic impedance of 300 Ω. The folded dipole is also convenient for 4-element arrays because 4 folded dipoles fed in parallel have a combined impedance which is close to the impedance of common transmission line types (i.e, 50 Ωand 75 Ω); more on this in Section 2.11.

• The bowtie (Figure 2.14(c)) and comparable antennas are examples of “fat dipoles”: dipoles with very small “effective” L/a, but not necessarily exhibiting the cylindrical cross-section presumed to this point. The principle advantage of this topology is increased bandwidth, which can be up to about 25% depending on the particular

In many applications where a dipole might be used, one or both of the following problems emerge: (1) the electrical
interface to the radio is single-ended (e.g., one terminal i s grounded), (2) mounting of the dipole is awkward due to spac e
constraints or the proximity of a large conducting surface w hich affects the dipole’s performance. Monopoles are typic ally
used in these cases. Let us first describe the monopole, and th en discuss why monopoles are often favored when
conditions (1) or (2) apply.

2.8.1 General Characteristics
The fundamental concept of the monopole is illustrated in Fi gure 2.15. Beginning with a dipole, an ideal monopole is
obtained by replacing one “arm” with a flat, perfectly-condu cting ground plane that extends to infinity in all directions .
From electromagnetic image theory, we know that the current s on the remaining arm should be identical to the currents on
the corresponding arm of the original dipole, and that the el ectromagnetic fields radiated by the monopole above the
ground plane should be identical to those of the dipole in the same region. Below the ground plane, however, the fields
radiated by the ideal monopole must be identically zero.
The facts allow us to quickly determine the directivity and i mpedance of a monopole, given the characteristics of the
corresponding dipole. Recall that directivity is power den sity divided by mean power density over a sphere enclosing th e
antenna. Below the ground plane, D(θ,φ ) = 0 since no power can be radiated into this region. Above the gro und plane,
D(θ,φ ) is twice the value for the corresponding dipole, since the po wer density is equal whereas mean power density is
reduced by one-half because D(θ,φ ) = 0 below the ground plane. Similarly the total power radiated b y a transmitting
ideal monopole is one-half that for the corresponding dipol e given the same terminal current IT , so from Equation 2.21 we
seeRrad for the ideal monopole must be one-half the corresponding va lue for the dipole. In fact, it is possible to show
(although beyond the scope of this text) that ZA (i.e., both real and imaginary components of the impedance) for the ideal
monopole is one-half ZA for the corresponding dipole.
It should be apparent that the electrical interface to the mo nopole is intrinsically single-ended, where the ground pla ne can
be interpreted as the datum. This is particularly convenien t when the connection between antenna and radio uses coaxial
cable, which is also intrinsically single-ended.

En muchas aplicaciones donde se puede utilizar un dipolo, surge uno o ambos de los siguientes problemas: (1) la interfaz eléctrica a la radio es de una sola forma (por ejemplo, una terminal está basada), (2) el montaje del dipole es incómodo debido a las limitaciones espaciales o la proximidad de una gran superficie de conducción que afecta al rendimiento del dipolo. 2.8.1 Las Características Generales

El concepto fundamental del monopolo se ilustra en la Figura 2.15. Comenzando por un dipolo, se obtiene un monopolo ideal reemplazando un “arma” con un plano plano plano plano de tierra plano y perfectamente conductor que se extiende a la infinidad en todas las direcciones. De la teoría de la imagen electromagnética, sabemos que las corrientes en el brazo restante deben ser idénticas a las corrientes en la rama correspondiente del dipolo original, y que los campos electromagnéticos irradiados por el monopolo sobre el plano terrestre deben ser idénticos a los del dipole en la misma región. Sin embargo, debajo del plano de tierra, los campos irradiados por un monopolo ideal deben ser idénticomente cero.

Los hechos nos permiten determinar rápidamente la directividad y la impedancia de un monopolo, dadas las características del dipolo correspondiente. Recordar que la directividad es densidad de potencia dividida por densidad de potencia media sobre una esfera que encierra la antena. Bajo el plano terrestre, D(θ, φ) = 0 ya que no se puede irradiar energía en esta región. Sobre el plano de tierra, D(θ, φ) es el doble del valor para el dipolo correspondiente, ya que la densidad de potencia es igual mientras que la densidad de potencia media se reduce por la mitad debido a D(θ, φ) = 0 debajo del plano de tierra. Del mismo modo el poder total irradiado por un monopolo ideal de transmisión es una mitad que para el dipolo correspondiente dada la misma corriente terminal IT, por lo tanto de la Ecuación 2.21 vemos Rrad para el monopolo ideal debe ser una mitad del valor correspondiente para el dipolo. De hecho, es posible mostrar (aunque más allá del alcance de este texto) que ZA (es decir, los componentes reales e imaginarios de la impedancia) para el monopolo ideal es un 1-half ZA para el dipolo correspondiente.

Debe ser evidente que la interfaz eléctrica al monopolo es intrínsecamente de un solo sentido, donde el plano terrestre puede interpretarse como datum. Esto es particularmente conveniente cuando la conexión entre la antena y la radio utiliza el cable coaxial, que también es intrónicamente de un solo soporte.

Por supuesto, variaciones significativas de la impedancia y patrón del ideal QWM se esperan cuando el plano de suelo se implementa de esta manera.

Como en el caso del dipolo, el número de variantes importantes es grande y un resumen de estas variantes está más allá del alcance de este libro; puntos de partida recomendados para información adicional incluyen [10] y [86]. In many applications where a dipole might be used, one or both of the following problems emerge: (1) the electrical interface to the radio is single-ended (e.g., one terminal is grounded), (2) mounting of the dipole is awkward due to space constraints or the proximity of a large conducting surface which affects the dipole’s performance. 2.8.1 General Characteristics

The fundamental concept of the monopole is illustrated in Figure 2.15. Beginning with a dipole, an ideal monopole is obtained by replacing one “arm” with a flat, perfectly-conducting ground plane that extends to infinity in all directions. From electromagnetic image theory, we know that the currents on the remaining arm should be identical to the currents on the corresponding arm of the original dipole, and that the electromagnetic fields radiated by the monopole above the ground plane should be identical to those of the dipole in the same region. Below the ground plane, however, the fields radiated by the ideal monopole must be identically zero.

The facts allow us to quickly determine the directivity and impedance of a monopole, given the characteristics of the corresponding dipole. Recall that directivity is power density divided by mean power density over a sphere enclosing the antenna. Below the ground plane, D(θ, φ) = 0 since no power can be radiated into this region. Above the ground plane, D(θ, φ) is twice the value for the corresponding dipole, since the power density is equal whereas mean power density is reduced by one-half because D(θ, φ) = 0 below the ground plane. Similarly the total power radiated by a transmitting ideal monopole is one-half that for the corresponding dipole given the same terminal current IT , so from Equation 2.21 we see Rrad for the ideal monopole must be one-half the corresponding value for the dipole. In fact, it is possible to show (although beyond the scope of this text) that ZA (i.e., both real and imaginary components of the impedance) for the ideal monopole is one-half ZA for the corresponding dipole.

It should be apparent that the electrical interface to the monopole is intrinsically single-ended, where the ground plane can be interpreted as the datum. This is particularly convenient when the connection between antenna and radio uses coaxial cable, which is also intrinsically single-ended.

2.9 Patch Antennas
A patch antenna consists of a planar metallic radiator which is separated from a ground plane by a slab of dielectric
material having thickness≪ λ. Figure 2.17(a) illustrates the design of a typical patch an tenna; in this case, for a handheld
GPS receiver. The patch may be fed using a conductor which pro trudes through the ground plane to some point on the
patch (as in Figure 2.17(a)), or alternatively using a micro strip transmission line connected to an edge of the patch. In
either case an electric field is created between the patch and the ground plane, which subsequently radiates from the edge s
of the patch.
Analysis of patches is difficult compared to dipoles and mono poles, and is beyond the scope of this text. However, a few
generally-applicable statements are in order. The patch an tenna exhibits greatest directivity in the direction perpe ndicular
to the ground plane. The maximum directivity of traditional patches is usually within a few dB of 8 dBi. This may be
confirmed by the following informal analysis: Assume the rad iation from the patch is well modeled as the radiation from
two parallel dipoles separated by the width of the patch. The n each dipole contributes a directivity of roughly 2 dBi, whi ch
is increased by roughly 3 dB by the presence of the ground plan e, since power remains constant whereas accessible solid
angle is reduced by one-half. Combining these dipoles incre ases the directivity by about 3 dB, yielding 8 dBi.
The impedance and polarization are determined by the dimens ions and shape of the patch, and the point of connection.
Square patches fed from near the center of the patch (as in Fig ure 2.17(a)) are typically resonant (i.e., have reactance
which is low relative to the radiation resistance) when the p erimeter of the patch is about λ/ √

2.9 Antenas de parche

Una antena de parche consiste en un radiador metálico plano que se separa de un plano de tierra por una losa de material dieléctrico con espesor ≪λ. Figura 2.17a) ilustra el diseño de una antena típica de parche; en este caso, para un portátil GPS receptor. El parche puede ser alimentado usando un conductor que protruye a través del plano del suelo hasta algún punto en el parche (como en la Figura 2.17(a)), o alternativamente utilizando una línea de transmisión de microstrip conectada a un borde del parche. En cualquier caso se crea un campo eléctrico entre el parche y el plano de tierra, que posteriormente irradia desde los bordes del parche.

El análisis de parches es difícil en comparación con dipoles y monopolos, y está más allá del alcance de este texto. Sin embargo, algunas declaraciones generalmente aplicables están en orden. La antena de parche muestra mayor directividad en la dirección perpendicular al plano de tierra. La máxima directividad de los parches tradicionales suele estar dentro de un poco dB de 8 dBi. Esto puede ser confirmado por el siguiente análisis informal: Asumir la radiación del parche está bien modelado como la radiación de dos dipoles paralelos separados por la anchura del parche. Luego cada dipolo contribuye una directividad de aproximadamente 2 dBi, que se aumenta en forma brusca 3 dB por la presencia del plano de tierra, ya que el poder permanece constante mientras que el ángulo sólido accesible se reduce por la mitad. Combinar estas dipoles aumenta la directividad por alrededor 3 dB, ceder 8 dBi.

La impedancia y la polarización se determinan por las dimensiones y la forma del parche, y el punto de conexión. Parches cuadrados alimentados desde cerca del centro del parche (como en la Figura 2.17(a)) son típicamente resonantes (es decir, tienen una reactancia baja en relación con la resistencia a la radiación) cuando el perímetro del parche se trata de λ/√ǫr, donde ǫr es la relativa permitividad de material de espaciamiento dieléctrico. El punto de conexión es ligeramente fuera del centro, lo que resulta en polarización circular. Los parches cuadrados que se alimentan desde un borde son típicamente resonantes cuando la longitud eléctrica del perímetro es 2λ/√ǫr,

y están linealmente poliarizados. La impedancia puede ser modificada más a través de conexiones cortas que conectan el parche al plano terrestre en otras ubicaciones.

Debido a que las antenas de parche consisten en la metalización por encima de un plano terrestre separado por una dieléctrica, son una opción natural cuando se desea la implementación en una placa de circuito impreso (PCB). En particular, es muy simple añadir una antena de parche a un circuito de radio que se ha implementado en un PCB.

Los parches tienen la característica atractiva adicional que su tamaño puede reducirse aumentando la constante dieléctrica del material de espaciamiento. ǫr of 4.5 (correspondiendo a un tipo popular de material epoxi de fibra de vidrio comúnmente utilizado en PCB), se puede hacer un parche cuadrado para resonar eficientemente cuando su longitud lateral es sólo alrededor λ/10. Esto hace que las antenas de parche sean extremadamente populares en electrónica de consumo, incluyendo teléfonos celulares y dispositivos de computación móvil.

Una antena de parche comúnmente contada es la antena planar invertida-F (PIFA), mostrada en la Figura 2.17(b). El PIFA se forma acortando un lado del parche, de modo que el parche, conductor de alimentación y sección de acortamiento forman una forma “F” vista desde un lado. Muchas de las antenas utilizadas en electrónica móvil moderna que operan en UHF o superior utilizan alguna variante del PIFA.

Ejemplo 2.5. La figura 2.18 muestra algunos ejemplos de PIFAs utilizados en teléfonos celulares celulares. La forma convocada del parche PIFA combinado con elementos parasitarios (sin conexión) resulta en baja reactancia a múltiples frecuencias, facilitando la operación multibanda.

Los principales inconvenientes de las antenas parche, en relación con dipoles y monopolos, son la eficiencia de radiación y el ancho de banda. Los parches suelen tener una mala eficiencia de radiación parcialmente porque el material de espaciamiento dieléctrico tiene alguna pérdida, pero también porque la antena puede interactuar fuertemente con materiales cercanos a la pérdida cuando se incrustan en dispositivos como teléfonos celulares. En los teléfonos celulares en particular, la eficiencia de radiación para un resonante PIFA está en el orden de 50%, y a veces mucho más bajo.6 El asunto ancho de banda surge porque parches resonantes son mucho más pequeños que dipoles o monopolos resonantes. Como veremos en el capítulo 12, el ancho de banda que una antena puede acomodar está inversamente relacionado con sus dimensiones generales relativas a una longitud de onda.

2.9 Patch Antennas

A patch antenna consists of a planar metallic radiator which is separated from a ground plane by a slab of dielectric material having thickness ≪λ. Figure 2.17(a) illustrates the design of a typical patch antenna; in this case, for a handheld GPS receiver. The patch may be fed using a conductor which protrudes through the ground plane to some point on the patch (as in Figure 2.17(a)), or alternatively using a microstrip transmission line connected to an edge of the patch. In either case an electric field is created between the patch and the ground plane, which subsequently radiates from the edges of the patch.

Analysis of patches is difficult compared to dipoles and monopoles, and is beyond the scope of this text. However, a few generally-applicable statements are in order. The patch antenna exhibits greatest directivity in the direction perpendicular to the ground plane. The maximum directivity of traditional patches is usually within a few dB of 8 dBi. This may be confirmed by the following informal analysis: Assume the radiation from the patch is well modeled as the radiation from two parallel dipoles separated by the width of the patch. Then each dipole contributes a directivity of roughly 2 dBi, which is increased by roughly 3 dB by the presence of the ground plane, since power remains constant whereas accessible solid angle is reduced by one-half. Combining these dipoles increases the directivity by about 3 dB, yielding 8 dBi.

The impedance and polarization are determined by the dimensions and shape of the patch, and the point of connection. Square patches fed from near the center of the patch (as in Figure 2.17(a)) are typically resonant (i.e., have reactance which is low relative to the radiation resistance) when the perimeter of the patch is about λ/√ǫr , where ǫr is the relative permittivity of dielectric spacing material. The point of connection is slightly off-center, resulting in circular polarization. Square patches which are fed from an edge are typically resonant when the electrical length of the perimeter is 2λ/√ǫr,

Figure 2.18: Mobile phones for 900/1800/1900 MHz GSM cellular systems using PIFA-type antennas. All dimensions are in mm. ©2012 IEEE. Reprinted and released under CC BY 4.0, with permission, from [69].

and are linearly-polarized. The impedance may be further modified using shorting connections which connect the patch to the ground plane at additional locations.

Example 2.4. The patch shown in Figure 2.17(a) is 20 mm × 21 mm in size and uses a ceramic material having relative permittivity ∼= 5.4. Confirm that this patch is suitable for GPS.

√

5.4 ∼= 82 mm. This yields λ ∼= 19.4 cm and thus f ∼= 1574.4 MHz. This is very close to the GPS L1 center frequency of 1575.42 MHz.

Solution: The perimeter of the patch is 82 mm and therefore patch should be resonant when λ/

Because patch antennas consist of metalization above a ground plane separated by a dielectric, they are a natural choice when implementation on a printed circuit board (PCB) is desired. In particular, it is quite simple to add a patch antenna to a radio circuit which has been implemented on a PCB.

Patches have the additional attractive feature that their size can be reduced by increasing the dielectric constant of the spacing material. For a typical ǫr of 4.5 (corresponding to a popular type of fiberglass epoxy material commonly used in PCBs), a square patch can be made to resonate efficiently when its side length is only about λ/10. This makes patch antennas extremely popular in consumer electronics, including mobile phones and mobile computing devices.

A commonly-encountered patch antenna is the planar inverted-F antenna (PIFA), shown in Figure 2.17(b). The PIFA is formed by shorting one side of the patch such that the patch, feed conductor, and shorting section form an “F” shape as viewed from one side. Many of the antennas used in modern mobile electronics operating at UHF or above utilize some variant of the PIFA.

2.10.text:
2.10 High Gain Antennas
Dipoles, monopoles, and patches are low-gain antennas. Som etimes, higher directivity is required or desired. There ar e at
least three broad classes of high gain antennas: beam antenn as (Section 2.10.1), reflector antennas (Section 2.10.2), a nd
certain types of arrays (Section 2.11).
From a transmit perspective, higher directivity is achieve d by increasing the power density in a specified direction.
Because an antenna is passive, the total radiated power is co nstant. Therefore increasing directivity one direction re sults in
reduced directivity in other directions.
The pattern of a typical high-gain antenna is shown in Figure 2.19. High directivity inevitably results in a more complex
pattern consisting of a main lobe, sidelobes, and (sometimes) a backlobe. As explained earlier in this chapter, Half power
beamwidth (HPBW) is the angular distance between points on the main lobe for which the directivity is one-half that of
the maximum directivity. Since E-plane and H-plane pattern s may be different, E-plane HPBW may be different from
H-plane HPBW.
Lobes other than the main lobe are referred to as sidelobes. T ypically the sidelobes adjacent to the main lobe have the
greatest directivity. The ratio of the directivity of a side lobe (typically the largest sidelobe) to that of the main lob e is
known as the sidelobe level. A backlobe is a sidelobe which is directly opposite the main lobe. Not all high-gain antennas
have an identifiable backlobe. When a backlobe exists, the rat io of maximum (i.e., main lobe) directivity to the maximum
directivity within the backlobe is known as the front-to-back ratio.
6As will be pointed out in Chapter 12, some part of this loss may be deliberately introduced as a technique for improving bandwi dth.

2.10.1 Beam Antennas; The Yagi
Beam antennas consist of a driver antenna whose directivity is increased through electromag netic (“parasitic”) interaction
with elements similar to the driver. 7 A beam antenna consisting of a HWD driver and dipole-type para sitic elements is
commonly known as a Yagi-Uda antenna or simply as a Yagi; see Figure 2.20(d) for an example. In a Y agi, the parasitic
elements consist of a reflector and some number of directors, and the direction of maximum directivity is in the directio n
of the directors. The driver, reflector, and directors are jo ined using a beam, which exists only for mechanical purposes and
normally has only a small effect on the electromagnetic char acteristics of the antenna. Beam antennas can be alternativ ely
be constructed from loops and certain other kinds of low-gai n elements.
The operation of the Y agi depends on electromagnetic interactions between the driver, reflector, and directors that can not
be described using simple closed-form equations. However i t is useful to know some basic design concepts. Beginning
with a HWD driver, the addition of a reflector which is slightly longer than the driver and which is separated by
0. 1λ–0. 25λ, as shown in Figure 2.20(b), results in an increase in direct ivity in the direction opposite the reflector by about
3–5 dB, to about 5–7 dBi. A similar improvement can be achieve d by adding a director which is slightly shorter than the
driver and with a similar spacing from the driver, as shown in Figure 2.20(c). These effects can be combined; a
properly-designed 3-element Y agi consisting of a driver, reflector, and director typically has a gain of about 9 dBi. Fur ther
increases in gain are achieved using additional equally-sp aced directors. Figure 2.20(d) shows an example of a Y agi usi ng
5 directors, having directivity of about 11.5 dBi. In princi ple directivity can be made arbitrarily large using increas ing
numbers of directors; albeit with diminishing returns.
The impedance, directivity, and pattern of practical beam a ntennas are quite difficult to determine without resorting t o a
numerical method (once again, method of moments and FDTD are popular choices) or to empirical solutions (e.g., tables

gain antenna; i.e., “beam” is taken to mean that the main lobe domi nates the pattern. By this definition, reflectors and arrays a re also “beam antennas”.
That is not quite what we mean here.

showing results for particular designs). For an introducti on to practical analysis and design techniques for beam ante nnas,
reference [78] is recommended.
Beam antennas are extremely popular for applications requi ring moderate gain at frequencies in the UHF band and below.
These applications include reception of terrestrial broad cast television and wireless data communications between fi xed
points. Beam antennas are less common above UHF, because (as noted above) greater directivity can typically be achieved
using reflector antennas (the topic of the next section) havi ng smaller overall size and a more convenient mechanical
design.
A common method for feeding a beam antenna using a coaxial cab le is to use a gamma match. An example is shown in
Figure 2.21. In this scheme the shield is grounded to center o f the driven element, and the inner conductor is connected to
the driven element a short distance from the center via a capa citive tuning stub. This allows the driven element and the
shield to be directly connected to the metallic boom, yeildi ng a simple and sturdy interface that obviates the need for a
balun.
2.10.2 Reflectors
A paraboloidal reflector can be used to dramatically increas e the directivity of a low- to moderate-gain antenna, known i n
this application as a feed. The concept is shown in Figure 2.22. The method of operation is most easily understood in
terms of geometrical optics (also known as ray optics), which is applicable if the minimum dimension and surface r adii of
curvature of the reflector are much greater than a wavelength . According to geometrical optics, the electromagnetic fiel d
scattered from each point on the reflector is approximately e qual to the field reflected by an infinite conducting plane
tangent to the surface. If the feed is located at the focus of t he paraboloid defining the reflector surface, then the field
reflected from each point on the reflector travels in the same d irection; that is, in parallel with the axis of revolution of the
paraboloid. Furthermore it can be shown that the phase of the reflected contributions is equal in any plane perpendicular to
the axis of the paraboloid. Thus the total reflected field is a p lane wave traveling along the axis.
The directivity of a reflector antenna system is limited by tw o factors: First, spillover; that is, some fraction of the feed
pattern does not illuminate the reflector. Second, diffraction from the edges of the paraboloid results in some fraction of
the power from the feed being scattered in other directions.
A good engineering approximation of the far-field pattern of a reflector antenna can be obtained using the following tenet
of antenna theory: The electric field in a planar aperture is r elated to the far-field pattern by the two-dimensional Fouri er
transform. In this case, we define a circular planar aperture in front of the dish, and note that according to the geometric al
optics approximation, the electric fields within that apert ure have uniform phase, and that the electric fields outside t his
aperture are identically zero. The pattern is therefore the Fourier transform of a two-dimensional function having
constant-phase within a circular aperture. The details of t his derivation are beyond the scope of this text, but the resu lts can

2.10 Antenas de alta ganancia

Las dipoles, los monopolos y los parches son antenas de baja ganancia. A veces, se requiere o desea una mayor directividad. Hay al menos tres clases amplias de antenas de alta ganancia: antenas de haz (Sección 2.10.1), antenas reflectoras (Sección 2.10.2), y ciertos tipos de arrays (Sección 2.11).

Desde una perspectiva de transmisión, la mayor directividad se logra aumentando la densidad de potencia en una dirección especificada. Debido a que una antena es pasiva, el poder radiado total es constante. Por lo tanto, aumentar la directividad una dirección resulta en menor directaidad en otras direcciones.

El patrón de una típica antena de alta ganancia se muestra en la Figura 2.19. La alta directividad inevitablemente resulta en un patrón más complejo que consiste en un lóbulo principal, sidelobes y (a veces) un backlobe. Como se explicó anteriormente en este capítulo, Media potencia de ancho de haz (HPBW) es la distancia angular entre puntos en el lóbulo principal para el cual la directividad es una mitad de la de la máxima directividad. Puesto que los patrones de E-plane y H-plane pueden ser diferentes, E-plane HPBW puede ser diferente de H-plane HPBW.

Los lobos que no son el lóbulo principal se denominan sidelobes. Típicamente los sidelobes adyacentes al lóbulos principal tienen la mayor directividad. La relación de la directividad de un sidelobe (típicamente el bódido más grande) con la del lóbula principal es conocida como el nivel de sidelobe. Un backlobe es un sidelobo que está directamente enfrente del lómero principal. Cuando existe un backlobe, la relación de máxima (es decir, lóbulo principal) directividad a la máxima directividad dentro del backlobe se conoce como la relación frontal-a-back.

2.10.1 Antenas de Beam; Los Yagi

Las antenas de haz consisten en una antena de conductor cuya directividad se aumenta mediante la interacción electromagnética (“parasitaria”) con elementos similares al controlador.La antena de haz 7 A que consiste en un controlador HWD y elementos parasitarios tipo dipole es comúnmente conocido como una antena Yagi-Uda o simplemente como un Yagi; vea la dirección 2.20(d) por ejemplo. El conductor, reflector y directores se unen usando una viga, que existe sólo para fines mecánicos y normalmente tiene un pequeño efecto sobre las características electromagnéticas de la antena. Las antenas de haz pueden ser construidas alternativamente a partir de bucles y ciertos otros tipos de elementos de baja ganancia.

La operación de los Yagi depende de interacciones electromagnéticas entre el conductor, reflector y directores que no pueden describirse usando ecuaciones simples de forma cerrada. Sin embargo, es útil conocer algunos conceptos básicos de diseño. Comenzando con un HWD conductor, la adición de un reflector que es un poco más largo que el conductor y que se separa por 0.1λ–0.25λ, como se muestra en la Figura 2.20b), se traduce en un aumento de la directividad en la dirección opuesta al reflector alrededor 3–5 dB, a casi 5–7 dBi. Una mejora similar se puede lograr mediante la adición de un director que es ligeramente más corto que el conductor y con un espaciado similar del conductor, como se muestra en la Figura 2.20(c). Estos efectos pueden combinarse; un Yagi de 3-element correctamente diseñado que consiste en un conductor, reflector y director normalmente tiene una ganancia de alrededor de 9 dBi. Se logran nuevos aumentos de ganancia utilizando directores adicionales igualmente espaciados. La Figura 2.20(d) muestra un ejemplo de un Yagi usando directores 5, con directividad de alrededor de11.5 dBi. En principio la directividad puede ser arbitrariamente grande utilizando números crecientes de dirección.

Por esta definición, los reflectores y arrays también son “ antenas de haz”. Eso no es lo que queremos decir aquí.

Figura 2.21: Un partido gamma utilizado para la interfaz de cable coaxial al elemento impulsado de un Yagi.

Para una introducción a técnicas prácticas de análisis y diseño para antenas de vigas, se recomienda referencia [78].

Las antenas de haz son extremadamente populares para aplicaciones que requieren ganancia moderada en frecuencias en la banda UHF y abajo. Estas aplicaciones incluyen recepción de televisión terrestre y comunicaciones inalámbricas de datos entre puntos fijos. Las antenas del haz son menos comunes por encima de UHF, porque (como se ha señalado anteriormente) una mayor directividad puede alcanzarse normalmente utilizando antenas reflectoras (el tema de la sección siguiente) con menor tamaño general y un diseño mecánico más conveniente.

Un método común para alimentar una antena de haz usando un cable coaxial es usar un partido gamma. Un ejemplo se muestra en la Figura 2.21. En este esquema el escudo se basa en el centro del elemento impulsado, y el conductor interno está conectado al elemento impulsado a corta distancia del centro a través de un ajuste capacitivo stub (tramo de línea). Esto permite que el elemento conducido y el escudo estén directamente conectados al boom metálico, yeilding una interfaz sencilla y robusta que evita la necesidad de un balun.

2.10.2 Reflectors

Un reflector paraboloidal puede ser utilizado para aumentar drásticamente la directividad de una antena de baja a moderada ganancia, conocida en esta aplicación como un pienso. El concepto se muestra en la Figura 2.22. El método de operación es más fácil de entender en términos de óptica geométrica (también conocido como ray óptica), que es aplicable si la dimensión mínima y radios superficiales de curvatura del reflector son mucho mayores que un wavele. Según la óptica geométrica, el campo electromagnético diseminado desde cada punto en el reflector es aproximadamente igual al campo reflejado por un plano de conducción infinito tangente a la superficie. Si el alimento se encuentra en el foco del paraboloide que define la superficie reflectora, entonces el campo reflejado desde cada punto sobre el reflector viaja en la misma dirección; es decir, en paralelo con el eje de revolución del parabooides. Además, se puede demostrar que la fase de las contribuciones reflejadas es igual en cualquier plano perpendicular al eje del paraboloide. Así el campo total reflejado es una onda plana que viaja a lo largo del eje.

La directividad de un sistema de antena reflectora está limitada por dos factores: Primero, el derrame; es decir, una parte del patrón de alimentación no ilumina al reflector. Segundo, la difracción de los bordes de los paraboloides resulta en alguna fracción de la potencia de la alimentación que se dispersa en otras direcciones.

Una buena aproximación de ingeniería del patrón de campo lejano de una antena reflectora se puede obtener utilizando el siguiente tene de la teoría de la antena: El campo eléctrico en una abertura planar está relacionado con el patrón de campo remoto por la transformación bidimensional Fourier. En este caso, definimos una abertura circular plana delante del plato y observamos que según la aproximación geométrica de óptica, los campos eléctricos dentro de esa abertura tienen fase uniforme, y que los campos eléctricoes fuera de esta abertura son idénticos cero. El patrón es por lo tanto el transformado Fourier de una función bidimensional que tiene fase constante dentro de una abertura circular. 2.10 High Gain Antennas

Dipoles, monopoles, and patches are low-gain antennas. Sometimes, higher directivity is required or desired. There are at least three broad classes of high gain antennas: beam antennas (Section 2.10.1), reflector antennas (Section 2.10.2), and certain types of arrays (Section 2.11).

From a transmit perspective, higher directivity is achieved by increasing the power density in a specified direction. Because an antenna is passive, the total radiated power is constant. Therefore increasing directivity one direction results in reduced directivity in other directions.

The pattern of a typical high-gain antenna is shown in Figure 2.19. High directivity inevitably results in a more complex pattern consisting of a main lobe, sidelobes, and (sometimes) a backlobe. As explained earlier in this chapter, Half power beamwidth (HPBW) is the angular distance between points on the main lobe for which the directivity is one-half that of the maximum directivity. Since E-plane and H-plane patterns may be different, E-plane HPBW may be different from H-plane HPBW.

Lobes other than the main lobe are referred to as sidelobes. Typically the sidelobes adjacent to the main lobe have the greatest directivity. The ratio of the directivity of a sidelobe (typically the largest sidelobe) to that of the main lobe is known as the sidelobe level. A backlobe is a sidelobe which is directly opposite the main lobe. Not all high-gain antennas have an identifiable backlobe. When a backlobe exists, the ratio of maximum (i.e., main lobe) directivity to the maximum directivity within the backlobe is known as the front-to-back ratio.

2.10.1 Beam Antennas; The Yagi

Beam antennas consist of a driver antenna whose directivity is increased through electromagnetic (“parasitic”) interaction with elements similar to the driver.7 A beam antenna consisting of a HWD driver and dipole-type parasitic elements is commonly known as a Yagi-Uda antenna or simply as a Yagi; see Figure 2.20(d) for an example. In a Yagi, the parasitic elements consist of a reflector and some number of directors, and the direction of maximum directivity is in the direction of the directors. The driver, reflector, and directors are joined using a beam, which exists only for mechanical purposes and normally has only a small effect on the electromagnetic characteristics of the antenna. Beam antennas can be alternatively be constructed from loops and certain other kinds of low-gain elements.

The operation of the Yagi depends on electromagnetic interactions between the driver, reflector, and directors that cannot be described using simple closed-form equations. However it is useful to know some basic design concepts. Beginning with a HWD driver, the addition of a reflector which is slightly longer than the driver and which is separated by 0.1λ–0.25λ, as shown in Figure 2.20(b), results in an increase in directivity in the direction opposite the reflector by about 3–5 dB, to about 5–7 dBi. A similar improvement can be achieved by adding a director which is slightly shorter than the driver and with a similar spacing from the driver, as shown in Figure 2.20(c). These effects can be combined; a properly-designed 3-element Yagi consisting of a driver, reflector, and director typically has a gain of about 9 dBi. Further increases in gain are achieved using additional equally-spaced directors. Figure 2.20(d) shows an example of a Yagi using 5 directors, having directivity of about 11.5 dBi. In principle directivity can be made arbitrarily large using increasing numbers of directors; albeit with diminishing returns.

The impedance, directivity, and pattern of practical beam antennas are quite difficult to determine without resorting to a numerical method (once again, method of moments and FDTD are popular choices) or to empirical solutions (e.g., tables

7Here we should note another common example of potentially confusing nomenclature: The term “beam antenna” is sometime used to mean any highgain antenna; i.e., “beam” is taken to mean that the main lobe dominates the pattern. By this definition, reflectors and arrays are also “beam antennas”. That is not quite what we mean here.

Figure 2.21: A gamma match used to interface coaxial cable to the driven element of a Yagi.

showing results for particular designs). For an introduction to practical analysis and design techniques for beam antennas, reference [78] is recommended.

Beam antennas are extremely popular for applications requiring moderate gain at frequencies in the UHF band and below. These applications include reception of terrestrial broadcast television and wireless data communications between fixed points. Beam antennas are less common above UHF, because (as noted above) greater directivity can typically be achieved using reflector antennas (the topic of the next section) having smaller overall size and a more convenient mechanical design.

A common method for feeding a beam antenna using a coaxial cable is to use a gamma match. An example is shown in Figure 2.21. In this scheme the shield is grounded to center of the driven element, and the inner conductor is connected to the driven element a short distance from the center via a capacitive tuning stub. This allows the driven element and the shield to be directly connected to the metallic boom, yeilding a simple and sturdy interface that obviates the need for a balun.

2.10.2 Reflectors

A paraboloidal reflector can be used to dramatically increase the directivity of a low- to moderate-gain antenna, known in this application as a feed. The concept is shown in Figure 2.22. The method of operation is most easily understood in terms of geometrical optics (also known as ray optics), which is applicable if the minimum dimension and surface radii of curvature of the reflector are much greater than a wavelength. According to geometrical optics, the electromagnetic field scattered from each point on the reflector is approximately equal to the field reflected by an infinite conducting plane tangent to the surface. If the feed is located at the focus of the paraboloid defining the reflector surface, then the field reflected from each point on the reflector travels in the same direction; that is, in parallel with the axis of revolution of the paraboloid. Furthermore it can be shown that the phase of the reflected contributions is equal in any plane perpendicular to the axis of the paraboloid. Thus the total reflected field is a plane wave traveling along the axis.

The directivity of a reflector antenna system is limited by two factors: First, spillover; that is, some fraction of the feed pattern does not illuminate the reflector. Second, diffraction from the edges of the paraboloid results in some fraction of the power from the feed being scattered in other directions.

A good engineering approximation of the far-field pattern of a reflector antenna can be obtained using the following tenet of antenna theory: The electric field in a planar aperture is related to the far-field pattern by the two-dimensional Fourier transform. In this case, we define a circular planar aperture in front of the dish, and note that according to the geometrical optics approximation, the electric fields within that aperture have uniform phase, and that the electric fields outside this aperture are identically zero. The pattern is therefore the Fourier transform of a two-dimensional function having constant-phase within a circular aperture. Los arrays plano de parches se emplean comúnmente cuando se requiere una antena alta ganancia pero las consideraciones espaciales requieren que la antena sea conforme a una superficie existente. Una aplicación común está en terminal móvil de abertura muy pequeña (VSAT) sistemas de comunicaciones por satélite instalados en vehículos como autobuses y aeronaves, en los que el haz puede ser “electrónicamente” dirigido para rastrear el satélite y en el que una antena de haz girado mecánicamente o reflector sería poco práctico. Los arrays de parche plano también se utilizan cada vez más como antenas de alta ganancia montables en pared de perfil bajo en exteriores punto a punto WLAN enlaces.

A common application is in mobile very small aperture terminal (VSAT) satellite communications systems installed in vehicles such as buses and aircraft, in which the beam can be “electronically” steered to track the satellite and in which a mechanically-steered beam or reflector antenna would be impractical. Planar patch arrays are also increasingly used as “low profile” wall-mountable high-gain antennas in outdoor point-to-point WLAN links.

2.12 Otras antenas de uso común

Las secciones anteriores han descrito unas pocas clases de antenas que ven uso generalizado en aplicaciones radiofónicas. Esta sección describe algunas clases más de antenas, que también son comúnmente contadas, pero para las cuales un debate más detallado está más allá del alcance de este texto.

La antena de bocina, mostrada en la Figura 2.26(a), es una antena moderadamente directa que se emplea frecuentemente como un pienso en los sistemas de antena reflectora. La antena del bocina también aparece en una variedad de aplicaciones que requieren una antena compacta y eficiente con más ganancia que una dipole o parche, pero menos ganancia que un haz o reflector. Las antenas de bocina suelen emplear una antena monopolea ubicada en el “tro” del bocina. El uso de un monopolo facilita la interfaz simplificada al cable coaxial, que es deseable en muchas aplicaciones. En transmisión, el poder irradiado del monopolo se dirige a una apertura con un área transversal mucho mayor que la garganta. Desde esta apertura, la fuente de la onda de radio puede interpretarse como la distribución de campo eléctrico que ha sido creada en la abertura de apertura. Como en el caso de la antena reflectora, la directividad nominal es aproximadamente 4πAphys/λ2 donde Aphys es el área física de la abertura. También como en el caso del reflector, la máxima directividad es menos debido a la no-uniformidad en la magnitud y fase del campo eléctrico creado en la abertura.

La antena helix axial-mode, mostrada en la Figura 2.26(b), es una antena de alta ganancia que es cualitativamente similar a una antena de haz. Esta antena es esencialmente una bobina que tiene una circunferencia de aproximadamente 1λ y un lanzamiento de alrededor 0.25λ en la frecuencia central deseada de operación. Cada vuelta de la bobina juega un papel análogo a un director dentro de una antena de haz. Una diferencia importante es que esta antena se poliariza circularmente, lo cual es un requisito en ciertas aplicaciones –por ejemplo, comunicaciones espaciales – donde la orientación relativa de las antenas en ambos extremos del enlace es desconocida o variable. Una ventaja de esta antena es ancho de banda relativamente grande (típicamente ∼= 20%) comparado con la mayoría de las antennas de haz.

La antena helix normal, mostrada en la Figura 2.26(c), es una bobina cuya circunferencia y longitud general son menos o mucho menos que λ/4. Esto resulta en un patrón similar al dipolo que es omnidireccional en el plano perpendicular al eje de la bobina. El helix de moda normal tiene una ventaja sobre los monopolos de la presión eléctrica que suelen usar. La bobina se encuentra típicamente encerrada en un material plástico o tipo goma para la protección, que a menudo da la falsa impresión de que la antena es un monopolo corto.

Concluimos este capítulo con la humilde antena de loopstick, mostrada en la Figura 2.26(d). El loopstick aparece en varias formas en las aplicaciones de las bandas MF y inferiores; en particular, en los receptores portátiles AM y radiodifusión de ondas cortas. En estas frecuencias, monopolos de corte eléctrico, dipoles, cálices y parches de alta gama son todos inexplicablemente grandes y tienen estrecha banda. Para lograr un pequeño tamaño y una actuación casi independiente de frecuencia, el loopstick utiliza un enfoque alternativo bastante diferente al utilizado por cualquier otra antena discutida anteriormente. Esta antena es esencialmente un inductor tipo bobina. En el receptor, el componente magnético de la onda de radio incidente induce una corriente que varia tiempo en la bobina que es proporcional a la inductancia. Esta corriente se entrega con impedancia muy baja pero puede ser sentido y transformado en una señal de impedancia moderada utilizando un amplificador adecuado (normalmente conocido como un amplificativo de “transimedance”). Sin embargo, se requiere una inductancia muy alta para obtener corrientes de magnitud usable, lo que requiere que la bobina tenga un número muy grande de vueltas alrededor de un núcleo ferrito. Esto a su vez significa pérdida ohmica alta, y por lo tanto muy baja eficiencia de radiación, que es la principal desventaja del lápiz labial en comparación con otras antenas eléctricamente pequeñas.

2.12.text_en_clean:
2.12 Other Commonly-Encountered Antennas

The previous sections have described a few classes of antennas that see widespread use in radio applications. This section describes a few more classes of antennas that are also commonly-encountered, but for which a more detailed discussion is beyond the scope of this text.

The horn antenna, shown in Figure 2.26(a), is a moderately-directive antenna which is frequently employed as a feed in reflector antenna systems. The horn antenna also appears in a variety of applications requiring a compact, efficient antenna with more gain than a dipole or patch, but less gain than an beam or reflector. Horn antennas typically employ a monopole-type antenna located in the “throat” of the horn. The use of a monopole facilitates simplified interface to coaxial cable, which is desirable in many applications. In transmission, the power radiated from the monopole is directed to an opening having much larger cross-sectional area than the throat. From this opening, the source of the radio wave can be interpreted to be the electric field distribution which has been created in the opening aperture. As in the case of the reflector antenna, the nominal directivity is roughly 4πAphys/λ2 where Aphys is the physical area of the aperture. Also as in the case of the reflector, the maximum directivity is less due to non-uniformity in the magnitude and phase of the electric field created in the aperture.

The axial-mode helix antenna, shown in Figure 2.26(b), is a high-gain antenna which is qualitatively similar to a beam antenna. This antenna is essentially a coil having a circumference of about 1λ and a pitch of about 0.25λ at the desired center frequency of operation. Each turn of the coil plays a role analogous to a director within a beam antenna. An important difference is that this antenna is circularly-polarized, which is a requirement in certain applications – e.g., space communications – where the relative orientation of the antennas on either end of the link is unknown or variable. An advantage of this antenna is relatively large bandwidth (typically ∼= 20%) compared to most beam antennas.

The normal-mode helix antenna, shown in Figure 2.26(c), is a coil whose circumference and overall length are both less than or much less than λ/4. This results in a dipole-like pattern which is omnidirectional in the plane perpendicular to the axis of the coil. The normal-mode helix has an advantage over electrically-short monopoles of comparable size in that they tend to have somewhat higher radiation resistance. For this reason they are sometimes used as external antennas in handheld radios. The coil is typically enclosed in a plastic or rubber-type material for protection, which often gives the false impression that the antenna is a short monopole.

We conclude this chapter with the humble loopstick antenna, shown in Figure 2.26(d). The loopstick appears in various forms in applications in the MF bands and lower; in particular, in portable AM and shortwave broadcast receivers. At these frequencies, electrically-short monopoles, dipoles, helices and high-ǫr patches are all unacceptably large and have hopelessly narrow bandwidth. To achieve small size and roughly frequency-independent performance, the loopstick uses an alternative approach quite unlike that used by any other antenna discussed previously. This antenna is essentially a coil-type inductor. On receive, the magnetic component of the incident radio wave induces a time-varying current in the coil which is proportional to the inductance. This current is delivered with very low impedance but can be sensed and transformed into a moderate impedance signal using an appropriate amplifier (typically known as a “transimpedance” amplifier). However very high inductance is required in order to obtain currents of usable magnitude, which requires that the coil have a very large number of turns around a ferrite core. This in turn means high ohmic loss, and thus very low radiation efficiency, which is the primary disadvantage of the loopstick compared to other electrically-small antennas.

3.1 Introduction
In Chapter 2, a radio wave was defined as an electromagnetic fie ld that transfers power over a distance and persists in the
absence of its source. In this chapter our primary concern is what happens to radio waves between antennas, and how the
information borne by radio waves is affected. This chapter i s organized as follows: In Section 3.2, we begin with the
simplest possible case – propagation in free space – and intr oduce the concept of path loss. In Section 3.3 we review
reflection and transmission, including the important probl ems of reflection from the Earth’s surface and scattering by
buildings and terrain. In Section 3.4 we derive the path loss associated with ground reflection. In Section 3.5 we conside r
the effect of scattering in the terrestrial propagation cha nnel, develop models for the channel impulse response, and
introduce metrics used to concisely describe these models i n terms useful for practical radio systems engineering. The n we
get specific about the nature of propagation in 30 MHz – 6 GHz (S ection 3.6), 6 GHz and above (Section 3.7), and
30 MHz and below (Section 3.8). This chapter concludes with a discussion of a few additional mechanisms for
propagation that are sometimes important to consider (Sect ion 3.9).

3.1 Introducción

En el capítulo 2, se definió una onda radiofónica como un campo electromagnético que traspasa el poder a distancia y persiste en ausencia de su fuente. En este capítulo nuestra preocupación principal es lo que sucede con las ondas de radio entre las antenas, y cómo la información transmitida por las ondas radiales se ve afectada. En la Sección3.4 se deriva la pérdida del camino asociada a la reflexión terrestre. En la sección 3.5 se considera el efecto de dispersión en el canal de propagación terrestre, desarrollar modelos para la respuesta del impulso del canal e introducir métricas utilizadas para describir concisamente estos modelos en términos útiles para la ingeniería práctica de sistemas de radio. Luego nos damos cuenta de la naturaleza de la propagación en 30 MHz – 6 GHz (Sección 3.6), 6 GHz y arriba (Sección 3.7), y 30 MHz y abajo (Sección 3.8). Este capítulo concluye con una discusión de algunos mecanismos adicionales para la propagación que a veces son importantes para considerar (Sección 3.9).

3.2 Propagation in Free Space; Path Loss

Consider an antenna transmitting a sinusoidal signal in free space; that is, in a region in which there is no ground, terrain, buildings, or other objects capable of interacting with the radio wave. Assuming the antenna is located at r = 0 (i.e., the origin of the coordinate system), the radio wave has the following general form in the far field of the transmitter:

E(r, θ, φ) = ˆe(θ, φ) V0(θ, φ) e−jβr
r
(3.1)

where ˆe(θ, φ) is a unit vector describing the polarization of the electric field and V0(θ, φ) represents the antenna pattern as well as the magnitude and phase of the signal applied to the antenna. Let us temporarily ignore the phase response of the antenna; i.e., let us assume for the moment that ∂V0/∂θ = ∂V0/∂φ = 0. In this case Equation 3.1 is a spherical wave; that is, surfaces of constant phase are concentric spheres centered on the antenna at r = 0. However for large r the radius of curvature of the phase front becomes so large that it appears “locally” to be a plane wave; that is, from the perspective of an observer far from the antenna, the phase appears nearly constant over the plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation.1 For antennas of practical interest, ∂V0/∂θ and ∂V0/∂φ change slowly with both θ and φ, so this effect remains after we reintroduce the phase due to the antenna.

1A good analogy is the fact that the curvature of the Earth’s surface is not apparent to an observer on the ground; i.e., the Earth appears “locally” to be flat.

A corollary to the derivation presented in Section 2.2.2 is that the far-field electric field intensity is always polarized in the plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation; i.e., ˆe(θ, φ) · ˆr = 0. Therefore one may write:

ˆe(θ, φ) = ˆθeθ(θ, φ) + ˆφeθ(θ, φ)
(3.2)

This fact will become useful when we consider reflection, since it reduces the number of possible orthogonal components of polarization from 3 to just 2, both perpendicular to the direction of propagation. In fact ˆθ and ˆφ are not the only possible choices for these two components, nor are they necessarily the most convenient choices, as we shall see in the next section.

Once the field is expressed in the form of Equation 3.1, it is easy to compute the power density Save (W/m2) at any point (r, θ, φ):

where we have assumed E is expressed in peak (as opposed to RMS) units. Note that the power density decreases by r2

over the same distance. This weakening is typically the dominant mechanism of “loss” in a radio link, and is attributable entirely to the “spreading out” of power with increasing distance from the antenna.

Usually the quantity Save is not quite what we need. The usual problem is this: Given a certain power PT (units of W) applied to the transmitting antenna, what is the power PR (also units of W) captured by the receiving antenna? A further wrinkle is that one typically prefers an answer in which the effect of the patterns of the transmit and receive antennas can be separated from the loss due to spreading and other mechanisms, for more complex channels. The reduction in power density with spreading is path loss, which we shall now derive for free space conditions.

Referring to Figure 3.1, imagine that PT is being delivered to an antenna which subsequently radiates this power isotropically (that is, uniformly in all directions), with |V0(θ, φ)| that is constant with respect to θ and φ. We no longer require an explicit global coordinate system, so let us represent the distance between between antennas using a different symbol, R. Save at a distance R from the transmit antenna is simply PT divided by the area of a sphere of radius R; i.e., Save = PT /(4πR2). If the antenna is not isotropic but instead has gain GT in the direction of the receiver, then the power density is increased by this factor, so SR = GT PT /(4πR2). Assuming the polarization of the receive antenna is perfectly matched to the polarization of the incident wave, PR is related to SR by the effective aperture Ae of the receive antenna. Ae is given by DRλ2/4π (Equation 2.44 of Chapter 2), where DR is the directivity of the receive antenna in the direction of the incident signal. 3.3 Reflection & Transmission
Aside from free space propagation, the simplest thing that c an happen to a radio wave in free space is that it can encounter
a planar boundary with some semi-infinite homogeneous diele ctric material as depicted in Figure 3.2. This is a pretty goo d
description of two important cases: (1) A radio wave inciden t on the ground; and (2) a radio wave at frequencies in the
upper VHF band or higher encountering certain kinds of terra in, or the wall, floor, or side of a building. When a radio
wave encounters such a boundary, we expect a reflected wave wi th magnitude and polarization determined by the material

Predecir la propagación fuera de estatura es extraordinariamente difícil. La segunda consideración adicional es la difusión, que se está dispersando de bordes y esquinas. En contraste con la reflexión, la difusión dispersa poder en todas direcciones. Así, la densidad de potencia significativa puede ser difraccionada en regiones exteriores que no son accesibles al campo reflejado desde las paredes exteriores. Estimar el campo diffractado es posible, pero es un tema avanzado más allá del alcance de este texto. (Una introducción recomendada a este tema y la propagación en edificios y alrededor de ellos es generalmente [6].) También cabe señalar que la difusión del terreno –en particular, cumbres de montaña y cresta– también es frecuentemente importante, por razones similares [44].

Aparte de la propagación espacial libre, lo más simple que puede suceder a una onda radio en espacio libre es que puede encontrar un límite plano con algún material dieléctrico semiinfinito homogéneo como se muestra en la Figura 3.2. Esta es una buena descripción de dos casos importantes: (1) Un incidente de onda de radio en el suelo; y (2) una onda de radiación en frecuencias en la parte superior VHF o en el suelo de encuentro. Cuando una onda de radio se encuentra con tal límite, esperamos una onda reflejada con magnitud y polarización determinada por las propiedades materiales de la superficie. Ahora trabajamos con algunos resultados de la teoría electromagnética básica.

3.3.2 La Reflexión de la Superficie de la Tierra

Los coeficientes de reflexión para la reflexión de la superficie de la Tierra dependen de la frecuencia, la permitividad, la conductividad y el ángulo de incidencia. La relativa permitividad de la superficie de la Tierra depende de la composición material específica, que depende de la geografía, y el contenido de humedad, que depende del clima. Un valor típico para el suelo (es decir, el suelo) es ǫr ∼15. La conductividad del suelo está normalmente en el rango 10−1 S/m para suelo húmedo, como tierras de cultivo, a 10−3 S/m para suelo descalificado típico de condiciones rocosas o arenosas. ǫr = 15 y σ = 10−2 S/m en la ecuación 3.16, obtenemos

• En la parte superior VHF banda y arriba, la superficie de la Tierra está bien aproximada como una dieléctrica sin pérdidas con ǫr ∼15. La reflexión es una ola de avión en el mismo sentido que el campo de incidentes es localmente una ola de avión.

• En el MF banda y abajo, la Tierra es un conductor imperfecto ̃ǫr que depende de la frecuencia. Sin embargo en este régimen λ > 100 m, por lo que las antenas se localizan típicamente dentro de una pequeña fracción de longitud de onda del suelo, y por lo tanto no es razonable suponer que el frente de fase radiada se puede interpretar como un incidente de onda plana en el suelo. Se requiere un análisis más sofisticado en este caso. Resulta que el mecanismo dominante no es ni "directo" ni reflejado, sino más bien la propagación de ondas terrestres. Véase Sección 3.8 para más acerca de esto.
• Comportamiento en las bandas HF y VHF inferiores es transitorio entre los casos anteriores.

Mientras que la situación es un poco inquieta para HF y abajo, podemos continuar productivamente restringiendo nuestra atención a las frecuencias en la banda superior VHF y arriba, haciendo la suposición de que el suelo está bien modelado como una pérdida baja

3.3.3 El estafador de las estructuras de Terrain

Los resultados de la Sección 3.3.1 pueden utilizarse para analizar la reflexión de ciertas características del terreno, como montañas; así como estructuras artificiales, tales como paredes interiores y exteriores, techos y suelos. Sin embargo hay algunas caveatillas y consideraciones adicionales.

Primero, debemos tener cuidado de restringir nuestra atención a las frecuencias en las que la longitud de onda asociada es pequeña relativa al área disponible para la reflexión, y la superficie debe ser aproximadamente lisa y plana relativa a una longitud de ondas; de lo contrario el dispersión no está bien modelado como reflejo de onda plana. Las montañas a menudo cumplen los requisitos "tamaño" y "smooth & plano" en la banda inferior VHF, pero falla el último requisito en frecuencia superior. Los edificios pueden tener dimensiones en el orden de decenas de metros y son lisos hasta dentro de un centímetro o así, por lo que el análisis de la Sección 3.3.1 es válido en las gamas UHF y SHF si el radio superficial de curvatura es grande relativo a una longitud de onda.

La composición material de los edificios es a menudo compleja. Las paredes interiores y exteriores son típicamente construidas a partir de varias combinaciones de hormigón2, ladrillo, madera, tablero de yeso y vidrio; y a veces de granito, mármol y otros materiales de tipo roca. ǫr en el rango 1.5–12, con una pérdida relativamente baja; es decir, con Im { ̃ǫr} ≪Re {\cHFF} ̃ǫr}. Para los fines del análisis que estamos a punto de hacer, es una aproximación razonable considerar que son materiales dieléctricos de baja pérdida con variación insignificante con frecuencia. Los coeficientes de reflexión resultante se comportan de forma similar a los identificados en la Figura 3.3 (que se calculó para ̃ǫr = 15). Los principales efectos de los valores más pequeños ǫr es reducir la magnitud de los coeficientes de reflexión para los valores de θi que no están cerca de la incidencia de pastoreo (θi →π/2), y cambiar el valor de θi en que Γ∥= 0 a valores inferiores θi. Asimismo, cabe señalar que

Desde la perspectiva de la propagación de ondas radiales, los suelos y techos caen en dos categorías amplias. En estructuras residenciales y ciertas estructuras comerciales, paredes y suelos se construyen principalmente de madera, que tiene ǫr ∼2. Por lo tanto los suelos y techos de madera reflejan de manera similar al suelo, pero con mucho menor ǫr. En la mayoría de las estructuras comerciales, el espacio entre niveles se construye a partir de varias combinaciones de acero y hormigón armado con acero, a menudo con suficiente contenido metálico adicional de los conductos HVAC y otras estructuras de utilidad para dar lugar a comportamientos que están más cerca de la de un plano terrestre perfectamente conductor.

Hay dos consideraciones adicionales que a menudo frustran intentos de modelar la dispersión en y alrededor de edificios como simple reflexión (ver Figura 3.4). Primero, debido a que las paredes tienen un espesor limitado, la transmisión en la estructura puede ser importante. En particular, una onda de radio puede penetrar en una estructura y luego ser dispersado de nuevo de la estructura con densidad de potencia significativa restante. En frecuencias en la banda UHF inferior y abajo, las pérdidas de absorción internas a edificios pueden resultar en densidad de potencia superada que es significativa en relación con la densidad de potencia reflejada desde el exterior. Predecir la propagación fuera de estatura es extraordinariamente difícil. La segunda consideración adicional es la difusión, que se está dispersando de bordes y esquinas. En contraste con la reflexión, la difusión dispersa poder en todas direcciones. Así, la densidad de potencia significativa puede ser difraccionada en regiones exteriores que no son accesibles al campo reflejado desde las paredes exteriores. Estimar el campo diffractado es posible, pero es un tema avanzado más allá del alcance de este texto. (Una introducción recomendada a este tema y la propagación en edificios y alrededor de ellos es generalmente [6].) También cabe señalar que la difusión del terreno –en particular, cumbres de montaña y cresta– también es frecuentemente importante, por razones similares [44].

3.3 Reflection & Transmission

Aside from free space propagation, the simplest thing that can happen to a radio wave in free space is that it can encounter a planar boundary with some semi-infinite homogeneous dielectric material as depicted in Figure 3.2. This is a pretty good description of two important cases: (1) A radio wave incident on the ground; and (2) a radio wave at frequencies in the upper VHF band or higher encountering certain kinds of terrain, or the wall, floor, or side of a building. When a radio wave encounters such a boundary, we expect a reflected wave with magnitude and polarization determined by the material properties of the surface. We now work this out using some results from basic electromagnetic theory.

3.3.1 Reflection from a Planar Interface

We established in Section 3.2 that a radio wave in free space, in the far field of the antenna which created it, can be approximated locally as a plane wave. Figure 3.2 depicts the situation when this plane wave encounters a semi-infinite

3.3.2 Reflection from the Surface of the Earth

Reflection coefficients for reflection from the surface of the Earth depend on frequency, permittivity, conductivity, and angle of incidence. The relative permittivity of the surface of the Earth depends on the specific material composition, which depends on geography; and moisture content, which depends on weather. A typical value for ground (i.e., soil) is ǫr ∼15. The conductivity of the ground is normally in the range 10−1 S/m for moist soil, such as farmland, to 10−3 S/m for dessicated soil typical of rocky or sandy conditions. Assuming typical values ǫr = 15 and σ = 10−2 S/m in Equation 3.16, we obtain
