5.6 Single Sideband (SSB)
Referring back to Figure 5.5, we see that DSB AM signals (both the -LC and -SC versions) include two versions of the
message spectrum: One version appearing at frequencies jus t above the carrier, and a second, spectrally-reversed vers ion
appearing below the carrier. The two versions are referred t o as the upper and lower sidebands, respectively. The
consequence of sending both sidebands is that the bandwidth of DSB AM is B = 2M .
The principle underlying single-sideband (SSB) modulatio n is to reduce the bandwidth by a factor of two by eliminating
one of the redundant sidebands. Thus SSB may be interpreted a s DSB-SC AM followed by filtering to pass only the upper
or lower sideband, as illustrated in Figure 5.16. These two v ersions of SSB are known as USB and LSB, respectively.
Aside from reduced bandwidth, an advantage of SSB over DSB-S C or DSB-LC is energy efficiency. The term “energy
efficiency”, when applied to an analog modulation, refers to the SNR achieved at the output of a demodulator compared to
the SNR delivered to the input of the demodulator. SSB has pot entially twice the energy efficiency of DSB-SC, since all
the transmit power in SSB lies within bandwidth W , and so the bandwidth of noise intercepted by a well-designe d SSB
receiver is alsoW ; whereas for DSB-SC a noise bandwidth of 2W is intercepted, resulting in the effective input SNR
being a factor of two less than the effective input SNR of SSB w hen the signal power is the same. This advantage is of
course even greater with respect to DSB-LC, since the power i n the carrier does not contribute the output SNR.

5.6.1 Generation of SSB
SSB can be generated using the method implied in Figure 5.16, but this is not always practical as the required filter must
have a very steep transition region in order to achieve suffic ient suppression of the undesired sideband without distort ing
the desired sideband. Such filters are quite difficult to impl ement, as we shall see in Chapters 13 and 18. This motivates
the Weaver and Hartley methods, which we shall now briefly des cribe.
The Weaver method is illustrated in Figures 5.17 and 5.18. We first convert m(t) to complex baseband representation by
shifting the spectrum of the message signal by +W/ 2 or−W/ 2, corresponding to LSB and USB respectively. This new
signal ism(t)e± j(W/2)t in the time domain and M (f± W/ 2) in the frequency domain. The undesired sideband is then
suppressed using a lowpass filter, which is practical becaus e this filter can be implemented with relatively large fracti onal
bandwidth. At this point we have the complex baseband repres entation of the desired SSB signal, so we may generate the
associated real-valued signal using quadrature upconvers ion as described at the end of Section 5.3. As an aside, it turn s out
that the “Weaver modulator” has applications beyond genera tion of SSB: see Section 14.5.2.
The Hartley method is an ingenious method for suppressing one sideband by cance llation, as opposed to filtering. The
method is illustrated in Figures 5.19 and 5.20. We first make a copy ofm(t) and apply a phase shift of +π/ 2 rad to the
copy (equivalently, multiply byj). Note that a phase shift of +π/ 2 rad for positive frequencies corresponds to a phase
shift of−π/ 2 rad for negative frequencies, since real-valued signals ha ve conjugate-symmetric spectrum. The resulting
spectrum is shown in Figure 5.20(b). Multiplying m(t) by cosω ct results in the spectrum shown in Figures 5.20(c); note
the positive side of the spectrum is now centered around +ω c. Multiplying the phase-shifted signal by − sinω ct results in

Hartley modulation has two big advantages over Weaver modul ation, and one big disadvantage. The two advantages are
(1) only one modulating frequency is required, as opposed tw o for the Weaver method, and (2) Cancellation of the
undesired sideband is essentially perfect for Hartley, whe reas suppression of the undesired sideband by the Weaver met hod
is only as good as the selectivity of the baseband lowpass filt er. The disadvantage of the Hartley method is that it is
relatively difficult to apply a frequency-independent π/ 2 phase shift to a real-valued signal. Specifically, this phas e shift

be interpreted as an allpass filter with unit magnitude respo nse and phase response equal to +π/ 2 or−π/ 2 for positive
and negative frequencies, respectively. This filter has infi nite impulse response, so any practical implementation is a n
approximation to the exact transform. On the other hand, a fin ite-length approximation can typically be made sufficientl y
good over the narrow range of frequencies occupied by the mes sage signal; and this becomes particularly easy using
digital signal processing techniques (more on this in Chapt er 18). Thus, the inconvenience associated with the Hilbert
transform is usually outweighed by the advantages of the Har tley method.
Like Weaver modulation, Hartley modulation has applicatio ns beyond generation of SSB: see Section 14.5.1.

Quadrature modulation turns out to be a recurring theme in ba ndwidth-efficient modulations, as we shall see in Chapter 6,
and also has implications for demodulation.
5.6.3 Demodulation and Performance of SSB
Because the carrier is suppressed in traditional SSB, only c oherent demodulation is possible. The methods described in
Section 5.5.4 work equally well for SSB; this is because the r eceived sideband is restored to it’s original frequency,
whereas the missing sideband is “automatically” restored s imply by virtue of taking the real part of the complex baseban d
signal (recall real-valued signals have conjugate-symmet ric spectrum).3
It is also possible to demodulate SSB using product detectio n without carrier phase estimation; i.e., as shown in
Figure 5.11 except using an LO with essentially random phase .4 The output in this case is obviously not properly
derotated in this scheme, but this is of little consequence s ince – being a quadrature modulation – SSB occupies both
dimensions of the signal space. The incorrect phase respons e imparted on the recovered message signal in this case has
little effect on the fidelity of the audio in voice communicat ions applications. In applications where the phase of the
message signal is important – e.g., m(t) is phase-modulated data – then this approach is clearly not a cceptable and carrier
phase estimation is required.
5.6.4 V estigial Sideband (VSB) Modulation
While SSB works great for voice signals, there are certain typ es of message signals for which traditional SSB becomes
awkward to implement. Prominent among these are analog vide o signals, for which much important spectral content is
concentrated at frequencies very close to DC. In SSB, this co ntent lies within the transition regions of the filter used to
suppress or cancel the undesired sideband. V estigial sideband(VSB) modulation is a more practical approach for such
signals. The difference between VSB and SSB is simple: The sp ectrum of the RF signal extends partially into the opposite
sideband, as opposed to being limited to the primary sideban d.
Analog VSB is becoming rare in modern communications system s for the simple reason that the message signals for
which it was designed – such as analog video – are being replac ed by digital versions. However – and perhaps ironically –
we shall find in Chapter 6 (Section 6.17) that the VSB concept i s central to the digital modulation scheme used by the
North American broadcast television system.
5.6.5 Pilot-Assisted SSB and VSB
One of the principle difficulties in implementing high-perf ormance SSB and VSB receivers is precise and robust
determination of carrier frequency and phase. This is becau se the carrier is absent, and so it’s properties must be infer red

5.6 Banda lateral única (SSB)

Refiriéndose a la Figura 5.5, vemos que DSB AM señalizaciones (tanto la -LC y...SC versiones) incluyen dos versiones del espectro de mensajes: Una versión que aparece en frecuencias justo por encima del transportista, y una segunda versión revisada espectralmente que aparece debajo del transportista. Las dos versiones se denominan las bandas laterales superior e inferior, respectivamente. La consecuencia de enviar ambas bandas laterales es que el ancho de banda de la banda de DSB AM es B = 2M.

El principio subyacente de la modulación de banda única (SSB) es reducir el ancho de banda por un factor de dos eliminando una de las bandas laterales redundantes. Así, SSB puede ser interpretado como DSB-SC AM seguido de filtrado para pasar sólo la banda lateral superior o inferior, como se ilustra en la Figura 5.16. Estas dos versiones de SSB son conocidas como USB y LSB, respectivamente.

Aparte de la reducción del ancho de banda, una ventaja de SSB sobre DSB-SC o DSB-LC es eficiencia energética. El término “eficiencia energética”, cuando se aplica a una modulación analógica, se refiere al SNR logrado en la salida de un demoldulador en comparación con el SNR entregado a la entrada del demodulador. SSB tiene potencialmente el doble de eficiencia energética DSB-SC, ya que todo el poder de transmisión en SSB se encuentra dentro del ancho de banda W, y por lo tanto el ancho de banda del ruido interceptado por un bien diseñado SSB receptor es también W; mientras que para DSB-SC un ancho de banda de ruido 2W es interceptado, lo que da lugar a la entrada efectiva SNR ser un factor de dos menos que la aportación efectiva SNR of of SSB cuando el poder de la señal es el mismo. Esta ventaja es, por supuesto, aún mayor con respecto a DSB-LC, ya que la potencia en el transportista no contribuye a la salida SNR.

5.6.1 Generación de SSB

SSB puede ser generado utilizando el método implícito en la Figura 5.16, pero esto no siempre es práctico ya que el filtro requerido debe tener una región de transición muy empinada para lograr la supresión suficiente de la banda lateral no deseada sin distorsionar la banda lateral deseada. Tales filtros son bastante difíciles de implementar, como veremos en los capítulos 13 y 18. Esto motiva los métodos Weaver y Hartley, que ahora describiremos brevemente.

El método Weaver se ilustra en las Figuras 5.17 y 5.18. Primero convertimos m(t) a la representación compleja de la banda base cambiando el espectro de la señal del mensaje por +W/2 o −W/2, correspondiente a LSB y USB Esta nueva señal es m(t)e±j(W/2)t en el dominio del tiempo y M(f ± W/2) en el dominio de frecuencia. La banda lateral no deseada es entonces suprimida utilizando un filtro de bajapass, que es práctico porque este filtro puede ser implementado con ancho de banda fraccional relativamente grande. En este punto tenemos la compleja representación de la banda base de la señal SSB deseada, por lo que podemos generar la señal real asociada utilizando la conversión de subconversión de cuadrícula como se describe al final de la sección 5.3. Como un lado, resulta que el “modulador de Weaver” tiene aplicaciones más allá de la generación de SSB: ver Sección 14.5.2.

El método Hartley es un método ingenioso para suprimir una banda lateral por cancelación, en lugar de filtrar. El método se ilustra en las Figuras 5.19 y 5.20. Primero hacemos una copia de m(t) y aplicamos un cambio de fase de +π/2 rad a la copia (equivalentemente, multiplicar por j). Tenga en cuenta que un cambio de fase de +π/2 rad para frecuencias positivas corresponde a un cambio de fase −π/2 rad for negative frecuencias, since real-valued signals have conjugate-symmetric spectrum. El espectro resultante se muestra en la Figura 5.20(b). Multiplying m(t) por cos ωct resultados en el espectro mostrado en las Figuras 5.20(c); note que el lado positivo del espectro ahora está centrado alrededor de +ωc. La modulación de Hartley tiene dos grandes ventajas sobre la modulación de Weaver, y una gran desventaja. Las dos ventajas son (1) sólo se requiere una frecuencia modulada, en lugar de dos para el método Weaver y (2) Cancelación de la banda lateral no deseada es esencialmente perfecta para Hartley, mientras que la supresión de la banda anchas por el método Weever es tan buena como la selectividad de los filtros de baja banda base. La desventaja del método Hartley es que es relativamente difícil aplicar un cambio de fase π/2 independiente a una señal de valor real. Específicamente, este cambio de fase se puede lograr en una frecuencia exactamente introduciendo el retraso apropiado, o mediante un circuito de desplazamiento de fases de banda estrecha (véase por ejemplo la Figura 14.9). Para lograrlo sobre todas las frecuencias requiere una transformación Hilbert. La transformación de Hilbert puede interpretarse como un filtro de alpaso con respuesta de magnitud unitaria y respuesta de fase igual a +π/2 o −π/2 para frecuencias positivas y negativas, respectivamente. Este filtro tiene una respuesta de impulso infinita, por lo que cualquier implementación práctica es una aproximación a la transformación exacta. Por otro lado, una aproximación de longitud finita puede ser hecha normalmente suficientemente buena sobre la estrecha gama de frecuencias ocupadas por la señal del mensaje; y esto se vuelve particularmente fácil utilizando técnicas digitales de procesamiento de señales (más en este capítulo 18). Así, la inconveniencia asociada con el transformador Hilbert suele superarse por las ventajas del método Hartley.

Como modulación Weaver, la modulación Hartley tiene aplicaciones más allá de la generación de SSB: ver Sección 14.5.1.

Esto es en contraste con AM, para el cual sq(t) ≡0. Así, las señales SSB ocupan ambas dimensiones en el plano real-imaginario. Por esta razón nos referimos a SSB como modulación de la cuadratura.

5.6.3 La Demodulación y el Rendimiento de SSB

Debido a que el portador es suprimido en SSB, sólo es posible desmodulación coherente. Los métodos descritos en la Sección 5.5.4 funcionan igualmente bien para SSB; esto es porque la banda lateral recibida se restaura a su frecuencia original, mientras que la banda lateral desaparecida es "automáticamente" restaurada simplemente por la parte real de la señal compleja de banda base (reconocidos señales reales tienen espectro conjugado-simétrico).3

También es posible desmoronar SSB mediante detección de productos sin estimación de fases de portador; es decir, como se muestra en la Figura 5.11 excepto usando un LO con fase esencialmente aleatoria.4 La salida en este caso obviamente no está debidamente desrotada en este esquema, pero esto es de poca consecuencia ya que – siendo una modulación de cuadratura – SSB ocupa ambas dimensiones del espacio de señal. La respuesta incorrecta de la fase impartida en la señal de mensaje recuperada en este caso tiene poco efecto sobre la fidelidad del audio en las aplicaciones de comunicación de voz. En las aplicaciones donde la fase de la señal de mensajes es importante – por ejemplo, m(t) es datos modulados por fases – entonces este enfoque no es claramente aceptable y se requiere estimación de fase de portador.

5.6.4 La modulación Vestigial Sideband (VSB)

Mientras tanto SSB funciona muy bien para las señales de voz, hay ciertos tipos de señales de mensaje para los que tradicionalmente SSB se vuelve incómodo para implementar. Destacan entre ellos las señales de vídeo analógicas, para las cuales el contenido espectral muy importante se concentra en frecuencias muy cercanas a DC. In SSB, este contenido se encuentra dentro de las regiones de transición del filtro utilizado para suprimir o cancelar la banda lateral no deseada.VSB) modulación es un enfoque más práctico para tales señales. La diferencia entre VSB y SSB es simple: El espectro de la señal RF se extiende parcialmente en la banda lateral opuesta, en lugar de limitarse a la banda lateral principal.

Analog VSB se está volviendo raro en los sistemas de comunicaciones modernos por la simple razón de que las señales de mensaje para las cuales fue diseñada –como el vídeo analógico– están siendo reemplazadas por versiones digitales. Sin embargo – y quizás irónicamente – encontraremos en Capítulo 6 (Sección 6.17) que el concepto VSB es central al esquema de modulación digital utilizado por el sistema de televisión de radiodifusión norteamericano.

5.6.5 SSB y VSB

Una de las principales dificultades para implementar receptores SSB y VSB de alto rendimiento es la determinación precisa y robusta de frecuencia y fase del transportista. Esto se debe a que el transportista está ausente, por lo que sus propiedades deben ser inferidas de la señal. Un compromiso es añadir una señal de portador explícita antes de la transmisión. Esto hace que SSB/VSB sea esencialmente análogo a DSB-LC, pero la motivación es bastante diferente. En primer lugar, el transportista se utiliza únicamente para estimar la frecuencia y la fase, y no permite demodulación incoherente. Segundo, la relación de potencia en el portador a la energía en las bandas laterales se hace generalmente relativamente pequeña; es decir, lo suficientemente grande como para facilitar la estimación de la frecuencia y fase con suficiente precisión. En esta aplicación, el transportador se denomina más precisamente una señal piloto, y esta técnica se denomina modulación experimental. De nuevo, veremos que esta técnica reaparece en nuestra discusión sobre el sistema de televisión digital de América del Norte en la Sección 6.17.

5.6 Single Sideband (SSB)

Referring back to Figure 5.5, we see that DSB AM signals (both the -LC and -SC versions) include two versions of the message spectrum: One version appearing at frequencies just above the carrier, and a second, spectrally-reversed version appearing below the carrier. The two versions are referred to as the upper and lower sidebands, respectively. The consequence of sending both sidebands is that the bandwidth of DSB AM is B = 2M.

The principle underlying single-sideband (SSB) modulation is to reduce the bandwidth by a factor of two by eliminating one of the redundant sidebands. Thus SSB may be interpreted as DSB-SC AM followed by filtering to pass only the upper or lower sideband, as illustrated in Figure 5.16. These two versions of SSB are known as USB and LSB, respectively.

Aside from reduced bandwidth, an advantage of SSB over DSB-SC or DSB-LC is energy efficiency. The term “energy efficiency”, when applied to an analog modulation, refers to the SNR achieved at the output of a demodulator compared to the SNR delivered to the input of the demodulator. SSB has potentially twice the energy efficiency of DSB-SC, since all the transmit power in SSB lies within bandwidth W, and so the bandwidth of noise intercepted by a well-designed SSB receiver is also W; whereas for DSB-SC a noise bandwidth of 2W is intercepted, resulting in the effective input SNR being a factor of two less than the effective input SNR of SSB when the signal power is the same. This advantage is of course even greater with respect to DSB-LC, since the power in the carrier does not contribute the output SNR.

SSB is generally preferred over DSB AM for modern analog voice communications, especially in the crowded HF spectrum where narrow bandwidth is a huge advantage. The sections that follow cover the basics of SSB. For additional details, the reader is referred to [72, Chapter 2].

5.6.1 Generation of SSB

SSB can be generated using the method implied in Figure 5.16, but this is not always practical as the required filter must have a very steep transition region in order to achieve sufficient suppression of the undesired sideband without distorting the desired sideband. Such filters are quite difficult to implement, as we shall see in Chapters 13 and 18. This motivates the Weaver and Hartley methods, which we shall now briefly describe.

The Weaver method is illustrated in Figures 5.17 and 5.18. We first convert m(t) to complex baseband representation by shifting the spectrum of the message signal by +W/2 or −W/2, corresponding to LSB and USB respectively. This new signal is m(t)e±j(W/2)t in the time domain and M(f ± W/2) in the frequency domain. The undesired sideband is then suppressed using a lowpass filter, which is practical because this filter can be implemented with relatively large fractional bandwidth. At this point we have the complex baseband representation of the desired SSB signal, so we may generate the associated real-valued signal using quadrature upconversion as described at the end of Section 5.3. As an aside, it turns out that the “Weaver modulator” has applications beyond generation of SSB: see Section 14.5.2.

The Hartley method is an ingenious method for suppressing one sideband by cancellation, as opposed to filtering. The method is illustrated in Figures 5.19 and 5.20. We first make a copy of m(t) and apply a phase shift of +π/2 rad to the copy (equivalently, multiply by j). Note that a phase shift of +π/2 rad for positive frequencies corresponds to a phase shift of −π/2 rad for negative frequencies, since real-valued signals have conjugate-symmetric spectrum. The resulting spectrum is shown in Figure 5.20(b). Multiplying m(t) by cos ωct results in the spectrum shown in Figures 5.20(c); note the positive side of the spectrum is now centered around +ωc. Multiplying the phase-shifted signal by −sin ωct results in

the spectrum shown in Figure 5.20(d). This is because −sin ωct imparts a phase shift of −π/2 rad relative to + cos ωct, which is equivalent to multiplication by −j. Adding the latter result to the former result, the lower sideband is cancelled whereas the upper sideband is preserved. A simple modification (see Problem 5.8) results in LSB as opposed to USB.

Hartley modulation has two big advantages over Weaver modulation, and one big disadvantage. The two advantages are (1) only one modulating frequency is required, as opposed two for the Weaver method, and (2) Cancellation of the undesired sideband is essentially perfect for Hartley, whereas suppression of the undesired sideband by the Weaver method is only as good as the selectivity of the baseband lowpass filter. The disadvantage of the Hartley method is that it is relatively difficult to apply a frequency-independent π/2 phase shift to a real-valued signal. Specifically, this phase shift can be achieved at one frequency exactly by introducing the appropriate delay, or by using a narrowband phase-shifting circuit (see e.g. Figure 14.9). To achieve this over all frequencies requires a Hilbert transform. The Hilbert transform can be interpreted as an allpass filter with unit magnitude response and phase response equal to +π/2 or −π/2 for positive and negative frequencies, respectively. This filter has infinite impulse response, so any practical implementation is an approximation to the exact transform. On the other hand, a finite-length approximation can typically be made sufficiently good over the narrow range of frequencies occupied by the message signal; and this becomes particularly easy using digital signal processing techniques (more on this in Chapter 18). Thus, the inconvenience associated with the Hilbert transform is usually outweighed by the advantages of the Hartley method.

Like Weaver modulation, Hartley modulation has applications beyond generation of SSB: see Section 14.5.1.

5.6.2 SSB as a Quadrature Modulation

A second look at Figure 5.19 reveals something interesting: the Hartley modulator can be interpreted as a two-step process in which the first step is generation of a complex baseband signal, and the second step is quadrature upconversion (as in Figure 5.1). The complex baseband signal is s(t) = si(t) + jsq(t) (as usual) with si(t) = m(t) (as in AM) and sq(t) = H {m(t)} where H {·} is the Hilbert Transform. This is in contrast to AM, for which sq(t) ≡0. Thus, SSB signals occupy both dimensions in the real-imaginary plane. For this reason we refer to SSB as a quadrature modulation.

Quadrature modulation turns out to be a recurring theme in bandwidth-efficient modulations, as we shall see in Chapter 6, and also has implications for demodulation.

5.6.3 Demodulation and Performance of SSB

Because the carrier is suppressed in traditional SSB, only coherent demodulation is possible. The methods described in Section 5.5.4 work equally well for SSB; this is because the received sideband is restored to it’s original frequency, whereas the missing sideband is “automatically” restored simply by virtue of taking the real part of the complex baseband signal (recall real-valued signals have conjugate-symmetric spectrum).3

It is also possible to demodulate SSB using product detection without carrier phase estimation; i.e., as shown in Figure 5.11 except using an LO with essentially random phase.4 The output in this case is obviously not properly derotated in this scheme, but this is of little consequence since – being a quadrature modulation – SSB occupies both dimensions of the signal space. The incorrect phase response imparted on the recovered message signal in this case has little effect on the fidelity of the audio in voice communications applications. In applications where the phase of the message signal is important – e.g., m(t) is phase-modulated data – then this approach is clearly not acceptable and carrier phase estimation is required.

5.6.4 Vestigial Sideband (VSB) Modulation

While SSB works great for voice signals, there are certain types of message signals for which traditional SSB becomes awkward to implement. Prominent among these are analog video signals, for which much important spectral content is concentrated at frequencies very close to DC. In SSB, this content lies within the transition regions of the filter used to suppress or cancel the undesired sideband. Vestigial sideband (VSB) modulation is a more practical approach for such signals. The difference between VSB and SSB is simple: The spectrum of the RF signal extends partially into the opposite sideband, as opposed to being limited to the primary sideband.

Analog VSB is becoming rare in modern communications systems for the simple reason that the message signals for which it was designed – such as analog video – are being replaced by digital versions. However – and perhaps ironically – we shall find in Chapter 6 (Section 6.17) that the VSB concept is central to the digital modulation scheme used by the North American broadcast television system.

5.6.5 Pilot-Assisted SSB and VSB

One of the principle difficulties in implementing high-performance SSB and VSB receivers is precise and robust determination of carrier frequency and phase. This is because the carrier is absent, and so it’s properties must be inferred from the signal. A compromise is to add an explicit carrier signal before transmission. This makes SSB/VSB essentially analogous to DSB-LC, but the motivation is quite different. First, the carrier is used solely for estimation of frequency and phase, and does not permit incoherent demodulation. Second, the ratio of power in the carrier to power in the sidebands is typically made relatively small; i.e., just large enough to facilitate the estimation of frequency and phase with sufficient accuracy. In this application, the carrier is more accurately referred to as a pilot signal, and this technique is referred to as pilot-assisted modulation. Again, we’ll see this technique reappears in our discussion of the North American digital broadcast television system in Section 6.17.

3One obvious exception, just to be clear: Estimation of φp using the method implied by Equation 5.19 will not work for SSB, because SSB is a quadrature modulation extending in both dimensions in the complex plane, whereas the method of Equation 5.19 requires the modulation to be limited to one dimension.

4Amateur radio enthusiasts will be most familiar with this method.

5.7 Frequency Modulation (FM)
The third major category of analog modulations remaining in common use in modern radio communications systems is
frequency modulation (FM). As indicated in Table 5.1, FM is t he representation of m(t) as a variation in the frequency of
the carrier. This single aspect of FM results in three advant ages which have made FM immensely popular. First, FM may
be generated using non-linear (primarily “Class C”) power a mplifiers, which are simpler and more power-efficient than th e
linear (Class A or AB) amplifiers required for AM and SSB (more on this in Chapter 17). Second, FM benefits from
relatively high immunity to additive noise and interferenc e, since these affect primarily the magnitude and phase of th e
signal as opposed to the frequency. Third, there is no risk of fast fading being interpreted as part of the message signal,
which makes FM somewhat better suited for use in terrestrial communications at VHF and above. However these
advantages come at the cost of significantly greater bandwid th, as we shall see below.
The following sections provide a brief but reasonably compl ete overview of FM in modern radio communications systems.
Among all modulations FM is arguably the most difficult to ana lyze in a rigorous mathematical way, and so we shall
sidestep all but the most essential aspects of that analysis here. For additional mathematical details some recommende d
references include [32] and [43, Ch. 8].
5.7.1 Characterization of FM
Since FM involves representing information as variations i n frequency, a useful starting point is to determine the
instantaneous frequency of the signal in Equation 5.1. Writing that equation here with A(t) = Ac (a constant), we have
sRF (t) = Ac cos [ω ct +φ(t)] (5.20)

To better understand the spectrum of FM signals, consider th e role of β in Equation 5.27. If β≪ 2π , then

said to give rise to narrowband FM (NBFM).
FM modulation which is not obviously NBFM is considered wideband FM (WBFM). There is no clear dividing line
between NBFM and WBFM in terms of β . However, whenβ≫ 1, Carson’s rule becomes B≈ 2βW ; i.e., we observe

increasing distance from a peak value at the carrier frequen cy, although typically not as smoothly as is the case for NBFM .
Example 5.1. Broadcast FM stations transmit an audio signal with 15 kHz ba ndwidth using a maximum
instantaneous frequency deviation of 75 kHz. (See Figure B. 1 (Appendix B) for an example of the spectrum of this

Solution: Here ∆f = 75 kHz andW = 15 kHz, so the modulation index β = ∆f/W = 5. Transmitted bandwidth
is estimated by Carson’s Rule: B≈ 2 (β + 1)W = 180 kHz.β is not≪ 2π here, so this is considered WBFM.
In practice, broadcast FM channels are 200 kHz wide – slight w ider than necessary in order to lessen receiver
selectivity requirements. Also, 10% of the maximum frequen cy deviation of a broadcast FM signal is given over to

In practice, ∆f up to 5 kHz or so is tolerated as the spectrum of voice signals i s not flat, but rather tends to be
concentrated around 1 kHz.
5.7.2 Generation of FM
The two primary methods used to generate FM signals are known as the direct method and the indirect method,
respectively. The direct method is as implied by Equation 5.22: m(t) is used as the frequency control signal for a
variable-frequency oscillator. This may be implemented in either the analog domain using a VCO or the digital domain
using an NCO; for more details see Sections 16.6 or 16.9 respe ctively. The VCO technique is sometimes referred to as
reactance modulation, which refers to the use of a varactor – a diode whose capacita nce is a function of voltage – as the
means to control the frequency of the VCO. The indirect method consists of first generating an NBFM signal, and then
using frequency multiplication to increase the frequency d eviation of the signal. Either method can be applied directl y to
the carrier, or alternatively implemented in complex baseb and form and then converted to sRF (t) as a subsequent step.
5.7.3 Demodulation
There are two popular methods for demodulation of FM. One met hod is simply to differentiate sRF (t) (or it’s complex
baseband representation) with respect to time, which yield s a DSB-LC AM signal. For example, from Equation 5.26:

Nowm(t) may be recovered using any method suitable for DSB-LC AM, inc luding envelope detection. The
differentiation may be implemented in a number of ways. If th e signal has been digitized, then the derivative is
proportional to the difference between adjacent time sampl es. In the analog domain, essentially the same operation can be
implemented using analog delay lines or by slope detection, including the venerable F oster-Seeley discriminator.
The second method employs a PLL, as shown in Figure 5.21. Here the phase of the FM-modulated signal is compared to
the phase of a reference signal provided by a VCO (analog doma in implementation) or NCO (digital domain
implementation). The frequency of the VCO/NCO is determine d by the magnitude of the error signal created by the phase
comparator. Specifically, the VCO/NCO frequency is increas ed if the phase comparator determines that the input
frequency is greater than the reference frequency, and the V CO/NCO frequency is decreased if the phase comparator
determines that the input frequency is less than the referen ce frequency. Thus the phase comparator output is proportio nal
to the instantaneous frequency deviation, and is therefore also proportional to m(t). PLL design entails a number of
considerations that must be addressed for this method to be s uccessful: For example, how exactly to measure phase
difference, how fast to change frequency as a function of pha se comparator output, and how to initialize the PLL and
maintain “lock” in the presence of noise and interference. T hese issues are specific to PLL design and therefore somewhat
beyond the scope of this chapter. However they are addressed in Section 16.8.
Most FM demodulators implement some form of fast AGC and/or limiting to normalize the signal magnitude prior to
demodulation. The basic idea is that the magnitude of the FM w aveform contains no information, only
propagation-induced variations and noise. Also, there is t ypically a limited range of magnitude over which analog

An extreme version of this concept is so-called “hard limiti ng” followed by zero-crossing detection, which constitute s a

converting zero-crossings of the modulated waveform into s hort pulses, and then integrating over the resulting pulse t rain
to obtain a waveform whose magnitude is proportional to freq uency.
5.7.4 Preemphasis
One unique aspect of FM is that the differentiation that is in trinsic to FM demodulation tends to exaggerate the impact of
noise at frequencies farthest from the carrier. This is beca use FM demodulation converts large frequencies into large
magnitudes. Thus, input noise at frequencies far from the ca rrier is converted to output noise in the message signal that is
relatively strong, whereas input noise at frequencies clos e to the carrier, but having the same power spectral density, is
converted to output noise in the message signal that is relat ively weak. Ironically, the spectrum of audio signals tends to be
concentrated around 1 kHz, with relatively less content at h igher frequencies. Therefore it makes sense to modify the
spectrum of audio signals before modulation such that more p ower is present at higher frequencies and less power is
present at lower frequencies, as this equalizes the SNR as a f unction of frequency after the signal is demodulated. This
technique is known as preemphasis, and the reciprocal operation at the demodulator is known as deemphasis. This process
significantly improves the perceived quality of audio that h as been transmit using FM, and so is nearly universally
employed.
5.7.5 Performance in Varying SNR; Threshold Effect
It is quite difficult to precisely estimate the output SNR of F M as a function of SNR. Not only does this relationship
depend on the message signal characteristics and modulatio n parameters in a complex way, but also propagation
characteristics and audio processing techniques play a rol e. Suffice it to say that FM typically requires input SNR on the
order of 3–6 dB for intelligible voice, and perhaps more like 10–15 dB for quality audio. However there are some other
aspects of this issue that are worth knowing about.
One reason for the popularity of FM is that it achieves relati vely high output SNR relative to input SNR when compared to
AM. However this only occurs when the input SNR is above a cert ain threshold, and below this threshold the ratio of
output SNR to input SNR is significantly worse than that for AM . This characteristic of FM is is known as threshold effect,
and the critical SNR is sometimes referred to as the capture threshold. In audio applications, exceeding the capture
threshold is perceived as quieting; i.e., an apparent reduction of background noise. The condi tion in which background
noise seems to be have been essentially completely suppress ed – which is the demodulator operating fully in the capture
region – is referred to as full quieting. No such effect is apparent in AM.


114 CHAPTER 5. ANALOG MODULA TION
Threshold effect makes FM superior for audio communication s applications in which the capture threshold – typically on
the order of 10 dB – can reasonably be expected to be achieved. This is the normally the case for FM broadcasting and
LMR systems. Conversely, AM is a better choice for audio comm unications in which the SNR can not reasonably be
expected to be consistently greater than the FM capture thre shold. This is more likely to be the case in low-power or
long-range communications systems, especially those vuln erable to propagation uncertainties such as HF skywave
communications.
This property of FM also applies to interference. A classic e xample pertains to broadcast FM, as follows: Since broadcas t
FM frequencies are reused, it is not uncommon for two station s to be individually strong enough to be received with
sufficient SNR at a given location. However the weaker statio n will be strongly suppressed in the audio output as long as
the stronger station exceeds the capture threshold. It is ra re to hear FM broadcast stations interfering with each other , as
this requires both stations to be significantly below the FM c apture threshold at the same time. This is in contrast to
broadcast AM, in which multiple stations are frequently aud ible in the output.

5.7 Modulación de frecuencia (FM)

La tercera categoría principal de modulación analógica que permanece en uso común en los sistemas modernos de radio comunicación es la modulación de frecuencia (FM). Como se indica en la Tabla 5.1, FM es la representación de m(t) como una variación en la frecuencia del transportista. Este solo aspecto de FM resulta en tres ventajas que han hecho FM inmensamente popular. En primer lugar, FM puede generarse usando amplificadores de potencia no lineales (principalmente Clase C), que son más simples y más eficientes que los amplificadores lineales (clase A o AB) requeridos para AM y SSB (más sobre esto en el capítulo 17). Segundo, FM se beneficia de inmunidad relativamente alta a ruido e interferencia aditivo, ya que estos afectan principalmente la magnitud y fase de la frecuencia. En tercer lugar, no hay riesgo de que se interprete la desactivación rápida como parte de la señal del mensaje, lo que hace que FM sea más adecuado para su uso en comunicaciones terrestres en VHF y superior. Sin embargo, estas ventajas vienen a costa de un ancho de banda significativamente mayor, como veremos a continuación.

Las siguientes secciones ofrecen una breve pero razonablemente completa visión general de FM en sistemas modernos de comunicaciones radio. Entre todas las modulaciones FM es posiblemente la más difícil de analizar de una manera matemática rigurosa, y por lo tanto vamos a hacer un paso todos los aspectos más esenciales de ese análisis aquí. Para detalles matemáticos adicionales algunas referencias recomendadas incluyen [32] y [43, Ch. 8].

5.7.2 Generación de FM

Los dos métodos primarios utilizados para generar señales FM son conocidos como el método directo y el método indirecto, respectivamente. El método directo es tan implícito por Ecuación 5.22: m(t) se utiliza como la señal de control de frecuencia para un oscilador de frecuencia variable. Esto puede ser implementado en el dominio analógico utilizando un VCO o el dominio digital usando un NCO; para más detalles ver secciones 16.6 o 16.9 respectivamente La técnica VCO se denomina a veces modulación de la reactancia, que se refiere al uso de un varactor – un diodo cuya capacitancia es una función de tensión – como los medios para controlar la frecuencia del VCO. El método indirecto consiste en generar primero una señal NBFM, y luego utilizar multiplicación de frecuencia para aumentar la desviación de frecuencia de la señal. Cualquier método puede aplicarse directamente al transportista, o bien se implementa alternativamente en forma compleja de banda base y luego se convierte a sRF (t) como paso posterior.

5.7.4 Preemfasis

Un aspecto único de FM es que la diferenciación que es intrínseca a la demodulación FM tiende a exagerar el impacto del ruido en frecuencias más alejadas del portador. Esto se debe a que la demodulación FM convierte grandes frecuencias en grandes magnitudes. Así, el ruido de entrada a frecuencias lejos del transportista se convierte en ruido de salida en la señal de mensaje que es relativamente fuerte, mientras que el ruido de la entrada a las frecuencias cercanas al portador, pero teniendo la misma densidad espectral de potencia, se convierte en sonido de salida en el mensaje de señal que es relativamente débil. Irónicamente, el espectro de señales de audio tiende a concentrarse alrededor de 1 kHz, con un contenido relativamente menor en frecuencias más altas. Por lo tanto, tiene sentido modificar el espectro de señales de audio antes de la modulación, de manera que más potencia está presente en frecuencias superiores y menos potencia está presente a frecuencias inferiores, ya que esto equipara al SNR como función de frecuencia después de que la señal se demodula. Esta técnica es conocida como preemfasis, y la operación recíproca en el demodulador se conoce como deemfasis. Este proceso mejora significativamente la calidad percibida de audio que se ha transmitido utilizando FM, y por lo tanto es casi universalmente empleado.

5.7.5 El rendimiento en Varying SNR; Efecto de Umbral

Es bastante difícil calcular con precisión la producción SNR of of FM como función de SNR. No sólo esta relación depende de las características de señal de mensaje y los parámetros de modulación de una manera compleja, sino también las características de propagación y las técnicas de procesamiento de audio juegan un papel. FM típicamente requiere entrada SNR sobre el orden 3–6 dB para la voz inteligible, y tal vez más como 10–15 dB para audio de calidad. Sin embargo, hay algunos otros aspectos de esta cuestión que vale la pena saber.

Una razón para la popularidad de FM es que alcanza una salida relativamente alta SNR relativa a la entrada SNR en comparación con AM. Sin embargo esto sólo ocurre cuando la entrada SNR está por encima de un determinado umbral, y debajo de este umbral la relación de salida SNR a la entrada de SNR es significativamente peor que la de AM. Esta característica de FM se conoce como el umbral, y el SNR crítico es a veces se refiere a capturar En aplicaciones de audio, superando el umbral de captura se percibe como un silencio; es decir, una reducción aparente del ruido de fondo. La condición en la que el ruido de fondo parece haber sido esencialmente suprimido completamente –que es el demodulador que opera plenamente en la región de captura – se refiere a la total quietud. Ningún efecto es evidente en AM.

El efecto Threshold hace que FM sea superior para las aplicaciones de comunicación de audio en las que se pueda esperar que el umbral de captura, normalmente en orden de 10 dB, sea posible. Este es el caso normal de los sistemas FM y LMR. Por el contrario, AM es una mejor opción para comunicaciones de audio en los que el SNR no puede razonablemente ser esperado consistentemente mayor que el umbral FM de captura. Es más probable que esto sea el caso de sistemas de comunicaciones de baja potencia o largo alcance, especialmente aquellos vulnerables a incertidumbres de propagación como las comunicaciones de ondas de cielo HF.

Esta propiedad de FM también se aplica a la interferencia. Un ejemplo clásico pertenece a la emisión FM, como sigue: Como las frecuencias de radiodifusión FM se reutilizan, no es raro que dos estaciones sean lo suficientemente fuertes individualmente para ser recibidas con suficiente SNR en un lugar dado. Sin embargo, la estación más débil será fuertemente suprimida en la salida de audio mientras la estación más fuerte supere el umbral de captura. Es raro escuchar a las emisoras FM interfiriendo entre sí, ya que esto requiere que ambas estaciones estén significativamente por debajo del umbral de captura FM al mismo tiempo. Esto es en contraste con la emisión AM, en la que muchas estaciones son audibles frecuentemente en la salida.

blocks_es_mx.text: 5.7 Modulación de frecuencia (FM)

La tercera categoría principal de modulación analógica que permanece en uso común en los sistemas modernos de radio comunicación es la modulación de frecuencia (FM). Como se indica en la Tabla 5.1, FM es la representación de m(t) como una variación en la frecuencia del transportista. Este solo aspecto de FM resulta en tres ventajas que han hecho FM inmensamente popular. En primer lugar, FM puede generarse usando amplificadores de potencia no lineales (principalmente Clase C), que son más simples y más eficientes que los amplificadores lineales (clase A o AB) requeridos para AM y SSB (más sobre esto en el capítulo 17). Segundo, FM se beneficia de inmunidad relativamente alta a ruido e interferencia aditivo, ya que estos afectan principalmente la magnitud y fase de la frecuencia. En tercer lugar, no hay riesgo de que se interprete la desactivación rápida como parte de la señal del mensaje, lo que hace que FM sea más adecuado para su uso en comunicaciones terrestres en VHF y superior. Sin embargo, estas ventajas vienen a costa de un ancho de banda significativamente mayor, como veremos a continuación.

Las siguientes secciones ofrecen una breve pero razonablemente completa visión general de FM en sistemas modernos de comunicaciones radio. Entre todas las modulaciones FM es posiblemente la más difícil de analizar de una manera matemática rigurosa, y por lo tanto vamos a hacer un paso todos los aspectos más esenciales de ese análisis aquí. Para detalles matemáticos adicionales algunas referencias recomendadas incluyen [32] y [43, Ch. 8].

PLL y, por lo tanto, algo más allá del alcance de este capítulo. Sin embargo, se abordan en la Sección 16.8.

Los detectores y convertidores analógicos funcionan de manera más efectiva. Fast AGC aplica ganancia inversa en proporción al aumento de propagación dinámicamente variable, sin embargo, a menudo no es práctico tener AGC variar a la velocidad necesaria para realizar un seguimiento preciso de esta variación. Una versión extrema de este concepto es la llamada “dud limiting” seguida por la detección de cero cruce, que constituye una tercera clase importante de demoduladores FM. En este esquema la frecuencia instantánea de la señal de entrada se determina mediante la conversión de cero cruces de la forma de onda modulada en pulsos cortos, y luego la integración en el tren de pulso resultante para obtener una forma de ondas cuya magnitud es proporcional a frecuencia.
5.7.4 Preemfasis

Un aspecto único de FM es que la diferenciación que es intrínseca a la demodulación FM tiende a exagerar el impacto del ruido en frecuencias más alejadas del portador. Esto se debe a que la demodulación FM convierte grandes frecuencias en grandes magnitudes. Así, el ruido de entrada a frecuencias lejos del transportista se convierte en ruido de salida en la señal de mensaje que es relativamente fuerte, mientras que el ruido de la entrada a las frecuencias cercanas al portador, pero teniendo la misma densidad espectral de potencia, se convierte en sonido de salida en el mensaje de señal que es relativamente débil. Irónicamente, el espectro de señales de audio tiende a concentrarse alrededor de 1 kHz, con un contenido relativamente menor en frecuencias más altas. Por lo tanto, tiene sentido modificar el espectro de señales de audio antes de la modulación, de manera que más potencia está presente en frecuencias superiores y menos potencia está presente a frecuencias inferiores, ya que esto equipara al SNR como función de frecuencia después de que la señal se demodula. Esta técnica es conocida como preemfasis, y la operación recíproca en el demodulador se conoce como deemfasis. Este proceso mejora significativamente la calidad percibida de audio que se ha transmitido utilizando FM, y por lo tanto es casi universalmente empleado.
5.7.5 El rendimiento en Varying SNR; Efecto de Umbral

Es bastante difícil calcular con precisión la producción SNR of of FM como función de SNR. No sólo esta relación depende de las características de señal de mensaje y los parámetros de modulación de una manera compleja, sino también las características de propagación y las técnicas de procesamiento de audio juegan un papel. FM típicamente requiere entrada SNR sobre el orden 3–6 dB para la voz inteligible, y tal vez más como 10–15 dB para audio de calidad. Sin embargo, hay algunos otros aspectos de esta cuestión que vale la pena saber.

Una razón para la popularidad de FM es que alcanza una salida relativamente alta SNR relativa a la entrada SNR en comparación con AM. Sin embargo esto sólo ocurre cuando la entrada SNR está por encima de un determinado umbral, y debajo de este umbral la relación de salida SNR a la entrada de SNR es significativamente peor que la de AM. Esta característica de FM se conoce como el umbral, y el SNR crítico es a veces se refiere a capturar En aplicaciones de audio, superando el umbral de captura se percibe como un silencio; es decir, una reducción aparente del ruido de fondo. La condición en la que el ruido de fondo parece haber sido esencialmente suprimido completamente –que es el demodulador que opera plenamente en la región de captura – se refiere a la total quietud. Ningún efecto es evidente en AM.

El efecto Threshold hace que FM sea superior para las aplicaciones de comunicación de audio en las que se pueda esperar que el umbral de captura, normalmente en orden de 10 dB, sea posible. Este es el caso normal de los sistemas FM y LMR. Por el contrario, AM es una mejor opción para comunicaciones de audio en los que el SNR no puede razonablemente ser esperado consistentemente mayor que el umbral FM de captura. Es más probable que esto sea el caso de sistemas de comunicaciones de baja potencia o largo alcance, especialmente aquellos vulnerables a incertidumbres de propagación como las comunicaciones de ondas de cielo HF.

Esta propiedad de FM también se aplica a la interferencia. Un ejemplo clásico pertenece a la emisión FM, como sigue: Como las frecuencias de radiodifusión FM se reutilizan, no es raro que dos estaciones sean lo suficientemente fuertes individualmente para ser recibidas con suficiente SNR en un lugar dado. Sin embargo, la estación más débil será fuertemente suprimida en la salida de audio mientras la estación más fuerte supere el umbral de captura. Es raro escuchar a las emisoras FM interfiriendo entre sí, ya que esto requiere que ambas estaciones estén significativamente por debajo del umbral de captura FM al mismo tiempo. Esto es en contraste con la emisión AM, en la que muchas estaciones son audibles frecuentemente en la salida.

5.7 Frequency Modulation (FM)

The third major category of analog modulations remaining in common use in modern radio communications systems is frequency modulation (FM). As indicated in Table 5.1, FM is the representation of m(t) as a variation in the frequency of the carrier. This single aspect of FM results in three advantages which have made FM immensely popular. First, FM may be generated using non-linear (primarily “Class C”) power amplifiers, which are simpler and more power-efficient than the linear (Class A or AB) amplifiers required for AM and SSB (more on this in Chapter 17). Second, FM benefits from relatively high immunity to additive noise and interference, since these affect primarily the magnitude and phase of the signal as opposed to the frequency. Third, there is no risk of fast fading being interpreted as part of the message signal, which makes FM somewhat better suited for use in terrestrial communications at VHF and above. However these advantages come at the cost of significantly greater bandwidth, as we shall see below.

The following sections provide a brief but reasonably complete overview of FM in modern radio communications systems. Among all modulations FM is arguably the most difficult to analyze in a rigorous mathematical way, and so we shall sidestep all but the most essential aspects of that analysis here. For additional mathematical details some recommended references include [32] and [43, Ch. 8].

5.7.1 Characterization of FM

Since FM involves representing information as variations in frequency, a useful starting point is to determine the instantaneous frequency of the signal in Equation 5.1. Writing that equation here with A(t) = Ac (a constant), we have

Simple expressions for the spectrum in the more general case are not available. However it is possible to generalize the above results in a manner that is approximate, but nevertheless useful. The above expression is known as Carson’s Rule. Note this expression is consistent with the result suggested by Equation 5.27: B increases approximately linearly with β (or, equivalently, with kf). However this tells us nothing about the spectrum of the resulting signal.

To better understand the spectrum of FM signals, consider the role of β in Equation 5.27. If β ≪2π, then β sin ωmt ≪2π regardless of ωm; whereas the carrier phase can vary over the full range [0, 2π]. Thus the spectrum of sRF (t) must be very narrow and the line spectrum described above must roll off very quickly with increasing distance from the carrier. If we further assume β ≪1, then from Carson’s rule B ≈2W; i.e., bandwidth depends only on the bandwidth of m(t). One expects a qualitatively similar result if we replace the sinusoidal message signal with an arbitrary message signal having lowpass bandwidth W. The associated spectrum becomes a “smeared” version of the line spectrum, rolling off continuously but rapidly from the peak value at the carrier frequency. Modulation with β ≪2π is said to give rise to narrowband FM (NBFM).

FM modulation which is not obviously NBFM is considered wideband FM (WBFM). There is no clear dividing line between NBFM and WBFM in terms of β. However, when β ≫1, Carson’s rule becomes B ≈2βW; i.e., we observe approximately linear dependence of B on β. The spectrum of WBFM representation of audio typically also rolls off with increasing distance from a peak value at the carrier frequency, although typically not as smoothly as is the case for NBFM.

Example 5.1. Broadcast FM stations transmit an audio signal with 15 kHz bandwidth using a maximum instantaneous frequency deviation of 75 kHz. (See Figure B.1 (Appendix B) for an example of the spectrum of this signal.) Determine the modulation index, transmitted bandwidth, and classify as NBFM or WBFM.

Solution: Here ∆f = 75 kHz and W = 15 kHz, so the modulation index β = ∆f/W = 5. Transmitted bandwidth is estimated by Carson’s Rule: B ≈2 (β + 1) W = 180 kHz. β is not ≪2π here, so this is considered WBFM. In practice, broadcast FM channels are 200 kHz wide – slight wider than necessary in order to lessen receiver selectivity requirements. Also, 10% of the maximum frequency deviation of a broadcast FM signal is given over to

“subcarriers” located at frequencies above the primary 15 kHz audio lowpass channel. One of these subcarriers is used to transmit information required to generate the stereo audio signal.

Example 5.2. Some LMR systems use FM designed to transmit voice signals having 3 kHz bandwidth within 12.5 kHz channels. Estimate the modulation index, maximum instantaneous frequency deviation, and classify as NBFM or WBFM.

Solution: Assuming W = 3 kHz for voice, we find from Carson’s Rule that β < B/2W −1 = 1.08 since B must be less than 12.5 kHz. Therefore ∆f = βW < 3.24 kHz. This is considered narrowband FM because β ≪2π. In practice, ∆f up to 5 kHz or so is tolerated as the spectrum of voice signals is not flat, but rather tends to be concentrated around 1 kHz.

5.7.2 Generation of FM

The two primary methods used to generate FM signals are known as the direct method and the indirect method, respectively. The direct method is as implied by Equation 5.22: m(t) is used as the frequency control signal for a variable-frequency oscillator. This may be implemented in either the analog domain using a VCO or the digital domain using an NCO; for more details see Sections 16.6 or 16.9 respectively. The VCO technique is sometimes referred to as reactance modulation, which refers to the use of a varactor – a diode whose capacitance is a function of voltage – as the means to control the frequency of the VCO. The indirect method consists of first generating an NBFM signal, and then using frequency multiplication to increase the frequency deviation of the signal. Either method can be applied directly to the carrier, or alternatively implemented in complex baseband form and then converted to sRF (t) as a subsequent step.

5.7.3 Demodulation

There are two popular methods for demodulation of FM. One method is simply to differentiate sRF (t) (or it’s complex baseband representation) with respect to time, which yields a DSB-LC AM signal. For example, from Equation 5.26:

Now m(t) may be recovered using any method suitable for DSB-LC AM, including envelope detection. The differentiation may be implemented in a number of ways. If the signal has been digitized, then the derivative is proportional to the difference between adjacent time samples. In the analog domain, essentially the same operation can be implemented using analog delay lines or by slope detection, including the venerable Foster-Seeley discriminator.

The second method employs a PLL, as shown in Figure 5.21. Here the phase of the FM-modulated signal is compared to the phase of a reference signal provided by a VCO (analog domain implementation) or NCO (digital domain implementation). The frequency of the VCO/NCO is determined by the magnitude of the error signal created by the phase comparator. Specifically, the VCO/NCO frequency is increased if the phase comparator determines that the input frequency is greater than the reference frequency, and the VCO/NCO frequency is decreased if the phase comparator determines that the input frequency is less than the reference frequency. Thus the phase comparator output is proportional to the instantaneous frequency deviation, and is therefore also proportional to m(t). PLL design entails a number of considerations that must be addressed for this method to be successful: For example, how exactly to measure phase difference, how fast to change frequency as a function of phase comparator output, and how to initialize the PLL and maintain “lock” in the presence of noise and interference. These issues are specific to PLL design and therefore somewhat beyond the scope of this chapter. However they are addressed in Section 16.8.

Most FM demodulators implement some form of fast AGC and/or limiting to normalize the signal magnitude prior to demodulation. The basic idea is that the magnitude of the FM waveform contains no information, only propagation-induced variations and noise. Also, there is typically a limited range of magnitude over which analog

Fast AGC applies gain in inverse proportion to the dynamically-varying propagation gain, however it is often not practical to have AGC vary at the rate required to accurately track this variation. (See Section 15.8 for more about this.) Limiting finishes the job by allowing a moderate amount of “clipping” of the waveform prior to demodulation.

An extreme version of this concept is so-called “hard limiting” followed by zero-crossing detection, which constitutes a third major class of FM demodulators. In this scheme the instantaneous frequency of the input signal is determined by converting zero-crossings of the modulated waveform into short pulses, and then integrating over the resulting pulse train to obtain a waveform whose magnitude is proportional to frequency.

5.7.4 Preemphasis

One unique aspect of FM is that the differentiation that is intrinsic to FM demodulation tends to exaggerate the impact of noise at frequencies farthest from the carrier. This is because FM demodulation converts large frequencies into large magnitudes. Thus, input noise at frequencies far from the carrier is converted to output noise in the message signal that is relatively strong, whereas input noise at frequencies close to the carrier, but having the same power spectral density, is converted to output noise in the message signal that is relatively weak. Ironically, the spectrum of audio signals tends to be concentrated around 1 kHz, with relatively less content at higher frequencies. Therefore it makes sense to modify the spectrum of audio signals before modulation such that more power is present at higher frequencies and less power is present at lower frequencies, as this equalizes the SNR as a function of frequency after the signal is demodulated. This technique is known as preemphasis, and the reciprocal operation at the demodulator is known as deemphasis. This process significantly improves the perceived quality of audio that has been transmit using FM, and so is nearly universally employed.

5.7.5 Performance in Varying SNR; Threshold Effect

It is quite difficult to precisely estimate the output SNR of FM as a function of SNR. Not only does this relationship depend on the message signal characteristics and modulation parameters in a complex way, but also propagation characteristics and audio processing techniques play a role. Suffice it to say that FM typically requires input SNR on the order of 3–6 dB for intelligible voice, and perhaps more like 10–15 dB for quality audio. However there are some other aspects of this issue that are worth knowing about.

One reason for the popularity of FM is that it achieves relatively high output SNR relative to input SNR when compared to AM. However this only occurs when the input SNR is above a certain threshold, and below this threshold the ratio of output SNR to input SNR is significantly worse than that for AM. This characteristic of FM is is known as threshold effect, and the critical SNR is sometimes referred to as the capture threshold. In audio applications, exceeding the capture threshold is perceived as quieting; i.e., an apparent reduction of background noise. The condition in which background noise seems to be have been essentially completely suppressed – which is the demodulator operating fully in the capture region – is referred to as full quieting. No such effect is apparent in AM.

Threshold effect makes FM superior for audio communications applications in which the capture threshold – typically on the order of 10 dB – can reasonably be expected to be achieved. This is the normally the case for FM broadcasting and LMR systems. Conversely, AM is a better choice for audio communications in which the SNR can not reasonably be expected to be consistently greater than the FM capture threshold. This is more likely to be the case in low-power or long-range communications systems, especially those vulnerable to propagation uncertainties such as HF skywave communications.

This property of FM also applies to interference. A classic example pertains to broadcast FM, as follows: Since broadcast FM frequencies are reused, it is not uncommon for two stations to be individually strong enough to be received with sufficient SNR at a given location. However the weaker station will be strongly suppressed in the audio output as long as the stronger station exceeds the capture threshold. It is rare to hear FM broadcast stations interfering with each other, as this requires both stations to be significantly below the FM capture threshold at the same time. This is in contrast to broadcast AM, in which multiple stations are frequently audible in the output.

5.8 Techniques for Improving Audio
Analog modulations are used predominantly to transmit audi o. Thus it is appropriate to consider techniques that can be
used to improve the performance of these modulations specifi cally when transmitting audio. We have already noted one
example: preemphasis in FM (Section 5.7.4). Preemphasis an d other forms of equalization are routinely used in amplitud e
modulations as well, but for somewhat different reasons. Th ese reasons include compensating for missing high-frequen cy
content due to narrow bandwidth, and improving fidelity in th e presence of non-ideal noise and interference.
Squelch is the silencing of the audio output of a receiver when there i s no signal present, or when the input SNR drops
below a specified threshold. Squelch is particularly import ant in LMR applications because it inhibits the noise (“stat ic”)
that would otherwise be heard when no one is transmitting. Sq uelch is typically not implemented in receivers using
amplitude modulation, because there is no obvious threshol d SNR that can be universally considered to indicate the
presence of an intelligible signal. In FM, however, the capt ure threshold serves this purpose. Thus, squelch in FM
receivers is typically set such that audio is enabled only wh en the demodulator has achieved quieting or full quieting.
Squelch is considered so desirable that FM modulators in LMR systems typically embedded a tone in the audio signal that
can be used by the demodulator to confirm the presence of an int elligible signal, providing an extremely robust squelch
that requires no user adjustment. See [67, Section 9.3] for a dditional reading on this topic.
Noise blanking is the disabling of the audio output of a receiver when an inte rfering RF pulse is detected. As explained
Section 4.5, such pulses are emitted by a variety of circuits and machines, and may also originate from systems which are
deliberately producing pulses, such as HF-band radar. 5 Since amplitude modulations (including SSB) represent
information as amplitude, these pulses contribute directl y to the demodulated output, and may also interfere with the
operation of the receiver’s AGC. However, these pulses are a lso typically quite short – typically on the order of 1μ s – and
occur with low duty cycle. A noise blanker disables the recei ver for the duration of the pulse, which significantly improv es
the quality of the audio output relative to the result if the i mpulse is not blanked. This also prevents the pulse from
disrupting the AGC. Noise blanking circuits can be quite sop histicated; see [67, Section 9.2] and [72, Section 7.3] for
additional reading on this topic.
5.8.text_es_mx:
5.8 Técnicas para mejorar el audio

Las modulaciones analógicas se utilizan predominantemente para transmitir audio. Por lo tanto, es apropiado considerar técnicas que pueden utilizarse para mejorar el rendimiento de estas modulación específicamente al transmitir audio. Ya hemos observado un ejemplo: preemfasis en FM (Sección 5.7.4). La preemfasia y otras formas de igualación son usadas rutinariamente en modulación de amplitud, pero por razones algo diferentes. Estas razones incluyen la compensación por el contenido de alta frecuencia perdido debido al ancho de banda estrecho, y la mejora de la fidelidad en presencia de ruido e interferencia no-ideal.

Squelch es el silenciamiento de la salida de audio de un receptor cuando no hay señal presente, o cuando la entrada SNR cae por debajo de un umbral especificado. Squelch tiene especial importancia en aplicaciones LMR porque inhibe el ruido (“estático”) que de otra manera se escucharía cuando nadie está transmitiendo. Squelch normalmente no se implementa en receptores usando modulación de amplitud, porque no hay umbral obvio SNR que puede ser considerado universalmente para indicar la presencia de una señal inteligible. En FM, sin embargo, el umbral de captura sirve este propósito. Por lo tanto, squelch en los receptores FM es típicamente establecido tal que el audio está habilitado sólo cuando el demodulador ha logrado calmar o silencio completo. Squelch es considerado tan deseable que los moduladores FM en sistemas LMR normalmente incrustan un tono en la señal de audio que puede ser utilizado por el demodulador para confirmar la presencia de una señal inteligible, proporcionando un squelch extremadamente robusto que no requiere ajuste del usuario. Véase [67, Sección 9.3] para lectura adicional sobre este tema.

El en blanco ruidoso es el desactivamiento de la salida de audio de un receptor cuando se detecta un pulso RF interfiriendo. Como se explica Sección 4.5, estos pulsos son emitidos por una variedad de circuitos y máquinas, y también pueden originarse de sistemas que producen deliberadamente pulsos, como el radar HF-band.5 Dado que las modulaciones de amplitud (incluyendo SSB) representan información como amplitud, estos pulsoes contribuyen directamente a la salida demodulado, y también puede interferir con el funcionamiento del receptor AGC. Sin embargo, estos pulsos también son típicamente bastante cortos – típicamente en el orden de 1 μs – y ocurre con el ciclo de bajo nivel. Un en blanco de ruido desactiva al receptor durante la duración del pulso, lo que mejora significativamente la calidad de la salida de audio en relación con el resultado si el impulso no está en blanco. Esto también evita que el pulso interrumpa AGC. Los circuitos de en blanco ruidoso pueden ser bastante sofisticados; ver [67, Sección 9.2] y [72, Sección 7.3] para leer más sobre este tema.

5.8 Techniques for Improving Audio

Analog modulations are used predominantly to transmit audio. Thus it is appropriate to consider techniques that can be used to improve the performance of these modulations specifically when transmitting audio. We have already noted one example: preemphasis in FM (Section 5.7.4). Preemphasis and other forms of equalization are routinely used in amplitude modulations as well, but for somewhat different reasons. These reasons include compensating for missing high-frequency content due to narrow bandwidth, and improving fidelity in the presence of non-ideal noise and interference.

Squelch is the silencing of the audio output of a receiver when there is no signal present, or when the input SNR drops below a specified threshold. Squelch is particularly important in LMR applications because it inhibits the noise (“static”) that would otherwise be heard when no one is transmitting. Squelch is typically not implemented in receivers using amplitude modulation, because there is no obvious threshold SNR that can be universally considered to indicate the presence of an intelligible signal. In FM, however, the capture threshold serves this purpose. Thus, squelch in FM receivers is typically set such that audio is enabled only when the demodulator has achieved quieting or full quieting. Squelch is considered so desirable that FM modulators in LMR systems typically embedded a tone in the audio signal that can be used by the demodulator to confirm the presence of an intelligible signal, providing an extremely robust squelch that requires no user adjustment. See [67, Section 9.3] for additional reading on this topic.

Noise blanking is the disabling of the audio output of a receiver when an interfering RF pulse is detected. As explained Section 4.5, such pulses are emitted by a variety of circuits and machines, and may also originate from systems which are deliberately producing pulses, such as HF-band radar.5 Since amplitude modulations (including SSB) represent information as amplitude, these pulses contribute directly to the demodulated output, and may also interfere with the operation of the receiver’s AGC. However, these pulses are also typically quite short – typically on the order of 1 μs – and occur with low duty cycle. A noise blanker disables the receiver for the duration of the pulse, which significantly improves the quality of the audio output relative to the result if the impulse is not blanked. This also prevents the pulse from disrupting the AGC. Noise blanking circuits can be quite sophisticated; see [67, Section 9.2] and [72, Section 7.3] for additional reading on this topic.

6.1 Introducción

En la Sección 5.1 definimos la modulación como la representación de la información en un formulario adecuado para la transmisión. La modulación digital podría definirse como la representación del dato como una secuencia de símbolos dibujados a partir de un alfabeto finito de posibles símbolos. Esta definición no es completamente satisfactoria, ya que parece incluir una variedad de técnicas que muchos practicantes considerarían como modulaciones analógicas; éstas incluyen señalización continua (CW) (el uso de un portador interrumpible para enviar código Morse). En la Sección 5.1 nos establecimos sobre la noción de que la modulación digital también requiere que la información sea transmitida para ser representada en forma digital (no simplemente discreta-time) en algún momento del proceso de modulación,1 mientras que esto no es necesario en modulación analógica.

6.1.1 La visión general de un enlace de comunicación digital " Organización de este Capítulo

Con esta definición en mente, la Figura 6.1 muestra una visión general de un enlace de comunicación digital. Aquí está el flujo de señal habitual:

• El punto de partida del enlace es la codificación fuente, que es el procesamiento de datos y/o señales analógicas digitalizadas de mensajes – por ejemplo, voz – para hacer los datos en una forma mejor adaptada para la modulación digital. Un objetivo común en la codificación de fuentes es la compresión; es decir, reducción de la tasa de datos para reducir el ancho de banda requerido. La codificación de fuentes se aborda en la sección 6.2.

• Los datos son a menudo cifrados para la seguridad. Los principios de encriptación no son específicos para las comunicaciones radiofónicas y por lo tanto no se abordan más en este libro.

• La codificación de canales es el procesamiento de datos con el objetivo de hacerlo más robusto para los deterioros del canal de propagación, incluyendo ruido, multiruta e interferencia. La codificación de canal se aborda en las secciones 6.13 (codificación de control de terror) y 6.14 (interleaving).

• En este punto los datos son procesados por lo que se considera tradicionalmente la “modulación”. El resultado es una señal analógica que representa un mensaje de alfabeto finito discreto-tiempo, y que es adecuado para la conversión de frecuencia y amplificación. Es esta forma de la señal que se transmite finalmente al otro extremo del enlace. La modulación se aborda en secciones 6.3, 6.4, y porciones de secciones 6.10–6.12, 6.18 y 6.19.

• En el receptor, las operaciones recíprocas se aplican en orden inverso: desmodulación, decodificación de canales, desciframiento, decodificaciones de fuentes y conversión digital a análog (para señales analógicas). La demolición se aborda en secciones 6.4.1-6.9 y porciones de secciones 6.10-6.12, 6.18 y 6.19.

1 “Tiempo descreto” significa simplemente “cambiar sólo en tiempos específicos”; mientras que “digital” implica cuantización y reducción a binario también.
