8.5 Stability & Gain
We now consider the issue of two-port stability, and the impl ications for the usable gain of active two-ports. After an
introduction to the concept of stability in Section 8.5.1, w e consider methods for determining the conditions under whi ch a
two-port may be considered stable (Section 8.5.2). Section 8.5.3 introduces simultaneous conjugate matching, which
maximizes the TPG of a stable two-port. In Section 8.5.4 we co nsider the question of how to estimate the maximum TPG
of an active two-port, taking into account the potential for instability.
8.5.1 Instability & Oscillation
Stability is the absence of instability. Instability is a pr operty of some two-ports which are active and have internal
feedback. The concept is best demonstrated by example. Consider a vol tage amplifier circuit. The voltage amplifier
produces an output voltage which is larger than the input vol tage. If there is perfect isolation between output and input , the
amplifier will be stable. If on the other hand some fraction of the voltage at the output makes its way to the input, then
there is feedback, but not necessarily instability. In fact , properly implemented “negative” feedback is often desira ble in
voltage amplifiers. Instability occurs when the voltage fee dback creates a “vicious cycle” in which the modified input
voltage results in a significant increase in the output volta ge, which increases the feedback voltage, which further inc reases
the output voltage, and so on. In this scenario, the apparent voltage gain of the amplifier is continuously increasing, ev en
though the input voltage has remained constant.


200 CHAPTER 8. TWO-PORT CONCEPTS
It is clear that this continuous increase is not sustainable , since the power available from the power supply is presumab ly
bounded. Instead, the characteristics of the amplifier must change so as to stop the unbounded escalation of the output
voltage. This “change in characteristics” might be as simpl e (and dramatic) as the self-destruction of the amplifier.
Typically, however, what happens is that the intrinsic gain of the amplifier decreases with increasing output so that the
combined input-plus-feedback voltage results in a sustain able output voltage. This nonlinear behavior is known as gain
compression and is addressed further in Section 11.2.3. A second phenome non associated with instability is oscillation,
which for our purposes here can be defined as a periodically-v arying output in response to a constant (or zero) input.
While oscillation has applications (see Chapter 16), it is no t desirable in most active two ports, and is especially
undesirable in amplifiers.
In practice, all practical active two-ports have some degre e of internal feedback and therefore are potentially unstab le.
Even if this internal feedback is negligible, supporting ci rcuitry (e.g., bias circuitry in the case of transistors) an d reflection
from impedance mismatches provide paths for feedback that c an lead to instability. This raises the question: Is it possi ble
to characterize the stability of an embedded two-port from i t’s s-parameters and the source and load impedances? The
answer is yes, and this is the topic of the next section.
8.5.2 Determination of Stability
The instability of an embedded two-port can be recognized fr om outside the two-port as a condition in which incident
power waves result in “reflected” power waves with greater ma gnitude; i.e.,|Γin|> 1 or|Γout|> 1. (The term “reflected”
is in quotes here because the power flowing in the opposite dir ection is not simply a fraction of the incident power, but
rather a sum of simply-reflected power plus power entering th e two-port some other way; i.e., from a power supply or
through the input.) Thus we can write the conditions for stab ility in terms of Equations 8.35 and 8.36 as follows:

We should also be clear that the conditions assume that the so urce and load are themselves well-behaved, with |ΓS|< 1
and|ΓL|< 1.
If the above conditions are satisfied for all possible ΓS & ΓL with magnitudes less than 1, then the two-port is said to be
unconditionally stable. If the above conditions are satisfied only for some combinat ions of ΓS and ΓL, then the two-port is
said to be conditionally stable. Unconditionally stable two-ports are highly-valued in pr actical design, as the task of
impedance matching is unencumbered by concern that the matc h may make the two-port unstable. However conditionally
stable two-ports are hard to avoid in many circumstances; so me techniques for dealing with this possibility in amplifier
design are considered in Chapter 10.
It is also important to note that the stability of a two-port m ay depend on frequency. It it quite common for a two-port to be
stable at one frequency and unstable at a different frequenc y. Furthermore: If some device within the two-port begins to
oscillate because it has been stimulated by a signal at a freq uency at which the two-port is unstable, then the two-port’s
performance may be affected at all frequencies. Therefore i t is important to consider the two-port’s stability over a
frequency range that contains all possible input signals th at might exist; not just the signals for which the two-port is
intended.
We now consider the question of how to determine the stabilit y of a two-port. There are four ways to go about this: (1)
sample testing, (2) exhaustive (“brute force”) testing, (3 ) stability circles and (4) computing a stability metric. We now
consider each of these in turn.
Sample Testing. If we wish to test for stability given the s-parameters with ΓS and ΓL (or, equivalently, withZS andZL),
then we can simply substitute these values into Equations 8. 42 and 8.43 and see if the inequalities are satisfied. If they a re,
then the two-port is stable for that choice of ΓS and ΓL, and the two-port must be either conditionally or unconditi onally
stable at that frequency.

8.5 Estabilidad y ganancia

Consideramos ahora la cuestión de la estabilidad de dos puertos y las implicaciones para el beneficio útil de dos puertos activos. Después de una introducción al concepto de estabilidad en la Sección 8.5.1, consideramos métodos para determinar las condiciones bajo las cuales un puerto de dos puertos puede considerarse estable (Sección 8.5.2). La sección 8.5.3 introduce coincidencias simultáneas conjugadas, lo que maximiza el TPG de un dos puertos estable. En la Sección 8.5.4 consideramos la cuestión de cómo estimar el máximo TPG de un dos puertos activo, teniendo en cuenta el potencial de inestabilidad.

8.5.1 La inestabilidad " Oscilación

La inestabilidad es una propiedad de dos puertos que son activos y tienen retroalimentación interna. El concepto es mejor demostrado por ejemplo. Considere un circuito amplificador de tensión. El amplificador del voltaje produce un voltaje de salida más grande que el voltaje del insumo. Si hay aislamiento perfecto entre la salida y la entrada, el amplificador será estable. Si por otro lado, una fracción del voltaje en la salida hace su camino a la entrada, entonces hay retroalimentación, pero no necesariamente inestabilidad. De hecho, la retroalimentacion “negativa” correctamente implementada es deseable en amplificadores de tensión. La inestabilidad ocurre cuando el retroalimentario de voltaje crea un “ciclo vicioso” en el que el voltaje de entrada modificado resulta en un aumento significativo en el voltímetro de salida, lo cual aumenta el voltretroceso de retroceso de salida, y así. En este escenario, la aparente ganancia de voltaje del amplificador aumenta continuamente, aunque el voltaje de entrada ha permanecido constante.

Es evidente que este aumento continuo no es sostenible, ya que la potencia disponible de la fuente de alimentación está presumiblemente atada. En lugar de ello, las características del amplificador deben cambiar para detener la escalada sin límites del voltaje de salida. Este “cambio de características” puede ser tan simple (y dramático) como la autodestrucción del amplificante. Típicamente, sin embargo, lo que sucede es que la ganancia intrínseca del amplificador disminuye con la producción creciente de modo que el voltaje combinado de entrada y alimentación resulta en un voltaje de salida sostenible. Este comportamiento no lineal se conoce como compresión de ganancia y se aborda más adelante en la sección 11.2.3. Un segundo fenómeno asociado con inestabilidad es oscilación, que para nuestros propósitos aquí puede definirse como una salida de entrada de carga periódica en respuesta a un cero constante (sinúmero). Aunque la oscilación tiene aplicaciones (ver Capítulo 16), no es deseable en la mayoría de los puertos activos, y es especialmente indeseable en amplificadores.

En la práctica, todos los dos puertos activos prácticos tienen cierto grado de retroalimentación interna y por lo tanto son potencialmente inestables. Incluso si esta retroalimentacion interna es insignificante, el apoyo a circuitos (por ejemplo, bias circuito en el caso de transistores) y la reflexión de las deficiencias de impedancia proporcionan caminos para la retroalimentaciones que pueden conducir a la inestabilidad. La respuesta es sí, y este es el tema de la siguiente sección.

8.5.2 La determinación de la estabilidad

La inestabilidad de un doble puerto incrustado puede ser reconocida desde fuera de los dos puertos como una condición en la que las ondas de potencia incidental resultan en ondas de potencia “reflexión” con mayor magnitud; es decir, |Γin| > 1 o |Γout| > 1. (El término “reflejado” es citado aquí porque el poder que fluye en la dirección opuesta no es simplemente una fracción de la potencia del incidente, sino más bien una suma de energía simplemente reflexiva más la potencia que entra en el dos puertos de otra manera; es decir, de un suministro de energía o a través de la entrada.) blocks_es_mx.text: 8.5 Estabilidad y ganancia

Consideramos ahora la cuestión de la estabilidad de dos puertos y las implicaciones para el beneficio útil de dos puertos activos. Después de una introducción al concepto de estabilidad en la Sección 8.5.1, consideramos métodos para determinar las condiciones bajo las cuales un puerto de dos puertos puede considerarse estable (Sección 8.5.2). La sección 8.5.3 introduce coincidencias simultáneas conjugadas, lo que maximiza el TPG de un dos puertos estable. En la Sección 8.5.4 consideramos la cuestión de cómo estimar el máximo TPG de un dos puertos activo, teniendo en cuenta el potencial de inestabilidad.
8.5.1 La inestabilidad " Oscilación

La inestabilidad es una propiedad de dos puertos que son activos y tienen retroalimentación interna. El concepto es mejor demostrado por ejemplo. Considere un circuito amplificador de tensión. El amplificador del voltaje produce un voltaje de salida más grande que el voltaje del insumo. Si hay aislamiento perfecto entre la salida y la entrada, el amplificador será estable. Si por otro lado, una fracción del voltaje en la salida hace su camino a la entrada, entonces hay retroalimentación, pero no necesariamente inestabilidad. De hecho, la retroalimentacion “negativa” correctamente implementada es deseable en amplificadores de tensión. La inestabilidad ocurre cuando el retroalimentario de voltaje crea un “ciclo vicioso” en el que el voltaje de entrada modificado resulta en un aumento significativo en el voltímetro de salida, lo cual aumenta el voltretroceso de retroceso de salida, y así. En este escenario, la aparente ganancia de voltaje del amplificador aumenta continuamente, aunque el voltaje de entrada ha permanecido constante.

Es evidente que este aumento continuo no es sostenible, ya que la potencia disponible de la fuente de alimentación está presumiblemente atada. En lugar de ello, las características del amplificador deben cambiar para detener la escalada sin límites del voltaje de salida. Este “cambio de características” puede ser tan simple (y dramático) como la autodestrucción del amplificante. Típicamente, sin embargo, lo que sucede es que la ganancia intrínseca del amplificador disminuye con la producción creciente de modo que el voltaje combinado de entrada y alimentación resulta en un voltaje de salida sostenible. Este comportamiento no lineal se conoce como compresión de ganancia y se aborda más adelante en la sección 11.2.3. Un segundo fenómeno asociado con inestabilidad es oscilación, que para nuestros propósitos aquí puede definirse como una salida de entrada de carga periódica en respuesta a un cero constante (sinúmero). Aunque la oscilación tiene aplicaciones (ver Capítulo 16), no es deseable en la mayoría de los puertos activos, y es especialmente indeseable en amplificadores.

En la práctica, todos los dos puertos activos prácticos tienen cierto grado de retroalimentación interna y por lo tanto son potencialmente inestables. Incluso si esta retroalimentacion interna es insignificante, el apoyo a circuitos (por ejemplo, bias circuito en el caso de transistores) y la reflexión de las deficiencias de impedancia proporcionan caminos para la retroalimentaciones que pueden conducir a la inestabilidad. La respuesta es sí, y este es el tema de la siguiente sección.
8.5.2 La determinación de la estabilidad

La inestabilidad de un doble puerto incrustado puede ser reconocida desde fuera de los dos puertos como una condición en la que las ondas de potencia incidental resultan en ondas de potencia “reflexión” con mayor magnitud; es decir, |Γin| > 1 o |Γout| > 1. (El término “reflejado” es citado aquí porque el poder que fluye en la dirección opuesta no es simplemente una fracción de la potencia del incidente, sino más bien una suma de energía simplemente reflexiva más la potencia que entra en el dos puertos de otra manera; es decir, de un suministro de energía o a través de la entrada.) Así podemos escribir las condiciones para la estabilidad en términos de Ecuaciones 8.35 y 8.36 como sigue:
También debemos ser claros que las condiciones suponen que la fuente y la carga son bien hechos, con |ΓS| < 1 y |ΓL| < 1.

Si las condiciones anteriores están satisfechas para todo lo posible ΓS & ΓL con magnitudes inferiores a 1, entonces se dice que el dos puertos es incondicionalmente estable. Si las condiciones mencionadas anteriormente se satisfacen sólo para algunas combinaciones de ΓS y ΓL, entonces se dice el dos-puerto está condicionalmente estable. Los dos puertos incondicionales son altamente valorados en diseño práctico, ya que la tarea de impedancia que coinciden Sin embargo, dos puertos condicionalmente estables son difíciles de evitar en muchas circunstancias; algunas técnicas para tratar esta posibilidad en el diseño amplificador se consideran en el Capítulo 10.

También es importante señalar que la estabilidad de un dos puertos puede depender de la frecuencia. Es bastante común que un dos-puerto sea estable a una frecuencia e inestable a otra frecuencia. Además: Si algún dispositivo dentro del dos-port comienza a oscilar porque ha sido estimulado por una señal a una frecuencia en la que el dos-puerto es inestable, entonces el rendimiento de dos-ports puede ser afectado en todas las frecuencias. Por lo tanto, es importante considerar la estabilidad de dos puertos en un rango de frecuencias que contiene todas las señales posibles de entrada que podrían existir; no sólo las señales para las cuales se pretende el dos puertos.

Ahora consideramos la cuestión de cómo determinar la estabilidad de un dos puertos. Hay cuatro maneras de hacer esto: (1) pruebas de muestra, (2) pruebas exhaustivas (“fuerza bruta”), círculos de estabilidad (3) y (4) computando una métrica de estabilidad. Ahora consideramos cada uno de estos a su vez.

8.5 Stability & Gain

We now consider the issue of two-port stability, and the implications for the usable gain of active two-ports. After an introduction to the concept of stability in Section 8.5.1, we consider methods for determining the conditions under which a two-port may be considered stable (Section 8.5.2). Section 8.5.3 introduces simultaneous conjugate matching, which maximizes the TPG of a stable two-port. In Section 8.5.4 we consider the question of how to estimate the maximum TPG of an active two-port, taking into account the potential for instability.

8.5.1 Instability & Oscillation

Stability is the absence of instability. Instability is a property of some two-ports which are active and have internal feedback. The concept is best demonstrated by example. Consider a voltage amplifier circuit. The voltage amplifier produces an output voltage which is larger than the input voltage. If there is perfect isolation between output and input, the amplifier will be stable. If on the other hand some fraction of the voltage at the output makes its way to the input, then there is feedback, but not necessarily instability. In fact, properly implemented “negative” feedback is often desirable in voltage amplifiers. Instability occurs when the voltage feedback creates a “vicious cycle” in which the modified input voltage results in a significant increase in the output voltage, which increases the feedback voltage, which further increases the output voltage, and so on. In this scenario, the apparent voltage gain of the amplifier is continuously increasing, even though the input voltage has remained constant.

It is clear that this continuous increase is not sustainable, since the power available from the power supply is presumably bounded. Instead, the characteristics of the amplifier must change so as to stop the unbounded escalation of the output voltage. This “change in characteristics” might be as simple (and dramatic) as the self-destruction of the amplifier. Typically, however, what happens is that the intrinsic gain of the amplifier decreases with increasing output so that the combined input-plus-feedback voltage results in a sustainable output voltage. This nonlinear behavior is known as gain compression and is addressed further in Section 11.2.3. A second phenomenon associated with instability is oscillation, which for our purposes here can be defined as a periodically-varying output in response to a constant (or zero) input. While oscillation has applications (see Chapter 16), it is not desirable in most active two ports, and is especially undesirable in amplifiers.

In practice, all practical active two-ports have some degree of internal feedback and therefore are potentially unstable. Even if this internal feedback is negligible, supporting circuitry (e.g., bias circuitry in the case of transistors) and reflection from impedance mismatches provide paths for feedback that can lead to instability. This raises the question: Is it possible to characterize the stability of an embedded two-port from it’s s-parameters and the source and load impedances? The answer is yes, and this is the topic of the next section.

8.5.2 Determination of Stability

The instability of an embedded two-port can be recognized from outside the two-port as a condition in which incident power waves result in “reflected” power waves with greater magnitude; i.e., |Γin| > 1 or |Γout| > 1. (The term “reflected” is in quotes here because the power flowing in the opposite direction is not simply a fraction of the incident power, but rather a sum of simply-reflected power plus power entering the two-port some other way; i.e., from a power supply or through the input.) Thus we can write the conditions for stability in terms of Equations 8.35 and 8.36 as follows:

We should also be clear that the conditions assume that the source and load are themselves well-behaved, with |ΓS| < 1 and |ΓL| < 1.

If the above conditions are satisfied for all possible ΓS & ΓL with magnitudes less than 1, then the two-port is said to be unconditionally stable. If the above conditions are satisfied only for some combinations of ΓS and ΓL, then the two-port is said to be conditionally stable. Unconditionally stable two-ports are highly-valued in practical design, as the task of impedance matching is unencumbered by concern that the match may make the two-port unstable. However conditionally stable two-ports are hard to avoid in many circumstances; some techniques for dealing with this possibility in amplifier design are considered in Chapter 10.

It is also important to note that the stability of a two-port may depend on frequency. It it quite common for a two-port to be stable at one frequency and unstable at a different frequency. Furthermore: If some device within the two-port begins to oscillate because it has been stimulated by a signal at a frequency at which the two-port is unstable, then the two-port’s performance may be affected at all frequencies. Therefore it is important to consider the two-port’s stability over a frequency range that contains all possible input signals that might exist; not just the signals for which the two-port is intended.

We now consider the question of how to determine the stability of a two-port. There are four ways to go about this: (1) sample testing, (2) exhaustive (“brute force”) testing, (3) stability circles and (4) computing a stability metric. We now consider each of these in turn.

Sample Testing. If we wish to test for stability given the s-parameters with ΓS and ΓL (or, equivalently, with ZS and ZL), then we can simply substitute these values into Equations 8.42 and 8.43 and see if the inequalities are satisfied. If they are, then the two-port is stable for that choice of ΓS and ΓL, and the two-port must be either conditionally or unconditionally stable at that frequency.

Exhaustive (“Brute Force”) Testing. If we do not have a specific ΓS and ΓL in mind and instead wish to know all values resulting in a stable embedded two-port, then we can systematically test all possible combinations of ΓS and ΓL. This is not quite as bad as it sounds, as long as you are content to let a computer do it. The reason this approach is tractable is because we have already constrained |ΓS| < 1 and |ΓL| < 1; that is, all allowed values of these reflection coefficients lie inside a circle of radius 1 on the real-imaginary plane. The astute reader will observe that this is essentially the famous “Smith chart”. However there is no specific need to invoke the Smith chart or associated methods for the work at hand.

Example 8.7. Table 8.1 shows the s-parameters of the Avago AT-41511 transistor in common-emitter configuration, biased at VCE = 2.7 V and IC = 5 mA, for three frequencies. Perform an exhaustive search to determine all values of source and load impedance for which this transistor is unstable at 1 GHz.

Solution: First, realize that we can save ourselves a lot of work by doing the search over ΓS and ΓL, since these parameters map one-to-one with ZS and ZL but have the advantage of being constrained to have magnitude less than 1 – i.e., fall within the unit circle. Figure 8.12 shows the regions within the unit circle for which ΓS satisfies Equation 8.42 and for which ΓL satisfies Equation 8.43. As long as both inequalities are satisfied over some part of the unit circle, the embedded two-port is at least conditionally stable; we see that this is true in this example. If both conditions are satisfied over the entire unit circle, then the two-port is unconditionally stable; this is not true in this example. Therefore the AT-41511 is conditionally stable at 1 GHz, and the values of source and load impedance leading to instability correspond to the unshaded regions in Figure 8.12.

However, note from the example in Figure 8.12 that the boundaries between regions associated with stability and instability appear as arcs in the real-imaginary plane. 8.5.4 Maximum Stable Gain

If a two-port is only conditionally stable, and a stable simultaneous conjugate match is not possible, then which values of ΓS and ΓL maximize TPG? The short answer to this question is that there is no simple answer. We have seen above that given the s-parameters of the embedded two-port, it is possible to identify the values of ΓS and ΓL that result in stable operation. We can also test for the possibility of a stable simultaneous conjugate matching solution, which guarantees maximum TPG but only if the resulting values of ΓS and ΓL result in stable operation. A quite reasonable option is to test all sets of values of ΓS and ΓL for which the two-port is stable using Equation 8.41, with the goal of determining the choices that that maximize GT . Again, this is tractable because all reasonable choices for ΓS and ΓL have magnitudes ≤1 (i.e., lie within the unit circle), so there is a finite and simply-bounded domain within which all possibilities lie. (This same procedure can also be used to determine all possible combinations of ΓS and ΓL which yield a specified TPG.)

Example 8.11. For the Avago AT-41511 transistor at 1 GHz (previously considered in Examples 8.7–8.10), determine maximum TPG.

Solution: In Example 8.9 we found the transistor is not unconditionally stable at 1 GHz; therefore the maximum TPG is not equal to MAG. We estimate the maximum TPG instead using MSG, which is found to be 18.5 dB.

Another approach to this problem is a brute force search over ΓS and ΓL, seeking the maximum TPG over the domain of values for which the two-port is stable. In practical design, it would be quite risky to intentionally choose such a solution, since small errors in component values or changes due to temperature could cause the two-port to drift over the line into instability. Revising the search to build in some margin – e.g., to requiring |Γin| < 0.95 and |Γout| < 0.95, is a good idea. Common alternative conventions for specifying t parameters involve swapping a and b in the input and output vectors, and swapping port 1 and port 2 in Equation 8.63. There is no one “correct” definition, so one must take care to be aware of the convention in effect.

Example 8.12. The conversions between t and s parameters given in Figure 8.14 were provided without derivation. However, we can devise a simple check. Recall that the s-parameters for a parallel impedance Z are given in Equations 8.24 and 8.25. Calculate the s-parameters for a cascade of two parallel impedances, each equal to Z0 (a) using basic circuit theory and then (b) using the s-parameter cascade approach.

Solution: (a) The parallel combination of two impedances, each equal to Z0, is an impedance Z0Z0/(Z0 + Z0) = Z0/2. From Equations 8.24 and 8.25, we find the s-parameters for a parallel impedance Z = Z0/2 are s11 = s22 = −1/2 and s12 = s21 = +1/2. (b) The s parameters for a parallel impedance Z = Z0 are s11 = s22 = −1/3 and s12 = s21 = +2/3. The associated t parameters are t11 = t21 = +1/2, t12 = −1/2, and t22 = +3/2. The t parameters for a cascade of two such parallel impedances is t11 = 0, t12 = −1, t21 = +1, t22 = +2. Converting this back to s parameters, we find s11 = s22 = −1/2 and s12 = s21 = +1/2, in agreement with (a).

An important application of t parameters is the evaluation of TPG of cascaded two-ports when the port impedances are mismatched. When the impedances of the connecting ports are connected in a reflectionless match (note: not the same as conjugate match!) then TPG with respect to Z0 is simply the product of the intrinsic forward power gains of the individual two-ports; i.e., |s(1)

Example 8.13. As we shall find in Chapter 10, one of the principal headaches in amplifier design is ensuring the stability of transistors. One way to accomplish this is by resistive loss stabilization (Section 10.4.3) which can be accomplished using a resistor across the output; i.e., from collector to emitter in a common-emitter BJT design. The s-parameters of the parallel resistance are simple to calculate (Section 8.2.2), and from this we can calculate the s-parameters of a two-port cascade consisting of the transistor and the stabilization resistor. From the s-parameters of the cascade, it is possible to reevaluate stability (e.g., using the Rollett criterion) and to simultaneously determine the effect – usually deleterious – on gain. Although gain is reduced, the advantage in terms of improved stability is often worth the trouble. So here’s the problem: In Example 8.9 we examined the AT-41511 NPN BJT in common emitter configuration and found it to be potentially unstable at 1 GHz. Make this transistor unconditionally stable at 1 GHz by adding a resistor in parallel with the output.

8.7 Differential Circuits
So far in this chapter we have made an implicit assumption tha t signals are single-ended: That is, voltages are defined as a
potential differences with respect to a datum or “ground”, a s shown in Figures 8.16(a) and 8.17(a). In circuits which are
designed to process single-ended signals, currents emerge from sources, are processed, and return to the source via gro und
(hence, the term “circuit”). But this is not the only possibi lity.5
A prominent alternative to single-ended design is differential design, as illustrated in Figures 8.16(b) and 8.17(b). In th is
scheme, sources and loads are arranged symmetrically aroun d the datum, voltage signals are defined as the potential
differences between symmetric nodes (as opposed to being de fined with respect to the datum), and an explicit ground is
not necessary. Independence from an explicit ground is perh aps the most important distinction between single-ended an d
differential circuits: In differential circuits, the curr ent return path is an integral component of the signal, where as in a
single-ended circuit, currents are merely “sunk” at a groun d node which is assumed to be at the same potential as the
ground node nearest the source, often with no explicitly-de fined return path. As a result, currents in a single-ended cir cuit
can return to the source by any path with sufficiently low potential difference. If not care fully managed, these paths may
be prone to interference pick-up and can lead to instability , resulting in some unpleasant surprises.
8.7.1 Applications of Differential Circuits
There are four principal applications for differential cir cuits in radio engineering. The first pertains to sources and loads
which are inherently differential: prominent among these a re dipole antennas. Examination of Figures 2.1 and 2.15 reve als
that dipoles are inherently differential (in reception, as sources; in transmission, as loads), whereas monopoles are
inherently single-ended, with the ground plane serving as b oth datum and ground. 6 We can expect that there will be some
potential for mischief when we attempt to connect a dipole to a single-ended radio circuit without accounting for the
5If you read Chapter 2, then this would be a good time to review Se ction 2.6.2.
6At this point it should be noted that the single-ended equiva lent circuits shown in Figures 2.4 and 2.6 are technically co rrect for the monopole and
other single-ended antennas, but should properly be shown a s differential circuits when used to model dipoles and other d ifferential-mode antennas.
Nevertheless, there is no harm done in using the simpler singl e-ended models for the purposes of Chapter 2.

differential nature of the dipole. The same distinction app lies to transmission lines. In particular, parallel wire
transmission line is intrinsically differential, whereas coaxial transmission line (in which the shield is typically used as
both datum and ground) is intrinsically single-ended. For c onvenience, the situation is summarized in Table 8.2.
Another common application for differential circuits is to improve immunity to common mode interference. This is most
easily explained by example. Consider a circuit in close pro ximity to another circuit which is radiating electromagnet ic
interference (a common offender: switching-mode DC power s upplies). This interference adds to the desired signal.
However, the effect is quite different for single-ended and differential circuits, as illustrated in Figure 8.18. The
single-ended circuit has no immunity to the interference. I n the differential circuit, the common mode interference is
effectively canceled in the final interpretation of the sign al as the difference between the conductor potentials. The
immunity offered by differential circuits to common-mode i nterference becomes essential in compact designs, and
especially in designs in which disparate circuits must coex ist on a single integrated circuit.
A third application for differential circuits is ability to handle higher power. All devices used in radio receive and tr ansmit
circuits are ultimately limited in the amount of power they c an process. In both transmitters and receivers, the limits m ay
be due to non-linearity; for example, the inability of an amp lifier to deliver a specified gain once the signal power exceed s
a certain threshold. In transmitters, the situation is some times further aggravated by heating due large currents
encountering the unavoidable intrinsic resistance of mate rials. In a differential circuit, power is distributed acro ss two
identical circuits, so in principle a differential circuit can handle twice the power at the same level of performance as a
single-ended circuit using identical hardware.
A fourth application for differential circuits is transmis sion of signals in situations in which the current return pat h
between single-ended circuits becomes ambiguous. This com monly occurs on printed circuit boards, in which the desired
(or assumed) return path is intended to be through a ground la yer, but in which other paths exist over which the impedance
is sufficiently low to attract significant amounts of current . In particular: When the intended connection to a ground plan e
does not have sufficiently low impedance, a significant fract ion of current may return via a highly undesirable path, such
as through a power supply. This problem is largely mitigated when the signal is conveyed differentially because the
current return path is intrinsic to the signal path.

8.7.2 Interfaces between Differential and Single-Ended Cir cuits
Since both single-ended and differential circuits are comm only used, one commonly encounters the problem of how to
connect one to the other. A direct connection which simply ig nores the difference between the two types of circuits is not
necessarily out of the question: For example, dipole antenn as are often connected directly to single-ended radio circu its.
However, such connections typically yield degraded perfor mance and often unintended consequences: In the case of
dipoles, such connections result in modified distributions of current on the dipole, and the circuit itself radiates and
receives as part of the dipole. (For more on this topic, see Se ctions 2.6.2 and 12.7.)
In general, an explicit conversion between signal modes is d esirable. A device which performs this conversion is known a s
a balun. Perhaps the simplest device that can be used as balun is a tra nsformer, as shown in Figure 8.19(a). In this scheme,
the single-ended and differential ports are electrically i solated, connected only by the magnetic flux linking the coil s. Thus
the explicit datum required by the single-ended port can be i mplemented with no effect on the differential port. This
particular scheme is often of interest since it can be used to simultaneously change impedance – more on that in Chapter 9.
Another way to use a transformer as a balun is as shown in Figur e 8.19(b). In this scheme the transformer is wound so that
the magnetic field associated with the current at the single- mode port excites a current in the other coil that flows in the
opposite direction, yielding a differential current at the opposite port. V ariations on this idea are the Guanella and Ruthroff
baluns, which use multiple transformers to simultaneously perform impedance transformation.
The above schemes can also be implemented using transmissio n line techniques in lieu of transformers. Transmission
lines yield a variety of additional strategies for converti ng between single-ended and differential signals; see Sect ion 12.7
for more on this topic.
Finally, we note one other approach: The LC balun is comprised of discrete inductors (L’s) and capacitors (C’ s) arranged
to implement the necessary phase shifts. A useful introduct ion to this class of devices can be found in [45, Sec. 15.3]. Th e
advantage of this approach is that the balun may be very small . The disadvantages of this approach are (1) it is difficult to
achieve large bandwidth and (2) discrete L’s and C’s of suffic ient quality may be difficult to find, especially for frequenc ies
in the UHF band and above.
8.7.3 Analysis of Differential Circuits
Given the advantages and prevalence of differential circui try in radio systems, it seems reasonable expect that the
single-endeds-parameter methods presented in this chapter could be exten ded to deal with differential two-ports, as well
as to combinations of differential and single-ended two-po rts. In fact, the necessary “mixed-mode” s-parameter analysis is
a relatively recent development [8]. In practice, it is ofte n possible to avoid the complexity of mixed-mode analysis.
Differential circuits are frequently designed and analyze d first as single-ended circuits, and then converted to equiv alent
differential forms as a final step. Interfaces between singl e-ended and differential circuits, such as baluns, can ofte n be
accommodated by initially assuming ideal conversion betwe en single-ended and differential signal modes. Explicit
mixed-mode analysis becomes important when the conversion between single-ended and differential modes cannot
reasonably be approximated as ideal. This is sometimes the c ase when the mode conversion is considered over very large
bandwidths, and in integrated circuit implementations.

8.7 Circuitos diferenciales

Hasta el momento en este capítulo hemos hecho una suposición implícita de que las señales son de un solo soporte: es decir, las tensiones se definen como una posible diferencia con respecto a un dato o “tierra”, como se muestra en las Figuras 8.16a) y 8.17a) En circuitos diseñados para procesar señales de un solo sentido, las corrientes emergen de fuentes, se procesan y regresan a la fuente por tierra (por lo tanto, el término “circuito”). Pero esta no es la única posibilidad.5

Una alternativa prominente al diseño de un solo soporte es el diseño diferencial, como se ilustra en las Figuras 8.16(b) y 8.17(b). En este esquema, las fuentes y cargas se organizan simétricamente alrededor del dato, las señales de tensión se definen como las diferencias potenciales entre los nodos simétricos (en lugar de ser definido con respecto al datum), y un terreno explícito no es necesario. La independencia de un terreno explícito es quizás la distinción más importante entre circuitos mono-denominados y diferenciales: En los circuitos diferenciales, el camino de retorno actual es un componente integral de la señal, mientras que en un circuito único las corrientes son meramente "sunk" en un nodo terrestre que se supone que está en el mismo potencial que el nodo de tierra más cercano a la fuente, a menudo sin un camino de retorno explícitamente definido. Como resultado, las corrientes en un circuito de una sola orden pueden regresar a la fuente por cualquier camino con una diferencia potencial suficientemente baja. Si no se administran cuidadosamente, estos caminos pueden ser propensos a la captación de interferencias y pueden conducir a la inestabilidad, lo que da lugar a algunas sorpresas desagradables.

8.7.1 Las aplicaciones de los circuitos diferenciales

Hay cuatro aplicaciones principales para circuitos diferenciales en ingeniería radiofónica. La primera se refiere a fuentes y cargas que son inherentemente diferenciales: prominente entre ellas son antenas dipolas. El examen de las Figuras 2.1 y 2.15 revela que los dipoles son inherentemente diferenciales (en recepción, como fuentes; en transmisión, como cargas), mientras que los monopolos son inherentemente mono-denominado, con el plano terrestre que sirve como datum y tierra.6 Podemos esperar que habrá algún potencial de error cuando intentamos conectar un dipole a un circuito de radio de un solo-des sin contabilizar para el

Sin embargo, no hay daño en el uso de los modelos de un solo sentido más simple para los propósitos del Capítulo 2.

la misma distinción se aplica a las líneas de transmisión. En particular, la línea de transmisión paralela del alambre es intrínsecamente diferencial, mientras que la línea de transmisiones coaxial (en la que el escudo se utiliza normalmente como datum y tierra) es intrónicamente única. Para comodidad, la situación se resume en la tabla 8.2.

Otra aplicación común para circuitos diferenciales es mejorar la inmunidad a la interferencia del modo común. Esto se explica más fácilmente por ejemplo. Considere un circuito cerca de otro circuito que está irradiando interferencia electromagnética (un ofensor común: conmutación-modo DC fuente de alimentación). Esta interferencia añade a la señal deseada. Sin embargo, el efecto es bastante diferente para los circuitos mono-mensión y diferencial, como se ilustra en la Figura 8.18. El circuito de un solo combo no tiene inmunidad a la interferencia. En el circuito diferencial, la interferencia del modo común se cancela efectivamente en la interpretación final de la señal como la diferencia entre los potenciales del conductor. La inmunidad ofrecida por circuitos diferenciales a la interferencia del movimiento común se hace esencial en diseños compactos, y especialmente en diseños en los que los dispares deben coexistir en un único circuito integrado.

Una tercera aplicación para circuitos diferenciales es la capacidad de manejar mayor potencia. Todos los dispositivos utilizados en los circuitos radio reciben y transmiten son, en última instancia, limitados en la cantidad de potencia que pueden procesar. Tanto en transmisores como receptores, los límites pueden ser debido a no linealidad; por ejemplo, la incapacidad de un amplificador para entregar una ganancia especificada una vez que la potencia de señal supere un determinado umbral. En los transmisores, la situación a veces se agrava más por el calentamiento debido a las grandes corrientes que encuentran la resistencia intrínseca inevitable de los materiales. En un circuito diferencial, la energía se distribuye en dos circuitos idénticos, por lo que en principio un circuito diferenciado puede manejar el doble de potencia al mismo nivel de rendimiento que un circuito de una sola serie utilizando hardware idéntico.

Una cuarta aplicación para circuitos diferenciales es la transmisión de señales en situaciones en las que el camino de retorno actual entre circuitos de un solo combo se vuelve ambiguo. Esto ocurre comúnmente en tableros de circuito impresos, en los cuales el camino de regreso deseado (o asumido) está destinado a ser a través de una capa terrestre, pero en los que existen otros caminos sobre los cuales la impedancia es suficientemente baja para atraer cantidades significativas de corriente. En particular: Cuando la conexión prevista a un plano terrestre no tiene suficiente impedancia baja, una fracción significativa de corriente puede regresar por un camino altamente indeseable, como por ejemplo mediante una fuente de alimentación. Este problema se mitiga en gran medida cuando la señal se transmite de manera diferente porque el camino de retorno actual es intrínseco al camino de señalización.

8.7.2 Las interfaces entre los circuitos diferenciales y de un solo cuerpo

Como los circuitos de un solo combo y diferencial son utilizados comúnmente, uno se encuentra con el problema de cómo conectarse uno a otro. Una conexión directa que simplemente ignora la diferencia entre los dos tipos de circuitos no necesariamente está fuera de la pregunta: Por ejemplo, las antenas dipole están a menudo conectadas directamente a los circuitos radiológicos de un único combo. Sin embargo, estas conexiones suelen producir rendimiento degradado y a menudo consecuencias no deseadas: En el caso de las dipoles, tales conexiones resultan en distribuciones modificadas de corriente en el dipolo, y el circuito mismo irradia y recibe como parte del dipolo. (Para más sobre este tema, véase Secciones 2.6.2 y 12.7.)

En general, es deseable una conversión explícita entre modos de señal. Un dispositivo que realiza esta conversión se conoce como balun. Tal vez el dispositivo más simple que puede ser utilizado como balun es un transformador, como se muestra en la Figura 8.19(a). En este esquema, los puertos mono-contenidos y diferenciales son aislados eléctricamente, conectados sólo por el flujo magnético que conecta las bobinas. Este esquema en particular es a menudo de interés ya que puede ser utilizado para cambiar simultáneamente impedancia – más sobre eso en el Capítulo 9.

Otra manera de utilizar un transformador como balun es como se muestra en la Figura 8.19(b). En este esquema el transformador está herido para que el campo magnético asociado con la corriente en el puerto de un solo movimiento excite una corriente en la otra bobina que fluye en la dirección opuesta, dando lugar a una corriente diferencial en el puerto opuesto. Variaciones sobre esta idea son el Guanella y Ruthroff balunes, que utilizan múltiples transformadores para realizar simultáneamente.

Los esquemas anteriores también se pueden implementar utilizando técnicas de línea de transmisión en lugar de transformadores. Las líneas de transmisión ofrecen una variedad de estrategias adicionales para la conversión entre señales individuales y diferenciales; véase la sección 12.7 para más sobre este tema.

Finalmente, tomamos nota de otro enfoque: El LC balun está compuesto por inductores discretos (L) y capacitores (C) dispuestos a implementar los cambios de fase necesarios. Una introducción útil a esta clase de dispositivos se puede encontrar en [45, Sec. 15.3]. La ventaja de este enfoque es que el balun puede ser muy pequeño. Las desventajas de este enfoque son (1) es difícil lograr ancho de banda grande y (2) discreto L’s y C de calidad suficiente puede ser difícil de encontrar, especialmente para las frecuencias en la banda UHF y arriba.

8.7.3 El análisis de los circuitos diferenciales

Dada las ventajas y prevalencia de los circuitos diferenciales en sistemas radiofónicos, parece razonable esperar que los métodos de parámetros de un solo sentido presentados en este capítulo puedan ampliarse para tratar los dos puertos diferenciales, así como combinaciones de dos puertos diferenciados y mono-dedos. De hecho, el análisis de es-parametro necesario "mixed-mode" es un desarrollo relativamente reciente [8]. En la práctica, evitar la complejidad mixta es a menudo posible. Los circuitos diferenciales se diseñan y analizan con frecuencia primero como circuitos de un solo soporte, y luego se convierten en formas diferenciales equivalentes como paso final. Las interfaces entre circuitos de una sola vez y diferencial, como balunes, pueden ser atendidas inicialmente asumiendo la conversión ideal entre modos de señal de un solo sentido y diferencial. El análisis de modo mixto explícito se vuelve importante cuando la conversión entre modos mono-denominados y diferenciales no puede razonablemente aproximarse como ideal. Esto es a veces el caso cuando la conversión del modo se considera sobre anchos de banda muy grandes, y en implementaciones de circuito integrado.

Para comodidad, la situación se resume en la tabla 8.2.

Otra aplicación común para circuitos diferenciales es mejorar la inmunidad a la interferencia del modo común. Esto se explica más fácilmente por ejemplo. Considere un circuito cerca de otro circuito que está irradiando interferencia electromagnética (un ofensor común: conmutación-modo DC fuente de alimentación). Esta interferencia añade a la señal deseada. Sin embargo, el efecto es bastante diferente para los circuitos mono-mensión y diferencial, como se ilustra en la Figura 8.18. El circuito de un solo combo no tiene inmunidad a la interferencia. En el circuito diferencial, la interferencia del modo común se cancela efectivamente en la interpretación final de la señal como la diferencia entre los potenciales del conductor. La inmunidad ofrecida por circuitos diferenciales a la interferencia del movimiento común se hace esencial en diseños compactos, y especialmente en diseños en los que los dispares deben coexistir en un único circuito integrado.

Una tercera aplicación para circuitos diferenciales es la capacidad de manejar mayor potencia. Todos los dispositivos utilizados en los circuitos radio reciben y transmiten son, en última instancia, limitados en la cantidad de potencia que pueden procesar. Tanto en transmisores como receptores, los límites pueden ser debido a no linealidad; por ejemplo, la incapacidad de un amplificador para entregar una ganancia especificada una vez que la potencia de señal supere un determinado umbral. En los transmisores, la situación a veces se agrava más por el calentamiento debido a las grandes corrientes que encuentran la resistencia intrínseca inevitable de los materiales. En un circuito diferencial, la energía se distribuye en dos circuitos idénticos, por lo que en principio un circuito diferenciado puede manejar el doble de potencia al mismo nivel de rendimiento que un circuito de una sola serie utilizando hardware idéntico.

Una cuarta aplicación para circuitos diferenciales es la transmisión de señales en situaciones en las que el camino de retorno actual entre circuitos de un solo combo se vuelve ambiguo. Esto ocurre comúnmente en tableros de circuito impresos, en los cuales el camino de regreso deseado (o asumido) está destinado a ser a través de una capa terrestre, pero en los que existen otros caminos sobre los cuales la impedancia es suficientemente baja para atraer cantidades significativas de corriente. En particular: Cuando la conexión prevista a un plano terrestre no tiene suficiente impedancia baja, una fracción significativa de corriente puede regresar por un camino altamente indeseable, como por ejemplo mediante una fuente de alimentación. Este problema se mitiga en gran medida cuando la señal se transmite de manera diferente porque el camino de retorno actual es intrínseco al camino de señalización.

8.7.2 Las interfaces entre los circuitos diferenciales y de un solo cuerpo

Como los circuitos de un solo combo y diferencial son utilizados comúnmente, uno se encuentra con el problema de cómo conectarse uno a otro. Una conexión directa que simplemente ignora la diferencia entre los dos tipos de circuitos no necesariamente está fuera de la pregunta: Por ejemplo, las antenas dipole están a menudo conectadas directamente a los circuitos radiológicos de un único combo. Sin embargo, estas conexiones suelen producir rendimiento degradado y a menudo consecuencias no deseadas: En el caso de las dipoles, tales conexiones resultan en distribuciones modificadas de corriente en el dipolo, y el circuito mismo irradia y recibe como parte del dipolo. (Para más sobre este tema, véase Secciones 2.6.2 y 12.7.)

En general, es deseable una conversión explícita entre modos de señal. Un dispositivo que realiza esta conversión se conoce como balun. Tal vez el dispositivo más simple que puede ser utilizado como balun es un transformador, como se muestra en la Figura 8.19(a). En este esquema, los puertos mono-contenidos y diferenciales son aislados eléctricamente, conectados sólo por el flujo magnético que conecta las bobinas. Este esquema en particular es a menudo de interés ya que puede ser utilizado para cambiar simultáneamente impedancia – más sobre eso en el Capítulo 9.

Otra manera de utilizar un transformador como balun es como se muestra en la Figura 8.19(b). En este esquema el transformador está herido para que el campo magnético asociado con la corriente en el puerto de un solo movimiento excite una corriente en la otra bobina que fluye en la dirección opuesta, dando lugar a una corriente diferencial en el puerto opuesto. Variaciones sobre esta idea son el Guanella y Ruthroff balunes, que utilizan múltiples transformadores para realizar simultáneamente.

Los esquemas anteriores también se pueden implementar utilizando técnicas de línea de transmisión en lugar de transformadores. Las líneas de transmisión ofrecen una variedad de estrategias adicionales para la conversión entre señales individuales y diferenciales; véase la sección 12.7 para más sobre este tema.

Finalmente, tomamos nota de otro enfoque: El LC balun está compuesto por inductores discretos (L) y capacitores (C) dispuestos a implementar los cambios de fase necesarios. Una introducción útil a esta clase de dispositivos se puede encontrar en [45, Sec. 15.3]. La ventaja de este enfoque es que el balun puede ser muy pequeño. Las desventajas de este enfoque son (1) es difícil lograr ancho de banda grande y (2) discreto L’s y C de calidad suficiente puede ser difícil de encontrar, especialmente para las frecuencias en la banda UHF y arriba.
8.7.3 El análisis de los circuitos diferenciales

Dada las ventajas y prevalencia de los circuitos diferenciales en sistemas radiofónicos, parece razonable esperar que los métodos de parámetros de un solo sentido presentados en este capítulo puedan ampliarse para tratar los dos puertos diferenciales, así como combinaciones de dos puertos diferenciados y mono-dedos. De hecho, el análisis de es-parametro necesario "mixed-mode" es un desarrollo relativamente reciente [8]. En la práctica, evitar la complejidad mixta es a menudo posible. Los circuitos diferenciales se diseñan y analizan con frecuencia primero como circuitos de un solo soporte, y luego se convierten en formas diferenciales equivalentes como paso final. Las interfaces entre circuitos de una sola vez y diferencial, como balunes, pueden ser atendidas inicialmente asumiendo la conversión ideal entre modos de señal de un solo sentido y diferencial. El análisis de modo mixto explícito se vuelve importante cuando la conversión entre modos mono-denominados y diferenciales no puede razonablemente aproximarse como ideal. Esto es a veces el caso cuando la conversión del modo se considera sobre anchos de banda muy grandes, y en implementaciones de circuito integrado.

8.7 Differential Circuits

So far in this chapter we have made an implicit assumption that signals are single-ended: That is, voltages are defined as a potential differences with respect to a datum or “ground”, as shown in Figures 8.16(a) and 8.17(a). In circuits which are designed to process single-ended signals, currents emerge from sources, are processed, and return to the source via ground (hence, the term “circuit”). But this is not the only possibility.5

A prominent alternative to single-ended design is differential design, as illustrated in Figures 8.16(b) and 8.17(b). In this scheme, sources and loads are arranged symmetrically around the datum, voltage signals are defined as the potential differences between symmetric nodes (as opposed to being defined with respect to the datum), and an explicit ground is not necessary. Independence from an explicit ground is perhaps the most important distinction between single-ended and differential circuits: In differential circuits, the current return path is an integral component of the signal, whereas in a single-ended circuit, currents are merely “sunk” at a ground node which is assumed to be at the same potential as the ground node nearest the source, often with no explicitly-defined return path. As a result, currents in a single-ended circuit can return to the source by any path with sufficiently low potential difference. If not carefully managed, these paths may be prone to interference pick-up and can lead to instability, resulting in some unpleasant surprises.

8.7.1 Applications of Differential Circuits

There are four principal applications for differential circuits in radio engineering. The first pertains to sources and loads which are inherently differential: prominent among these are dipole antennas. Examination of Figures 2.1 and 2.15 reveals that dipoles are inherently differential (in reception, as sources; in transmission, as loads), whereas monopoles are inherently single-ended, with the ground plane serving as both datum and ground.6 We can expect that there will be some potential for mischief when we attempt to connect a dipole to a single-ended radio circuit without accounting for the

Nevertheless, there is no harm done in using the simpler single-ended models for the purposes of Chapter 2.

differential nature of the dipole. The same distinction applies to transmission lines. In particular, parallel wire transmission line is intrinsically differential, whereas coaxial transmission line (in which the shield is typically used as both datum and ground) is intrinsically single-ended. For convenience, the situation is summarized in Table 8.2.

Another common application for differential circuits is to improve immunity to common mode interference. This is most easily explained by example. Consider a circuit in close proximity to another circuit which is radiating electromagnetic interference (a common offender: switching-mode DC power supplies). This interference adds to the desired signal. However, the effect is quite different for single-ended and differential circuits, as illustrated in Figure 8.18. The single-ended circuit has no immunity to the interference. In the differential circuit, the common mode interference is effectively canceled in the final interpretation of the signal as the difference between the conductor potentials. The immunity offered by differential circuits to common-mode interference becomes essential in compact designs, and especially in designs in which disparate circuits must coexist on a single integrated circuit.

A third application for differential circuits is ability to handle higher power. All devices used in radio receive and transmit circuits are ultimately limited in the amount of power they can process. In both transmitters and receivers, the limits may be due to non-linearity; for example, the inability of an amplifier to deliver a specified gain once the signal power exceeds a certain threshold. In transmitters, the situation is sometimes further aggravated by heating due large currents encountering the unavoidable intrinsic resistance of materials. In a differential circuit, power is distributed across two identical circuits, so in principle a differential circuit can handle twice the power at the same level of performance as a single-ended circuit using identical hardware.

A fourth application for differential circuits is transmission of signals in situations in which the current return path between single-ended circuits becomes ambiguous. This commonly occurs on printed circuit boards, in which the desired (or assumed) return path is intended to be through a ground layer, but in which other paths exist over which the impedance is sufficiently low to attract significant amounts of current. In particular: When the intended connection to a ground plane does not have sufficiently low impedance, a significant fraction of current may return via a highly undesirable path, such as through a power supply. This problem is largely mitigated when the signal is conveyed differentially because the current return path is intrinsic to the signal path.

8.7.2 Interfaces between Differential and Single-Ended Circuits

Since both single-ended and differential circuits are commonly used, one commonly encounters the problem of how to connect one to the other. A direct connection which simply ignores the difference between the two types of circuits is not necessarily out of the question: For example, dipole antennas are often connected directly to single-ended radio circuits. However, such connections typically yield degraded performance and often unintended consequences: In the case of dipoles, such connections result in modified distributions of current on the dipole, and the circuit itself radiates and receives as part of the dipole. (For more on this topic, see Sections 2.6.2 and 12.7.)

In general, an explicit conversion between signal modes is desirable. A device which performs this conversion is known as a balun. Perhaps the simplest device that can be used as balun is a transformer, as shown in Figure 8.19(a). In this scheme, the single-ended and differential ports are electrically isolated, connected only by the magnetic flux linking the coils. Thus the explicit datum required by the single-ended port can be implemented with no effect on the differential port. This particular scheme is often of interest since it can be used to simultaneously change impedance – more on that in Chapter 9.

Another way to use a transformer as a balun is as shown in Figure 8.19(b). In this scheme the transformer is wound so that the magnetic field associated with the current at the single-mode port excites a current in the other coil that flows in the opposite direction, yielding a differential current at the opposite port. Variations on this idea are the Guanella and Ruthroff baluns, which use multiple transformers to simultaneously perform impedance transformation.

The above schemes can also be implemented using transmission line techniques in lieu of transformers. Transmission lines yield a variety of additional strategies for converting between single-ended and differential signals; see Section 12.7 for more on this topic.

Finally, we note one other approach: The LC balun is comprised of discrete inductors (L’s) and capacitors (C’s) arranged to implement the necessary phase shifts. A useful introduction to this class of devices can be found in [45, Sec. 15.3]. The advantage of this approach is that the balun may be very small. The disadvantages of this approach are (1) it is difficult to achieve large bandwidth and (2) discrete L’s and C’s of sufficient quality may be difficult to find, especially for frequencies in the UHF band and above.

8.7.3 Analysis of Differential Circuits

Given the advantages and prevalence of differential circuitry in radio systems, it seems reasonable expect that the single-ended s-parameter methods presented in this chapter could be extended to deal with differential two-ports, as well as to combinations of differential and single-ended two-ports. In fact, the necessary “mixed-mode” s-parameter analysis is a relatively recent development [8]. In practice, it is often possible to avoid the complexity of mixed-mode analysis. Differential circuits are frequently designed and analyzed first as single-ended circuits, and then converted to equivalent differential forms as a final step. Interfaces between single-ended and differential circuits, such as baluns, can often be accommodated by initially assuming ideal conversion between single-ended and differential signal modes. Explicit mixed-mode analysis becomes important when the conversion between single-ended and differential modes cannot reasonably be approximated as ideal. This is sometimes the case when the mode conversion is considered over very large bandwidths, and in integrated circuit implementations.

9.1 Introduction

In Chapter 8 we noted the central role two-port theory plays in RF circuit design, and especially the role of reflection coefficients in determining the stability and gain of two-ports. Reflection coefficients were introduced as surrogates for source and load impedance (recall Equations 8.32 and 8.37), facilitating the use of scattering parameters. In this chapter we consider impedance matching, which is the process of converting impedances (equivalently, embedded reflection coefficients) from a given value to some other value.

Applications for impedance matching include (1) maximizing power transfer between two-ports, (2) eliminating reflections (not the same thing!), and (3) converting from a given impedance to another impedance necessary for setting the stability and/or gain of a two-port. In each of these cases, the problem is essentially as shown in Figure 9.1: We wish to design a passive two-port that converts the output impedance of the source, ZS = RS + jXS, into the desired input impedance for the load, ZL = RL + jXL. Usually we would like to achieve this with a TPG as close to 1 as possible, and often there is frequency span over which a minimum TPG must be achieved. At the design frequency, the nominal embedded input impedance Zin of the matching two-port is either Z∗

S for maximum power transfer or ZS for reflectionless matching. Similarly, the nominal embedded output impedance Zout of the matching two-port is either Z∗

L or ZL at the design frequency.

The organization of this chapter is as follows. In Section 9.2 we consider some rudimentary approaches to impedance matching, including resistive matching, transformer matching, and reactance canceling. Section 9.3 introduces narrowband matching using two discrete reactances in an “L” configuration, which is useful both as a standalone technique

Section 9.4 considers the issue of bandwidth, and introduces the concept of quality factor to provide some insight into how the bandwidth of matching circuits is determined and can be manipulated. In Section 9.5 we combine the concepts of previous sections to develop impedance matching circuits having bandwidth which can be wider or narrower than that obtained using discrete two-reactance matching. Section 9.6 explains how to obtain differential versions of the single-ended circuits developed in earlier sections. In Section 9.7 we introduce distributed matching devices, which use transmission lines in lieu of discrete reactances and thereby find application at higher frequencies, where discrete inductors and capacitors become difficult to use. Por otro lado, este enfoque vale la pena tener en cuenta porque tiene una característica extremadamente útil: Tiene ancho de banda infinito.1 En otras palabras, si RS y RL son constantes con frecuencia, entonces el dos puertos asociado tendrá TPG que es constante con frecuencia.

Coincidiendo con impedancias reales usando un transformador. Digamos XS = XL = 0 y usted es serio acerca de lograr TPG≈1. Mejor aún, los transformadores son capaces de ancho de banda muy grande. Otra ventaja de este enfoque tiene que ver con la conversión de modo individual a diferencial: Si usted necesita hacer esto, podría utilizar el mismo transformador para lograr tanto la conversión del modo (como se explica en la sección 8.7.2) como la transformación de impedancia simultáneamente.2

9.3 Discrete Two-Component (“L”) Matching

For reasons listed in the previous section, transformers (with or without canceling of source reactance) are often unacceptable as impedance matching devices. This is the case even though they achieve the desired impedance transformation with less loss than resistive matching, and even though they can deliver very large bandwidth for real-to-real valued impedance transformation. The alternative is to design two-port circuits that explicitly meet the requirements inferred by Figure 9.1 using combinations of discrete or distributed reactances. In this section, we describe the design and performance of the simplest of this class of two-ports: The discrete two-component match, also known as the “L-match”.3

To simplify subsequent discussion, we shall assume XL = 0; that is, the matching is from a complex- (or real-) valued impedance to a real-valued impedance. This is not a fundamental limitation of the L-match, but greatly simplifies the analysis and addresses the vast majority of practical applications. In cases where complex-to-complex impedance matching cannot be avoided, it is possible to use the complex-to-real L-match technique first to match the real part of the

We observed in the previous sections that impedance matchin g is inherently sensitive to frequency; i.e., it is quite sim ple
to achieve a perfect match at a specified frequency, but the pe rformance of the resulting design degrades at higher or lowe r
frequencies. In other words, the matching techniques consi dered so far are narrowband.4 Sometimes narrowband
4Here, we use the term “narrowband” to refer to circuits designed for nominal performance at a specific frequency, ignoring all other frequencies. Often,
but not always, such circuits also have very narrow bandwidt h. A counter-example in which narrowband design yields large bandwidth is Problem 9.8
(75 Ω to 50 Ω match).

Se observó en las secciones anteriores que la impedancia de adaptación es inherentemente sensible a la frecuencia; es decir, es bastante simple lograr un partido perfecto a una frecuencia especificada, pero el rendimiento del diseño resultante se degrada a frecuencias superiores o inferiores. En otras palabras, las técnicas de coincidencia consideradas hasta ahora son banda estrecha.4 A veces banda estrecha

4Aquí, utilizamos el término “banda estrecha” para referirse a circuitos diseñados para un rendimiento nominal a una frecuencia específica, ignorando todas las demás frecuencias. A menudo, pero no siempre, tales circuitos también tienen ancho de banda muy estrecho. Un contra-ejemplo en el que el diseño de banda angosta produce ancho de banda grande es Problema 9.8 (75 Ωto 50 Ωmatch).

Los circuitos de adaptación son aceptables, y tal vez incluso preferir ya que también proporcionan un grado de selectividad. A menudo, sin embargo, el ancho de banda obtenido usando técnicas de unión estrecha es demasiado pequeño. En algunos otros casos, el ancho de la banda puede ser mayor que el deseado. En esta sección desarrollamos una teoría relativa al ancho de banda de los circuitos de coincidencia, y en la Sección 9.5 aplicamos esta teoría para desarrollar circuitos de matchth con ancho de banda más grande o menor. En el Capítulo 13 retomaremos este tema, considerando el problema de cómo lograr una respuesta de frecuencia específica.

El primer orden de negocio debe ser establecer una definición rigurosa del ancho de banda. De hecho, es útil tener dos definiciones. La primera y muy común definición del ancho de grupo es el ancho de banda medio potencia BHP (también conocido como “3 dB ancho de banda”): Esta es la separación entre frecuencias en las que el beneficio de potencia transductor del dos puertos ha degradado por un factor de valor relativo nominal a 2 Como ejemplo, el ancho de banda de media potencia para Ejemplo 9.2 (Figura 9.9) es 15.2 MHz y 15.5 MHz para las versiones paralelas del capacitor y inductor paralelo, respectivamente.

Para los propósitos de esta sección, es útil emplear una segunda definición. Esta definición asume un dos-puerto pasivo que consiste en componentes reactivas o resistivos, impulsados por una fuente sinusoidal y operando en condiciones de estado estable (es decir, cualquier respuesta transitoria se ha reducido a un nivel insignificante). La energía inyectada en tal dos-puerto por la fuente puede hacer una de dos cosas: Puede escapar, o puede ser almacenado. Los dos posibles métodos de escape energético son la disipación (conversión al calor a través de la resistencia) y la transferencia a través de su salida. El almacenamiento energético es por contención en el campo eléctrico de capacitores y/o el campo magnético de inductores. Con esta perspectiva, podemos definir un ancho de banda BQ como sigue:

Siguiente, note que si el dos-puerto no es capaz de almacenar energía (por ejemplo, quizás porque no contiene capacitores o inductores), entonces Ust = 0 y por lo tanto BQ →∞. Esto es precisamente el comportamiento esperado: Por ejemplo, la impedancia coincide con un grupo de tensión resistivo Si por otro lado Ust > 0 pero Ues/T = 0 para T > 0, entonces no hay escape de energía; sólo almacenamiento de energía. En este caso, el dos-puerto es “frozen” y no hay posibilidad de pasar una señal de tiempo-varying a través de él: BQ →0 y ancho de banda (por cualquier definición) es esencialmente cero. Este ancho de banda no es claramente idéntico al ancho de banda de media potencia, sin embargo, y en particular difiere en que BQ es una evaluación del ancho de banda específica a una frecuencia f = 1/T. Dicho de otra manera, BQ(f) es una evaluación de ancho de banda basada en el cambio en TPG con la frecuencia cambiante en el barrio de f = 1/T.

Este concepto resulta estar estrechamente relacionado con el concepto de resonancia. A los efectos de esta sección, la resonancia es un estado en el que todas las reactancias internas a una cancelación sin pérdidas de dos puertos, de tal manera que las impedancias de entrada y salida se vuelven completamente valoradas. Además, según Ecuación 9.9, Q depende sólo de Rhi/Rlo (es decir, la relación de las impedancias del puerto), y no directamente reaccionan.

Como ejemplo, revisemos la solución del Ejemplo 9.2 (Figura 9.9). Aquí, Q ∼= 9.95, por lo que BQ = ω0/Q ∼= 47.4 MHz. Este valor es muy diferente de BHP: 15.2 MHz y 15.5 MHz para las dos soluciones posibles. Esto destaca que ambas definiciones de ancho de banda miden cosas diferentes. En este caso, BQ se aproxima más al ancho de banda de 10 dB. Para valores de Q suficientemente grandes, es decir, Q ≫ 2π, se obtiene

Desde entonces BQ ∝Q−1, también debe ser cierto que el ancho de banda del dos-port coincidente es inversamente proporcional a Rhi/Rlo. En otras palabras, ancho de banda es grande si la relación de impedancia es pequeña (tal vez obvio que el ancho de banda debe ser infinito si la relación es 1) y ancho de banda es pequeño si la relación de impedancia es grande.

Con estas ideas en mente, ahora estamos preparados para abordar el problema de cómo aumentar el ancho de banda de un dos-puerto coincidente: La clave es disminuir la Q del dos-port. Se puede reducir Q disminuyendo aumentando la pérdida interna (ya que esto aumenta Ues), o disminuyendo Ust. Ambos métodos tienen aplicaciones, pero generalmente el último es preferido ya que por lo general prefiere TPG ≈1 de interés superior.

9.4 Bandwidth and Q

We observed in the previous sections that impedance matching is inherently sensitive to frequency; i.e., it is quite simple to achieve a perfect match at a specified frequency, but the performance of the resulting design degrades at higher or lower frequencies. In other words, the matching techniques considered so far are narrowband.4 Sometimes narrowband

4Here, we use the term “narrowband” to refer to circuits designed for nominal performance at a specific frequency, ignoring all other frequencies. matching circuits are acceptable, and perhaps even preferred since they also provide a degree of selectivity. Often, however, the bandwidth obtained using narrowband matching techniques is too small. In some other cases, the bandwidth may be larger than desired. In this section we develop some theory pertaining to the bandwidth of matching circuits, and in Section 9.5 we apply this theory to develop matching circuits with larger or smaller bandwidth. In Chapter 13 we will take up this topic again, considering the problem of how to achieve a specific frequency response.

The first order of business should be to establish a rigorous definition of bandwidth. In fact, it is useful to have two definitions. The first and very common definition of bandwidth is half-power bandwidth BHP (also known as “3 dB bandwidth”): This is the separation between frequencies at which the transducer power gain of the two-port has degraded by a factor of 2 relative to the nominal (peak) value. As an example, half-power bandwidth for Example 9.2 (Figure 9.9) is 15.2 MHz and 15.5 MHz for the parallel capacitor and parallel inductor versions, respectively.

For the purposes of this section, it is useful to employ a second definition. This definition assumes a passive two-port consisting of reactive or resistive components, driven by a sinusoidal source, and operating in steady-state conditions (i.e., any transient response has reduced to an insignificant level). Energy injected into such a two-port by the source can do one of two things: It can escape, or it can be stored. The two possible methods of energy escape are dissipation (conversion to heat through resistance) and transfer through the output. Energy storage is by containment in the electric field of capacitors and/or the magnetic field of inductors. With this perspective, we can define a bandwidth BQ as follows:

BQ ≡Ues/T

(9.12)

Ust

where the numerator is the escaped energy Ues per period T of the sinusoidal stimulus; and Ust is the energy stored, which is remains constant given the steady-state assumption made above.

How is this a definition of bandwidth? First, note that it is dimensionally correct, having units of 1/time. Next, note that if the two-port is unable to store energy (e.g., perhaps because it contains no capacitors or inductors), then Ust = 0 and therefore BQ →∞. This is precisely the expected behavior: For example, impedance matching using a resistive voltage divider has no energy storage and has bandwidth (by any definition) which is essentially infinite. If on the other hand Ust > 0 but Ues/T = 0 for T > 0, then there is no energy escape; only energy storage. In this case, the two-port is “frozen” and there is no possibility of passing a time-varying signal through it: BQ →0 and bandwidth (by any definition) is essentially zero. In the intermediate case in which both Ues > 0 and Ues/T > 0, the rate at which a voltage or current

signal passing through the two-port can be varied (another way to say “bandwidth”) increases with increasing Ues/T. Thus Equation 9.12 is a definition of bandwidth.

This bandwidth is clearly not identical to half-power bandwidth, however, and in particular differs in that BQ is an evaluation of bandwidth specific to a frequency f = 1/T. Said differently, BQ(f) is a assessment of bandwidth based on the change in TPG with changing frequency in the neighborhood of f = 1/T.

This concept turns out to be closely related to the concept of resonance. For the purposes of this section, resonance is a state in which all reactances internal to a lossless two-port cancel, such that the input and output impedances become completely real-valued. In particular: For 2-component discrete “L” matches between real valued impedances, there is precisely one resonance, and it occurs at the design frequency. f0. Let this frequency be expressed as the angular frequency ω0 = 2πf0, having units of rad/s.

The ratio of ω0 to BQ(f0) is a unitless quantity known as the quality factor Q:

The concept of quality factor has multiple applications in radio engineering. An important one is the characterization of the lossiness of practical inductors and cavity resonators. However Q plays a distinct and important role in analysis and design of impedance matching circuits, as we shall now explain.

Let’s begin by working out the Q for the matching circuit shown in Figure 9.8(a). First, recall that the capacitor and inductor in an LC circuit share the same stored energy, transferring all energy from inductor to capacitor and back, once per period. Therefore we can determine Q based on the energy storage in the series inductor only, and know that that is the same value obtained if we considered the parallel capacitor only, or the entire circuit at once.
