Remarkably, we have independently derived the “+”-signed case of Equation 9.11, in which Q was simply a parameter we defined to simplify the equations. The Q parameter of Section 9.3 is in fact the quality factor Q defined in Equation 9.13. Furthermore, according to Equation 9.9, Q depends only on Rhi/Rlo (that is, the ratio of the port impedances), and not directly on the reactances used in the two-port.

As an example, let us reexamine the solution to Example 9.2 (Figure 9.9). Here, Q ∼= 9.95, so BQ = ω0/Q ∼= 47.4 MHz. This is quite different from BHP, which we found to be 15.2 MHz and 15.5 MHz for the two possible solutions; this underscores the fact that these two definitions of bandwidth are measuring different things. Here one finds BQ is closer to the 10-dB bandwidth. For sufficiently large Q (i.e., Q ≫2π) one finds

Since BQ ∝Q−1, it must also be true that the bandwidth of the matching two-port is inversely proportional to Rhi/Rlo. In other words, bandwidth is large if the impedance ratio is small (perhaps obvious since bandwidth should be infinite if the ratio is 1) and bandwidth is small if the impedance ratio is large.

With these insights in mind, we are now prepared to address the problem of how to increase the bandwidth of a matching two-port: The key is to decrease the Q of the two-port. Decreased Q can be achieved by increasing internal loss (since this increases Ues), or by decreasing Ust. Both methods have applications, but usually the latter is preferred since we usually prefer TPG ≈1 over the bandwidth of interest.

9.5 Modifying Bandwidth Using Higher-Order Circuits
Section 9.3 presented the simplest possible scheme for loss less impedance matching, using two reactances in an “L”
configuration. In Section 9.4 we found the half-power bandwi dth of such a match was limited: This bandwidth is often
found to be insufficient, especially when the impedance rati o (Rhi/R lo) is large, resulting in high Q. When the impedance
ratio is low,Q is low and bandwidth may be quite large. In some applications where this occurs, it is desirable to reduce
bandwidth. A good example of this appears in Chapter 10, in wh ich reducing the bandwidth of matching circuits used in
transistor amplifiers can reduce the likelihood of undesira ble oscillation. Thus, we find there are a variety of reasons w hy
we might desire matching two-ports with bandwidth either la rger or smaller than that provided by the two-reactance
matches of the type considered in Section 9.3.
9.5.1 Increasing Bandwidth using Cascades of Two-Reactance Matching Circuits
Increasing or decreasing the bandwidth of a matching two-po rt can be accomplished with little or no reduction in nominal
TPG using higher-order circuits; that is, using circuits co ntaining additional discrete reactances. A simple but effe ctive
method is to implement the change in impedance in smaller ste ps, with each step implemented using a discrete
two-reactance two-port of the type described in the previou s section. This results in a cascade of two-reactance “L”
two-ports having the so-called “ladder” topology. Typical ly the intermediate impedance Rmid is selected to be the
geometrical mean of Rhi andRlow; i.e.,√
RhiRlo, which results in the two stages having the same Q. Because each stage
implements a smaller change in impedance than a single two-p ort implementing the entire change at once, the former has
smallerQ and thus larger bandwidth. Generally the overall bandwidth of a cascade of impedance transformations arranged
in this way will also be greater than that of a single impedanc e transformation from the initial to final value.
Example 9.3. Recall in Example 9.2 we designed matching circuits that tra nsformedRhi = 5000 Ω toRlo = 50 Ω
at 75 MHz using 2 discrete reactances in an “L” configuration. Design a two-stage “L” match with increased
bandwidth.
Solution: The first stage will reduce 5000 Ω to an intermediate impedance Rmid, and the second state will reduce

Bandwidth can be further increased in four ways:
• The “divide and conquer” strategy followed above can be ext ended to 3 or more stages, resulting in longer cascades
of “L” type circuits matching smaller impedance ratios. In p rinciple there is no limit to the bandwidth that can be
achieved in this way, since in the limit as the number of stage s increases to infinity, the impedance ratio per stage
approaches 1, and therefore each stage can have essentially zeroQ and essentially infinite bandwidth. In practice,
the number of stages is that can be effectively implemented i s limited by unavoidable dissipative losses and
precision of component values, as well as size and cost.
• Additional resonances can be employed in order to extend th e bandwidth. We see evidence of this effectiveness of
this strategy in Example 9.3, as noted above. Generalizing t his idea, we could attempt to design the circuit with
specific constraints on the frequency response: For example , requiring TPG = 1 (or some other high value) at
multiple frequencies distributed over the desired passban d. An impedance matching circuit which achieves a
specified frequency response is essentially a filter. Filter design is addressed in Chapter 13.
• Bandwidth can always be increased by introducing dissipat ive loss. This is because dissipative loss increases Pes
without necessarily affectingUst, thereby decreasing Q. The obvious disadvantage is that the passband TPG is
degraded. Odd it may seem, this is often a reasonable tradeof f: For example, this technique is commonly used to
increase the usable bandwidth of antennas embedded in handh eld devices; see e.g. Example 12.11 (Chapter 12).
• Combinations of the above approaches are frequently emplo yed; for example, a three-stage “divide and conquer”
design with additional loss to increase the bandwidth by som e additional amount which could not otherwise be
achieved due to limitations in the available reactances.
It is prudent to make one additional point since we are on the t opic of increasing bandwidth: As in the “divide and
conquer” strategy, there is a fundamental limit on the maxim um TPG that can be achieved over a specified frequency
range using a given number of reactances. The most commonly- cited expression of this limit is the Fano-Bode relation
[19] (more on this in Section 12.5). However this limit is qui te difficult to apply to practical problems. Here there is a “n o
free lunch” principle in action: For any given number of reac tances employed in a matching circuit, the maximum TPG
that can be uniformly achieved over a specified bandwidth is f undamentally constrained, no matter how cleverly the circu it
is designed.
9.5.2 Decreasing Bandwidth Using “Pi” and “T” Circuits
At the beginning of Section 9.5.1 we considered how the bandw idth of a matching circuits could be increased by adding
additional sections, with an intermediate impedance Rmid betweenRlo andRhi. Similarly, the bandwidth of an

appear in parallel with each other, and therefore can be comb ined into a single parallel reactance. This results in the “T ”

9.5.3 Other Considerations and Variants
There may be other considerations when designing matching c ircuits as described in the previous sections. We have

9.5 Modificación del ancho de banda con circuitos de orden superior

La sección 9.3 presentó el esquema más simple posible para la impedancia sin pérdidas que coincide, utilizando dos reactancias en una configuración de “L”. En la Sección 9.4 encontramos el ancho de banda de media potencia de tal partido fue limitado: Este ancho de banda es a menudo insuficiente, especialmente cuando la relación de impedancia (Rhi/Rlo) es grande, resultando en alta Q. Cuando la relación de la impedance es bastante baja, Q es deseable Un buen ejemplo de esto aparece en el Capítulo 10, en el que reducir el ancho de banda de circuitos de coincidencia utilizados en amplificadores transistores puede reducir la probabilidad de oscilación indeseable. Por lo tanto, encontramos que hay una variedad de razones por las cuales podríamos desear que coincidan dos puertos con ancho de banda sea más grande o menor que la proporcionada por los partidos de dos reactancias del tipo considerado en la Sección 9.3.

9.5.1 El aumento del ancho de banda utilizando cascadas de circuitos de adaptación de dos funciones

El aumento o disminución del ancho de banda de un dos puertos coincidente se puede lograr con poca o ninguna reducción en TPG nominal utilizando circuitos de mayor orden; es decir, usando circuitos que contienen reactancias discretas adicionales. Un método simple pero eficaz es implementar el cambio de impedancia en pasos más pequeños, con cada paso implementado utilizando un doble retroceso discreto del tipo descrito en la sección anterior. Esto resulta en una cascada de dos-reactancias “L” dos puertos que tienen la llamada topología “escalera”. Típicamente, la impedancia intermedia Rmid es seleccionada para ser la media geométrica de Rhi y Rlow; es decir, √RhiRlo, que resulta en las dos etapas que tienen la misma Q. Debido a que cada etapa implementa un cambio más pequeño en la impedance que un solo doble-puerto En general, el ancho de banda general de una cascada de transformaciones de impedancia dispuestas de esta manera también será mayor que el de una sola transformación de impedance del valor inicial a final.

De manera similar, el ancho de banda de un partido de impedancia puede disminuirse utilizando un 2- cascada de escenario de circuitos de juego tipo “L” en los que Rmid es seleccionado para ser inferior a Rlo o superior a Rhi. Un método simple pero eficaz es implementar el cambio de impedancia en pasos más pequeños, con cada paso implementado utilizando un doble retroceso discreto del tipo descrito en la sección anterior. Típicamente, la impedancia intermedia Rmid es seleccionada para ser la media geométrica de Rhi y Rlow; es decir, √RhiRlo, que resulta en las dos etapas que tienen la misma Q. 9.5 Modifying Bandwidth Using Higher-Order Circuits

Section 9.3 presented the simplest possible scheme for lossless impedance matching, using two reactances in an “L” configuration. In Section 9.4 we found the half-power bandwidth of such a match was limited: This bandwidth is often found to be insufficient, especially when the impedance ratio (Rhi/Rlo) is large, resulting in high Q. When the impedance ratio is low, Q is low and bandwidth may be quite large. In some applications where this occurs, it is desirable to reduce bandwidth. A good example of this appears in Chapter 10, in which reducing the bandwidth of matching circuits used in transistor amplifiers can reduce the likelihood of undesirable oscillation. Thus, we find there are a variety of reasons why we might desire matching two-ports with bandwidth either larger or smaller than that provided by the two-reactance matches of the type considered in Section 9.3.

9.5.1 Increasing Bandwidth using Cascades of Two-Reactance Matching Circuits

Increasing or decreasing the bandwidth of a matching two-port can be accomplished with little or no reduction in nominal TPG using higher-order circuits; that is, using circuits containing additional discrete reactances. A simple but effective method is to implement the change in impedance in smaller steps, with each step implemented using a discrete two-reactance two-port of the type described in the previous section. This results in a cascade of two-reactance “L” two-ports having the so-called “ladder” topology. Typically the intermediate impedance Rmid is selected to be the geometrical mean of Rhi and Rlow; i.e., √RhiRlo, which results in the two stages having the same Q. Because each stage implements a smaller change in impedance than a single two-port implementing the entire change at once, the former has smaller Q and thus larger bandwidth. Generally the overall bandwidth of a cascade of impedance transformations arranged in this way will also be greater than that of a single impedance transformation from the initial to final value.

Example 9.3. Recall in Example 9.2 we designed matching circuits that transformed Rhi = 5000 Ωto Rlo = 50 Ω at 75 MHz using 2 discrete reactances in an “L” configuration. Design a two-stage “L” match with increased bandwidth.

The apparent agreement here is a bit of a fluke: Normally BQ/2 overestimates BHP when Q is not ≫2π, however BHP itself is larger than might otherwise be expected because the two-stage match has four reactances as opposed to two, with a second resonance at 82.9 MHz. This second resonance has further increased the BHP, and is not taken into account by the simple “Q1 + Q2” calculation.

Bandwidth can be further increased in four ways:

• The “divide and conquer” strategy followed above can be extended to 3 or more stages, resulting in longer cascades of “L” type circuits matching smaller impedance ratios. In principle there is no limit to the bandwidth that can be achieved in this way, since in the limit as the number of stages increases to infinity, the impedance ratio per stage approaches 1, and therefore each stage can have essentially zero Q and essentially infinite bandwidth. In practice, the number of stages is that can be effectively implemented is limited by unavoidable dissipative losses and precision of component values, as well as size and cost.

• Additional resonances can be employed in order to extend the bandwidth. We see evidence of this effectiveness of this strategy in Example 9.3, as noted above. Generalizing this idea, we could attempt to design the circuit with specific constraints on the frequency response: For example, requiring TPG = 1 (or some other high value) at multiple frequencies distributed over the desired passband. An impedance matching circuit which achieves a specified frequency response is essentially a filter. Filter design is addressed in Chapter 13.

• Bandwidth can always be increased by introducing dissipative loss. This is because dissipative loss increases Pes without necessarily affecting Ust, thereby decreasing Q. The obvious disadvantage is that the passband TPG is degraded. Odd it may seem, this is often a reasonable tradeoff: For example, this technique is commonly used to increase the usable bandwidth of antennas embedded in handheld devices; see e.g. Example 12.11 (Chapter 12).

• Combinations of the above approaches are frequently employed; for example, a three-stage “divide and conquer” design with additional loss to increase the bandwidth by some additional amount which could not otherwise be achieved due to limitations in the available reactances.

It is prudent to make one additional point since we are on the topic of increasing bandwidth: As in the “divide and conquer” strategy, there is a fundamental limit on the maximum TPG that can be achieved over a specified frequency range using a given number of reactances. The most commonly-cited expression of this limit is the Fano-Bode relation [19] (more on this in Section 12.5). However this limit is quite difficult to apply to practical problems. Here there is a “no free lunch” principle in action: For any given number of reactances employed in a matching circuit, the maximum TPG that can be uniformly achieved over a specified bandwidth is fundamentally constrained, no matter how cleverly the circuit is designed.

9.5.2 Decreasing Bandwidth Using “Pi” and “T” Circuits

At the beginning of Section 9.5.1 we considered how the bandwidth of a matching circuits could be increased by adding additional sections, with an intermediate impedance Rmid between Rlo and Rhi. Similarly, the bandwidth of an impedance match can be decreased using a 2-stage cascade of “L” type matching circuits in which Rmid is selected to be either lower than Rlo or higher than Rhi. These two strategies are illustrated in Figure 9.12. In the first strategy, Rmid is chosen to be less than Rlo. This results in two “L” matches in which the series reactances appear in series with each other, and therefore can be combined into a single series reactance. This results in the “Pi” topology (so-named for it’s resemblance to the Greek letter π). Because Rhi/Rmid and Rlo/Rmid are both greater than Rhi/Rlo, the Q of the Pi circuit is greater than the Q of a single-stage match. Therefore the bandwidth of the Pi circuit is less, and the degree to which it is less depends on how much lower Rmid is than Rlo and Rhi.

Alternatively, Rmid can be chosen to be greater than Rhi. This results in two “L” matches in which the parallel reactances appear in parallel with each other, and therefore can be combined into a single parallel reactance. This results in the “T”

The choice between a Pi configuration and a T configuration for a reduced-bandwidth impedance match depends primarily on the requirements of interfacing circuits; e.g., whether DC signals should be shorted to ground or simply blocked, and the ability to absorb components in adjacent stages into the design so as to decrease overall parts count.

We noted in the previous section that the Q of a multi-stage matching circuit can be estimated as the sum of the Q of the stages, if all Qs are sufficiently high. Similarly, the bandwidth of the Pi and T circuits can be roughly estimated as the sum of quality factors of the original two “L” match sections. This provides an approximate method for specified-bandwidth design: Bandwidth implies overall Q, which in turn constrains Rmid to one of two possible values; one for Pi variant and one for the T variant. 9.5.3 Other Considerations and Variants

There may be other considerations when designing matching circuits as described in the previous sections. We have already noted the intrinsic lowpass/highpass behavior of various matching circuits, and suggested that this might influence the selection of a circuit. However, recall from elementary electronics that the delta-wye transformation5 may be used to transform any T-type impedance matching circuit into a Pi-type circuit, and vice versa. The circuits will be equivalent at the frequency assumed for the transformation, but will behave differently away from this frequency. There are a number of reasons why such a transformation may be desirable: For example, it may yield more favorable component values, it may avoid a DC short circuit or provide DC blocking at the input or output, or may position a component in such a way that the component may be “absorbed” into the adjacent stage, thereby reducing the parts count.

in differential matching circuits. One method is as follows : First, design a single-ended circuit which matches one-ha lf the
desired source impedance to one-half the desired load imped ance. Next, combine the resulting circuit with a mirror imag e
of itself using a common datum. Finally, eliminate the commo n datum and combine any series reactances.
Example 9.5. Design a circuit that matches a 10 kΩ differential source impedance to a 100 Ω differential load
impedance at 75 MHz. Use the differential version of the “L” m atch technique.

(single-ended). This is precisely the problem we solved in E xample 9.2. Figure 9.15 shows the corresponding
differential matching circuits.

Las técnicas desarrolladas en secciones anteriores, aunque presentadas como de un solo soporte, se modifican directamente para su uso en circuitos diferenciales de coincidencia. Un método es el siguiente: Primero, diseña un circuito de un solo combo que coincide con la mitad del impedancia de fuente deseada a una mitad del impetuoso de carga deseado. Luego, combina el circuito resultante con una imagen de espejo de sí mismo utilizando un datum común.

Ejemplo 9.5. Diseñar un circuito que coincida con un 10 kΩdifferential impedancia de la fuente a un 100 Ωdifferential impedancia de carga 75 MHz. Usar la versión diferencial de la técnica del partido “L”.

Solución: Primero, identificamos el circuito de adaptación de un solo prototipo: Es 5000 Ω(single-ended) a 50 Ω (single -ended). Este es precisamente el problema que resolvimos en Ejemplo 9.2. La Figura 9.15 muestra los circuitos de coincidencia diferencial correspondientes.

9.6 Impedance Matching for Differential Circuits

The techniques developed in previous sections, although presented as single-ended, are straightforwardly modified for use in differential matching circuits. One method is as follows: First, design a single-ended circuit which matches one-half the desired source impedance to one-half the desired load impedance. Next, combine the resulting circuit with a mirror image of itself using a common datum. Finally, eliminate the common datum and combine any series reactances.

Example 9.5. Design a circuit that matches a 10 kΩdifferential source impedance to a 100 Ωdifferential load impedance at 75 MHz. Use the differential version of the “L” match technique.

Solution: First, we identify the “prototype” single-ended matching circuit: It is 5000 Ω(single-ended) to 50 Ω (single-ended). This is precisely the problem we solved in Example 9.2. Figure 9.15 shows the corresponding differential matching circuits.

9.7 Estructuras distribuidas de adaptación

En secciones anteriores de este capítulo hemos considerado circuitos de adaptación impedancia sin pérdidas utilizando capacitores e inductores discretos. Este enfoque es generalmente aplicable para frecuencias hasta unos pocos cientos de MHz, y a frecuencias más altas si los comportamientos no-ideales de estos componentes pueden ser tenidos en cuenta adecuadamente. Ejemplos comunes de comportamientos no ideales que se vuelven importantes en frecuencias más altas incluyen: La capacitancia entre giros en las bobinas utilizadas en inductores, la inductancia asociada con los terminales de capacitores, y en ambos casos la resistencia de materiales puede llegar a ser significativa en relación con la reactancia nominal. Aunque es posible compensar estos efectos bien en el régimen SHF, suficiente precisión y repetibilidad es normalmente bastante difícil de lograr.

Afortunadamente, hay una alternativa a las reactancias discretas que funciona bien en frecuencias más altas: líneas de transmisión. El concepto esencial se muestra en la Figura 9.16: Cuando la salida de una línea de transmisión con longitud l y impedancia característica Zc se termina en una impedancia de carga ZL, la impedancia del entrada Zin es dada por

En secciones anteriores de este capítulo hemos considerado circuitos de adaptación impedancia sin pérdidas utilizando capacitores e inductores discretos. Este enfoque es generalmente aplicable para frecuencias hasta unos pocos cientos de MHz, y a frecuencias más altas si los comportamientos no-ideales de estos componentes pueden ser tenidos en cuenta adecuadamente. Ejemplos comunes de comportamientos no ideales que se vuelven importantes en frecuencias más altas incluyen: La capacitancia entre giros en las bobinas utilizadas en inductores, la inductancia asociada con los terminales de capacitores, y en ambos casos la resistencia de materiales puede llegar a ser significativa en relación con la reactancia nominal. Aunque es posible compensar estos efectos bien en el régimen SHF, suficiente precisión y repetibilidad es normalmente bastante difícil de lograr.

Afortunadamente, hay una alternativa a las reactancias discretas que funciona bien en frecuencias más altas: líneas de transmisión. El concepto esencial se muestra en la Figura 9.16: Cuando la salida de una línea de transmisión con longitud l y impedancia característica Zc se termina en una impedancia de carga ZL, la impedancia del entrada Zin es dada por

9.7 Distributed Matching Structures

In previous sections of this chapter we have considered lossless impedance matching circuits using discrete capacitors and inductors. This approach is generally applicable for frequencies up to a few hundred MHz, and to higher frequencies if the non-ideal behaviors of these components can be properly taken into account. Common examples of non-ideal behaviors that become important at higher frequencies include: The capacitance between turns in the coils used in inductors, the inductance associated with the leads of capacitors, and in both cases the resistance of materials may become significant relative to the nominal reactance. Although is possible to compensate for these effects well into the SHF regime, sufficient accuracy and repeatability is typically quite difficult to achieve.

Fortunately, there is an alternative to discrete reactances that works well at higher frequencies: transmission lines. The essential concept is shown in Figure 9.16: When the output of a transmission line having length l and characteristic impedance Zc is terminated into a load impedance ZL, the input impedance Zin is given by

9.7.3 Single-Stub Matching

The single-stub matching technique, illustrated in Figure 9.19, allows any complex-valued impedance ZL to be transformed to any complex-valued source impedance Zin, represented in the figure as the source admittance Yin = 1/Zin. The essential idea is to use a transmission line to match the real part of YS, and then to use a stub attached in parallel to match the transmission line + stub combination to the imaginary part of YS. We prefer to work with admittances as opposed to impedances on the source side because this greatly simplifies the math: the admittance of the parallel combination of the transmission line and the stub is simply the sum of the associated admittances, whereas the the impedance of the parallel combination of the transmission line and the stub is given by a much more complex expression.

The single-stub design procedure is as follows:

1. Select a transmission line and determine its characteristic impedance Zc1. Zc1 is commonly, but not necessarily, chosen to be equal to either the desired real component of the transformed load impedance, or the reference impedance for s-parameters employed in the design. Thus, Zc1 = 50 Ωis quite common. Similarly, select a transmission line type for the stub and determine its characteristic impedance Zc2. The transmission line and transmission line stub are commonly, but not necessarily, chosen to be identical transmission line types, differing only in length and termination; thus, Zc2 = Zc1 typically.

2. Design the primary (in-line) transmission line section. This is illustrated in Figure 9.20. Note that Y1, the input admittance of the transmission line, is given by Equation 9.22. Use this equation to find the smallest value of l1/λ that makes G1 (the real part of Y1) equal to GS (the real part of YS). The resulting imaginary value of the admittance (B1) is unimportant at this step. This step can be done graphically using a Smith chart; however accuracy of 3 or more significant figures is possible with just a few rounds of trial and error with Equation 9.22 using a short computer program or a simple spreadsheet.

3. Determine the required stub input susceptance Bstub. For a conjugate match, the imaginary part of the source admittance BS should be equal to −(B1 + Bstub), where jBstub is the input admittance of the stub. Therefore Bstub = −BS −B1 for a conjugate match. For a reflectionless match, BS should be equal to +(B1 + Bstub), and therefore Bstub = +BS −B1 in this case.

4. Design the stub. This is illustrated in Figure 9.21. Using Equations 9.30 and 9.31, find a stub that has an input admittance jBstub as selected in the previous step. Since stubs can be either open- or short-circuited, you should check both possibilities. Typically – but not always – the shorter stub is desired (more on this below).

We should add a final step: Check your work. It’s pretty easy to make a mistake in the design process, but such mistakes are easily found simply by computing Yin for the candidate design, and confirming that it is the correct value.

Impedance inverters have a number of applications beyond im pedance matching. Before moving on, it is worthwhile to
identify at least two of these applications. One applicatio n is the replacement of inductors with capacitors, using an
impedance inverter to change the sign of the capacitor’s rea ctance. This is useful at frequencies in the UHF band and

9.8.text_es_mx:
9.8 Inversión de impedancias

El partido de cuarto de onda pertenece a una clase de dispositivos de adaptación de impedancia conocidos como inversores de impedancia. Un inversor de impedancia es un dispositivo de dos puertos para el cual la impedancia de entrada es proporcional a la reciprocal de la impedancia de carga. Para el partido de cuarto de onda, esto está claro desde la Ecuación 9.33. Los inversores de impedancia también se pueden construir a partir de reactancias discretas; por ejemplo, la impedancia de entrada del circuito de Pi que se muestra en la Figura 9.24 es

(9.35)
Zin = X2
ZL

que se ve tener la misma forma que Ecuación 9.33. (El producto de esto es dejado como un ejercicio para el lector; vea Problema 9.8.)

Los inversores de impedancia tienen una serie de aplicaciones más allá de la coincidencia de impedance. Antes de seguir adelante, vale la pena identificar al menos dos de estas aplicaciones. Una aplicación es el reemplazo de inductores con capacitores, utilizando un inversor de impedencia para cambiar el signo de la reactancia del capacitor. Esto es útil en frecuencias de la banda UHF y arriba, donde los inductores (1) se vuelven muy difíciles de usar mientras que los capacitores son algo más fáciles de trabajar con, y (2) las líneas de transmisión de cuarto de onda son suficientemente pequeñas para adaptarse a PCB.

Una segunda aplicación de la inversión de impedancia es la inyección de DC poder en RF circuitos. Como se mencionó anteriormente, y como veremos muchas veces en Capítulo 10, es a menudo necesario para DC poder para compartir caminos utilizados por RF señales. Sin embargo, también es importante mantener RF señalización de los circuitos de suministro de energía. En frecuencias inferiores, este aislamiento es posible utilizando un inductor de serie, que pasa DC mientras se bloquea RF. Sin embargo, los inductores adecuados se vuelven difíciles de encontrar en las frecuencias RF en la banda VHF y más alto. Una alternativa es utilizar un inversor de impedancia entre la fuente de alimentación, que tiene baja impedancia de salida, y el punto de inyección de potencia. La línea de transmisión de cuarto de onda transforma la impedancia de baja salida de la fuente de alimentación en una impedancia AC alta, de modo que RF se bloquea mientras DC pase libremente.

9.8 Impedance Inversion

The quarter-wave match belongs to a class of impedance matching devices known as impedance inverters. An impedance inverter is a two-port device for which the input impedance is proportional to the reciprocal of the load impedance. For the quarter-wave match, this is clear from Equation 9.33. Impedance inverters can also be constructed from discrete reactances; for example, the input impedance of the Pi circuit shown in Figure 9.24 is

(9.35)

ZL

which is seen to have the same form as Equation 9.33. (Proof of this is left as an exercise for the reader; see Problem 9.8.)

Impedance inverters have a number of applications beyond impedance matching. Before moving on, it is worthwhile to identify at least two of these applications. One application is the replacement of inductors with capacitors, using an impedance inverter to change the sign of the capacitor’s reactance. This is useful at frequencies in the UHF band and above, where (1) inductors become very difficult to use whereas capacitors are somewhat easier to work with, and (2) quarter-wave transmission lines are sufficiently small to fit on PCBs.

A second application of impedance inversion is injection of DC power into RF circuits. As mentioned earlier, and as we shall see many times in Chapter 10, it is often necessary for DC power to share paths used by RF signals. The quarter-wave transmission line transforms the low output impedance of the power supply into a high AC impedance, so that RF is blocked while DC passes freely.

10.1.text:
10.1 Introduction
The primary purpose of most amplifiers used in radio frequenc y systems is to increase signal magnitude. This is necessary
in receivers because propagation path loss results in a sign al arriving with voltage or current which is far too small to b e
digitized or directly demodulated. Amplification appears i n transmitters when it is convenient to synthesize a signal a t low
power and amplify it, as opposed to synthesizing signals dir ectly at the intended transmit power; the latter is difficult for
all but very simple analog modulations.
This chapter is organized as follows. Section 10.2 introduc es the transistor, its use as a gain device, provides a brief
summary of transistor types and device technologies. The de sign of narrowband single-transistor amplifiers is introdu ced
in four parts: Biasing (Section 10.3), small-signal design to meet gain requirements (Section 10.4), designing for noi se
figure (Section 10.5), and designing for voltage standing wa ve ratio (Section 10.6). Section 10.7 presents a design exam ple
intended to demonstrate the principles of amplifier design a s laid out in the previous sections. Section 10.8 introduces the
concepts of multistage, differential, and broadband trans istor amplifiers. Section 10.9 describes the implementatio n of
transistor amplifiers as integrated circuits.
10.1.text_es_mx:
10.1 Introducción

El objetivo principal de la mayoría de los amplificadores utilizados en sistemas de frecuencias radiofónicas es aumentar la magnitud de la señal. Esto es necesario en receptores porque la pérdida del camino de propagación resulta en una señal que llega con tensión o corriente, que es demasiado pequeña para ser digitalizada o directamente demodulada. La amplificación aparece en los transmisores cuando es conveniente sintetizar una señal a baja potencia y amplificarla, en lugar de sintetizando las señales directamente en la potencia de transmisión prevista; este último es difícil para todas pero muy simples modulaciones analógicas.

Este capítulo se organiza de la siguiente manera. 10.2 presenta al transistor, su uso como dispositivo de ganancia, proporciona un breve resumen de los tipos de transistores y las tecnologías de dispositivos. El diseño de amplificadores de banda angosta de un solo transistor se introduce en cuatro partes: Biasing (Sección) 10.3), diseño pequeño-signal para satisfacer los requisitos de ganancia (Sección 10.4), diseño para la figura de ruido (Sección) 10.5), y diseño para la relación de onda de tensión (Sección) 10.6). La sección 10.7 presenta un ejemplo de diseño destinado a demostrar los principios del diseño amplificador establecidos en las secciones anteriores. La sección 10.8 introduce los conceptos de amplificadores transistores multietapa, diferencial y banda ancha. La sección 10.9 describe la implementación de amplificadoras transistoras como circuitos integrados.

10.1 Introduction

The primary purpose of most amplifiers used in radio frequency systems is to increase signal magnitude. This is necessary in receivers because propagation path loss results in a signal arriving with voltage or current which is far too small to be digitized or directly demodulated. Amplification appears in transmitters when it is convenient to synthesize a signal at low power and amplify it, as opposed to synthesizing signals directly at the intended transmit power; the latter is difficult for all but very simple analog modulations.

This chapter is organized as follows. Section 10.2 introduces the transistor, its use as a gain device, provides a brief summary of transistor types and device technologies. The design of narrowband single-transistor amplifiers is introduced in four parts: Biasing (Section 10.3), small-signal design to meet gain requirements (Section 10.4), designing for noise figure (Section 10.5), and designing for voltage standing wave ratio (Section 10.6). Section 10.7 presents a design example intended to demonstrate the principles of amplifier design as laid out in the previous sections. Section 10.8 introduces the concepts of multistage, differential, and broadband transistor amplifiers. Section 10.9 describes the implementation of transistor amplifiers as integrated circuits.

10.2 Transistors as Amplifiers
The fundamental building block of modern radio frequency am plifiers is the transistor. 1 A transistor is a three-terminal
semiconductor device in which the current between two termi nals can be manipulated using the voltage or current at a
third terminal. The application to RF design is most easily e xplained in the context of a particular device – For our
purposes, the silicon (Si) bipolar junction transistor (BJT) is a good place to start.
10.2.1 Bipolar Transistors
A BJT is depicted in Figure 10.1. The three terminals of a BJT a re known as the base, the collector, and the emitter. The
associated terminal currents and voltages are as defined in F igure 10.1. The Si BJT comes in two varieties, known as
“NPN” and “PNP”, referring to the geometry of semiconductor materials within the device. The NPN variant is somewhat
more common in RF applications and is specifically considere d here (and shown in Figure 10.1); the PNP variant is
relatively easily understood once the NPN variant is master ed.

albeit somewhat eclectic – applications for vaccuum tubes.

An important step in using a BJT as an amplifier is to select an o perating point that results in forward-active mode and is

Finally, to get this scheme to work, we need to interface an in put signal to the transistor and extract an output signal fro m
the transistor. It’s unlikely that the transistor will have the appropriate input and output impedances as-is, so imped ance
matching will typically be necessary. Also, because the tra nsistor is being used as an active device, stability must be
considered.
In summary, the process of transistor amplifier design boils down to two parts: biasing, which sets the operating point and
is addressed in more detail in Section 10.3; and impedance ma tching with stability constraints, addressed in more detai l in
Section 10.4.

Si BJTs are but one category from an expansive family of quali tatively similar devices, which we shall refer to as bipolar
transistors. Whereas the maximum useful frequency of Si BJTs is on the order of a few GHz, frequencies up to about
10 GHz are possible by replacing Si with various combination s of alternative semiconductor materials to form what is
known as a heterojunction bipolar transistor (HBT). HBTs are typically identified by their constituent ma terials, which
may include gallium arsenide (GaAs), silicon geranium (SiG e), indium phosphide (InP), indium gallium phosphide
(InGaP), and indium GaAs nitride (InGaAsN). Bipolar transi stors may also be implemented directly in complementary
metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS) devices using manufactu ring processes such as BiCMOS, enabling the compact
implementation of large and complex radio frequency circui ts as single integrated circuit (IC) devices (more on this in
Section 10.9).
The primary driver for alternative transistor technologie s is the quest for improved gain, noise figure, and linearity a t
ever-increasing frequencies. The maximum usable frequenc y of a transistor depends on the application. A common and
useful characterization is unity-gain bandwidth,fT . The concept is that the realizable gain inevitably decreas es with
frequency, and eventually becomes unity; i.e., no gain. For bipolar transistors in amplifier applications, the decline in gain
with frequency is due to the capacitance of the base-emitter junction, and “realizable gain” is most conveniently define d as
the “short circuit gain” ∆IC/ ∆IB; i.e., the value of β applicable to small excursions around a specified operating
operating point. In this terminology, Si BJTs have fT in the range 100 MHz – 4 GHz, whereas HBTs have fT up to about
100 GHz.
10.2.2 Field Effect Transistors
A distinct and equally important category of transistors is known as field effect transistors (FETs). A circuit schematic
depiction of a FET is shown in Figure 10.3. The three terminal s are known as the gate, drain, and source; these are
analogous to the base, collector, and emitter, respectivel y, of the bipolar transistor. A fourth terminal, known vario usly as
body or base, is sometimes identified but is typically important only in i ntegrated circuit applications.
A big difference between FETs and bipolar transistors is tha tIG (analogous toIB for bipolar transistors) is often small
enough that it may be neglected, with the result that IS∼

particular, MOSFETs – are sometimes shown with a fourth (“bo dy”) terminal.
In terms of performance relative to bipolar transistors, FE Ts dominate above about 4 GHz, and appear in applications up
to 100 GHz and beyond. Below 4 GHz, the primary advantage of FE Ts over bipolar transistors is low noise figure,
although there are copious applications for both technolog ies throughout the MF–SHF bands.
As with bipolar transistors, FETs constitute a broad class o f devices. Although a detailed discussion is beyond the scop e of
this book, it is useful to know something about the family tre e of FET devices so that they may be recognized when
encountered. First, FETs come in two varieties: depletion-mode devices, and enhancement-mode devices. The primary
distinction is that depletion-mode FETs require VGS to be negative for use as an amplifier, which affects the desig n of bias
circuitry. FETs also come in “N-channel” and “P-channel” va riants, which are analogous to NPN and PNP for bipolar
transistors. Many types of FETs have appeared over the years as a result of the never-ending quest to improve gain, noise
figure, and linearity at ever-increasing frequencies. Mode rn applications are dominated by metal-oxide semiconductor
FETs (MOSFETs), metal-epitaxy-semiconductor FETs (MESFETs), and high electron mobility transistors (HEMTs).
MOSFETs appear primarily in applications at UHF and below, a nd include the increasingly popular category of
laterally-diffused MOS (LDMOS) devices. MESFETs are commonly constructed from GaA s, known as GaAsFETs, and
increasingly from Gallium Nitride (GaN) and Silicon carbid e (SiC). HEMTs are heterojunction devices, analogous to
HBTs, utilizing AlGaAs on GaAs; AlGaAs-InGaAs layers on GaA s, known as pseudomorphic HEMTs (PHEMTs); and
“lattice-matched” AlInAs-GaInAs layers on InP . Also notable are the modulation doped FET (MODFET), and the
venerable junction FET (JFET), which was the first popular FET technology but is now l argely deprecated in favor of
newer variants.
10.2.3 Designing with Transistors
Given the dizzying array of bipolar and FET device technolog ies, it might seem that a broadly-applicable design
methodology is not in the cards. In practice, the situation i s not quite that bad. The process of designing amplifiers from
transistors inevitably boils down to the problems of biasin g and small-signal design, as explained above. The particul ars of
biasing of bipolars and FETs may be somewhat different, but t he considerations and methods are, in a broad sense, the
same. Once the operating point is set, the transistor may be r educed to a two-port model (e.g., s-parameters) which is
essentially technology-independent; thus the design proc ess from that point proceeds in essentially the same way
regardless of the device family in use.

Si BJTs son sólo una categoría de una familia expansiva de dispositivos cualitativamente similares, a la que nos referiremos como transistores bipolares. Mientras que la frecuencia máxima útil de Si BJTs está en el orden de unos pocos GHz, frecuencias hasta cerca 10 GHz son posibles reemplazando Si con varias combinaciones de materiales semiconductores alternativos para formar lo que se conoce como un transistor bipolar heterojunción (HBT). Los HBTs son identificados típicamente por sus materiales constitutivos, que pueden incluir arsénico de gallium (GaAs), geranio de silicio (SiGe), fosfido de indio (InP), fósfido del galio indio (inGaP) y nitrido de GaAs indio (INGaAsN). Los transistores bipolares también pueden implementarse directamente en dispositivos semiconductores complementarios de metal-óxido (CMOS) utilizando procesos de fabricación como BiCMOS, permitiendo la implementación compacta de circuitos de radio grandes y complejos como únicos dispositivos de circuito integrado (IC) (más en esta sección 10.9).

El principal impulsor de tecnologías transistoras alternativas es la búsqueda de mejores ganancias, figuras de ruido y linealidad en frecuencias cada vez mayores. La frecuencia máxima usable de un transistor depende de la aplicación. Una caracterización común y útil es el ancho de banda de ganancia de unidad, fT . El concepto es que el logro realizable disminuye inevitablemente con frecuencia, y eventualmente se convierte en unidad; es decir, no hay ganancia. Para los transistores bipolares en aplicaciones amplificadoras, la disminución de la ganancia con frecuencia se debe a la capacitancia de la unión base emitter, y “ganancia realizable” se define más convenientemente como el “ganancia de circuito corto” ∆IC/∆IB; es decir, el valor de β aplicable a pequeñas excursiones alrededor de un punto operativo especificado. En esta terminología, Si BJTs tienen fT en el rango 100 MHz – 4 GHz, mientras que los HBT tienen hasta cerca 100 GHz.

También son notables la modulación dopada FET (MODFET), y el venerable cruce FET (JFET), que fue la primera tecnología popular FET pero ahora está deprecatado en gran parte a favor de nuevas variantes.

10.2.3 Diseñando con Transistores

Dado el divergente conjunto de tecnologías bipolar y FET, puede parecer que una metodología de diseño amplia no está en las tarjetas. En la práctica, la situación no es tan mala. El proceso de diseñar amplificadores de los transistores inevitablemente se reduce a los problemas de diseño sesgador y pequeño-signal, como se explica anteriormente. Los detalles de parcialización de los sentidos y los diferentes pueden ser un poco más. Una vez que se establece el punto de funcionamiento, el transistor puede reducirse a un modelo de dos puertos (por ejemplo, s-parameters) que es esencialmente dependiente de la tecnología; por lo tanto el proceso de diseño desde ese punto procede esencialmente de la misma manera independientemente de la familia del dispositivo en uso.

En resumen, el proceso de diseño de amplificador transistor se reduce a dos partes: la polarización, que establece el punto de funcionamiento y se aborda en mayor detalle en la Sección 10.3; y la adaptación de impedancias con las limitaciones de estabilidad, abordada en más detalle en la sección 10.4.

Si BJTs son sólo una categoría de una familia expansiva de dispositivos cualitativamente similares, a la que nos referiremos como transistores bipolares. Mientras que la frecuencia máxima útil de Si BJTs está en el orden de unos pocos GHz, frecuencias hasta cerca 10 GHz son posibles reemplazando Si con varias combinaciones de materiales semiconductores alternativos para formar lo que se conoce como un transistor bipolar heterojunción (HBT). Los HBTs son identificados típicamente por sus materiales constitutivos, que pueden incluir arsénico de gallium (GaAs), geranio de silicio (SiGe), fosfido de indio (InP), fósfido del galio indio (inGaP) y nitrido de GaAs indio (INGaAsN). Los transistores bipolares también pueden implementarse directamente en dispositivos semiconductores complementarios de metal-óxido (CMOS) utilizando procesos de fabricación como BiCMOS, permitiendo la implementación compacta de circuitos de radio grandes y complejos como únicos dispositivos de circuito integrado (IC) (más en esta sección 10.9).

El principal impulsor de tecnologías transistoras alternativas es la búsqueda de mejores ganancias, figuras de ruido y linealidad en frecuencias cada vez mayores. La frecuencia máxima usable de un transistor depende de la aplicación. Una caracterización común y útil es el ancho de banda de ganancia de unidad, fT . El concepto es que el logro realizable disminuye inevitablemente con frecuencia, y eventualmente se convierte en unidad; es decir, no hay ganancia. Para los transistores bipolares en aplicaciones amplificadoras, la disminución de la ganancia con frecuencia se debe a la capacitancia de la unión base emitter, y “ganancia realizable” se define más convenientemente como el “ganancia de circuito corto” ∆IC/∆IB; es decir, el valor de β aplicable a pequeñas excursiones alrededor de un punto operativo especificado. En esta terminología, Si BJTs tienen fT en el rango 100 MHz – 4 GHz, mientras que los HBT tienen hasta cerca 100 GHz.
10.2.2 Los transistores de efectos de campo

Una categoría distinta e igualmente importante de transistores se conoce como transistores de efectos de campo (FETs). Una representación esquemática de circuito de un FET se muestra en la Figura 10.3. Los tres terminales son conocidos como la puerta, el drenaje y la fuente; estos son análogos a la base, el coleccionista y el emisor, respectivamente, del transistor bipolar. En cuanto a rendimiento en relación con transistores bipolar, los FET dominan sobre 4 GHz y aparecen en aplicaciones hasta 100 GHz y más allá. Debajo de 4 GHz, la principal ventaja de los FETs sobre transistores biopolar es baja figura de ruido, aunque hay aplicaciones copiosos para ambas tecnologías en todas las bandas MF-SHF.

Como con transistores bipolares, los FET constituyen una amplia clase de dispositivos. Aunque un debate detallado está más allá del alcance de este libro, es útil saber algo sobre el árbol familiar de los dispositivos FET para que puedan ser reconocidos cuando se encuentran. Primero, los FTE vienen en dos variedades: dispositivos de amortiguación y dispositivos de mejora de modo. La principal distinción es que los FETs de impulso negativo requieren VGS para ser diseño de amplificador Los FET también vienen en variantes “N-canal” y “P-canal”, que son análogas a NPN y PNP para transistores bipolares. Muchos tipos de FET han aparecido a lo largo de los años como resultado de la búsqueda interminable para mejorar el beneficio, la figura del ruido y la linealidad en frecuencias cada vez mayores. MOSFETs aparecen principalmente en aplicaciones de UHF y abajo, e incluyen la categoría cada vez más popular de dispositivos MOS (LDMOS) disfrazados lateralmente. Los MESFETs se construyen comúnmente desde GaAs, conocidos como GaAsFETs, y cada vez más desde Gallium Nitride (GaN) y Silicon Carbide (SiC). También son notables la modulación dopada FET (MODFET), y el venerable cruce FET (JFET), que fue la primera tecnología popular FET pero ahora está deprecatado en gran parte a favor de nuevas variantes.
10.2.3 Diseñando con Transistores

Dado el divergente conjunto de tecnologías bipolar y FET, puede parecer que una metodología de diseño amplia no está en las tarjetas. En la práctica, la situación no es tan mala. El proceso de diseñar amplificadores de los transistores inevitablemente se reduce a los problemas de diseño sesgador y pequeño-signal, como se explica anteriormente. Los detalles de parcialización de los sentidos y los diferentes pueden ser un poco más. Una vez que se establece el punto de funcionamiento, el transistor puede reducirse a un modelo de dos puertos (por ejemplo, s-parameters) que es esencialmente dependiente de la tecnología; por lo tanto el proceso de diseño desde ese punto procede esencialmente de la misma manera independientemente de la familia del dispositivo en uso.

10.2 Transistors as Amplifiers

The fundamental building block of modern radio frequency amplifiers is the transistor.1 A transistor is a three-terminal semiconductor device in which the current between two terminals can be manipulated using the voltage or current at a third terminal. The application to RF design is most easily explained in the context of a particular device – For our purposes, the silicon (Si) bipolar junction transistor (BJT) is a good place to start.

10.2.1 Bipolar Transistors

A BJT is depicted in Figure 10.1. The three terminals of a BJT are known as the base, the collector, and the emitter. The associated terminal currents and voltages are as defined in Figure 10.1. The Si BJT comes in two varieties, known as “NPN” and “PNP”, referring to the geometry of semiconductor materials within the device. The NPN variant is somewhat more common in RF applications and is specifically considered here (and shown in Figure 10.1); the PNP variant is relatively easily understood once the NPN variant is mastered.

1Full disclosure: Very high power applications continue to use devices such as traveling wave tubes and klystrons, and there continue to be a few – albeit somewhat eclectic – applications for vaccuum tubes.

The properties of the semiconductor materials and the physical principles at work are sometimes useful to know but somewhat beyond the scope of this book. (A useful reference for additional details on all types of transistors considered in this chapter is [50, Chapter 2].) For our immediate purposes, it suffices to know that that the BJT can be used as an amplifier when operating in the forward-active mode. This mode is achieved by constraining VCE ≡VC −VE to be greater than about 0.3 V, which results in the base-emitter junction behaving as a diode with VBE ≡VB −VE ≈0.65 V when appropriately biased. Under these conditions, there are two useful descriptions of the behavior of the transistor. The first is the following approximate version of the Ebers-Moll model:

IC ≈IC0eVBE/VT

where k is Boltzmann’s constant, T is physical temperature, and q is the charge of an electron (1.6 × 10−19 coulomb). The primary application of this model will come in Chapter 11 (Section 11.2.2), when we consider linearity issues.

For amplifier design, a somewhat more useful model is the equivalent circuit of Figure 10.2. Note IC = βIB, where β, also known as the DC current gain and sometimes by the symbol hF E, is a constant value on the order of 10 to a few hundred. Thus, small changes in IB cause large and proportional changes in IC, assuming a power supply exists to provide the necessary collector current. The specific value of β depends primarily on VCE and IC; these two quantities together are known as the operating point of the transistor.2

An important step in using a BJT as an amplifier is to select an operating point that results in forward-active mode and is able to support the necessary variation around VCE (“signal swing”) for a specified supply voltage VCC. Then small variations around IB result in proportionally larger variations around the selected value of IC. Note that the increase in power is not provided by the transistor, but rather by the power supply; the transistor merely moderates the flow of collector current.

Finally, to get this scheme to work, we need to interface an input signal to the transistor and extract an output signal from the transistor. It’s unlikely that the transistor will have the appropriate input and output impedances as-is, so impedance matching will typically be necessary. Also, because the transistor is being used as an active device, stability must be considered.

In summary, the process of transistor amplifier design boils down to two parts: biasing, which sets the operating point and is addressed in more detail in Section 10.3; and impedance matching with stability constraints, addressed in more detail in Section 10.4.

Si BJTs are but one category from an expansive family of qualitatively similar devices, which we shall refer to as bipolar transistors. Whereas the maximum useful frequency of Si BJTs is on the order of a few GHz, frequencies up to about 10 GHz are possible by replacing Si with various combinations of alternative semiconductor materials to form what is known as a heterojunction bipolar transistor (HBT). HBTs are typically identified by their constituent materials, which may include gallium arsenide (GaAs), silicon geranium (SiGe), indium phosphide (InP), indium gallium phosphide (InGaP), and indium GaAs nitride (InGaAsN). Bipolar transistors may also be implemented directly in complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS) devices using manufacturing processes such as BiCMOS, enabling the compact implementation of large and complex radio frequency circuits as single integrated circuit (IC) devices (more on this in Section 10.9).

The primary driver for alternative transistor technologies is the quest for improved gain, noise figure, and linearity at ever-increasing frequencies. The maximum usable frequency of a transistor depends on the application. A common and useful characterization is unity-gain bandwidth, fT . The concept is that the realizable gain inevitably decreases with frequency, and eventually becomes unity; i.e., no gain. For bipolar transistors in amplifier applications, the decline in gain with frequency is due to the capacitance of the base-emitter junction, and “realizable gain” is most conveniently defined as the “short circuit gain” ∆IC/∆IB; i.e., the value of β applicable to small excursions around a specified operating operating point. In this terminology, Si BJTs have fT in the range 100 MHz – 4 GHz, whereas HBTs have fT up to about 100 GHz.

10.2.2 Field Effect Transistors

A distinct and equally important category of transistors is known as field effect transistors (FETs). A circuit schematic depiction of a FET is shown in Figure 10.3. The three terminals are known as the gate, drain, and source; these are analogous to the base, collector, and emitter, respectively, of the bipolar transistor. A fourth terminal, known variously as body or base, is sometimes identified but is typically important only in integrated circuit applications.

A big difference between FETs and bipolar transistors is that IG (analogous to IB for bipolar transistors) is often small enough that it may be neglected, with the result that IS ∼= ID. When used as an RF amplifier, a FET is essentially a voltage-controlled current source: The drain current ID is controlled by the gate-to-source voltage VGS according to the following relationship:

P-channel variants are indicated by reversing the direction of the arrow on the gate, or moving the arrow from source to drain. Some transistors of both varieties – in particular, MOSFETs – are sometimes shown with a fourth (“body”) terminal.

In terms of performance relative to bipolar transistors, FETs dominate above about 4 GHz, and appear in applications up to 100 GHz and beyond. Below 4 GHz, the primary advantage of FETs over bipolar transistors is low noise figure, although there are copious applications for both technologies throughout the MF–SHF bands.

As with bipolar transistors, FETs constitute a broad class of devices. Although a detailed discussion is beyond the scope of this book, it is useful to know something about the family tree of FET devices so that they may be recognized when encountered. First, FETs come in two varieties: depletion-mode devices, and enhancement-mode devices. The primary distinction is that depletion-mode FETs require VGS to be negative for use as an amplifier, which affects the design of bias circuitry. FETs also come in “N-channel” and “P-channel” variants, which are analogous to NPN and PNP for bipolar transistors. Many types of FETs have appeared over the years as a result of the never-ending quest to improve gain, noise figure, and linearity at ever-increasing frequencies. Modern applications are dominated by metal-oxide semiconductor FETs (MOSFETs), metal-epitaxy-semiconductor FETs (MESFETs), and high electron mobility transistors (HEMTs). MOSFETs appear primarily in applications at UHF and below, and include the increasingly popular category of laterally-diffused MOS (LDMOS) devices. MESFETs are commonly constructed from GaAs, known as GaAsFETs, and increasingly from Gallium Nitride (GaN) and Silicon carbide (SiC). HEMTs are heterojunction devices, analogous to HBTs, utilizing AlGaAs on GaAs; AlGaAs-InGaAs layers on GaAs, known as pseudomorphic HEMTs (PHEMTs); and “lattice-matched” AlInAs-GaInAs layers on InP. Also notable are the modulation doped FET (MODFET), and the venerable junction FET (JFET), which was the first popular FET technology but is now largely deprecated in favor of newer variants.

10.2.3 Designing with Transistors

Given the dizzying array of bipolar and FET device technologies, it might seem that a broadly-applicable design methodology is not in the cards. In practice, the situation is not quite that bad. The process of designing amplifiers from transistors inevitably boils down to the problems of biasing and small-signal design, as explained above. The particulars of biasing of bipolars and FETs may be somewhat different, but the considerations and methods are, in a broad sense, the same. Once the operating point is set, the transistor may be reduced to a two-port model (e.g., s-parameters) which is essentially technology-independent; thus the design process from that point proceeds in essentially the same way regardless of the device family in use.

10.3 Biasing of Transistor Amplifiers
Biasing involves designing a circuit around the transistor which results in DC operation at the desired operating point , and
which facilitates interfacing of the AC (in our case, RF) sig nal. The operating point determines the small-signal two-p ort
behavior – e.g., the s-parameters – so once biased, the circuit can be reduced to a t wo-port model for subsequent analysis
of RF behavior and the design of impedance matching networks , as described in Section 10.4.
10.3.1 Bipolar Transistors
The most common (but certainly not only) topology for an RF am plifier using an NPN bipolar transistor is the common
emitter configuration. In this configuration, the input signal is app lied to the base, the output signal is extracted from the
collector, and the emitter serves as a datum. For bipolar tra nsistors, the common emitter configuration results in high
current gain and high output impedance, which is often what i s needed in an amplifier. For simplicity, we’ll assume
common emitter configuration throughout this section, and d efer discussion of other configurations to Section 10.3.3.
Once the configuration is settled, there are two possible str ategies for selecting the operating point. The classical an d
rigorous strategy is based on an analysis of the characteristic curves of the transistor. For a bipolar transistor in common
emitter configuration, these curves are simply plots of IC as a function of VCE for various values of IB. The trick is to
choose a combination of IC andVCE that yields desirable small-signal characteristics and al lows sufficient “swing” in the
output signal with respect to the collector supply voltage VCC while keeping the transistor firmly biased in the
forward-active mode (see e.g. [74, Chapter 5]). This strate gy is not always practical because such data is typically not
available; especially for UHF and above. The simpler and mor e common strategy is simply to refer to the manufacturer’s
data sheet for a recommended operating point. For RF transis tors of modern vintage, manufacturers typically document a
set of nominal operating points in advance, providing also t he associateds-parameters, noise figure parameters, and other
potentially useful information. Even for older transistor s, the trend is provide data that allows one to quickly grasp t he
range of reasonable operating points and the implications o f various choices within that range, in lieu of characterist ic
curves. Alternatively, a sufficiently detailed equivalent circuit (“device model”) for the transistor can be used in si mulation
to determine a suitable bias point.
Example 10.1. The Avago A T-41511 (previously considered in Chapter 8) is a modern NPN Si BJT. Seek out the
data sheets for this device and determine some reasonable op erating points.
Solution: The data sheet for this device is readily available on the int ernet, through the manufacturer. Y ou’ll find that
this device is very well-characterized for IC = 5 mA and 25 mA, and VCE = 2. 7 V and 5 V; i.e., four operating
points. The data sheet provides s-parameters and noise figure characterization data for thes e operating points. This is
certainly not to say that other operating points are not poss ible or recommended; however, this represents a pretty
good set of options for our initial design. For many applicat ions, one of these would probably be sufficient without
modification.
Example 10.2. An example of an older NPN Si BJT still appearing in radios is t he 2N3904, offered by a variety of
manufacturers (and under a variety of different model names , associated with different packaging options). Seek out
the data sheet and determine some reasonable operating poin ts.

recommendations. Y ou probably will see a lot of data for IC in the range 0.1–100 mA and VCE in the range 1–10 V ,
which indicate relevant tradeoffs and can be used to narrow d own the range of possibilities. In the absence of any
particular constraint, it should be apparent that a pretty g ood starting point for the 2N3904 is IC = 10 mA and
VC = 5 V , as the device is typically well-characterized for operating points near those values. Y ou will most likely

10.3.3 Beyond Common Emitter and Common Source
As explained above, the common emitter configuration (for bi polar transistors) and common source configuration (for
FETs) account for most of the amplifier designs seen in radio c ircuits. However, transistors are three-terminal devices , and
so there are two other configurations for attaching input and output signals, shown in Figure 10.11. If you need low output
impedance as opposed to high output impedance, then the bett er choice is the common collector (bipolar) and common
drain (FET) configurations. A bipolar transistor in common c ollector configuration is also known as an emitter follower.
These configurations tend to show up in applications where th e output needs to drive a low-impedance load with a lot of
current – the classic example is a cable driver, which is a low-gain amplifier whose output drives a long sect ion of coaxial
transmission line. If you require low input impedance and are OK with relatively low gain, then the bette r choice is the
common base (bipolar) and common gate (FET) configurations. A typical application for these configurations is in some
low noise amplifiers which are directly attached to resonant antennas with low resistive impedance. In this application ,
low gain is an advantage because the lack of preselection (se e Section 15.4) makes the amplifier vulnerable to compressio n
due to out-of-band signals unless the gain is low.

10.3 Polarización de amplificadores con transistores

El biasing implica diseñar un circuito alrededor del transistor que resulte en DC operación en el punto de funcionamiento deseado, y que facilita la interfase del AC (en nuestro caso, RF) señal. El punto de funcionamiento determina el comportamiento de dos puertos pequeño-signal – por ejemplo, los s-parameters – así que una vez sesgado, el circuito puede ser reducido a un modelo de dos puertos para el análisis posterior de RF comportamiento y el diseño de las redes de adaptación de impedancia, como se describe en la Sección 10.4.

10.3.1 Los transistores bipolares

La topología más común (pero ciertamente no sólo) para un amplificador RF utilizando un transistor bipolar NPN es la configuración de emisor común. En esta configuración, la señal de entrada se aplica a la base, la señal se extrae del colector y el emisor sirve como datum. Para los transistores bipolares, la configuración de emisión común resulta en ganancia alta corriente y una impedancia de salida elevada, que es a menudo un amplificante. Para la simplicidad, asumiremos la configuración común de emisores en toda esta sección y aplazaremos el debate de otras configuraciones a la Sección 10.3.3.

Una vez que se resuelve la configuración, hay dos posibles estrategias para seleccionar el punto de funcionamiento. La estrategia clásica y rigurosa se basa en un análisis de las curvas características del transistor. Para un transistor bipolar en la configuración común de emisores, estas curvas son simplemente parcelas de IC como una función de VCE para varios valores de IB. El truco es elegir una combinación de IC y VCE que produce características pequeñas y deseables y permite suficiente “swing” en la señal de salida con respecto al voltaje de suministro del coleccionista VCC mientras mantiene el transistor firmemente sesgado en el modo de avance (véase por ejemplo [74, Capítulo 5]). Esta estrategia no siempre es práctica porque tales datos normalmente no están disponibles; especialmente para UHF y La estrategia más simple y más común es simplemente referirse a la hoja de datos del fabricante para un punto de funcionamiento recomendado. Para los transistores RF de la moderna cosecha, los fabricantes suelen documentar un conjunto de puntos de operación nominales con antelación, proporcionando también los parámetros de s asociados, parámetros de figura de ruido y otra información potencialmente útil. Incluso para los transistores mayores, la tendencia es proporcionar datos que permiten captar rápidamente el rango de puntos de funcionamiento razonables y las implicaciones de varias opciones dentro de ese rango, en lugar de curvas características. Alternativamente, un circuito equivalente suficientemente detallado (“modelo de dispositivo”) para el transistor puede ser utilizado en simulación para determinar un punto de polarización adecuado.

Ejemplo 10.1. El Avago AT-41511 (previamente considerado en el Capítulo 8) es un NPN Si BJT moderno. Busque las hojas de datos para este dispositivo y determine algunos puntos de funcionamiento razonables.

Solución: La hoja de datos para este dispositivo está disponible fácilmente en Internet, a través del fabricante. Encontrarás que este dispositivo está muy bien definido para IC = 5 mA y 25 mA, y VCE = 2.7 V y 5 V; es decir, cuatro puntos operativos. La hoja de información proporciona datos de caracterización de figuras s-paramétricas y ruido para estos puntos operativos . Esto no es ciertamente decir que otros puntos operativos no son posibles o recomendados; sin embargo, esto representa un buen conjunto de opciones para nuestro diseño inicial. Para muchas aplicaciones, uno de estos probablemente sería suficiente sin modificaciones.

Ejemplo 10.2. Un ejemplo de un NPN Si BJT más antiguo que todavía aparece en las radios es el 2N3904, ofrecido por una variedad de fabricantes (y bajo una variedad de nombres de modelos diferentes, asociados con diferentes opciones de embalaje). Busque la hoja de datos y determine algunos puntos de funcionamiento razonables.

Solución: Las hojas de datos para este dispositivo están disponibles fácilmente en Internet. Diferentes fabricantes proporcionarán los datos en formatos algo diferentes. Sin embargo, probablemente no encontrará recomendaciones específicas de puntos operativos. Probablemente verá muchos datos para IC en el rango 0.1-100 mA y VCE en el rango de 1-10 V, que indican los tradeoffs relevantes y se pueden utilizar para reducir la gama de posibilidades. En ausencia de cualquier limitación particular, debe ser evidente que un punto de partida bastante bueno para el 2N3904 es IC = 10 mA y VC = 5 V, ya que el dispositivo suele estar bien definido para puntos de funcionamiento cerca de esos valores. Es probable que no encuentre datos de caracterización de figuras s-paramétricas o ruido proporcionados como parte de la hoja de datos.

Una vez que se decide el punto de funcionamiento, un circuito que establece esos valores puede diseñarse. Para los transistores bipolares, hay una variedad de técnicas, descritas a continuación.

Bias fijas. polarización fijo para transistores bipolar emisor comunes se muestra en la figura 10.4. En primer lugar, observe algunos elementos que tienden a aparecer en todos los esquemas de polarización: los Capacidores en los terminales de entrada y salida aíslan la polarización (DC) voltajes y corrientes de los RF entrada y salida. Los circuitos de inductor-capacitor “L” aparecen dentro de las cajas sombreadas de la Figura 10.4 forma filtros de baja velocidad destinados a mantener RF señales fuera de la fuente de alimentación. Los incluimos aquí por dos razones: (1) Para tener en cuenta la posibilidad de que sean necesarios, y (2) Encontraremos más tarde que estos componentes pueden necesitar ser considerados en el diseño pequeño-signal, y puede resultar de hecho útil para la adaptación de impedancias. Para los fines de nuestra discusión sobre la polarización, es seguro asumir que todos los capacitores son circuitos abiertos y todos los inductores son cortocircuitos.

La idea detrás de la polarización fijo es bastante simple: Primero IC usando R1, y luego establecer VCE utilizando RC. Para ver cómo funciona esto, primero aplicar la Ley de Voltaje de Kirchoff (KVL)3 al camino desde VCC aunque la base a tierra:

A pesar de su aparente elegancia, la polarización fijo es generalmente una mala idea. Un gran problema es la estabilidad térmica. El problema surge como sigue: VBE varía un poco como una función de temperatura física; como regla brusca del pulgar, VBE disminuye en aproximadamente 2 mV para cada aumento de temperatura 1 °C. Los dispositivos electrónicos aumentan la temperatura después de ser encendido, por lo que lo que

es esto: VBE disminuye ligeramente, por lo que IB aumenta ligeramente. IC = βIB, y β es un gran valor, por lo tanto IC aumenta en mucho. Esto ya es malo, porque el transistor se está alejando de su punto de operación previsto. Sin embargo, lo que también sucede es que el aumento de IC hace que la temperatura del transistor aumente una cantidad adicional, que posteriormente disminuye VBE más. En este punto, tenemos un escape térmico: un mecanismo de retroalimentación positivo en el que IC es impulsado a valores cada vez mayores, aumentando la temperatura del transistor y posiblemente causando daños.

Otro problema con la polarización fijo es que no es particularmente robusto a las variaciones de las características del dispositivo. En particular, las variaciones en β se traducen a variaciones en el punto operativo y posteriormente en los parámetros s. Esto es una preocupación porque los valores de β varían considerablemente, incluso entre dispositivos aparentemente idénticos.

Ahora cuando IC comienza a aumentar debido a la temperatura creciente, VC disminuye, y por lo que el aumento en IB debido a la disminución VBE se mitiende.

La desventaja de reducir R1 se incrementa significativamente el consumo de energía, como lo representa la corriente total. Si se especificase para este circuito, probablemente no sería necesario el inductor y capacitor en el suministro de colector, ya que RC por sí mismo proporcionaría una impedancia muy alta a RF relativa al 50 Ω especificado. Si la impedancia de salida especificada fuera mayor, podría ser necesario utilizar estas reactancias para aumentar la impedencia en el suministro eléctrico relativo a la impedibilidad de salida. Una consideración similar se aplica al inductor y capacitor en el suministro base: Si se especifica la impedancia de entrada del amplificador 50 Ω, entonces probablemente estos no serían necesarios R1 = 10 kΩ, pero probablemente sería importante R1 = 100 Ω. La necesidad de DC-bloquear capacitores en entrada y salida depende de los circuitos adyacentes. Por supuesto, estos capacitores son necesarios si la impedancia DC mirando hacia fuera la entrada o salida es pequeña, o si los circuitos adyacentes afirman un voltaje DC en la entrada o la salida.

Autobios con Dividente de Voltaje Base. El principal inconveniente en la degeneración del emisor es posible dificultad para hacer RE “desaparecido” a la frecuencia de operación, y sin reactancia residual para complicar el diseño de pequeña señal. Una alternativa más segura en UHF y arriba puede ser en lugar de “acelerar” el esquema de autobias con un resistor adicional para crear un dividedor de tensión base y por lo tanto un grado adicional de libertad. Esto se ilustra en la Figura 10.8, junto con una versión que contiene un tweak adicional: Un resistor en el terminal base para un mejor control de la compensación entre estabilización y consumo de energía. El análisis y diseño de estos esquemas es muy similar a los de los esquemas anteriores.

Bias activas. En algunas aplicaciones, no hay una combinación de esquemas pasivos de polarización – por los que nos referimos a cualquiera de las técnicas anteriores – que proporciona un nivel aceptable de robustez a variaciones en la temperatura y β. En algunos diseños puede ser difícil mantener el punto de funcionamiento de cambiar en respuesta a otras cosas que están pasando en el circuito, lo que conduce a fluctuaciones en VCC, por ejemplo. En estos casos, la alternativa es diseñar e implementar fuentes de corriente y tensión alrededor del transistor que fijan el punto de funcionamiento deseado, con retroalimentación para “clamp” IC y VCE a sus valores nominales. Esto se conoce como parcial activo. Las fuentes adicionales normalmente consisten en los propios transistores, por lo que no es raro encontrar circuitos amplificadores que consisten en varios transistores , pero en los cuales sólo uno está haciendo el trabajo.

10.3.2 Las FETs

La versión FET de la configuración común del emisor es una configuración de fuente común: la entrada está coronada por AC a la puerta, la salida es AC-coupled desde el drenaje, y el truco es encontrar un punto de operación (VDS, ID) que produce el beneficio deseado con suficiente oscilación de señal de salida en relación con el voltaje de suministro VDD. A continuación, VGS se puede determinar utilizando Ecuación 10.3 (o leer desde la hoja de datos), y un circuito de polarización está diseñado para fijar estos valores con un ojo hacia la estabilidad térmica y minimizar la sensibilidad a las variaciones de fabricación. Al igual que con transistores bipolar, los fabricantes suelen proporcionar orientación en cuanto a puntos de operación nominales.

Para dispositivos de mejora del movimiento de canales N, VGS es positivo y las técnicas de la sección 10.3.1 se aplican; de hecho la polarización se simplifica considerablemente por el hecho de que la corriente de la puerta puede ser descuidada, tanto porque es pequeña como porque no tiene mucho efecto en el sesgado (recordar: FET son esencialmente fuentes de corriente controladas por tensión). VGS también puede ser positivo para los dispositivos de amortiguación de póleo (N)
