11.1.text_es_mx:
11.1 Introducción

Capítulos anteriores han descrito dispositivos de dos puertos en términos de tres aspectos: Impedancia, ganancia y ruido interno. En este capítulo, presentamos un cuarto aspecto: linealidad.

Un sistema es lineal si su comportamiento es independiente de su entrada. Esto implica también que la salida es proporcional a la entrada, aunque la constante de proporcionalidad puede ser una función de frecuencia. Una breve revisión de las características de los transistores (en particular, Ecuaciones 10.1 y 10.3) revela que los amplificadores transistor no pueden ser formalmente lineales; uno sólo puede alcanzar una aproximación a la linearidad en las proximidades del punto de operación. (Los dispositivos de pasividad también son intrínsecamente no lineales, aunque la aproximación es generalmente mucho mejor.)

Las secciones 11.2 y 11.3 introducen formalmente el concepto de linearidad, las consecuencias de la no linealidad, y las diversas métricas que se utilizan para cuantificar estos efectos en los sistemas RF.

El próximo tema principal en este capítulo es el análisis de la ganancia, el ruido interno y la linealidad de RF sistemas compuestos por múltiples dos puertos organizados en cascada. Las características de una cascada de dos puertos pueden determinarse fácilmente por la ganancia, el ruido interno y la linealidad de los dos puertos individuales (las “etapas”) si las etapas se pueden suponer que son impedancia-matched. Primero consideramos la linearidad de dos puertos cascadas en la Sección 11.4. La sección 11.5 explica la técnica del “análisis de escenarios/cascadas” y demuestra su aplicación en el diseño de sistemas prácticos RF. La Sección 11.6 explica los conceptos de MDS y suelo de ruido, ambas descripciones alternativas de la sensibilidad de un sistema RF.

El tercer tema principal de este capítulo es el rango dinámico (Sección 11.7). En términos generales, rango dinámico se refiere a la capacidad de un sistema para procesar correctamente señales muy fuertes sin sensibilidad inaceptablemente degradante a las señales débiles.

11.1.text_en_clean:
11.1 Introduction

Previous chapters have described two-port devices in terms of three aspects: Impedance, gain, and internal noise. In this chapter, we introduce a fourth aspect: linearity.

A system is linear if its behavior is independent of its input. This also implies that the output is proportional to the input, although the constant of proportionality may be a function of frequency. A brief review of the characteristics of transistors (in particular, Equations 10.1 and 10.3) reveals that transistor amplifiers cannot be formally linear; one may only achieve an approximation to linearity in the vicinity of the operating point. (Passive devices are also intrinsically non-linear, although the approximation is typically much better.)

Sections 11.2 and 11.3 formally introduce the concept of linearity, the consequences of non-linearity, and the various metrics that are used to quantify these effects in RF systems.

The next major topic in this chapter is the analysis of the gain, internal noise, and linearity of RF systems consisting of multiple two-ports arranged in cascade. The characteristics of a cascade of two-ports may be readily determined from the gain, internal noise, and linearity of the individual two-ports (the “stages”) if the stages can be assumed to be impedance-matched. We first consider the linearity of cascaded two-ports in Section 11.4. Section 11.5 explains the technique of “stage/cascade analysis” and demonstrates its application in the design of practical RF systems. Section 11.6 explains the concepts of MDS and noise floor, both alternative descriptions of the sensitivity of an RF system.

The third major topic of this chapter is dynamic range (Section 11.7). Broadly speaking, dynamic range refers to the ability of a system to properly process very strong signals without unacceptably degrading sensitivity to weak signals.

11.2 Characterization of Linearity
The term linearity, as it is used in modern radio engineering, has several possi ble interpretations; some leading to informal
definitions that can be confusing to the uninitiated. Let us b egin with a formal definition and then proceed to some of the
more common interpretations in the context of radio enginee ring.

11.2.1 Linearity as Independence of Response
A formal definition of linearity is as follows. 1 Consider a system consisting of a single two-port, or consis ting of a
two-port cascade which may be described as a single two-port . Such a system may be characterized in terms of its impulse
responseh(t), which is its output when the input is the Dirac delta functio nδ(t).2 When a signal x1(t) is applied to this
system, the output is given by
y1(t) = x1(t)∗h(t)
where “∗” denotes convolution. In a separate experiment, a signal x2(t) is applied to the same system, resulting in output
y2(t) = x2(t)∗h(t)
The systemh(t) is formally linear if, for any constants a1 anda2:
[a1x1(t) +a2x2(t)]∗h(t) = a1y1(t) +a2y2(t) (11.1)
wherex1(t),y1(t),x2(t), andy2(t) also satisfy the previous equations. This might also be refe rred to as the “scaling and
superposition” definition of linearity: We say a system is li near if its response to inputs one at a time tells us everythin g we
need to know about the system’s response to linear combinati ons of those inputs. The frequency domain version of the
“scaling and superposition” definition of linearity is
[a1X1(f ) +a2X2(f )]H(f ) = a1Y1(t) +a2Y2(t) (11.2)
where the upper-case quantities are Fourier transforms of t he lower case quantities, and, in particular, H(f ) is the
frequency response of the system.
Now, how does this apply to an RF system? x1(t) andx2(t), as well as y1(t) andy2(t), may be either voltages or currents,
andh(t) can be a description of any two-port, including cascades of t wo-ports. Equations 11.1 and 11.2 are essentially
statements that the system is not affected by the input. A cas e where this is trivially true is the “null” system h(t) = δ(t)
(equivalently,H(f ) = 1 ), which is just a pair of wires connecting the input terminal s to the output terminals. In this case
it’s easy to verify that Equations 11.1 and 11.2 apply, and it ’s also clear that h(t) does not depend on x(t). An ideal
amplifier can be modeled as h(t) = gδ(t) whereg is a constant (equivalently,H(f ) = g); again it’s clear that this is
formally linear, and the response of the system does not depe nd on the input.
For any practical amplifier, g cannot be completely independent of the input. For an exampl e, just look back to
Section 10.3, where it is noted that the gain of a transistor a mplifier varies as a function of the operating point. When the
input current strays too far from the operating point, the ou tput current becomes significantly distorted by the change i nβ
over the resulting output signal swing. In effect, g – not just y(t) – becomes a function of x(t). It is only in a relatively
small range around the operating point that the apparent gai n of the amplifier is approximately independent of the input t o
the amplifier. In this region Equation 11.1 holds – albeit app roximately – and in that region we may reasonably refer to the
amplifier as “linear”. Generalizing, it is common to refer to a two-port device as linear if it’s transfer function is
independent – at least approximately – of its input. Convers ely, a two-port is said to be non-linear if this condition cannot
reasonably be assumed.
11.2.2 Linearity of Systems with Memoryless Polynomial Respo nse
A memoryless system is one in which the output does not depend on past values of the input. Many two-ports encountered
in radio engineering are either electrically small or dispe rsionless, and thus may be assumed to be memoryless. Excepti ons
include certain power amplifiers (more on those beginning in Section 17.4).
Any system that can be described as a memoryless two-port has a response which can, in principle, be described by the
following infinite sum:
y(t) = a0 +a1x(t) +a2x2(t) +a3x3(t) +... (11.3)

FET amplifiers used for as small-signal amplifiers typically have have lower P1 when designed for optimal or near-optimal
noise figure, which is one reason why bipolar transistors con tinue to be used in some low-noise applications at UHF and
above.

11.2.6 AM-PM Conversion
In previous sections we have considered only constant-powe r sinusoids. When the power in a signal varies, the
non-linearity of a system may manifest in more complex ways. Primary among these is AM-PM conversion. The concept
can be explained as follows: Consider an amplitude-modulat ed (AM) signal applied to a two-port. The two-port may be
arbitrarily simple or complex, but let us assume for the sake of illustration that it consists of at least one capacitor, a nd let
us assume that the signal creates sufficient voltage across t he capacitor that non-linear effects are apparent. Recalli ng that
non-linearity is fundamentally the dependence of response on input, this means that the capacitance C of the capacitor is a
function of the applied voltage, and that this variation in c apacitance is significant. The impedance of a capacitor is
−j/ωC ; therefore the reactance of this capacitor varies with the i nput signal magnitude, which is varying due to the
modulation. Since there are also real-valued impedances in the system, and since these impedances are either not varyin g
significantly or are varying independently of C, the phase response of the system must be time-varying. Thus , the
non-linear capacitance is essentially converting the ampl itude-modulated input signal into a signal which also conta ins
phase modulation (PM). AM-PM conversion can also be attribu ted to inductors (also reactances), transistors (which
exhibit capacitive terminal-to-terminal impedances), an d gain compression relative to independently-nonlinear re actances
– all that is needed for the system phase response to become a f unction of the input magnitude.
AM-PM conversion is typically not a concern for AM signals, s ince the erroneous PM component does not affect the
information, which is represented in the amplitude. AM-PM c onversion is also typically not of much concern in systems
using FM or PSK, since these signals have constant modulus. H owever digital modulations employing sinusoidal carrier
modulation with non-constant modulus – most notably, QAM – r eally suffer, as the PM component significantly distorts

11.2 Caracterización de la linealidad

El término linealidad, como se utiliza en la ingeniería moderna de radio, tiene varias interpretaciones posibles; algunas conducen a definiciones informales que pueden confundirse con los no iniciados. Comencemos con una definición formal y luego procedamos a algunas de las interpretaciones más comunes en el contexto de la ingeniería radio.

11.2.1 La linealidad como la independencia de la respuesta

Una definición formal de linearidad es la siguiente.1 Considere un sistema consistente en una sola cascada de dos puertos, o que consiste en una cascada de dos niveles que puede describirse como un solo dos puertos. Tal sistema se puede caracterizar en términos de su respuesta de impulso h(t), que es su salida cuando la entrada es la función Dirac delta δ(t).2 Cuando una señal x1(t) se aplica a este sistema,

y1(t) = x1(t) ∗h(t)

donde “∗” denota la convolución. En un experimento separado, se aplica una señal x2(t) al mismo sistema, dando lugar a la salida

y2(t) = x2(t) ∗h(t)

El sistema h(t) es formalmente lineal si, para cualquier constante a1 y a2:

[a1x1(t) + a2x2(t)] ∗h(t) = a1y1(t) + a2y2(t)
(11.1)

donde x1(t), y1(t) x2(t), and y2(t) también satisfacen las ecuaciones anteriores. Esto también podría denominarse la definición de “scaling y superposición” de linearidad: Decimos que un sistema es lineal si su respuesta a los insumos uno a la vez nos dice todo lo que necesitamos saber sobre la respuesta del sistema a combinaciones lineales de esos insumos.

[a1X1(f) + a2X2(f)] H(f) = a1Y1(t) + a2Y2(t)
(11.2)

donde las cantidades de la maleta superior son Fourier transforma de las cantidades inferiores del caso, y, en particular, H(f) es la respuesta de frecuencia del sistema.

Ahora, ¿cómo se aplica esto a un RF sistema? x1(t) y x2(t), así como y1(t) y y2(t), pueden ser voltajes o corrientes, y h(t) puede ser una descripción de cualquier dos puertos, incluyendo cascadas de dos puertos. 11.1 y 11.2 son esencialmente declaraciones que el sistema no se ve afectado por la entrada. Un caso en el que esto es trivialmente cierto es el sistema “null” h(t) = δt) (equivalentemente, H(f) = 1), que es sólo un par de cables que conectan los terminales de entrada a los terminales de salida. En este caso es fácil verificar que Ecuaciones 11.1 y 11.2 aplicar, y también está claro que h(t) no depende de x(t). Un amplificador ideal puede ser modelado como h(t) = gδ(t) where g is a constant (equivallently, H(f) = g); again it’s clear that this is formally linear, and the response of the system does not depend on the input.

Para cualquier amplificador práctico, g no puede ser completamente independiente de la entrada. Por ejemplo, sólo mira hacia atrás a la Sección 10.3, donde se observa que el aumento de un amplificador transistor varía como una función del punto operativo. Cuando la corriente de entrada se aleja demasiado lejos del punto de funcionamiento, la corriente de salida se distorsiona significativamente por el cambio en β sobre el oscilación de señal de salida resultante. En efecto, g – no sólo y Es sólo en una gama relativamente pequeña alrededor del punto operativo que la ganancia aparente del amplificador es aproximadamente independiente de la entrada al amplificador. En esta región Ecuación 11.1 sostiene – aunque aproximadamente – y en esa región podemos razonablemente referirnos al amplificante como “linear”. Generalizando, es común referirse a un dispositivo de dos puertos como lineal si su función de transferencia es independiente – por lo menos aproximadamente – de Por el contrario, se dice que un doble puerto no es lineal si esta condición no puede razonablemente ser asumida.

11.2.2 La linealidad de sistemas con respuesta polinomio sin memoria

Un sistema sin memoria es uno en el que la salida no depende de los valores pasados de la entrada. Muchos dos puertos encontrados en la ingeniería radio son eléctricamente pequeños o dispersionless, y por lo tanto puede ser asumido como sin memoria. Las excepciones incluyen ciertos amplificadores de potencia (más sobre los que comienzan en la Sección 17.4).

Este métrica también se puede expresar con respecto a la salida. El punto de compresión 1-dB de salida se define como la magnitud de la producción para la cual el beneficio aparente del fundamental es 1 dB menos que la ganancia lineal nominal. Esto es simplemente TENA1 VENDA; es decir, la entrada y salida 1-dB puntos de compresión están relacionados por la magnitud de las ganancias lineales nominales a1.

Como se ha formulado anteriormente, 1 dB punto de compresión se expresa en términos de voltaje o corriente. 1 dB El punto de compresión también se puede expresar en términos de potencia, ya que las tres cantidades (voltaje, corriente y potencia) están relacionadas con la impedancia. Las unidades de potencia son normalmente más convenientes para la medición, y las hojas de datos del fabricante utilizan normalmente las cantidades de potencia. 1 dB punto de compresión en las unidades de potencia es típicamente representado por el símbolo P1dB, P1, OP1 (“O” para la salida). La compresión de entrada 1 dB es a veces representada por el símbolo IP1, y está relacionada con el punto de compresión 1 dB de salida por la ganancia de potencia; es decir, OP1 = G · IP1. Las hojas de datos frecuentemente no hacen la distinción entre las cantidades de entrada y salida-referida, en cuyo caso es típicamente la cantidad referenciada a la salida que se indica; sin embargo, siempre es una buena idea para comprobar.

Debido a que los amplificadores transistores bipolares emisores comunes aparecen prominentemente en RF el diseño del sistema, es útil estar al tanto de algunas reglas-de-thumb aplicables a estos dispositivos. Debido a que los transistores bipolares son fuentes de corriente controladas esencialmente, la linealidad depende más directamente de la corriente de polarización del coleccionista IC. Amplificador de emisor común con una corriente de polarización de coleccionista 20 mA y que se termina en 50Ωwill típicamente tienen un producto 1 dB punto de compresión de alrededor +10 dBm. Generalmente, disminuir la polarización del coleccionista actual o disminuir la impedancia de carga tiende a disminuir P1.

Los amplificadores FET utilizados como amplificadores de pequeña señal suelen tener P1 inferior cuando se diseñó para una figura de ruido óptima o casi óptima, lo que es una razón por la cual los transistores bipolar siguen siendo utilizados en algunas aplicaciones de baja densidad en UHF y superior.

11.2.4 La Intermodulación; Intermodulación de Tercer Orden

En la sección anterior asumimos un solo sinusoide en la entrada. Una entrada ligeramente más complicada es dos sinusoides:

x(t) = A1 cos ω1t + A2 cos ω2t

Los resultados se resumen en la tabla 11.1. Tenga en cuenta que los productos de salida incluyen no sólo los fundamentos y sus armónicos, sino también productos adicionales cuyas frecuencias dependen de ambos ω1 y ω2. Estos productos adicionales se denominan intermodulación. Los productos de intermodulación asociados con a2 son conocidos como intermodulación de segundo orden (IM2) y los asociados con a3 se conocen como intermodulador de terceros (IM3).

Como se indica en el cuadro 11.1 la producción fundamental (desirada) para cada tono se modifica no sólo a3 (como en el caso de una sola tonelada), sino ahora también por a2 y por la magnitud del otro tono. Entre todos los productos restantes, los dos de mayor preocupación son generalmente los IM3 productos a 2ω1 −ω2 y 2ω2 −ω1. Esto se debe a que la separación entre cada uno de estos productos y el fundamental más cercano es igual a la separación entre los fundamentos; por ejemplo, (2ω2 −ω1) −ω2 = ω2 −ω1. Si ambos fundamentales aparecen en la misma banda, es probable que estos productos IM3 estén también en la banda ancha, o lo suficientemente cerca para presentar un desafío de diseño de filtros.

No sólo son los IM3 productos potencialmente difíciles de filtrar, pero también son potencialmente bastante grandes. 11.1 vemos que la magnitud de una IM3 producto para fundamentos de igualdad de densidad (por ejemplo, A1 = A2 A) 3a3A3/4; es decir, cada uno IM3 el producto es proporcional a A3, mientras que la producción básica nominal (lineal) es proporcional a A. En otras palabras: Cuando A aumenta por un factor de α, el IM3 los productos aumentan por un factor α3. Por esta razón, la vulnerabilidad del sistema a IM3 se caracteriza a menudo utilizando una cantidad conocida como el punto de interceptación de tercera orden (IP3), ilustrado en la Figura 11.2. El concepto es el siguiente: Los productos IM3 aumentan más rápidamente con el aumento tenciónA sufrimiento que los propios fundamentos; por lo tanto, para algún valor de TENA soportar las magnitudes de los productos IM3 deben ser en principio iguales a las magnitud de los productos fundamentales (linear). El valor de TENA SUPERVISIÓN en el que esto ocurre es la entrada IP3 (IIP3), y el valor asociado de TENAPA1A VENT es la salida IP3 (OIP3).

Tenga en cuenta que IP3 no es el valor de TENA TARDIS para el cual la magnitud del IM3 es igual a la magnitud real (por ejemplo, comprimido) de la producción fundamental. Por lo tanto, IP3 no puede ser medido "directamente" en el sentido de aumentar TENA SUPERVISIÓN hasta que los productos IM3 sean iguales a los fundamentos y tomando ese valor de ANTEA permanecer para ser el IIP3. (No sólo esto no es consistente con la definición, pero es potencialmente peligroso para el dispositivo bajo prueba!) IP3 se puede medir fácilmente (y con seguridad) de la siguiente manera: Usando niveles de entrada relativamente bajos, se mide la ganancia lineal nominal como la pendiente de la curva de potencia de salida a entrada, y también la IM3 para los mismos niveles de entrada. Cuando se trama en un diagrama de registro, estas curvas pueden ser linealmente-extrapoladas hasta el punto donde se encuentran, como se muestra en la Figura 11.2.

Como es el caso 1 dB punto de compresión, IP3 se expresa comúnmente en las unidades de energía, OIP3 = G · IIP3, y las hojas de datos generalmente reportan la cantidad referida de salida (OIP3). El IIP3 de los receptores típicos va desde cerca −30 dBm a +10 dBm, dependiendo de la aplicación. Por ejemplo, un típico IIP3 especificación para un celular GSM receptor es −18 dBm, y una especificación típica para un celular CDMA receptor es −13 dBm. Las especificaciones de linearidad para receptores en aplicaciones HF y LMR tienden a ser mucho más altas.

En la práctica se encuentra Ecuación 11.18 no es una mala conjetura, pero se aplican cavernas. Los dispositivos pasivos no lineales a menudo están bien modelados como compresivo de tercera orden, en cuyo caso Ecuación 11.18 es una buena estimación. Para los dispositivos activos, esto normalmente no es una suposición segura. Véase [12] para más información sobre este tema.

Comportamiento similar se ve en la mayoría RF amplificadores transistores, para los cuales IP3 es común 12-14 dB superior a la superior P1dB [12]. Otros tipos de amplificadores pueden mostrar mayores diferencias; en particular los amplificadores operativos (“op-amps”), para los cuales no existe una relación esencialmente consistente entre IP3 y P1dB. La interpretación y los obstáculos apropiados de la caracterización del sistema en términos de P1dB y IP3 son un tema permanente de la investigación [14].

11.2.5 La Intermodulación Segunda Orden

Se señaló en la sección anterior que entre los muchos productos indicados en la tabla 11.1, el IM3 productos a 2ω2 −ω1 y 2ω1 −ω2 otro producto de especial preocupación es el IM2 producto en ω2 −ω1. Por razones históricas, esta frecuencia se conoce a veces como la frecuencia de los golpes, y el asociado IM2 el producto es conocido como el producto de latidos. El producto de la vencida es a menudo una preocupación porque se produce relativamente cerca de DC, que (como veremos en el capítulo 15) es donde las etapas finales del procesamiento de señales analógicas (es decir, digitalización o demodulación) se realizan a menudo. En tales receptores el producto de la batida es propenso a interferir con la señal deseada en las etapas finales de la receptora.

La línea de desgarrada muestra la relación esperada de la Ecuación 11.18. Los puntos indican amplificadores y diamantes de una sola orden indican amplificadores diferenciales.

El producto de la ventosa se produce a una frecuencia relativamente baja porque la frecuencia de la ventosas es igual a la separación entre los tonos, que generalmente es pequeña en relación con la frecuencia central de la banda de pases. Como IM3, el producto de la batida tiende a ser relativamente fuerte, por lo tanto puede ser difícil suprimir este producto suficientemente utilizando el filtrado analógico – más sobre eso en capítulos posteriores.

11.2.6 La conversión AM-PM

En secciones anteriores hemos considerado sólo sinusoides de potencia constante. Cuando el poder en una señal varía, la no linealidad de un sistema puede manifestarse de maneras más complejas. Entre ellas se encuentra la conversión AM-PM. El concepto se explica como sigue: Considere una señal de amplitud modulada (AM) aplicada a dos puertos. El dos puertos puede ser arbitrariamente simple o complejo, pero asumamos por el bien de la ilustración que consiste en al menos un capacitor, y asumimos que la señal crea tensión suficiente en el capacitor que los efectos no lineales son aparentes. Recordando que la no linearidad es fundamentalmente la dependencia de respuesta sobre la entrada, esto significa que la capacitancia C del capacitor es una función de la tensión aplicada, y que esta variación en la capacitancia es significativa La impedancia de un capacitor es −j/ωC; por lo tanto, la reactancia de este capacitor varía con la magnitud de la señal de entrada, que varia según la modulación. Como también hay impedancias reales en el sistema, y dado que estas impedanciaes no varían significativamente o están variar independientemente de C, la respuesta fase del sistema debe ser de tiempo-varía. Así, la capacitancia no lineal es esencialmente convertir la señal de entrada modulada de amplitud en una señal que también contiene modulación de fase (PM). La conversión AM-PM también puede atribuirse a inductores (también reactancias), transistores (que exhiben impedancias terminales capacitivas a término) y ganar compresión relativa a las reactancias no lineales de forma independiente – todo lo que se hace necesaria para la respuesta del sistema

AM-PM Por lo general, la conversión no es motivo de preocupación AM las señales, desde las señales erróneas PM componente no afecta la información, que está representada en la amplitud. AM-PM La conversión no suele ser motivo de gran preocupación en los sistemas que utilizan FM o PSK, ya que estas señales tienen un modulo constante. Sin embargo, modulaciones digitales empleando modulación de portador sinusoidal con módulo no constante – sobre todo, QAM – realmente sufrir, como el PM componente distorsiona significativamente

blocks_es_mx.text: 11.2 Caracterización de la linealidad

El término linealidad, como se utiliza en la ingeniería moderna de radio, tiene varias interpretaciones posibles; algunas conducen a definiciones informales que pueden confundirse con los no iniciados. Comencemos con una definición formal y luego procedamos a algunas de las interpretaciones más comunes en el contexto de la ingeniería radio.
11.2.1 La linealidad como la independencia de la respuesta

Una definición formal de linearidad es la siguiente.1 Considere un sistema consistente en una sola cascada de dos puertos, o que consiste en una cascada de dos niveles que puede describirse como un solo dos puertos. Tal sistema se puede caracterizar en términos de su respuesta de impulso h(t), que es su salida cuando la entrada es la función Dirac delta δ(t).2 Cuando una señal x1(t) se aplica a este sistema,
donde “∗” denota la convolución. En un experimento separado, se aplica una señal x2(t) al mismo sistema, dando lugar a la salida
El sistema h(t) es formalmente lineal si, para cualquier constante a1 y a2:

donde x1(t), y1(t) x2(t), and y2(t) también satisfacen las ecuaciones anteriores. Esto también podría denominarse la definición de “scaling y superposición” de linearidad: Decimos que un sistema es lineal si su respuesta a los insumos uno a la vez nos dice todo lo que necesitamos saber sobre la respuesta del sistema a combinaciones lineales de esos insumos.
donde las cantidades de la maleta superior son Fourier transforma de las cantidades inferiores del caso, y, en particular, H(f) es la respuesta de frecuencia del sistema.

Ahora, ¿cómo se aplica esto a un RF sistema? x1(t) y x2(t), así como y1(t) y y2(t), pueden ser voltajes o corrientes, y h(t) puede ser una descripción de cualquier dos puertos, incluyendo cascadas de dos puertos. 11.1 y 11.2 son esencialmente declaraciones que el sistema no se ve afectado por la entrada. Un caso en el que esto es trivialmente cierto es el sistema “null” h(t) = δt) (equivalentemente, H(f) = 1), que es sólo un par de cables que conectan los terminales de entrada a los terminales de salida. En este caso es fácil verificar que Ecuaciones 11.1 y 11.2 aplicar, y también está claro que h(t) no depende de x(t). Un amplificador ideal puede ser modelado como h(t) = gδ(t) where g is a constant (equivallently, H(f) = g); again it’s clear that this is formally linear, and the response of the system does not depend on the input.

Para cualquier amplificador práctico, g no puede ser completamente independiente de la entrada. Por ejemplo, sólo mira hacia atrás a la Sección 10.3, donde se observa que el aumento de un amplificador transistor varía como una función del punto operativo. Cuando la corriente de entrada se aleja demasiado lejos del punto de funcionamiento, la corriente de salida se distorsiona significativamente por el cambio en β sobre el oscilación de señal de salida resultante. En efecto, g – no sólo y Es sólo en una gama relativamente pequeña alrededor del punto operativo que la ganancia aparente del amplificador es aproximadamente independiente de la entrada al amplificador. En esta región Ecuación 11.1 sostiene – aunque aproximadamente – y en esa región podemos razonablemente referirnos al amplificante como “linear”. Generalizando, es común referirse a un dispositivo de dos puertos como lineal si su función de transferencia es independiente – por lo menos aproximadamente – de Por el contrario, se dice que un doble puerto no es lineal si esta condición no puede razonablemente ser asumida.
11.2.2 La linealidad de sistemas con respuesta polinomio sin memoria

Un sistema sin memoria es uno en el que la salida no depende de los valores pasados de la entrada. Muchos dos puertos encontrados en la ingeniería radio son eléctricamente pequeños o dispersionless, y por lo tanto puede ser asumido como sin memoria. Las excepciones incluyen ciertos amplificadores de potencia (más sobre los que comienzan en la Sección 17.4).
Cualquier sistema que pueda describirse como un dos-puerto sin memoria tiene una respuesta que puede, en principio, ser descrita por la siguiente suma infinita:

11.2.6 La conversión AM-PM

En secciones anteriores hemos considerado sólo sinusoides de potencia constante. Cuando el poder en una señal varía, la no linealidad de un sistema puede manifestarse de maneras más complejas. Entre ellas se encuentra la conversión AM-PM. El concepto se explica como sigue: Considere una señal de amplitud modulada (AM) aplicada a dos puertos. El dos puertos puede ser arbitrariamente simple o complejo, pero asumamos por el bien de la ilustración que consiste en al menos un capacitor, y asumimos que la señal crea tensión suficiente en el capacitor que los efectos no lineales son aparentes. Recordando que la no linearidad es fundamentalmente la dependencia de respuesta sobre la entrada, esto significa que la capacitancia C del capacitor es una función de la tensión aplicada, y que esta variación en la capacitancia es significativa La impedancia de un capacitor es −j/ωC; por lo tanto, la reactancia de este capacitor varía con la magnitud de la señal de entrada, que varia según la modulación. Como también hay impedancias reales en el sistema, y dado que estas impedanciaes no varían significativamente o están variar independientemente de C, la respuesta fase del sistema debe ser de tiempo-varía. Así, la capacitancia no lineal es esencialmente convertir la señal de entrada modulada de amplitud en una señal que también contiene modulación de fase (PM). La conversión AM-PM también puede atribuirse a inductores (también reactancias), transistores (que exhiben impedancias terminales capacitivas a término) y ganar compresión relativa a las reactancias no lineales de forma independiente – todo lo que se hace necesaria para la respuesta del sistema

11.2 Characterization of Linearity

The term linearity, as it is used in modern radio engineering, has several possible interpretations; some leading to informal definitions that can be confusing to the uninitiated. Let us begin with a formal definition and then proceed to some of the more common interpretations in the context of radio engineering.

11.2.1 Linearity as Independence of Response

A formal definition of linearity is as follows.1 Consider a system consisting of a single two-port, or consisting of a two-port cascade which may be described as a single two-port. Such a system may be characterized in terms of its impulse response h(t), which is its output when the input is the Dirac delta function δ(t).2 When a signal x1(t) is applied to this system, the output is given by

y1(t) = x1(t) ∗h(t)

where “∗” denotes convolution. In a separate experiment, a signal x2(t) is applied to the same system, resulting in output

y2(t) = x2(t) ∗h(t)

The system h(t) is formally linear if, for any constants a1 and a2:

[a1x1(t) + a2x2(t)] ∗h(t) = a1y1(t) + a2y2(t)
(11.1)

where x1(t), y1(t), x2(t), and y2(t) also satisfy the previous equations. This might also be referred to as the “scaling and superposition” definition of linearity: We say a system is linear if its response to inputs one at a time tells us everything we need to know about the system’s response to linear combinations of those inputs. The frequency domain version of the “scaling and superposition” definition of linearity is

[a1X1(f) + a2X2(f)] H(f) = a1Y1(t) + a2Y2(t)
(11.2)

where the upper-case quantities are Fourier transforms of the lower case quantities, and, in particular, H(f) is the frequency response of the system.

Now, how does this apply to an RF system? x1(t) and x2(t), as well as y1(t) and y2(t), may be either voltages or currents, and h(t) can be a description of any two-port, including cascades of two-ports. Equations 11.1 and 11.2 are essentially statements that the system is not affected by the input. A case where this is trivially true is the “null” system h(t) = δ(t) (equivalently, H(f) = 1), which is just a pair of wires connecting the input terminals to the output terminals. In this case it’s easy to verify that Equations 11.1 and 11.2 apply, and it’s also clear that h(t) does not depend on x(t). An ideal amplifier can be modeled as h(t) = gδ(t) where g is a constant (equivalently, H(f) = g); again it’s clear that this is formally linear, and the response of the system does not depend on the input.

For any practical amplifier, g cannot be completely independent of the input. For an example, just look back to Section 10.3, where it is noted that the gain of a transistor amplifier varies as a function of the operating point. When the input current strays too far from the operating point, the output current becomes significantly distorted by the change in β over the resulting output signal swing. In effect, g – not just y(t) – becomes a function of x(t). It is only in a relatively small range around the operating point that the apparent gain of the amplifier is approximately independent of the input to the amplifier. In this region Equation 11.1 holds – albeit approximately – and in that region we may reasonably refer to the amplifier as “linear”. Generalizing, it is common to refer to a two-port device as linear if it’s transfer function is independent – at least approximately – of its input. Conversely, a two-port is said to be non-linear if this condition cannot reasonably be assumed.

11.2.2 Linearity of Systems with Memoryless Polynomial Response

A memoryless system is one in which the output does not depend on past values of the input. Many two-ports encountered in radio engineering are either electrically small or dispersionless, and thus may be assumed to be memoryless. Exceptions include certain power amplifiers (more on those beginning in Section 17.4).

Any system that can be described as a memoryless two-port has a response which can, in principle, be described by the following infinite sum:

y(t) = a0 + a1x(t) + a2x2(t) + a3x3(t) + ...
(11.3)

1Hopefully this is familiar from an undergraduate course in signals and systems; if not, no worries. 2Reminder: δ(t) is defined as follows: δ(t) = 0 for t̸ = 0, and R +∞

−∞δ(t)dt = 1.

where x(t) is the input signal (voltage or current as appropriate), y(t) is the output signal (again, voltage or current, as appropriate), and the an’s are constants. This relationship may be viewed as a Taylor series representation, which provides a method for computing the coefficients. In this form, the system is seen to be formally linear when all coefficients except a1 are zero; in this case, the gain is a1. If a0̸ = 0, then the system can not satisfy the “scaling and superposition” definition of linearity. The remaining term, known as the fundamental and associated with a1, represents the nominally linear output and is located at the input frequency.

11.2.3 Gain Compression

Turning our attention to the fundamental, note that the apparent gain is a1 + (3a3/4)A2, whereas the nominal linear gain is simply a1. Practical devices are compressive, meaning they have apparent gain which decreases with increasing input magnitude, as illustrated in Figure 11.1.3 From this we can infer that a1 and a3 have opposite sign. This phenomenon is referred to as gain compression or simply compression.

A useful characterization of a compressive system is the 1-dB compression point. This metric may be expressed with respect to the input or the output. The input 1-dB compression point A1dB is defined as the magnitude of x(t) for which the apparent gain of the fundamental is 1 dB less than the nominal linear gain. For the system model and stimulus considered above, this condition may be expressed mathematically as

It should be no surprise that to make A1dB large, the ratio a1/a3 must be large. A little surprising is that A1dB does not depend on a2.

This metric may also be expressed with respect to the output. The output 1-dB compression point is defined as the magnitude of the output for which the apparent gain of the fundamental is 1 dB less than the nominal linear gain. This is simply |a1| A1dB; i.e., the input and output 1-dB compression points are related by the magnitude of the nominal linear gain a1.

As formulated above, the 1 dB compression point is expressed in terms of either voltage or current. The 1 dB compression point may also be expressed in terms of power, since all three quantities (voltage, current, and power) are related by impedance. Power units are typically more convenient for measurement, and manufacturer’s data sheets typically use power quantities. The output 1 dB compression point in power units is typically represented by the symbol P1dB, P1, or OP1 (“O” for output). The input 1 dB compression is sometimes represented by the symbol IP1, and is related to the output 1 dB compression point by the power gain; i.e., OP1 = G · IP1. Datasheets frequently do not make the distinction between the input- and output-referred quantities, in which case it is typically the output-referred quantity that is indicated; however, it is always a good idea to check.

Because common emitter bipolar transistor amplifiers figure prominently in RF system design, it is useful to be aware of some rules-of-thumb applicable to these devices. Because bipolar transistors are essentially controlled current sources, the linearity depends most directly on collector bias current IC. A common-emitter amplifier with a collector bias current of 20 mA and which is terminated into 50Ωwill typically have an output 1 dB compression point of about +10 dBm. Generally, decreasing the collector bias current or decreasing load impedance tends to decrease P1.

FET amplifiers used for as small-signal amplifiers typically have have lower P1 when designed for optimal or near-optimal noise figure, which is one reason why bipolar transistors continue to be used in some low-noise applications at UHF and above.

11.2.4 Intermodulation; Third-Order Intermodulation

In the previous section we assumed a single sinusoid at the input. A slightly more complicated input is two sinusoids:

x(t) = A1 cos ω1t + A2 cos ω2t
(11.15)

Following the procedure of the previous section, we apply this input to the system described by Equation 11.10. As in the previous section, it is useful to fully expand the result and then gather terms by frequency. The algebra is straightforward, but a bit tedious. The results are summarized in Table 11.1. Note that the output products include not only the fundamentals and their harmonics, but now also additional products whose frequencies depend on both ω1 and ω2. These additional products are referred to as intermodulation. Intermodulation products associated with a2 are known as second-order intermodulation (IM2) and those associated with a3 are known as third-order intermodulation (IM3).

As noted in Table 11.1 the fundamental (desired) output for each tone is modified by not only a3 (as in the single-tone case), but now also by a2 and by the magnitude of the other tone. Among all of the remaining products, the two of greatest concern are usually the IM3 products at 2ω1 −ω2 and 2ω2 −ω1. This is because the separation between each of these products and the nearest fundamental is equal to the separation between the fundamentals; e.g., (2ω2 −ω1) −ω2 = ω2 −ω1. If both fundamentals appear in the same passband, then these IM3 products are likely to be either also in the passband, or close enough to present a filter design challenge.

Not only are the IM3 products potentially difficult to filter out, but they are also potentially quite large. From Table 11.1 we see that the magnitude of an IM3 product for equal-magnitude fundamentals (e.g., A1 = A2 = A) is 3a3A3/4; that is, each IM3 product is proportional to A3, whereas the nominal (linear) fundamental output is proportional to A. In other words: When A increases by a factor of α, the IM3 products increase by a factor of α3. For this reason, the vulnerability of system to IM3 is often characterized using a quantity known as the third-order intercept point (IP3), illustrated in Figure 11.2. The concept is as follows: The IM3 products increase more quickly with increasing |A| than do the fundamentals themselves; therefore for some value of |A| the magnitudes of the IM3 products should in principle be equal to the magnitudes of the ideal (linear) fundamental products. The value of |A| at which this occurs is the input IP3 (IIP3), and the associated value of |a1A| is the output IP3 (OIP3).

Note that IP3 is not the value of |A| for which the magnitude of the IM3 is equal to the actual (e.g., compressed) magnitude of the fundamental output. Therefore, IP3 can not be measured “directly” in the sense of increasing |A| until the IM3 products are equal to the fundamentals and taking that value of |A| to be the IIP3. (Not only is this not consistent with the definition, but it is potentially dangerous to the device under test!) Nevertheless IP3 may be easily (and safely) measured as follows: Using relatively low input levels, one measures the nominal linear gain as the slope of the output-to-input power curve, and also the IM3 for the same input levels. When plotted on a log-log plot, these curves may be linearly-extrapolated to the point where they meet, as shown in Figure 11.2.

As is the case for 1 dB compression point, IP3 is commonly expressed in power units, OIP3 = G · IIP3, and datasheets usually report the output-referred quantity (OIP3). The IIP3 of typical receivers ranges from about −30 dBm to +10 dBm, depending on the application. For example, a typical IIP3 specification for a cellular GSM receiver is −18 dBm, and a typical specification for a cellular CDMA receiver is −13 dBm. Linearity specifications for receivers in HF and LMR applications tend to be much higher.

Remarkably, it turns out that the third-order intercept point is approximately 10 dB above the 1-dB compression point, independently of the model parameters (i.e., the an’s) or the magnitude of the applied tones. This observation provides a rough estimate of IP3 from P1 and vice-versa, knowing nothing else about the device.

In practice one finds Equation 11.18 is not a bad guess, but caveats apply. Passive non-linear devices are often well-modeled as third-order compressive, in which case Equation 11.18 is a good estimate. For active devices, this is typically not a safe assumption. To demonstrate, Figure 11.3 shows how this works out for modern commercially-available MMIC amplifiers: We find that Equation 11.18 underestimates IP3 given P1dB by somewhere between 1 dB and 5 dB on average, with the largest error occurring for the largest values of IP3. From this we can conclude that the linearity of commercially-available MMIC amplifiers is not always well-modeled as third-order compressive, so Equation 11.18 is, at best, a rough bound for these devices. See [12] for more on this topic.

Similar behavior is seen in most RF transistor amplifiers, for which IP3 is commonly 12-14 dB greater than P1dB [12]. Other types of amplifers may exhibit greater differences; in particular operational amplifiers (“op-amps”), for which there is essentially no consistent relationship between IP3 and P1dB. The proper interpretation and pitfalls of system characterization in terms of P1dB and IP3 are a continuing topic of research [14].

11.2.5 Second-Order Intermodulation

It was noted in the previous section that among the many products indicated in Table 11.1, the IM3 products at 2ω2 −ω1 and 2ω1 −ω2 were of particular concern. Another product of particular concern is the IM2 product at ω2 −ω1. For historical reasons, this frequency is sometimes referred to as the beat frequency, and the associated IM2 product is thus known as the beat product. The beat product is often a concern because it occurs relatively close to DC, which (as we shall see in Chapter 15) is where the final stages of analog signal processing (i.e., digitization or demodulation) are often performed. In such receivers the beat product is prone to interfere with the desired signal in the final stages of the receiver.

Figure 11.3: Relationship between input P1dB and IIP3 from a survey of 271 commercially-available MMIC amplifiers at 50 MHz operated at the recommended bias conditions, determined from datasheets. The dashed line shows the expected relationship from Equation 11.18. Dots indicate single-ended amplifiers and diamonds indicate differential amplifiers.

The beat product occurs at a relatively low frequency because the beat frequency is equal to the separation between the tones, which is generally small relative to the center frequency of the passband. Like IM3, the beat product tends to be relatively strong, therefore it may be difficult to suppress this product sufficiently using analog filtering – more on that in later chapters.

From Table 11.1 we see that the magnitude of the beat and sum products for equal-magnitude fundamentals is a2A2/2; that is, thes products are proportional to A2, whereas the nominal (linear) fundamental output is proportional to A. Therefore, when A increases by a factor of α, the beat product increases by a factor of α2. For this reason, the vulnerability of system to the beat product is often characterized using a quantity known as the second-order intercept point (IP2), illustrated in Figure 11.4. The concept is exactly analogous to IP3: The input IP2 (IIP2) is the value for which |A1| = |A2| = |A| results in a product having magnitude equal to the ideal (linear) fundamental product(s).4 The associated value of |a1A| is the output IP2 (OIP2). As in the case of IP3, IP2 is not the value of |A| for which the magnitude of the IM2 is equal to the actual (e.g., compressed) magnitude of the fundamental output; nevertheless IP2 may be conveniently measured using the same low-level extrapolation technique described in the previous section (and as implied by Figure 11.4).

11.2.6 AM-PM Conversion

In previous sections we have considered only constant-power sinusoids. When the power in a signal varies, the non-linearity of a system may manifest in more complex ways. Primary among these is AM-PM conversion. The concept can be explained as follows: Consider an amplitude-modulated (AM) signal applied to a two-port. The two-port may be arbitrarily simple or complex, but let us assume for the sake of illustration that it consists of at least one capacitor, and let us assume that the signal creates sufficient voltage across the capacitor that non-linear effects are apparent. Recalling that non-linearity is fundamentally the dependence of response on input, this means that the capacitance C of the capacitor is a function of the applied voltage, and that this variation in capacitance is significant. The impedance of a capacitor is −j/ωC; therefore the reactance of this capacitor varies with the input signal magnitude, which is varying due to the modulation. Since there are also real-valued impedances in the system, and since these impedances are either not varying significantly or are varying independently of C, the phase response of the system must be time-varying. Thus, the non-linear capacitance is essentially converting the amplitude-modulated input signal into a signal which also contains phase modulation (PM). AM-PM conversion can also be attributed to inductors (also reactances), transistors (which exhibit capacitive terminal-to-terminal impedances), and gain compression relative to independently-nonlinear reactances – all that is needed for the system phase response to become a function of the input magnitude.

AM-PM conversion is typically not a concern for AM signals, since the erroneous PM component does not affect the information, which is represented in the amplitude. AM-PM conversion is also typically not of much concern in systems using FM or PSK, since these signals have constant modulus. However digital modulations employing sinusoidal carrier modulation with non-constant modulus – most notably, QAM – really suffer, as the PM component significantly distorts

11.5.text:
11.5 Stage/Cascade Analysis; Significance of Stage Order
In Section 4.4.2, we worked out a procedure for determining t he sensitivity of a cascade of two-ports given the sensitivi ty
(specifically, noise figure or equivalent temperature) of th e constituent stages. Similarly, in earlier sections of thi s chapter
we have worked out procedures for determining the linearity of cascades of two-ports given the linearity (specifically, IIP3
and IIP2) of the constituent stages. Under the same assumptions the c ascade gain is simply the product of the stage gains;
that is
G =G1G2G3... (11.33)
Stage/cascade analysis typically consists of constructin g a table of stage gain, linearity, and sensitivity and the
corresponding quantities for the associated cascade. This type of analysis is known by many other names, and exists in
many different variants and presentations. The approach pr esented here is sufficiently generic that it should apply to m ost
other forms that the reader is likely to encounter. The purpo se of this analysis is to determine the impact of individual
stages on the overall performance, thereby providing insig ht into how best to arrange the stages, and how to specify the
stage characteristics when that flexibility exists. The con cept is most easily demonstrated by example:
Example 11.3. An LMR base station has a receive path consisting of a mast-mo unted antenna separated by a long
cable having 10 dB loss at the frequency of interest. The rece iver consists of two parts: A front end including the
antenna, cable, and two amplifiers; and a back end consisting of the rest of the receiver. The front end is specified to
have a gain of 35 dB. To accomplish this, two amplifiers are pro vided. Amplifier 1 has 15 dB gain, +5 dBm OIP 3,
and 4 dB noise figure. Amplifier 2 has 30 dB gain, +10 dB OIP 3, and 8 dB noise figure. The noise figure of the front
end is required to be 7 dB or better. Assume perfect impedance matching, and either amplifier may be installed at the
antenna side or receiver side of the cable. Design the front e nd.
Solution: This is a classic problem in radio engineering: Y ou have mult iple components and you need to arrange
them to achieve acceptable overall performance. Since this is a receiver problem, the relevant performance
considerations are sensitivity and linearity. In this appl ication, linearity is commonly characterized in terms of II P3,
whereas sensitivity is commonly characterized in terms of n oise figure or system temperature. The linearity of the
amplifiers is specified in terms of OIP 3 as opposed to IIP 3, but this poses no particular difficulty since IIP 3 is related
to OIP3 by the gain; thus we find IIP 3 =− 10 dBm and− 20 dBm for Amplifiers 1 and 2 respectively.

11.5 Análisis por etapas y de la cascada: importancia del orden de las etapas

En la Sección 4.4.2, hemos elaborado un procedimiento para determinar la sensibilidad de una cascada de dos puertos dada la sensibilidad (específicamente, figura de ruido o temperatura equivalente) de las etapas constitutivas. De igual modo, en secciones anteriores de este capítulo hemos elaborado procedimientos para determinar la linealidad de cascadas de dos puertos dado la linearidad (específico, IIP3 y IIP2) de las etapas constituyentes. Bajo las mismas suposiciones, la ganancia de cascada es simplemente el producto de los avances en estadio; es decir,

G = G1 G2 G3 ...
(11.33)

El análisis de estadio/cascada consiste típicamente en construir una tabla de ganancia, linealidad y sensibilidad y las cantidades correspondientes para la cascada asociada. Este tipo de análisis es conocido por muchos otros nombres, y existe en muchas variantes y presentaciones diferentes.El enfoque presentado aquí es suficientemente genérico que debe aplicar a la mayoría de otras formas que el lector probablemente encuentre. El objetivo de este análisis es determinar el impacto de las etapas individuales en el rendimiento general, proporcionando así información sobre la mejor manera de organizar las etapas y cómo especificar las características de la etapa cuando existe esa flexibilidad.El concepto se demuestra con mayor facilidad por ejemplo:

Ejemplo 11.3. LMR estación base tiene un camino de recepción que consiste en una antena montada en el mástil separada por un cable largo 10 dB pérdida a la frecuencia de interés. El receptor consta de dos partes: Un extremo frontal incluyendo la antena, cable y dos amplificadores; y un extremo posterior que consiste del resto del receptor. El extremo frontal se especifica para tener una ganancia de 35 dBPara lograr esto, se proporcionan dos amplificadores. 1 ha tenido 15 dB Ganancia, +5 dBm OIP3, y 4 dB figura de ruido. Amplificador 2 tiene ganancia 30 dB, +10 dB OIP3, y 8 dB. La figura de ruido del extremo frontal es necesaria para ser 7 dB o mejor. Asume perfecto impedance matching, y cualquiera amplificador puede ser instalado en el lado de la antena o receptor del cable. Diseñar el extremo delantero.

Solución: Este es un problema clásico en la ingeniería de radio: Usted tiene múltiples componentes y necesita organizarlos para lograr un rendimiento global aceptable. Como este es un problema receptor, las consideraciones de rendimiento relevantes son sensibilidad y linealidad. En esta aplicación, la linealidad se caracteriza comúnmente en términos de IIP3, mientras que la sensibilidad se caracteriza común en términos de figura de ruido o temperatura del sistema. La linealidad de los amplificadores se especifica en términos de OIP3 en contra de IIP3, pero esto no plantea ninguna dificultad particular desde IIP3 está relacionado con OIP3 por la ganancia; así encontramos IIP3 = −10 dBm y −20 dBm para amplificadores 1 y 2 la figura de ruido del amplificador 2 es más grande que la figura de ruido especificada para el extremo frontal, por lo que no habrá solución en la que amplificador 2 precedes Amplificador 1 en la cascada. Esto deja tres posibilidades: (1) El cable viene primero, y ambos amplificadores están en el lado receptor; (2) Amplificador 1 es montado en masa, seguido por el cable, seguido por amplificador 2, y (3) Amplificadores 1 y 2 son ambos montados en masa, seguida por el cable. Opción 1 vale la pena considerar sólo si el ruido del extremo delantero es menos Si asumimos que la temperatura física del cable es igual a la temperatura de referencia de la figura de ruido T0, entonces la figura de ruido del cable es simplemente la reciproca de la ganancia del cable (Si esto no está claro, vea Ecuación 4.19 y texto asociado). IEEE- temperatura de referencia estándar T0 = 290 K es una conjetura razonable para la temperatura física del cable, así que tomaremos la figura de ruido del cable para ser 10 dB. Esto es más grande que 7 dB, así que Opción 1 está fuera. Para elegir entre Opciones 2 y 3, es útil preparar un análisis de fase-cascada para cada opción, como se muestra en Tablas 11.2 y 11.3. Comparando los resultados, se observa un dilema familiar: Option 2 ofrece una mejor linealidad (IIP3), pero la opción 2 ofrece una mejor sensibilidad (F). Si interpretamos el requisito de la figura de ruido del estado problemático como una limitación (en oposición a la figura de sonido como algo que se debe optimizar), entonces Option 1 es preferido ya que cumple con la especificación de la figura del ruido al tiempo que optimiza el parámetro restante; es decir, cascada IIP3. En la práctica, probablemente se tomaría una decisión examinando las conclusiones de la cascada IIP3 y F de ambas opciones en el contexto de otras consideraciones a nivel de sistema, tal vez como parte de un proceso de diseño del sistema iterativo.

Tenga en cuenta que las Tablas 11.2 y 11.3 también muestran la temperatura de ruido equivalente en estadio y cascada. Específicamente, estas son las temperaturas de ruido equivalentes referenciadas a entrada.¿Qué valor hay en esto? Hay dos razones por las que esto es potencialmente útil. Primero, recuerde que asumimos que la temperatura física del cable era igual a la temperatura de referencia estándar IEEE para la figura de ruido, T0. En el ejemplo 4.4 señalamos que esta es una aproximación bastante buena sobre una amplia gama de temperaturas físicas. Sin embargo, si el cable está a una temperatura no cercana a T0 (tal vez se enrolla en una caja con electrónica caliente), es un poco más sencillo hacer la computación de sensibilidad en términos de temperatura de ruido, y luego

Solución: En primer lugar, recuerde de la Sección 4.5 que la temperatura de la antena TA es una descripción de la cantidad de ruido externo proveniente de la antena, y que 400 K es bastante típico para las aplicaciones de radio móvil en las bandas VHF-UHF. Recordar también de la Sección 7.4 que una manera conveniente de caracterizar la sensibilidad general, contando el ruido externo, es la temperatura del sistema. La temperatura del sistema Tsys es simplemente la suma de TA y la temperatura de ruido equivalente de entrada del extremo frontal, que se encontró con 1008 K y 487 K para Opciones 1 y 2 respectivamente. Así Tsys es 1408 K para Option 1 y 887 K para la opción 2. Con estos valores ahora podríamos proceder con el análisis de enlaces de radio como se describe en la sección 7.6.

El ejemplo anterior también puede resolverse comenzando con la figura de ruido cascada. Sin embargo, este enfoque requiere más trabajo porque se expresa la figura de ruido respecto a una temperatura de ruido predeterminada de entrada; es decir, T0, que normalmente se toma como 290 K. Por otro lado, si TA resulta ser ≈T0, entonces el enfoque de la figura del ruido es más fácil: La densidad espectral de potencia del ruido que se produce en la salida de la cascada es simplemente kT0FG (donde F y G son los valores de cascada), por lo que Tsys (ser referido por entrada) es simplemente T0F. Debido a que este es un cálculo tan simple, y debido a que es frecuentemente difícil determinar la temperatura real de la antena, es muy común asumir Tsys = T0F; sin embargo esto conduce a un error potencialmente muy grande a menos TA ∼= T0, TA ≪T0 (para que el ruido externo pueda ser descuidado).

11.5 Stage/Cascade Analysis; Significance of Stage Order

In Section 4.4.2, we worked out a procedure for determining the sensitivity of a cascade of two-ports given the sensitivity (specifically, noise figure or equivalent temperature) of the constituent stages. Similarly, in earlier sections of this chapter we have worked out procedures for determining the linearity of cascades of two-ports given the linearity (specifically, IIP3 and IIP2) of the constituent stages. Under the same assumptions the cascade gain is simply the product of the stage gains; that is

G = G1 G2 G3 ...
(11.33)

Stage/cascade analysis typically consists of constructing a table of stage gain, linearity, and sensitivity and the corresponding quantities for the associated cascade. This type of analysis is known by many other names, and exists in many different variants and presentations. The approach presented here is sufficiently generic that it should apply to most other forms that the reader is likely to encounter. The purpose of this analysis is to determine the impact of individual stages on the overall performance, thereby providing insight into how best to arrange the stages, and how to specify the stage characteristics when that flexibility exists. The concept is most easily demonstrated by example:

Example 11.3. An LMR base station has a receive path consisting of a mast-mounted antenna separated by a long cable having 10 dB loss at the frequency of interest. The receiver consists of two parts: A front end including the antenna, cable, and two amplifiers; and a back end consisting of the rest of the receiver. The front end is specified to have a gain of 35 dB. To accomplish this, two amplifiers are provided. Amplifier 1 has 15 dB gain, +5 dBm OIP3, and 4 dB noise figure. Amplifier 2 has 30 dB gain, +10 dB OIP3, and 8 dB noise figure. The noise figure of the front end is required to be 7 dB or better. Assume perfect impedance matching, and either amplifier may be installed at the antenna side or receiver side of the cable. Design the front end.

Solution: This is a classic problem in radio engineering: You have multiple components and you need to arrange them to achieve acceptable overall performance. Since this is a receiver problem, the relevant performance considerations are sensitivity and linearity. In this application, linearity is commonly characterized in terms of IIP3, whereas sensitivity is commonly characterized in terms of noise figure or system temperature. The linearity of the amplifiers is specified in terms of OIP3 as opposed to IIP3, but this poses no particular difficulty since IIP3 is related to OIP3 by the gain; thus we find IIP3 = −10 dBm and −20 dBm for Amplifiers 1 and 2 respectively. The noise figure of Amplifier 2 is larger than the noise figure specified for the front end, so there will be no solution in which Amplifier 2 precedes Amplifier 1 in the cascade. This leaves three possibilities: (1) The cable comes first, and both amplifiers are on the receiver side; (2) Amplifier 1 is mast-mounted, followed by the cable, followed by Amplifier 2, and (3) Amplifiers 1 and 2 are both mast-mounted, followed by the cable. Option 1 is worth considering only if the noise figure of the cable is less than the specified noise figure of the front end. If we assume the physical temperature of the cable is equal to the noise figure reference temperature T0, then the noise figure of the cable is simply the reciprocal of the gain of the cable (If this is not clear, see Equation 4.19 and associated text). The IEEE-standard reference temperature T0 = 290 K is a reasonable guess for the physical temperature of the cable, so we’ll take the noise figure of the cable to be 10 dB. This is greater than 7 dB, so Option 1 is out. To choose between Options 2 and 3, it is useful to prepare a stage-cascade analysis for each option, as shown in Tables 11.2 and 11.3. Comparing the results, a familiar dilemma is apparent: Option 2 offers better linearity (IIP3), but Option 2 offers better sensitivity (F). If we interpret the noise figure requirement from the problem statement as a constraint (as opposed to noise figure as being something to be optimized), then Option 1 is preferred since it meets the noise figure specification while optimizing the remaining parameter; i.e., cascade IIP3. In practice, a decision would probably be made by considering the cascade IIP3 and F findings from both options in the context of other system-level considerations, perhaps as part of an iterative system design process.

Note that Tables 11.2 and 11.3 also show the stage and cascade equivalent noise temperatures. Specifically, these are the input-referred equivalent noise temperatures. What value is there in this? There are two reasons why this is potentially useful. First, recall that we assumed the physical temperature of the cable was equal to the IEEE standard reference temperature for noise figure, T0. We noted in Example 4.4 that this is a pretty good approximation over a broad range of physical temperatures. However if the cable is at a temperature not close to T0 (perhaps it is coiled up in a box with hot electronics), it is a little more straightforward to do the sensitivity computation in terms of noise temperature, and then

Example 11.4. Continuing Example 11.3, consider the contribution of external noise to the sensitivity of front end Options 1 and 2. Work this out for an antenna temperature of 400 K.

Solution: First, recall from Section 4.5 that antenna temperature TA is a description of the amount of external noise delivered from the antenna, and that 400 K is pretty typical for mobile radio applications in the VHF-UHF bands. Recall also from Section 7.4 that a convenient way to characterize the overall sensitivity, accounting for external noise, is system temperature. The system temperature Tsys is simply the sum of TA and the input-referred equivalent noise temperature of the front end, which was found to be 1008 K and 487 K for Options 1 and 2 respectively. Thus Tsys is 1408 K for Option 1 and 887 K for Option 2. With these values we could now proceed with radio link analysis as described in Section 7.6.

The above example can also be solved beginning with the cascade noise figure. However this approach requires more work because noise figure is expressed with respect to a pre-determined input noise temperature; namely T0, which is typically taken to be 290 K. On the other hand, if TA just happens to be ≈T0, then the noise figure approach is actually easier: The noise power spectral density delivered at the output of the cascade is simply kT0FG (where F and G are the cascade values), so Tsys (being input-referred) is simply T0F. Because this is such a simple calculation, and because it is frequently difficult to determine the actual antenna temperature, it is very common to assume Tsys = T0F; however this leads to potentially very large error unless TA ∼= T0, or TA ≪T0 (so that external noise may be neglected).

11.6 Other Common Characterizations of Sensitivity
It was stated in Chapter 1 that we would find that receiver desi gn was essentially a three-way tradeoff between sensitivit y,
dynamic range, and bandwidth. We are now almost ready to quan tify the first two elements of this tradeoff. First, it is
useful to make two additional definitions, both related to se nsitivity. These are minimum discernible signal and noise floor.


11.6. OTHER COMMON CHARACTERIZA TIONS OF SENSITIVITY 295
11.6.1 Minimum Discernible Signal (MDS): Concept and Zero-Inp ut-Noise Expressions
In Section 7.5 we defined “formal sensitivity” as the inciden t power density of a radio wave required to achieve a specified
signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) at the input of a detector or dem odulator. We also noted that there are many alternative
definitions which are more or less appropriate depending on t he application. Let us now consider one of the alternative
definitions, known as minimum discernible signal (MDS).7 The MDS of a two-port (including a cascade of two-ports) is
the signal power applied to the input which results in a speci fied SNR at the output, assuming perfect impedance matching
at input and output, and assuming the bandwidth of the two-po rt is at least as large as the bandwidth of the signal. The
specified SNR is typically 1, and this will be our definition, b ut the reader should be aware that it is not uncommon to
define MDS to correspond to an SNR of 2, 3 dB (which is not exactl y 2), 10 dB, or other values. The reader should also
note that MDS is sometimes defined so as to account for a non-ze ro noise power applied to the input – more on that in the
next section. Summarizing: We shall initially assume a defin ition that assumes SNR = 1 and no noise entering from the
input.
MDS is useful primarily because it can be easily measured in a laboratory, since the effect of antennas and variable
external noise need not be considered. Here’s an example:
Example 11.5. A signal generator is applied to the input of a two-port casca de, and a power meter is attached to the
output of the cascade. It is found that an RF tone at − 127 dBm at the input results in a reading of +5 dBm on the
power meter. When the tone is turned off, the power meter reads +2 dBm. What is the MDS? Assume the signal
generator contributes negligible noise.
Solution: When the tone is turned off, the power meter is indicating the o utput-referred internal noise of the cascade.
Let’s call this quantity N . When the tone is turned on, the power meter is reading S +N whereS is the
output-referred signal power. (This of course assumes that the cascade remains utterly linear when the tone is turned
on; i.e.,N does not change once the signal is applied.) The ratio of the t wo readings is 3 dB∼
= 2; therefore
(S +N )/N ∼
= 2. Note (S +N )/N =S/N + 1 = SNR + 1, so we find that SNR = 1. Therefore MDS is (in this
case) equal to the applied power,− 127 dBm.
One can also calculate MDS from the cascade parameters. The o utput-referred internal noise power is N =kTeqBG
whereB is bandwidth and G is cascade gain. The output-referred signal power when the i nput power is equal to the MDS
isS = MDS·G. If the input power is equal to the MDS, then the output SNR is e qual to 1; i.e., kTeqBG = MDS·G.
Thus:
MDS =kTeqB (11.34)
This may also be expressed in terms of the cascade noise facto rF :
MDS =kT0 (F− 1)B (11.35)
where, as usual, T0 is the noise temperature used to define noise figure, and this i s usually, but not always, chosen to be the
IEEE standard value of 290 K.
11.6.2 Minimum Discernible Signal (MDS): Non-Zero-Input-Noi se Expressions
Equation 11.34 indicates that the zero-input-noise definit ion of MDS is really just another way of indicating the equiva lent
noise temperature of the receiver. This is not exactly the sa me as sensitivity, since sensitivity is also affected by ext ernal
noise applied to the input, which we assume to be zero in the pr evious section. The definition of MDS may be modified to
account for this by changing Equation 11.34 as follows:
MDS =kTsysB =k (Tin +Teq)B (11.36)
7This is sometimes written minimum detectable signal .


296 CHAPTER 11. LINEARITY , MULTISTAGE ANAL YSIS, AND DYNAMIC RANGE
whereTin is the noise temperature applied at the input; for example, Tin =TA if the input is connected to an antenna.
This raises the question of what value to use for Tin, since this is now intrinsic to the definition. One approach i s to specify
a value ofTin that corresponds to a value which is expected or typical when the two-port – which we might as well call a
“receiver” in this case – is in operation. However, it is very common to arbitrarily assume Tin =T0 for this purpose, as
noted in the last paragraph of Section 11.5. Of course it is pr etty uncommon for Tin to actually be equal to T0 – even
approximately – so this form of the definition is no less arbit rary than the zero-input-noise (Tin = 0) definition.
One nice feature of the Tin =T0 definition is a convenient simplification of the math, since i n this case we have
MDS =k (T0 +Teq)B =kT0B +kTeqB =kT0B +kT0 (F− 1)B
which reduces to
MDS =kT0FB assuming Tin =T0 (11.37)
This equation is readily expressible in a popular decibel fo rm:
MDS [dBm]∼
=− 174 dBm/Hz +F [dB] + 10 log10B (11.38)
where “dBm/Hz” is shorthand for “dB(mW/Hz)”. It should also b e noted that this definition of MDS is usually
approximately equal to the zero-input-noise definition if o utput-referred external noise is small compared to
output-referred internal noise (i.e., F is very large), since in that case it doesn’t matter what you a ssume about the external
noise.
Be careful to avoid the following pitfall: Given F you assume Equation 11.37 gives you the in situ sensitivity of the
receiver. This is clearly not true, since again the noise inp ut to the receiver may be (probably is!) very different from
− 174 dBm/Hz. Recall we noted precisely this type of error when dis cussing link budgets in Chapter 7 (see Section 7.6).
In summary, MDS defined in this manner is not really useful for evaluating in situ sensitivity; instead it’s utility is in
relating internal noise characteristics to sensitivity in laboratory conditions and other situations where it is conv enient to
specify a “standard” external noise condition.
Example 11.6. The bandwidth and noise figure of a receiver are 30 kHz and 5 dB, respectively. (a) What is the MDS
assuming the zero-input-noise definition? (b) What is the MDS assuming theTin =T0 definition?
Solution: NoteB = 30 kHz andF = 5 dB = 3. 2. For (a), we have from Equation 11.35 that MDS =
2. 60× 10− 16 W =− 125. 9 dBm. For (b), we have from Equation 11.37 that MDS = 3. 80× 10− 16 W =− 124. 2 dBm.
Note that the receiver is no less sensitive; it is simply that we have defined the input noise condition differently. In
case (b) we may also use Equation 11.38; then we find as expecte d:
MDS∼
=− 174 dBm/Hz + 5 dB + 44. 8 dB (Hz) =− 124. 2 dBm
Example 11.7. In Example 11.5, assume the bandwidth is 30 kHz. What is the noi se figure?
Solution: Assuming the noise figure was defined with respect to T0 = 290 K, then Equation 11.35 gives us
F = MDS +kT0B
kT0B (11.39)
MDS is− 127 dBm, andkT0B =− 129. 2 dBm, so we have
F = MDS +kT0B
kT0B = 2. 66 = 4. 2 dB (11.40)
We must not use Equation 11.37 to solve this problem, since it ’s assumption about the in situ input noise is incorrect.

the apparent level of the signal is independent of ∆B as long as the signal bandwidth is less than ∆B.
11.6.3 Noise Floor
V ery often the bandwidth of the signal (or signals) of intere st are less than the bandwidth of the receiver, resulting in a
situation such as the one shown in Figure 11.8. We have seen th is above: The signal is a tone (taken to mean that the signal
bandwidth is smaller than the spectral resolution), yet the bandwidth is 30 kHz. This realization leads us to the concept of
a noise floor. The noise floor is best defined as the average power spectral d ensity of the noise in the central region of the
passband, where the noise power spectral density is relativ ely flat. So, in Example 11.7, this is kTeqG =kT0(F− 1)G
referred to output, which is kT0(F− 1) =− 171. 8 dBm/Hz referred to input. An alternative and very common des cription
of the noise floor is in terms of power within a specified resolution bandwidth. Resolution bandwidth is simply the
bandwidth ∆B <B within which the power is measured.
Example 11.8. Returning to Example 11.7, let’s say the gain is 50 dB. (a) What is the output-referred noise floor in
terms of power spectral density? (b) Let’s say we terminate t he input into a very cold matched load, and observe the
output using an ideal (noiseless) spectrum analyzer with re solution bandwidth set to 1 kHz. What does the spectrum
analyzer indicate as the noise floor?
Solution: The output-referred noise floor is kTeqG =kT0(F− 1)G =− 171. 8 dBm/Hz + 50 dB
=− 121. 8 dBm/Hz, which is the answer to (a). Terminating the input int o a “very cold matched load” suggests that
the applied external noise is negligible compared to the int ernal noise, so the spectrum analyzer is measuring only
internal noise. Since the noise floor power spectral density is− 121. 8 dBm/Hz, and ∆B = 1 kHz, the spectrum
analyzer shows a trace at− 121. 8 dBm/Hz + 10 log10 ∆B =− 91. 8 dBm.
The above examples demonstrate that MDS and noise floor are cl osely-related concepts that have multiple definitions. To
further complicate the issue, the terms “MDS” and “noise floo r” are often used interchangeably. In practical problems on e
should always take great care to understand precisely how th ese terms are being used.
