18.6 Tecnologías de hardware para procesamiento digital de señales (DSP)

Por último, es apropiado discutir las implementaciones de hardware del DSP descrito a lo largo de este capítulo. Debido a que las capacidades de los equipos DSP están evolucionando rápidamente, los comentarios se limitarán a algunas observaciones generales que son más probables que sean aplicables para el futuro previsible.

18.6.1 CPUs, Sus Limitaciones y Alternativas

Los anchos de banda hasta unos pocos cientos de kHz en forma compleja de banda base pueden ser acomodados generalmente utilizando computación “propósito general”, que incluye computadoras personales y procesadores de menor rendimiento que se encuentran típicamente en dispositivos móviles. Estos dispositivos siguen un paradigma central de procesamiento (CPU), en el cual el procesamiento se define en software e implementado como una secuencia de operaciones matemáticas realizadas uno a la vez. Una clase de estos dispositivos que aparece comúnmente en las radios emplea dedicados DSP procesadores o coprocesadores que se pueden utilizar para acelerar ciertos tipos de operaciones, como FIR filtros y FFTs. Las ventajas de CPU- Basado en DSP en las radios es la reconfigurabilidad de software y facilidad de integración con funciones periféricas como codificación de fuentes/descodificación, redes e interfaces físicas.

La limitación principal de DSP basado en CPU es la ejecución esencialmente serie de operaciones. Dado que las modulaciones digitales modernas requieren miles a cientos de miles de operaciones matemáticas por muestra de salida, el paradigma de procesamiento basado en instrucciones en serie de arquitectura CPU se convierte en un embotellamiento cada vez más intrápido para anchos de banda mayores que unos pocos MHz, incluso cuando la velocidad de reloj de CPU está en el orden de unos pocos GHz. Incluso en anchos de banda inferiores donde las CPU son fácilmente capaces de mantenerse al día, el tamaño asociado, el peso, la energía y el costo son generalmente poco atractivos en comparación con otras alternativas (identificadas a continuación) a menos que una de las ventajas identificadas anteriormente sea bastante importante.

Para hacer mejor, se hace necesario abandonar la arquitectura secuencial de instrucciones en favor de esquemas que permiten que muchas operaciones se realicen en paralelo. Por ejemplo: En lugar de calcular un filtro orden-M FIR como multiplicaciones M + 1 uno a la vez, se puede calcular todas las multiplicaciones M+ 1 simultáneamente. Esto requiere multiplicadores de hardware M; por otro lado, los multiplicadores de entero son muy baratos, compactos. Esta paralelización permite que la velocidad del reloj esté en el orden de la tasa de muestra, en lugar del enfoque CPU que requiere una velocidad del reloj en el orden del tiempo de la frecuencia de la muestra el número de multiplicaciones por muestra, tiempos el número de ciclos del reloj requerido para realizar una multiplicación. Los dispositivos que entran en esta categoría incluyen circuitos integrados de función especial (IC), arrays de puertas programables de campo (FPGA) y circuitos integradoes específicos de aplicación (ASICs).7 Cada uno de ellos se considera brevemente abajo.

18.6.2 Los IC de Función Especial

Una función especial IC es precisamente lo que el nombre implica: Procesamiento digital implementado en un IC que ha sido diseñado para implementar una función específica. Actualmente la mayoría de las normas de comunicación inalámbrica están disponibles para su implementación en este formulario. Las ventajas de utilizar tales dispositivos son características de tamaño/peso/poder, relativamente bajo costo, y comodidad ya que el esfuerzo de diseño se reduce al problema de interfacing a la IC. La principal desventaja de este enfoque es la falta de flexibilidad: Por ejemplo, una función especial IEEE 802.11b IC normalmente no puede ser reconfigurado para utilizar una nueva variante de 802.11, o reconfigurado a implementar ZigBee (que comparte la misma banda de frecuencia), etc.

18.6.3 FPGAs

An FPGA es esencialmente una función especial reconfigurable IC. FPGA Los IC consisten en un gran número de unidades (que se denominan “células” o “blocks”) que realizan operaciones básicas (addición, multiplicación, memoria, etc.) que pueden combinarse de diversas maneras para implementar FIR Filtros, FFTs, etc. Las conexiones entre estas unidades se determinan por firmware descargado a la FPGA después de la potenciación; por lo tanto el término “campo programable”. Así, la ventaja principal de FPGAs es la flexibilidad: Tanto en términos de implementar completamente nuevo DSP, como en poder redefinir/reconfigurar DSP sin modificar el hardware, y tal vez incluso sin poder ciclista. La desventaja de FPAGs es que no pueden ser optimizados para tamaño, peso, potencia y costo hasta el grado que un IC de función especial puede, y una gran fracción de la capacidad de procesamiento innata inevitablemente Sin embargo, el uso de FPGAs en radios modernas aumenta constantemente, impulsado en parte por la demanda de reconfigurabilidad, y en parte debido a innovaciones técnicas que permiten a las FPGA emular y así sustituir CPU (es decir, procesamiento de softcore). Actualmente las FPAGs operan rutinariamente a velocidades de reloj de 100 MHz y más allá, y – con ciertas caveats – son generalmente capaces de alcanzar tasas de salida.

18.6.4 ASICs

ASICs son esencialmente optimizados implementaciones de hardware de FPGA firmware. Es un hecho bastante común que el procesamiento implementado en forma FPGA no requiere la reconfigurabilidad de un FPGA IC; sino más bien sólo el alto grado de paralelismo ofrecido por arquitectura FPGA. En este caso es posible sintetizar un IC de función especial que

7Y luego hay unidades de procesamiento gráfico (GPUs), que son esencialmente arrays de CPU rudimentarias. Aunque actualmente hay mucha experimentación con GPU como motores DSP de alto rendimiento personalizado para aplicaciones de radio, las GPU no aparecen ahora en aplicaciones de radio “principal”. Pero en el futuro? Tal vez.

implementa el diseño definido por el firmware FPGA, utilizando hardware optimizado para ese diseño particular. Esto resulta en un dispositivo que es generalmente mucho menos caro que el FPGA original (presuming large-quantity production) y con tamaño superior, peso y características de potencia. Así, ASICs combinan las ventajas de FPGAs y ICs de función especial.

18.6 DSP Hardware Technologies

Finally it is appropriate to discuss hardware implementations of the DSP described throughout this chapter. Because the capabilities of DSP hardware are always rapidly evolving, comments will be limited to a few general observations that are most likely to be applicable for the foreseeable future.

18.6.1 CPUs, Their Limitations, and Alternatives

Bandwidths up to a few hundred kHz in complex baseband form can usually be accommodated using “general purpose” computing, which includes personal computers and lower-performance processors typically found in mobile devices. Such devices follow a central processing unit (CPU) paradigm, in which processing is defined in software and implemented as a sequence of mathematical operations performed one at a time. A class of these devices that commonly appears in radios employs dedicated DSP processors or coprocessors which can be used to speed up certain types of operations, such as FIR filters and FFTs. The advantages of CPU-based DSP in radios is software reconfigurability and ease of integration with peripheral functions such as source coding/decoding, networking, and physical interfaces.

The principal limitation of CPU-based DSP is the essentially serial execution of operations. Since modern digital modulations require thousands to hundreds of thousands of mathematical operations per output sample, the serial instruction-based processing paradigm of CPU architecture becomes an increasingly intractable bottleneck for bandwidths greater than a few MHz, even when the CPU’s clock rate is on the order of a few GHz. Even at lower bandwidths where CPUs are easily able to keep up, the associated size, weight, power, and cost are typically unattractive compared to other alternatives (identified below) unless one of the advantages identified above is pretty important.

To do better, it becomes necessary to abandon sequential-instruction architecture in favor of schemes which allow many operations to be performed in parallel. For example: Rather than computing an order-M FIR filter as M + 1 multiplications one at a time, one might compute all M + 1 multiplications simultaneously. This requires M hardware multipliers; on the other hand, integer multipliers are very cheap, compact, and power-efficient compared to CPUs. This parallelization allows the clock rate to be on the order of the sample rate, as opposed to the CPU approach which requires a clock rate on the order of the sample rate times the number of multiplications per sample, times the number of clock cycles required to perform a multiplication. Devices falling into this category include special-function integrated circuits (ICs), field programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), and application specific integrated circuits (ASICs).7 Each of these is considered briefly below.

18.6.2 Special-Function ICs

A special function IC is precisely what the name implies: Digital processing implemented on an IC which has been designed to implement a specified function. Currently most wireless communications standards are available for implementation in this form. The advantages of using such devices are good size/weight/power characteristics, relatively low cost, and convenience since design effort is reduced to the problem of interfacing to the IC. The primary disadvantage of this approach is lack of flexibility: For example, a IEEE 802.11b special function IC typically can’t be reconfigured to use a newer variant of 802.11, or reconfigured to implement ZigBee (which shares the same frequency band), and so on.

18.6.3 FPGAs

FPGA ICs consist of large numbers of units (variously referred to as “cells” or “blocks”) performing basic operations (addition, multiplication, memory, and so on) that may be combined in various ways to implement FIR filters, FFTs, and so on. A.2 Hata Model
The form of Equation A.11 lends itself readily to empirical m odeling of mean path loss. The fundamental strategy in
empirical modeling is to collect a large number of measureme nts of mean path loss as a function of R,f ,h1 andh2, and
then to determine values of n andm, and functions L(h1) andL(h2), that result in the best fit of Equation A.11 to this
data. There is no expectation that the resulting model will y ield accurate estimates of
Lp on a case-by-case basis; however
the model will typically be good enough on a statistical basi s to permit informed design of specific radio links and to
facilitate engineering analyses of radio links generally.
The Hata model provides parameters for Equation A.11 based o n an empirical analysis of measurements of VHF and UHF
mobile radio path loss in Japan in the 1960s [23]. The Hata mod el is widely used in the design of mobile radio systems,
and also serves an important role as a “standard” or “referen ce” model facilitating comparative analyses of radio
technologies. The model is summarized in Table A.1.
In the Hata model, the parameter L0 depends on terrain classification. Categories of terrain ar e specified to be “urban”,
“suburban”, and “open rural”. The values of L0 are:
L0 = 69. 55 , urban (A.16)
L0 = 64. 15− 2
[
log10
(fMHz
28
)]2
, suburban (A.17)
L0 = 28. 61− 4. 78 [log10fMHz]2 + 18. 33 log10fMHz , open rural (A.18)


A.3. COST231-HA TA MODEL 489
There is no particular definition that precisely identifies t he difference between “urban”, “suburban”, and “open rural ”
environments; the user decides which form best suits the int ended application.
The primary application of the Hata model is to mobile radio s ystems consisting of mobile stations that communicate with
base stations. The parameter h1 is taken to be the height of the base station antenna, which is assumed to be at least 30 m.
The corresponding antenna height function for Equation A.1 1 is:
L1(h1) =− (13. 82 + 6. 55 log10Rkm) (log10h1) (A.19)
In the original Hata model, the mobile antenna is assumed to b e 1–10 m above ground, and the corresponding antenna
height function is specified only for the “urban” case and for 100<f MHz < 200 and 400<f MHz < 1500. Within these
limitations, Hata further distinguishes between various t ypes of urban environments. The specified antenna height fun ction
for “small/medium cities” is:
L2(h2) = 1. 56 log10fMHz− 0. 8 + (0. 7− 1. 1 log10fMHz)h2 (A.20)
The specified antenna height function for “large cities” and fMHz≥ 400 is:
L2(h2) = 4. 97− 3. 2 [log10 (11. 75h2)]2 (A.21)
The specified antenna height function for “large cities” and fMHz≤ 200 is:
L2(h2) = 1. 1− 8. 29 [log10 (1. 54h2)]2 (A.22)
Again, there is no definition that specifically identifies the difference between “small/medium cities” and “large citie s”; the
user decides which form best suits the intended application . A common (but nevertheless arbitrary) criterion used to ma ke
this distinction is mean building height: If greater than 15 m, the environment is considered to be “large city”; otherwi se
“small/medium city”.
The original Hata specification for L2(h2), as described above, leaves a few gaps. First, L2(h2) is not specified for
environments that are not considered “urban”. Traditional work-arounds for this issue are to use the “small/medium cit y”
height function, or simply to set L2(h2) to zero. There is usually not much harm done in either case, si nceL2(h2) is
typically small compared to the other terms in Equation A.11 for non-urban environments. Second, the original Hata
model provides no guidance on how to choose L2(h2) for 200<f MHz < 400 in a “large city” environment. The
traditional workaround is simply to use Equation A.21 for fMHz < 300 and Equation A.22 for fMHz > 300. Although
these choices are somewhat arbitrary, the impact on practic al problems is generally small, and in any case one must keep
in mind that the Hata model is never expected to yield accurat e “site specific” predictions anyway.

La forma de la Ecuación A.11 se presta fácilmente al modelado empírico de la pérdida del camino medio. A.2 Hata Model

The form of Equation A.11 lends itself readily to empirical modeling of mean path loss. The fundamental strategy in empirical modeling is to collect a large number of measurements of mean path loss as a function of R, f, h1 and h2, and then to determine values of n and m, and functions L(h1) and L(h2), that result in the best fit of Equation A.11 to this data. There is no expectation that the resulting model will yield accurate estimates of Lp on a case-by-case basis; however the model will typically be good enough on a statistical basis to permit informed design of specific radio links and to facilitate engineering analyses of radio links generally.

The Hata model provides parameters for Equation A.11 based on an empirical analysis of measurements of VHF and UHF mobile radio path loss in Japan in the 1960s [23]. The Hata model is widely used in the design of mobile radio systems, and also serves an important role as a “standard” or “reference” model facilitating comparative analyses of radio technologies. The model is summarized in Table A.1.

In the Hata model, the parameter L0 depends on terrain classification. Categories of terrain are specified to be “urban”, “suburban”, and “open rural”. The values of L0 are:

L0 = 69.55 , urban
(A.16)

2
L0 = 28.61 −4.78 [log10 fMHz]2 + 18.33 log10 fMHz , open rural (A.18)
L0 = 64.15 −2

fMHz

There is no particular definition that precisely identifies the difference between “urban”, “suburban”, and “open rural” environments; the user decides which form best suits the intended application.

The primary application of the Hata model is to mobile radio systems consisting of mobile stations that communicate with base stations. The parameter h1 is taken to be the height of the base station antenna, which is assumed to be at least 30 m. The corresponding antenna height function for Equation A.11 is:

L1(h1) = −(13.82 + 6.55 log10 Rkm) (log10 h1) (A.19)

In the original Hata model, the mobile antenna is assumed to be 1–10 m above ground, and the corresponding antenna height function is specified only for the “urban” case and for 100 < fMHz < 200 and 400 < fMHz < 1500. Within these limitations, Hata further distinguishes between various types of urban environments. The specified antenna height function for “small/medium cities” is:

L2(h2) = 1.56 log10 fMHz −0.8 + (0.7 −1.1 log10 fMHz) h2 (A.20)

The specified antenna height function for “large cities” and fMHz ≥400 is:

L2(h2) = 4.97 −3.2 [log10 (11.75h2)]2
(A.21)

The specified antenna height function for “large cities” and fMHz ≤200 is:

L2(h2) = 1.1 −8.29 [log10 (1.54h2)]2
(A.22)

Again, there is no definition that specifically identifies the difference between “small/medium cities” and “large cities”; the user decides which form best suits the intended application. A common (but nevertheless arbitrary) criterion used to make this distinction is mean building height: If greater than 15 m, the environment is considered to be “large city”; otherwise “small/medium city”.

The original Hata specification for L2(h2), as described above, leaves a few gaps. First, L2(h2) is not specified for environments that are not considered “urban”. Traditional work-arounds for this issue are to use the “small/medium city” height function, or simply to set L2(h2) to zero. There is usually not much harm done in either case, since L2(h2) is typically small compared to the other terms in Equation A.11 for non-urban environments. Second, the original Hata model provides no guidance on how to choose L2(h2) for 200 < fMHz < 400 in a “large city” environment. The traditional workaround is simply to use Equation A.21 for fMHz < 300 and Equation A.22 for fMHz > 300. Although these choices are somewhat arbitrary, the impact on practical problems is generally small, and in any case one must keep in mind that the Hata model is never expected to yield accurate “site specific” predictions anyway.

B.1 Broadcasting
Broadcasting is the delivery of audio, video, and/or data fr om a single transmitter to multiple receivers, primarily fo r
purposes of entertainment and public information. Broadca sting has enormous historical significance as the original
application of radio technology, and the legacy of technolo gy developed for early broadcast radio is evident in modern
radio systems of all types.
A few of the most common terrestrial broadcast systems now in common operation are identified in Table B.1. Some
additional details follow.
It should be noted that modern broadcast FM is not simply FM-m odulated audio. Modulated along with the audio are a
number of subcarriers that permit stereo audio and a rudimentary data service. The subcarriers are es sentially transparent
to a minimal (monaural audio) receiver, but are easily recov ered with a bit of additional signal processing.

OFDM-modulated signals that lie adjacent to existing chann el boundaries; see Figure B.1 for an example. In the US, the
In Band On Channel (IBOC) system (commonly known by the brand name “HD Radio”) i s common. The
digitally-modulated signal offers higher audio quality an d additional content and data services for suitably-equipp ed
receivers. The power in the digital overlay is limited to be b etween 1% and 10% of the power in the primary WBFM
signal. This, combined the fact that adjacent channels are t ypically not assigned in the same geographical region, miti gates

B.1 Radiodifusión

La radiodifusión es la entrega de audio, vídeo y/o datos de un único transmisor a múltiples receptores, principalmente para fines de entretenimiento e información pública. La radiodiversión tiene una enorme importancia histórica como la aplicación original de la tecnología de radio, y el legado de la tecnología desarrollada para la radio de transmisión temprana es evidente en los sistemas modernos de radio de todo tipo.

En el cuadro B.1 se identifican algunos de los sistemas de radiodifusión terrestre más comunes que se encuentran en funcionamiento común.

Cabe señalar que la radio moderna FM no es simplemente audio modulado por FM. Modulado junto con el audio son una serie de subcaríferos que permiten el audio estéreo y un servicio de datos rudimentario. Los subcaríteros son esencialmente transparentes a un receptor mínimo (aulio neuronal), pero se recuperan fácilmente con un poco de procesamiento adicional de señales.

Las transmisiones AM y FM de transmisión moderna incluyen a menudo una señal de sobrelevado digital. La superposición consiste en señales moduladas OFDM que se encuentran adyacentes a los límites de canales existentes; véase Figura B.1 por ejemplo. En el sistema US, el sistema In Band On Channel (IBOC) (comúnmente conocido por la marca “HD Radio”) es común. La potencia en la superposición digital se limita a estar entre 1% y 10% de la potencia en la señal WBFM primaria. La radiodifusión es la entrega de audio, vídeo y/o datos de un único transmisor a múltiples receptores, principalmente para fines de entretenimiento e información pública. La radiodiversión tiene una enorme importancia histórica como la aplicación original de la tecnología de radio, y el legado de la tecnología desarrollada para la radio de transmisión temprana es evidente en los sistemas modernos de radio de todo tipo.
En el cuadro B.1 se identifican algunos de los sistemas de radiodifusión terrestre más comunes que se encuentran en funcionamiento común.

Cabe señalar que la radio moderna FM no es simplemente audio modulado por FM. Modulado junto con el audio son una serie de subcaríferos que permiten el audio estéreo y un servicio de datos rudimentario. Los subcaríteros son esencialmente transparentes a un receptor mínimo (aulio neuronal), pero se recuperan fácilmente con un poco de procesamiento adicional de señales.

B.1 Broadcasting

Broadcasting is the delivery of audio, video, and/or data from a single transmitter to multiple receivers, primarily for purposes of entertainment and public information. Broadcasting has enormous historical significance as the original application of radio technology, and the legacy of technology developed for early broadcast radio is evident in modern radio systems of all types.

A few of the most common terrestrial broadcast systems now in common operation are identified in Table B.1. Some additional details follow.

It should be noted that modern broadcast FM is not simply FM-modulated audio. Modulated along with the audio are a number of subcarriers that permit stereo audio and a rudimentary data service. The subcarriers are essentially transparent to a minimal (monaural audio) receiver, but are easily recovered with a bit of additional signal processing.

Modern broadcast AM and FM transmissions often include a digital overlay signal. The overlay consists of OFDM-modulated signals that lie adjacent to existing channel boundaries; see Figure B.1 for an example. In the US, the In Band On Channel (IBOC) system (commonly known by the brand name “HD Radio”) is common. The digitally-modulated signal offers higher audio quality and additional content and data services for suitably-equipped receivers. The power in the digital overlay is limited to be between 1% and 10% of the power in the primary WBFM signal. This, combined the fact that adjacent channels are typically not assigned in the same geographical region, mitigates

Table B.1 identifies the digital television standards ATSC,1 which is used in North America, Central America, and South Korea; and DVB-T, which is used in much of the rest of the world. Another important digital television system is ISDB-T, which is a distinct OFDM-based digital television standard used primarily in South America and Japan. These standards replace the now largely-deprecated analog standards NTSC, PAL, and SECAM – although many stations using these standards remain in operation in various places around the world.

A similar transition is underway in the “shortwave” (HF) broadcast bands, where Digital Radio Mondiale (DRM) is now prevalant, but many DSB-LC AM broadcast stations and a few SSB broadcast stations remain operational.

An important class of broadcast systems not included in Table B.1 is direct broadcast satellite (DBS), which is essentially broadcast television transmit from a satellite in geostationary orbit. DBS is typically implemented at frequencies in the SHF (predominantly Ku) band.2

B.2 Land Mobile Radio
Land mobile radio (LMR) is a very broad class of radio systems intended for voice and data communications between
mobile terrestrial users. Applications include public saf ety (police, fire, etc.), business operations (taxi dispatc h, security,
etc.), personal/recreational use, and amateur radio. LMR i s distinct from cellular telecommunications (Section B.3) in that
there is no “telecommunication” – that is, users communicat e with other users either directly or through a repeater, and no
network switching or routing is required. However that dist inction is likely to become ambiguous in the future as some
LMR systems migrate to technologies originally intended fo r telecommunications – again see Section B.3 for more on this .
A few of the most common LMR systems now in common operation ap pear in Table B.2. As in broadcasting, a transition
to digital systems is underway, but is happening slowly. Ana log FM systems remain very common, and often the technical
emphasis is on reducing bandwidth (e.g., US efforts to trans ition to 6.25 kHz channels) as opposed to implementing new
digital systems.
P25 and TETRA are the digital standards most commonly employ ed in the US and in Europe, respectively. P25 uses a
version ofM = 4 FSK (4FSK) known as continuous 4-level FM (C4FM), where the word “continuous” refers to the pulse
shaping used to optimize the spectral efficiency. TETRA uses π
4 -DQPSK, which yields slightly better spectral efficiency
but requires better (more linear) power amplifiers. TETRA ch annels are wider, but TETRA employs an explicit TDMA
scheme with 4 users per channel; thus the spectral efficiency is similar to P25.
Many LMR systems employ trunking, which is a multiple access scheme in which frequency channe ls are used in groups
that are dynamically assigned, as opposed to being used indi vidually. This improves overall capacity by distributing t raffic
more uniformly over the available frequencies.
Typical transmit power for Analog FM, P25, and TETRA is on the order of 1–10 W for handheld units and 10–100 W for
fixed/vehicular units and repeaters. Typical maximum range is on the order of kilometers, although systems are often
interconnected using repeaters with high antennas to provi de coverage over a much larger area.
The US Citizens Band (CB) and Family Radio Service (FRS) are i ncluded in Table B.2 as examples of unlicensed LMR
systems used primarily for personal and recreational commu nications. Maximum transmit power for these systems is 4 W
and 500 mW, respectively. This yields range on the order of ki lometers using low-gain antennas close to the ground over
level terrain, although CB signals intermittently reach mu ch greater distances when ionospheric conditions permit.
Systems which are similar, although perhaps with slight dif ferences in technical parameters, exist throughout the wor ld.

B.2 Radiocomunicación móvil terrestre

La radio móvil terrestre (LMR) es una clase muy amplia de sistemas de radio destinados a comunicaciones de voz y datos entre usuarios terrestres móviles. Las aplicaciones incluyen seguridad pública (policía, fuego, etc.), operaciones comerciales (despacho de impuestos, seguridad, etc.) uso personal/recreativo, y radio amateur. LMR es distinto de las telecomunicaciones celulares (Sección B.3) en que no hay “telecomunicación” – es decir, los usuarios se comunican con otros usuarios directamente o a través de un repetidor, y no se requiere conmutación de red o enrutamiento. Sin embargo, esa distinción es probable que se vuelva ambigua en el futuro como algunos LMR los sistemas migran a las tecnologías originalmente destinadas a las telecomunicaciones – véase nuevamente la Sección B.3 por más en esto.

Algunos de los sistemas LMR más comunes que se encuentran en funcionamiento común aparecen en la Tabla B.2. Como en la radiodifusión, se está realizando una transición a los sistemas digitales, pero está ocurriendo lentamente. Los sistemas Analog FM siguen siendo muy comunes y a menudo el énfasis técnico es reducir el ancho de banda (por ejemplo, los esfuerzos US para la transición a canales 6.25 kHz) en vez de implementar nuevos sistemas digitales.

P25 y TETRA son las normas digitales más empleadas en US y en Europa, respectivamente. P25 usa una versión de M = 4 FSK (4FSK) conocido como continuo 4- nivel FM (C4FM), donde la palabra “continua” se refiere a la configuración del pulso utilizada para optimizar la eficiencia espectral. TETRA usos π

4 -DQPSK, que produce una eficiencia ligeramente mejor espectral, pero requiere mejores amplificadores de potencia (más lineales). Los canales TETRA son más anchos, pero TETRA emplea un esquema TDMA explícito con usuarios 4 por canal; así la eficiencia espectral es similar a P25.

Muchos sistemas LMR emplean el troque, que es un esquema de acceso múltiple en el que se utilizan canales de frecuencia en grupos que se asignan dinámicamente, en lugar de ser utilizados individualmente. Esto mejora la capacidad general distribuyendo el tráfico de manera más uniforme sobre las frecuencias disponibles.

El poder de transmisión típico para Analog FM, P25, y TETRA está en el orden de 1-10 W para unidades portátiles y 10-100 W para unidades fijas/vehiculares y repetidores. El rango máximo típico está en el pedido de kilómetros, aunque los sistemas a menudo se interconectan utilizando repetidores con altas antenas para proporcionar cobertura sobre una zona mucho mayor.

La Banda Ciudadana US (CB) y el Servicio de Radio Familia (FRS) se incluyen en la Tabla B.2 como ejemplos de sistemas LMR sin licencia utilizados principalmente para comunicaciones personales y recreativas. Potencia máxima de transmisión para estos sistemas es 4 W y 500 mW, respectivamente. Esto produce rango en el orden de kilómetros utilizando antenas de baja ganancia cerca del terreno sobre terreno, aunque CB señales de gran distancia entremitentes. Sistemas similares, aunque quizás con pequeñas diferencias en parámetros técnicos existen en todo el mundo.

B.2.text_en_clean:
B.2 Land Mobile Radio

Land mobile radio (LMR) is a very broad class of radio systems intended for voice and data communications between mobile terrestrial users. Applications include public safety (police, fire, etc.), business operations (taxi dispatch, security, etc.), personal/recreational use, and amateur radio. LMR is distinct from cellular telecommunications (Section B.3) in that there is no “telecommunication” – that is, users communicate with other users either directly or through a repeater, and no network switching or routing is required. However that distinction is likely to become ambiguous in the future as some LMR systems migrate to technologies originally intended for telecommunications – again see Section B.3 for more on this.

A few of the most common LMR systems now in common operation appear in Table B.2. As in broadcasting, a transition to digital systems is underway, but is happening slowly. Analog FM systems remain very common, and often the technical emphasis is on reducing bandwidth (e.g., US efforts to transition to 6.25 kHz channels) as opposed to implementing new digital systems.

P25 and TETRA are the digital standards most commonly employed in the US and in Europe, respectively. P25 uses a version of M = 4 FSK (4FSK) known as continuous 4-level FM (C4FM), where the word “continuous” refers to the pulse shaping used to optimize the spectral efficiency. TETRA uses π

4 -DQPSK, which yields slightly better spectral efficiency but requires better (more linear) power amplifiers. TETRA channels are wider, but TETRA employs an explicit TDMA scheme with 4 users per channel; thus the spectral efficiency is similar to P25.

Many LMR systems employ trunking, which is a multiple access scheme in which frequency channels are used in groups that are dynamically assigned, as opposed to being used individually. This improves overall capacity by distributing traffic more uniformly over the available frequencies.

Typical transmit power for Analog FM, P25, and TETRA is on the order of 1–10 W for handheld units and 10–100 W for fixed/vehicular units and repeaters. Typical maximum range is on the order of kilometers, although systems are often interconnected using repeaters with high antennas to provide coverage over a much larger area.

The US Citizens Band (CB) and Family Radio Service (FRS) are included in Table B.2 as examples of unlicensed LMR systems used primarily for personal and recreational communications. Maximum transmit power for these systems is 4 W and 500 mW, respectively. This yields range on the order of kilometers using low-gain antennas close to the ground over level terrain, although CB signals intermittently reach much greater distances when ionospheric conditions permit. Systems which are similar, although perhaps with slight differences in technical parameters, exist throughout the world.

B.3.text:
B.3 Mobile Telecommunications
In mobile telecommunications systems, users are connected to the network by radio, as opposed to wires. Mobile
telecommunications combined with wireless data networks ( the topic of the next section) account for the majority of
contemporary economic activity – and, subsequently, new te chnology development – in the field of radio.


B.3. MOBILE TELECOMMUNICA TIONS 493
B.3.1 General Characteristics
Whereas the emphasis in LMR is “one-to-many” communication, the emphasis in mobile telecommunications is
“one-to-one” communications between users, facilitated b y network switching with user-specific addressing; i.e., ph one
numbers and IP addresses. 3 Thus, mobile telecommunications systems are nominally sea mless extensions of the
worldwide telecommunications system. Nearly all mobile te lecommunications systems employ cellular architecture
(reminder: Figure 1.6 and associated text) in some form. Thi s category is not limited to terrestrial systems, since we ca n
also count satellite-based systems such as Iridium and Inma rsat as mobile telecommunications systems.
Existing terrestrial mobile telecommunications exist pri marily in the UHF band, with most systems implemented betwee n
700 MHz and 1 GHz, and within a few hundred MHz of 2 GHz. Certain segments of the latter are called the Personal
Communications Services (PCS) and Advanced Wireless Services (AWS) bands.4 The reasons why mobile cellular
telecommunications ended up in these bands are primarily hi storical. Although these terrestrial mobile
telecommunications systems could potentially perform muc h better in the VHF and lower UHF regime (where path loss is
much lower), these frequencies had been in use for televisio n broadcasting for decades before the first modern cellular
systems were were implemented in the 1980s, and remaining sp ectrum, primarily in the VHF band, was generally too
narrow. Similarly, legacy applications precluded impleme ntation of cellular systems between 1 GHz and about 1.8 GHz.
With a few exceptions, satellite-based mobile telecommuni cations systems operate primarily in narrow bands between
1.4 GHz and 1.7 GHz, which is shared with a variety of other sat ellite systems that are considered to be compatible from
an interference perspective.
What follows is a brief summary of terrestrial cellular syste ms, organized historically. It is quite difficult – and far be yond
the scope of this book – to summarize all potentially-releva nt aspects of modern cellular systems. Such a summary would
probably have limited utility anyway, given the rapidly evo lution of these systems in terms of both technology
development and deployment. Additional current informati on on these systems is probably best obtained from journals –
IEEE Communications Magazine is recommended in particular – and from the official document s that define the standards.
B.3.2 First, Second, and Third Generation Cellular Systems
It is common to classify terrestrial cellular telecommunic ations by “generation”. First-generation systems emerged in the
1980s, employed primarily analog modulations (NBFM in part icular), and are now essentially extinct. Second-generati on
(“2G”) technologies emerged in the mid 1990s and employed pr imarily low-order digital sinusoidal carrier modulations .
Notable among the 2G technologies are GSM and IS-95. GSM uses GMSK with 8 users per carrier in a TDMA scheme to
manage access to 200 kHz channels. IS-95 uses QPSK with DSSS, allowing a variable number of users to share a
1.25 MHz channel via CDMA.
Although operational 2G systems are becoming rare, the asso ciated technologies gave rise to a panoply of enhanced and
hybridized versions that are known collectively as third ge neration (“3G”) systems, in which the primary emphasis is
increased rates for data applications. The example in Secti on 7.8 is representative of the downlink (base station to mob ile
user link) in a PCS-band 3G cellular system, demonstrating h ow downlink rates between a few hundred kb/s to a few Mb/s
are achieved.
B.3.3 Fourth Generation Cellular Systems (“4G”) and LTE
Presently, 3G systems are nearly ubiquitous but are rapidly being overtaken by fourth generation (“4G”) systems. The
hallmarks of 4G technologies are OFDM, MIMO, carrier aggreg ation,5 and a transition from circuit-switched networking
3This is not always so clear-cut: Modern mobile telecommunicati ons systems may also provide a “push-to-talk” (PTT) capabilit y that emulates LMR,
and some modern LMR systems use technologies that would normally be considered telecommunications systems, such as LTE.
4The names do not infer any particular features aside from iden tifying specific frequency ranges.
5Reminder: See the last paragraphs of Section 7.8.


494 APPENDIX B. CHARACTERISTICS OF SOME COMMON RADIO SYSTEMS
(a legacy of the early emphasis on voice communications) to I P-based networking (to facilitate easier integration with
data).
Prominent among 4G technologies is Long Term Evolution (LTE).6 LTE itself is not really a single standard, but rather a
broad family of standards that that continues to evolve and i s being adapted to a variety of applications that have
traditionally been outside the domain of cellular telecomm unications – this includes LMR (especially in the public saf ety
arena) and wireless data networking (the topic of the next se ction).
The emerging primacy of LTE makes it appropriate to identify a few of the defining technical characteristics. The LTE
downlink uses OFDM with QPSK, 16QAM, or 64QAM. The atomic uni t of time-frequency utilization in LTE is the
resource block, which consists of 7 contiguous symbols × 12 contiguous subcarriers. Data are assigned to resource bl ocks
on a dynamic basis, which facilitates relatively efficient u tilization of available spectrum. In this sense LTE uses TDM A
and FDMA simultaneously. This offers considerable advanta ges over earlier technologies which are primarily FDMA
(albeit perhaps with TDMA within frequency channels), sinc e in traditional FDMA systems it is possible for capacity to
be limited because some frequency channels can remain idle w hile others are running at maximum capacity.
The symbol period T for the OFDM modulation in LTE is about 66.7 μ s; therefore the subcarrier spacing is
1/T ∼
= 15 kHz and subsequently a resource block is about 0.5 ms × 180 kHz. In the time domain, consecutive pairs of
resource blocks form 1 ms subframes, and 10 subframes are organized into 10 ms frames. In the frequency domain,
contiguous groups of resource blocks are combined to form ch annels having widths between 1.25 MHz and 20 MHz. In
principle, downlink data rates up to about 100 Mb/s can be ach ieved in ideal conditions.
For the uplink (mobile-to-base station link), LTE uses sing le-carrier QPSK or 16QAM with FDMA, commonly referred to
as “SC-FDMA ”, as opposed to OFDM. This avoids the problem of i mplementing efficient power amplifiers with sufficient
linearity to accommodate the high PAPR of OFDM. The maximum p ossible uplink data rate is about half the maximum
downlink rate, which is appropriate since data rate require ments in telecommunications systems tend to be highly
asymmetrical in this way.
B.3.4 Fifth Generation Cellular Systems (“5G”)
What’s next? The answer is, of course, fifth generation (“5G”) technology. 5G standards are being developed as this book
is being written, but features will certainly emphasize inc reased data rates and continued integration of voice and dat a
applications of all types across a variety of physical-laye r standards. Significant increases in data rates require add itional
spectrum which is simply unavailable in existing cellular t elecommunications bands; therefore a new emphasis in 5G wil l
be operation at frequencies in the SHF (3–30 GHz) and EHF (pri marily 30–80 GHz) bands, where wider bandwidths can
be accommodated. 5G will also likely accommodate emerging internet of things (IoT) and machine-to-machine (M2M;
alternatively known as device-to-device (D2D)) communications applications.

B.3 Telecomunicaciones móviles

En los sistemas de telecomunicaciones móviles, los usuarios están conectados a la red por radio, en lugar de cables. Las telecomunicaciones móviles combinadas con redes inalámbricas de datos (el tema de la próxima sección) representan la mayoría de la actividad económica contemporánea y, posteriormente, el desarrollo de nuevas tecnologías en el campo de la radio.

B.3.1 Las Características Generales

Mientras que el énfasis en LMR es la comunicación “una a la mayoría”, el énfasis en las telecomunicaciones móviles es las comunicaciones “una a una” entre los usuarios, facilitadas por la conmutación de la red con dirección específica del usuario; es decir, números de teléfono y IP direcciones.3 Por lo tanto, los sistemas de telecomunicaciones móviles son extensiones nominalmente sin costuras del sistema mundial de telecomunicaciones. Casi todos los sistemas de telecomunicaciones móviles emplean arquitectura celular (reminder: Figura 1.6 y texto asociado) en alguna forma. Esta categoría no se limita a los sistemas terrestres, ya que también podemos contar con sistemas basados en satélites como Iridium e Inmarsat como sistemas de telecomunicaciones móviles.

Existen telecomunicaciones móviles terrestres existentes principalmente en la banda UHF, con la mayoría de los sistemas implementados entre 700 MHz y 1 GHz, y dentro de unos pocos cientos MHz de 2 GHz. Algunos segmentos de estos últimos se llaman Servicios de Comunicación Personal (PCS) y Advanced Wireless Services (AWS) bands.4 Las razones por las que las telecomunicaciones celulares móviles terminaron en estas bandas son principalmente históricas. Aunque estos sistemas de telecomunicaciones móviles terrestres podrían funcionar mucho mejor en el VHF y inferior UHF régimen (donde la pérdida del camino es mucho menor), estas frecuencias habían estado en uso para la radiodifusión televisiva durante décadas antes de que los primeros sistemas celulares modernos fueran implementados en el decenio de 1980, y el espectro restante, principalmente en el VHF banda, era generalmente demasiado estrecha. De manera similar, las aplicaciones heredadas impedían la implementación de sistemas celulares entre 1 GHz y sobre 1.8 GHz. Con algunas excepciones, los sistemas de telecomunicaciones móviles basados en satélites funcionan principalmente en bandas estrechas entre 1.4 GHz y 1.7 GHz, que se comparte con una variedad de otros sistemas de satélites que se consideran compatibles desde la perspectiva de la interferencia.

Lo que sigue es un breve resumen de los sistemas celulares terrestres, organizados históricamente. Es bastante difícil –y mucho más allá del alcance de este libro– resumir todos los aspectos potencialmente relevantes de los sistemas móviles modernos. Tal resumen probablemente tendría una utilidad limitada de todas formas, dada la rápida evolución de estos sistemas en términos de desarrollo y despliegue tecnológico. La información actualizada adicional sobre estos sistemas probablemente se obtiene mejor de las revistas – IEEE Communications Magazine es recomendable en particular – y de los documentos oficiales que definen los estándares.

B.3.2 Los sistemas Celulares de Primera, Segunda y Tercera Generación

Es común clasificar las telecomunicaciones celulares terrestres por “generación”. Los sistemas de primera generación surgieron en el decenio de 1980, empleados principalmente modulaciones analógicas (NBFM en particular), y ahora están esencialmente extintas. Las tecnologías de segunda generación (“2G”) surgieron a mediados del decenio de 1990 y emplearon principalmente modulaciones de portadores sinusoidales digitales de baja orden. GSM y IS-95. GSM utiliza los usuarios GMSK con 8 por transportista en un esquema TDMA para gestionar el acceso a los canales 200 kHz. IS-95 utiliza QPSK con DSSS, permitiendo que un número variable de usuarios compartan un canal 1.25 MHz a través de CDMA.

Aunque los sistemas operativos 2G se están volviendo raros, las tecnologías asociadas dieron lugar a una panoplia de versiones mejoradas e híbridas que se conocen colectivamente como sistemas de tercera generación (“3G”), en los cuales el énfasis principal es mayor tasa para aplicaciones de datos. El ejemplo en la sección 7.8 es representativo del enlace descendente (estación de base a enlace móvil) en un sistema celular 3G de banda PCS, demostrando cómo las tasas de enlace entre unos pocos cientos/b

B.3.3 Los sistemas celulares de cuarta generación (“4G”) y LTE

Actualmente, los sistemas 3G son casi omnipresentes pero se están superando rápidamente por sistemas de cuarta generación (“4G”). Los distintivos de las tecnologías 4G son OFDM, MIMO, agregación de portadores,5 y una transición de redes de circuito-switched

3Esto no siempre es tan claro: Los sistemas modernos de telecomunicaciones móviles también pueden proporcionar una capacidad de “push-to-talk” (PTT) que emula LMR, y algunos sistemas modernos LMR utilizan tecnologías que normalmente serían consideradas sistemas de telecomunicaciones, como LTE.

4Los nombres no infiere ninguna característica particular aparte de identificar rangos de frecuencia específicos. 5Recordar: Vea los últimos párrafos de la sección 7.8.

(un legado del énfasis temprano en las comunicaciones de voz) a la creación de redes basadas en IP (para facilitar la integración con los datos).

Prominent among 4G technologies is Long Term Evolution (LTE).6 LTE no es realmente un estándar único, sino una amplia familia de estándares que sigue evolucionando y se está adaptando a una variedad de aplicaciones que tradicionalmente han estado fuera del dominio de las telecomunicaciones celulares – esto incluye LMR (especialmente en el ámbito de seguridad pública) y redes inalámbricas de datos (el tema de la próxima sección).

La primacía emergente de LTE hace que sea apropiado identificar algunas de las características técnicas definitorias. LTE usos del enlace descendente OFDM con QPSK, 16QAM, o 64QAM. La unidad atómica de la utilización de la frecuencia del tiempo en LTE es el bloque de recursos, que consiste en 7 símbolos contiguos × 12 subcarritos contiguos. Los datos se asignan a los bloques de recursos de forma dinámica, lo que facilita la utilización relativamente eficiente del espectro disponible. LTE usos TDMA y FDMA simultáneamente. Esto ofrece ventajas considerables sobre tecnologías anteriores que son principalmente FDMA (aunque quizás con TDMA dentro de canales de frecuencia), ya que en los sistemas tradicionales FDMA es posible que la capacidad sea limitada porque algunos canales de frecuencia pueden permanecer ociosos mientras otros se ejecutan a máxima capacidad.

El período de símbolo T para el OFDM modulación en el interior LTE Se trata de 66.7 μs; por lo tanto el espaciado subcarrier es 1/T ∼= 15 kHz y posteriormente un bloque de recursos está a punto 0.5 ms × 180 kHz. En el dominio del tiempo, se forman pares consecutivos de bloques de recursos 1 ms subframes, y 10 subframes are organized into 10 ms frames. En el dominio de frecuencia, grupos contiguos de bloques de recursos se combinan para formar canales que tienen anchos entre 1.25 MHz y 20 MHz. En principio, las tasas de datos de enlace descendente hasta aproximadamente 100 Mb/s pueden alcanzarse en condiciones ideales.

Para el enlace de red (enlace móvil a base), LTE utiliza un solo carrier QPSK o 16QAM con FDMA, comúnmente denominado “SC-FDMA”, en lugar de OFDM. Esto evita el problema de implementar amplificadores de potencia eficientes con suficiente linearidad para dar cabida al alto PAPR de OFDM. La tasa máxima posible de conexión es aproximadamente la mitad de los sistemas máximos de conexión

B.3.4 Los sistemas celulares de quinta generación (“5G”)

La respuesta es, por supuesto, la tecnología de quinta generación (“5G”). Se están desarrollando estándares 5G ya que este libro está siendo escrito, pero las características sin duda enfatizarán mayores tasas de datos y la integración continua de aplicaciones de voz y datos de todo tipo a través de una variedad de estándares de capas físicas. Los aumentos significativos de las tasas de datos requieren un espectro adicional que simplemente no está disponible en las bandas de telecomunicaciones celulares existentes; por lo tanto, un nuevo énfasis en 5G será operado en frecuencias en las SHF (3–30 GHz) y EHF (Primero) 30–80 GHz) bandas, donde se pueden acomodar anchos de banda más anchos. 5G también probablemente acomodar el Internet emergente de las cosas (IoT) y máquina a máquina (M2M; alternativamente conocido como dispositivo a dispositivo (D2D)) Aplicaciones de comunicaciones.

B.3.text_en_clean:
B.3 Mobile Telecommunications

In mobile telecommunications systems, users are connected to the network by radio, as opposed to wires. Mobile telecommunications combined with wireless data networks (the topic of the next section) account for the majority of contemporary economic activity – and, subsequently, new technology development – in the field of radio.

B.3.1 General Characteristics

Whereas the emphasis in LMR is “one-to-many” communication, the emphasis in mobile telecommunications is “one-to-one” communications between users, facilitated by network switching with user-specific addressing; i.e., phone numbers and IP addresses.3 Thus, mobile telecommunications systems are nominally seamless extensions of the worldwide telecommunications system. Nearly all mobile telecommunications systems employ cellular architecture (reminder: Figure 1.6 and associated text) in some form. This category is not limited to terrestrial systems, since we can also count satellite-based systems such as Iridium and Inmarsat as mobile telecommunications systems.

Existing terrestrial mobile telecommunications exist primarily in the UHF band, with most systems implemented between 700 MHz and 1 GHz, and within a few hundred MHz of 2 GHz. Certain segments of the latter are called the Personal Communications Services (PCS) and Advanced Wireless Services (AWS) bands.4 The reasons why mobile cellular telecommunications ended up in these bands are primarily historical. Although these terrestrial mobile telecommunications systems could potentially perform much better in the VHF and lower UHF regime (where path loss is much lower), these frequencies had been in use for television broadcasting for decades before the first modern cellular systems were were implemented in the 1980s, and remaining spectrum, primarily in the VHF band, was generally too narrow. Similarly, legacy applications precluded implementation of cellular systems between 1 GHz and about 1.8 GHz. With a few exceptions, satellite-based mobile telecommunications systems operate primarily in narrow bands between 1.4 GHz and 1.7 GHz, which is shared with a variety of other satellite systems that are considered to be compatible from an interference perspective.

What follows is a brief summary of terrestrial cellular systems, organized historically. It is quite difficult – and far beyond the scope of this book – to summarize all potentially-relevant aspects of modern cellular systems. Such a summary would probably have limited utility anyway, given the rapidly evolution of these systems in terms of both technology development and deployment. Additional current information on these systems is probably best obtained from journals – IEEE Communications Magazine is recommended in particular – and from the official documents that define the standards.

B.3.2 First, Second, and Third Generation Cellular Systems

It is common to classify terrestrial cellular telecommunications by “generation”. First-generation systems emerged in the 1980s, employed primarily analog modulations (NBFM in particular), and are now essentially extinct. Second-generation (“2G”) technologies emerged in the mid 1990s and employed primarily low-order digital sinusoidal carrier modulations. Notable among the 2G technologies are GSM and IS-95. GSM uses GMSK with 8 users per carrier in a TDMA scheme to manage access to 200 kHz channels. IS-95 uses QPSK with DSSS, allowing a variable number of users to share a 1.25 MHz channel via CDMA.

Although operational 2G systems are becoming rare, the associated technologies gave rise to a panoply of enhanced and hybridized versions that are known collectively as third generation (“3G”) systems, in which the primary emphasis is increased rates for data applications. The example in Section 7.8 is representative of the downlink (base station to mobile user link) in a PCS-band 3G cellular system, demonstrating how downlink rates between a few hundred kb/s to a few Mb/s are achieved.

B.3.3 Fourth Generation Cellular Systems (“4G”) and LTE

Presently, 3G systems are nearly ubiquitous but are rapidly being overtaken by fourth generation (“4G”) systems. The hallmarks of 4G technologies are OFDM, MIMO, carrier aggregation,5 and a transition from circuit-switched networking

3This is not always so clear-cut: Modern mobile telecommunications systems may also provide a “push-to-talk” (PTT) capability that emulates LMR, and some modern LMR systems use technologies that would normally be considered telecommunications systems, such as LTE.

4The names do not infer any particular features aside from identifying specific frequency ranges. 5Reminder: See the last paragraphs of Section 7.8.

(a legacy of the early emphasis on voice communications) to IP-based networking (to facilitate easier integration with data).

Prominent among 4G technologies is Long Term Evolution (LTE).6 LTE itself is not really a single standard, but rather a broad family of standards that that continues to evolve and is being adapted to a variety of applications that have traditionally been outside the domain of cellular telecommunications – this includes LMR (especially in the public safety arena) and wireless data networking (the topic of the next section).

The emerging primacy of LTE makes it appropriate to identify a few of the defining technical characteristics. The LTE downlink uses OFDM with QPSK, 16QAM, or 64QAM. The atomic unit of time-frequency utilization in LTE is the resource block, which consists of 7 contiguous symbols × 12 contiguous subcarriers. Data are assigned to resource blocks on a dynamic basis, which facilitates relatively efficient utilization of available spectrum. In this sense LTE uses TDMA and FDMA simultaneously. This offers considerable advantages over earlier technologies which are primarily FDMA (albeit perhaps with TDMA within frequency channels), since in traditional FDMA systems it is possible for capacity to be limited because some frequency channels can remain idle while others are running at maximum capacity.

The symbol period T for the OFDM modulation in LTE is about 66.7 μs; therefore the subcarrier spacing is 1/T ∼= 15 kHz and subsequently a resource block is about 0.5 ms × 180 kHz. In the time domain, consecutive pairs of resource blocks form 1 ms subframes, and 10 subframes are organized into 10 ms frames. In the frequency domain, contiguous groups of resource blocks are combined to form channels having widths between 1.25 MHz and 20 MHz. In principle, downlink data rates up to about 100 Mb/s can be achieved in ideal conditions.

For the uplink (mobile-to-base station link), LTE uses single-carrier QPSK or 16QAM with FDMA, commonly referred to as “SC-FDMA”, as opposed to OFDM. This avoids the problem of implementing efficient power amplifiers with sufficient linearity to accommodate the high PAPR of OFDM. The maximum possible uplink data rate is about half the maximum downlink rate, which is appropriate since data rate requirements in telecommunications systems tend to be highly asymmetrical in this way.

B.3.4 Fifth Generation Cellular Systems (“5G”)

What’s next? The answer is, of course, fifth generation (“5G”) technology. 5G standards are being developed as this book is being written, but features will certainly emphasize increased data rates and continued integration of voice and data applications of all types across a variety of physical-layer standards. Significant increases in data rates require additional spectrum which is simply unavailable in existing cellular telecommunications bands; therefore a new emphasis in 5G will be operation at frequencies in the SHF (3–30 GHz) and EHF (primarily 30–80 GHz) bands, where wider bandwidths can be accommodated. 5G will also likely accommodate emerging internet of things (IoT) and machine-to-machine (M2M; alternatively known as device-to-device (D2D)) communications applications.

B.4.text:
B.4 Wireless Data Networks
Wireless data networks connect computers to a data network b y radio, as opposed to wires or cables. Such networks are
referred to as wireless local area networks (WLANs), which ar e indoor or short-range outdoor networks; or wireless
metropolitan area networks (WMANs), which implies longer li nks, perhaps spanning a few kilometers. As noted in the
previous section, wireless data networks along with mobile telecommunications account for the majority of contempora ry
economic activity and new technology development in the fiel d of radio.
6Technically, early versions of LTE aren’t considered 4G bec ause they don’t meet some of the performance specifications that are considered to be
required for 4G. Later versions are considered 4G.


B.4. WIRELESS DA TA NETWORKS 495
B.4.1 IEEE 802.11 and 802.11b
In WLAN applications, the IEEE 802.11 family of standards cur rently dominate.7 The earliest realization of this standard,
known simply as “802.11” (alternatively as “802.11-1997” o r “802.11 Legacy”), achieved data rates up to about 2 Mb/s
using single-carrier DSSS or FHSS approaches in the 2.4 GHz u nlicensed band. This standard became popular in the late
1990s but was quickly superseded by 802.11b.
IEEE 802.11b, despite itself being superseded by multiple g enerations of standards (summarized below), remains
ubiquitous. It is so popular that its marketing name – “Wi-Fi ” – has become a synonym for WLAN in general. IEEE
802.11b uses a single-carrier modulation scheme known as complementary code keying (CCK) to transmit data at rates of
5.5 Mb/s or 11 Mb/s in channels up to 22 MHz wide in the 2.4 GHz un licensed band.8 In CCK, groups of 4 bits (for
5.5 Mb/s) or 8 bits (for 11 Mb/s) are mapped to a sequence of 8 QP SK symbols; this mapping is essentially a form of error
control coding. Transmit power is up to 100 mW, which yields a usable range of about 20 m indoors and about 100 m
outdoors assuming low-gain antennas.
Data rates perceived by the user are roughly half the theoret ical maximum data rates, attributable in part to the multipl e
access scheme used in 802.11b. This scheme is known as carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance
(CSMA/CA). In this scheme, a radio may transmit if it is unabl e to detect a transmission already underway in the same
channel. If the transmitting radio does not receive an ackno wledgement from the receiving radio – perhaps due to a
“collision” with another radio that began transmitting at t he same time – then the transmitter retransmits the affected data.9
Although there is considerable inefficiency associated wit h this unscheduled form of channel access, this scheme is sim pler
to implement than a rigid TDMA system and permits higher thro ughput when the number of users per channel is low.
B.4.2 IEEE 802.11a, -g, and -n
By the early 2000’s, advancements in technology permitted g reatly improved data rates, leading to the widespread
adoption of the standards 802.11a and 802.11g. IEEE 802.11a uses OFDM to send rates up to 54 Mb/s in channels of
about 20 MHz in the 5 GHz unlicensed band. 10 The primary benefit of 5 GHz is increased availability of spec trum,
allowing more RF channels and thus more simultaneous users. IEEE 802.11g is essentially 802.11a implemented in the
2.4 GHz band, providing a higher-rate alternative to 802.11 b. Like 802.11b, transmit power for 802.11a and 802.11g is
about 100 mW. IEEE 802.11a/g yields roughly twice the range o f 802.11b indoors, and improvement of tens of percent
outdoors. Since the mid 2000’s it has been practical and comm on for Wi-Fi radios to support all three standards: i.e.,
802.11b, -a, and -g.
The principal barrier to further increases in data rates was lack of available spectrum in the unlicensed 2.4 GHz and
5.8 GHz bands. This led to the IEEE 802.11n standard in 2009, w hich incorporates MIMO as well as a number of other
technical refinements that facilitate rates up to 600 Mb/s in 40 MHz channels in the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands. Like
802.11a/b/g, 802.11n uses about 100 mW transmit power, but a chieves about double the range; nominally up to about
70 m indoors and 250 m outdoors.
B.4.3 IEEE 802.11ac and ad
The two major emerging WLAN standards as this book is being wri tten are IEEE 802.11ac and IEEE 802.11ad, which
continue the OFDM+MIMO strategy but with significantly increased rates owing t o combinations of wider channels,

B.4.5 Las tendencias futuras

Por último, se debe observar el potencial de los sistemas de telecomunicaciones móviles 4G y 5G para subsumir parcialmente los sistemas WLAN y WMAN en el futuro. En un gran número de aplicaciones, los sistemas emergentes 4G ya son adecuados para servir como redes de datos inalámbricas. B.4.text_en_clean:
B.4 Wireless Data Networks

Wireless data networks connect computers to a data network by radio, as opposed to wires or cables. Such networks are referred to as wireless local area networks (WLANs), which are indoor or short-range outdoor networks; or wireless metropolitan area networks (WMANs), which implies longer links, perhaps spanning a few kilometers. As noted in the previous section, wireless data networks along with mobile telecommunications account for the majority of contemporary economic activity and new technology development in the field of radio.

6Technically, early versions of LTE aren’t considered 4G because they don’t meet some of the performance specifications that are considered to be required for 4G. Later versions are considered 4G.

B.4.1 IEEE 802.11 and 802.11b

In WLAN applications, the IEEE 802.11 family of standards currently dominate.7 The earliest realization of this standard, known simply as “802.11” (alternatively as “802.11-1997” or “802.11 Legacy”), achieved data rates up to about 2 Mb/s using single-carrier DSSS or FHSS approaches in the 2.4 GHz unlicensed band. This standard became popular in the late 1990s but was quickly superseded by 802.11b.

IEEE 802.11b, despite itself being superseded by multiple generations of standards (summarized below), remains ubiquitous. It is so popular that its marketing name – “Wi-Fi” – has become a synonym for WLAN in general. IEEE 802.11b uses a single-carrier modulation scheme known as complementary code keying (CCK) to transmit data at rates of 5.5 Mb/s or 11 Mb/s in channels up to 22 MHz wide in the 2.4 GHz unlicensed band.8 In CCK, groups of 4 bits (for 5.5 Mb/s) or 8 bits (for 11 Mb/s) are mapped to a sequence of 8 QPSK symbols; this mapping is essentially a form of error control coding. Transmit power is up to 100 mW, which yields a usable range of about 20 m indoors and about 100 m outdoors assuming low-gain antennas.

Data rates perceived by the user are roughly half the theoretical maximum data rates, attributable in part to the multiple access scheme used in 802.11b. This scheme is known as carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance (CSMA/CA). In this scheme, a radio may transmit if it is unable to detect a transmission already underway in the same channel. If the transmitting radio does not receive an acknowledgement from the receiving radio – perhaps due to a “collision” with another radio that began transmitting at the same time – then the transmitter retransmits the affected data.9

Although there is considerable inefficiency associated with this unscheduled form of channel access, this scheme is simpler to implement than a rigid TDMA system and permits higher throughput when the number of users per channel is low.

B.4.2 IEEE 802.11a, -g, and -n

By the early 2000’s, advancements in technology permitted greatly improved data rates, leading to the widespread adoption of the standards 802.11a and 802.11g. IEEE 802.11a uses OFDM to send rates up to 54 Mb/s in channels of about 20 MHz in the 5 GHz unlicensed band.10 The primary benefit of 5 GHz is increased availability of spectrum, allowing more RF channels and thus more simultaneous users. IEEE 802.11g is essentially 802.11a implemented in the 2.4 GHz band, providing a higher-rate alternative to 802.11b. Like 802.11b, transmit power for 802.11a and 802.11g is about 100 mW. IEEE 802.11a/g yields roughly twice the range of 802.11b indoors, and improvement of tens of percent outdoors. Since the mid 2000’s it has been practical and common for Wi-Fi radios to support all three standards: i.e., 802.11b, -a, and -g.

The principal barrier to further increases in data rates was lack of available spectrum in the unlicensed 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz bands. This led to the IEEE 802.11n standard in 2009, which incorporates MIMO as well as a number of other technical refinements that facilitate rates up to 600 Mb/s in 40 MHz channels in the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands. Like 802.11a/b/g, 802.11n uses about 100 mW transmit power, but achieves about double the range; nominally up to about 70 m indoors and 250 m outdoors.

B.4.3 IEEE 802.11ac and ad

The two major emerging WLAN standards as this book is being written are IEEE 802.11ac and IEEE 802.11ad, which continue the OFDM+MIMO strategy but with significantly increased rates owing to combinations of wider channels, higher-order modulations, beamforming, and increased number of MIMO streams. IEEE 802.11ac – also currently

7A pretty good summary of the IEEE 802.11 family of standards through 2010 (so, including 802.11b, -a, -g, and -n), containing many more details than are conveyed here, is [26].

8The exact frequencies vary from country to country, but generally 10’s of MHz somewhere just above 2.4 GHz. 9The “CA” in “CSMA/CA” refers to an feature in the protocol which allows a transmitter to reserve time for transmission; however this feature is rarely implemented. Thus 802.11 networks are typically just “CSMA”.

10Varies from country to country, but generally 100s of MHz between 5.1 GHz and 5.8 GHz.

referred to Very High Throughput (VHT) – is designed for 5 GHz (only) and uses subcarrier modulations up to 256-QAM and channel bandwidths up to 160 MHz to achieve data rates up to a few Gb/s.

IEEE 802.11ad – also currently referred to as “WiGig” – is designed for the 60 GHz unlicensed band,11 and is expected to consistently achieve rates above 2 Gb/s using 2.16 GHz-wide channels. In contrast to all previous standards, 802.11ad maximum transmit power will be about 10 mW (as opposed to about 100 mW), owing to the greater difficulty of efficient power amplifier design in this frequency regime. In addition, there is a factor of about 22 dB additional path loss associated with the increase in frequency relative to 5 GHz. The outcome is that range is limited to about 10 m in line-of-site conditions, and poor penetration into adjacent rooms in indoor deployments. On the other hand, any attempt to increase range significantly beyond 10s of meters would be complicated by oxygen absorption in this band (reminder: Section 3.7.3), which becomes dominant over free-space path loss for ranges greater than about 50 m. In fact, this last issue is considered a possible strength of IEEE 802.11ad from the perspective that interference between nearby systems (e.g., two systems located at opposite ends of a building, or in adjacent buildings) is reduced by a much greater extent than would be possible by relying on free-space path loss alone.

B.4.4 Longer Range Systems: IEEE 802.16 (WiMAX) and 802.11af (TVWS)

Although there are many more wireless data network technologies which are currently in use or are currently emerging, we now limit ourselves to just two more: IEEE 802.16 and 802.11af. The IEEE 802.16 family of standards – also known by the marketing title “WiMAX” – is properly classified as a WMAN technology. The principal distinction between WiMAX and the standards mentioned above is the intended use for “metropolitan area” outdoor data networks, delivering data rates up to 10s of Mb/s over ranges up to several kilometers in various frequency bands in the SHF regime.12 As this book is being written, the future of WiMAX is unclear; LTE seems to be emerging as a more popular alternative.

IEEE 802.11af facilitates 802.11-type data networking in unused broadcast television channels below 1 GHz. This is a response to two issues: Limited spectrum in the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz unlicensed bands, and desire for longer range facilitated by the reduced path loss of lower frequencies. Data rates of 10s to 100s of Mb/s at ranges up to 1 km or so are anticipated using single carrier and OFDM modulations in unused 6 MHz-wide television channels. IEEE 802.11af is also known by a number of other names, including Television White Spaces (TVWS),13 White-Fi, and Super Wi-Fi. The future of IEEE 802.11af is presently a bit murky, as it depends on co-existence with broadcast television – i.e., deciding what constitutes an “unused” television channel – and the nominal data rates are relatively low.

B.4.5 Future Trends

Finally, one should note the potential for 4G and 5G mobile telecommunications systems to partially subsume WLAN and WMAN systems in the future. In a large number of applications, emerging 4G systems are already suitable to serve as wireless data networks. However since spectrum available to mobile telecommunications systems will remain relatively small, it currently seems likely that distinct WLAN/WMAN systems will continue to be required to accommodate applications requiring the highest data rates.

B.5 Short-Range Data Communications
A distinct class of wireless data communications systems is comprised of systems that are optimized for relatively low
data rates over short range, and for which WLAN technology is t ypically overkill. Examples described below are
Bluetooth, ZigBee and the simplex systems used for remote ke yless entry and tire pressure monitoring in automobiles.

The purpose of these systems is to move relatively small amou nts of data in scenarios in which a wired connection would
be more expensive or inconvenient, and at the lowest possibl e power and device cost.
B.5.1 Bluetooth
Bluetooth is a scheme for point-to-point networking in supp ort of devices such as wireless computer peripherals, wirel ess
microphones and headphones; and for connections between sm art phones, computers, and entertainment devices. Such
systems are sometimes referred to as personal area networks (PANs). Bluetooth operates in the 2.4 GHz unlicensed band,
using FHSS multiple access at 1600 frequency hops per second . Data rates up to hundreds of kb/s over ranges up to a few
meters are achieved using channels of 1 MHz or 2 MHz with trans mit power in the range 1–100 mW. Bluetooth currently
employs a variety of modulations including BFSK with Gaussi an pulse shaping (commonly referred to as GFSK),
π
4 -DQPSK, and 8-DPSK. The latest versions of the standard supp ort data rates up to 3 Mb/s. Bluetooth was originally
conceived as IEEE 802.15.1, but the standard is now managed b y an industry consortium.
B.5.2 ZigBee
ZigBee – also known as IEEE 802.15.4 – serves a role similar to Bluetooth but is more commonly found in industrial
applications, such as networks interconnecting large numb ers of sensors. ZigBee is specified to operate in a number of
unlicensed UHF bands including 2.4 GHz. Data rates up to 250 k b/s over ranges up to 10s of meters are achieved using
DSSS OQPSK modulation in 5 MHz channels with transmit power i n the range 1–100 mW. A notable feature of ZigBee is
ad hoc mesh networking, which allows ZigBee radios which would nor mally be out of range to communicate by relaying
data through other ZigBee radios.
B.5.3 Automotive Applications: RKE and TPMS
Remote keyless entry (RKE) is the system that allows one to unlock an automobile fr om a distance, usually by pressing a
button on a “fob” attached to one’s key ring. There is no singl e standard for RKE, however most systems operate in
unlicensed spectrum in the lower UHF range (433 MHz is common in the US), typically sending bursts of a few kb/s using
either binary ASK or binary FSK at a level of a few milliwatts. RKE is strictly simplex.
A tire pressure monitoring system (TPMS) is the simplex system that conveys tire pressure data from a transmitter located
in the valve stem of a tire to a receiver located elsewhere in t he vehicle. In all other respects, TPMS closely resembles
RKE: Both use the simplest possible binary digital modulati ons in unlicensed spectrum below 1 GHz to send bursts of
very low rate data.
The primary considerations in both RKE and TPMS are low power (for long battery life), rugged implementation, and low
cost. For RKE there is, of course, the additional matter of se curity, which requires that RKE data be well-encrypted.
B.5.text_es_mx:
B.5 Comunicación de datos de corto alcance

Una clase distinta de sistemas de comunicaciones inalámbricas de datos está compuesta por sistemas optimizados para tasas de datos relativamente bajas a lo largo del corto alcance, y para los cuales la tecnología WLAN es normalmente demasiado alta. Los ejemplos que se describen a continuación son Bluetooth, ZigBee y los sistemas simples utilizados para la entrada remota sin llave y el monitoreo de presión de neumáticos en automóviles.

11Las frecuencias exactas varían de país a país, pero generalmente varias GHz en 57–66 GHz. 12Para recordar por qué es tan difícil ofrecer mayores tasas de datos a estas distancias, vea el ejemplo en la sección 7.8. 13Se debe notar que “TVWS” realmente se refiere a todos los esquemas (no sólo 802.11af) que utilizan canales de televisión de barbecho.

El propósito de estos sistemas es mover cantidades relativamente pequeñas de datos en escenarios en los que una conexión cableada sería más cara o inconveniente, y al menor costo de potencia y dispositivo posible.

B.5.1 Bluetooth

Bluetooth es un esquema para la creación de redes punto a punto en apoyo de dispositivos como periféricos de computadora inalámbrico, micrófonos inalámbricos y auriculares; y para conexiones entre teléfonos inteligentes, computadoras y dispositivos de entretenimiento. Estos sistemas se denominan a veces redes de área personal (PANs). Bluetooth opera en la banda sin licencia 2.4 GHz, utilizando el acceso múltiple FHSS en los audífonos de frecuencia 1600 por segundo. Los datos de hasta cientos de kb/s sobre rangos de hasta unos pocos metros se logran utilizando canales de 1 MHz o 2 MHz con potencia de transmisión en el rango 1-100 mW. Bluetooth actualmente emplea una variedad de modulación incluyendo BFSK con modelado de pulso gausiano (commonly denominado GFSK),

π 4 -DQPSK, y 8-DPSK. Las últimas versiones de los datos estándar de soporte hasta 3 Mb/s. Bluetooth fue concebido originalmente como IEEE 802.15.1, pero el estándar ahora es gestionado por un consorcio industrial.

B.5.2 ZigBee

ZigBee – también conocido como IEEE 802.15.4 – sirve un papel similar al Bluetooth, pero se encuentra más comúnmente en aplicaciones industriales, tales como redes interconectando grandes cantidades de sensores. ZigBee se especifica para operar en un número de sin licencia UHF bandas incluyendo 2.4 GHz. Tasas de datos hasta 250 kb/s sobre rangos de hasta 10 metros se logra utilizando DSSS OQPSK modulación en el interior 5 MHz canales con potencia de transmisión en el rango 1–100 mW. Una característica notable de ZigBee es la red de malla ad hoc, que permite radios ZigBea que normalmente estarían fuera de alcance para comunicarse retransmitiendo datos a través de otras radios ZigaBee.

B.5.3 Las aplicaciones automotrices: RKE y TPMS

Entrada sin llave remota (RKE) es el sistema que permite desbloquear un automóvil desde una distancia, generalmente pulsando un botón en un “fob” conectado a un anillo de llave. No hay un solo estándar para RKE, sin embargo la mayoría de los sistemas funcionan en el espectro sin licencia en la parte inferior UHF rango (433 MHz es común en el US), generalmente envía ráfagas de unos pocos kb/s utilizando ya sea binario ASK o binario FSK a un nivel de unos pocos milits. RKE Es estrictamente simple.

Un sistema de monitoreo de presión de neumáticos (TPMS) es el sistema simplex que transmite datos de presión de los neumáticos desde un transmisor situado en el tallo de válvula a un receptor ubicado en otro lugar del vehículo. En todos los demás aspectos, TPMS se asemeja estrechamente a RKE: Ambos utilizan las modulaciones digitales binarias más sencillas posibles en espectro sin licencia debajo de 1 GHz para enviar ráfagas de datos de muy baja velocidad.

Las consideraciones primarias tanto en RKE como TPMS son de baja potencia (para larga duración de la batería), aplicación robusta y bajo costo. Para RKE hay, por supuesto, la materia adicional de seguridad, que requiere que los datos RKE estén bien cifrados.
