B.6.text:
B.6 Radio Frequency Identification (RFID)
RFID encompasses a broad class of technologies for determin ing the identity and (sometimes) the status of objects over
ranges of 10s to 100s of meters. The “killer app” for RFID is in ventory control; i.e., tracking the location of large numbe rs
of items such as products in retail stores, medical instrume nts and pharmacy items in hospitals, and so on. The
fundamental elements of an RFID system are tags, which are attached to the objects of interest; and readers, whose
locations are known and are able to wirelessly communicate w ith the tags. The communication is typically initiated by th e
reader, which broadcasts a radio signal that all tags within range should be able to detect. This is referred to as
interrogation. In response, the tags transmit a signal which includes info rmation that allows the reader to uniquely identify
the tag. Detection of a tag’s signal indicates that the assoc iated object must within range of the reader.


498 APPENDIX B. CHARACTERISTICS OF SOME COMMON RADIO SYSTEMS
Figure B.2: A tag used in a 900 MHz-band passive RFID system. T his tag is about 10 cm × 1 cm. The IC is the small
rectangular device located near the center of the tag. The antenna is essentially a resonant dipole which has been compressed
in length using a combination of “meandering” and end loadin g. Trademark and ©ALIEN. Used under fair use.
RFID systems can be broadly categorized as active, passive, or semi-passive. In an active RFID system, the tags are
battery-powered and the system operates more or less as a tra ditional half-duplex radio communications system. Active
RFID systems typically operate in the lower UHF band (e.g., u nlicensed spectrum around 430 MHz), which is tradeoff
that accommodates the relatively small size of the tags, whi ch can accommodate only small antennas. The principal
drawbacks of active RFID systems pertain to the tags, which a re too bulky and expensive for tracking large numbers of
small objects. Therefore active RFID is used mainly for trac king relatively small numbers of large or valuable objects;
e.g., shipping containers.
In a passive RFID system, the tag is powered by the received si gnal. When a signal is received, the power in the signal is
converted to DC, used to power-up the electronics (typicall y a small IC), which in turn controls the response. Because th e
available power is extremely limited, passive tags typical ly do not actually transmit a response signal. Instead, the t ag’s
antenna is connected to a varying impedance under the contro l of the tag’s electronics. The tag’s antenna re-radiates th e
incident power with a magnitude and phase that is determined by the connected impedance. A common scheme employs
two states: One state in which the antenna is severely mismat ched, resulting in most of the incident signal being
re-radiated; and another state in which the antenna is well- matched, resulting in relatively low re-radiation. Thus th e
response signal received by the reader is the “backscatter” from the tag, with the information from the tag represented a s
variation in the magnitude and/or phase of this backscatter . This strategy offers the huge advantage that passive RFID t ags
can be made very inexpensively and with nearly-negligible b ulk. For example, Figure B.2 shows a passive RFID tag
designed for the operation in the 900 MHz unlicensed band. 14 The tag is small, flat, and flexible so that it is easily attache d
to curved surfaces.
The backscatter strategy employed by passive RFID systems i mposes severe constraints on the modulation. The 900 MHz
band systems now in common use employ a form of binary ASK know n as pulse interval encoding (PIE). In this scheme,
each bit period begins with an interval during which the carr ier is always on, and the difference between a “0” and a “1” is
represented by the total fraction of the bit period during wh ich the carrier remains on. This scheme ensures that the tag
receives enough power to remain energized while responding . The backscattered signal from tag to reader is typically
modulated using one of two schemes: “FM0” or Miller modulation. In these schemes the bits are represented by the
number of state changes during a bit period. In FM0, for examp le, zero changes in a bit period indicates a “1” whereas one
change in a bit period indicates a “0”.
Data rates in passive RFID are typically in the range of 10s to 100s of kb/s. The incentive for high data rates is to reduce
the length of transmissions, so as to minimize contention fo r spectrum. Range for passive systems operating in the
900 MHz band is typically 10s of meters with reader transmit l evels of a few watts. Also common are HF-band
(13.56 MHz in the U.S.) passive RFID systems, which have much shorter range but also have advantages in some
scenarios where UHF-band propagation is problematic; this includes in particular tags affixed to containers of liquid.
Active and passive RFID systems also appear in bands around 1 50 kHz, 2.4 GHz, and in the 3–10 GHz range; each having
various advantages and disadvantages.
Semi-passive RFID tags are passive RFID tags that also inclu de a battery, which is used to implement functions that must
be maintained even when the tag is not within range of a reader , or for which the power provided by the reader’s signal is
inadequate. Typical applications include tags used as sens ors to monitor temperature or other environmental conditio ns.
14Exact frequencies vary between countries.

B.6.text_es_mx:
B.6 Identificación por radiofrecuencia (RFID)

RFID abarca una amplia clase de tecnologías para determinar la identidad y (a veces) el estado de los objetos sobre rangos de 10 a 100 metros. La “app de asesino” para RFID es control de inventario; es decir, rastrear la ubicación de un gran número de artículos como productos en tiendas minoristas, instrumentos médicos y productos farmacéuticos en hospitales, etc. Los elementos fundamentales de un sistema RFID son etiquetas, que se adjuntan a los objetos de interés; y lectores, cuyos lugares son conocidos y pueden comunicarse inalámbricamente con las etiquetas. La comunicación es típicamente iniciada por el lector, que transmite una señal de radio que todas las etiquetas dentro del rango deben ser capaces de detectar. Esto se conoce como interrogatorio. En respuesta, las etiquetas transmiten una señal que incluye información que permite al lector identificar de forma única la etiqueta. La detección de la señal de una etiqueta indica que el objeto asociado debe estar dentro del rango del lector.

Figura B.2: Una etiqueta usada en un sistema RFID pasivo de banda 900 MHz. Esta etiqueta es sobre 10 cm × 1 cm. El IC es el pequeño dispositivo rectangular situado cerca del centro de la etiqueta. La antena es esencialmente una dipole resonante que se ha comprimido en longitud utilizando una combinación de “meandering” y carga final. Marca comercial y ©ALIEN usado bajo uso justo.

Los sistemas RFID pueden clasificarse ampliamente como activos, pasivos o semipasivos. En un sistema activo RFID, las etiquetas son propulsadas por batería y el sistema funciona más o menos como un sistema tradicional de comunicaciones de radio de punto medio. Los sistemas Active RFID normalmente funcionan en la banda UHF inferior (por ejemplo, espectro sin licencia alrededor de 430 MHz), que es un intercambio que acomoda el tamaño relativamente pequeño de etiquetas ante Los principales inconvenientes de los sistemas RFID activos corresponden a las etiquetas, que son demasiado voluminosos y costosos para rastrear grandes cantidades de objetos pequeños. Por lo tanto, el RFID activo se utiliza principalmente para rastrear números relativamente pequeños de objetos grandes o valiosos; por ejemplo, contenedores de envío.

En un sistema RFID pasivo, la etiqueta está alimentada por la señal recibida. Cuando se recibe una señal, la potencia en la señal se convierte a DC, utilizada para encender la electrónica (típicamente un pequeño IC), que a su vez controla la respuesta. Debido a que la potencia disponible es extremadamente limitada, las etiquetas pasivas normalmente no transmiten una señal de respuesta. En lugar, la antena de la etiqueta está conectada a un control electrónico variable. La antena de la etiqueta re-radia el poder del incidente con una magnitud y fase que se determina por la impedancia conectada. Un esquema común emplea dos estados: Un estado en el cual la antena es severamente disuelta, dando lugar a la mayoría de la señal del incidente siendo re-radiada; y otro estado en el que la antena está bien emparejada, resultando en una re-radicion relativamente baja. Así la señal de respuesta recibida por el lector es el “backscatter” de la etiqueta, con la información de la etiqueta representada como variación en la magnitud y/o fase de este backscatter. Esta estrategia ofrece la enorme ventaja de que las etiquetas pasivo RFID pueden ser hechas muy barato y con casi nítida granel. Por ejemplo, la Figura B.2 muestra una etiqueta RFID pasiva diseñada para la operación en la banda sin licencia 900 MHz.14 La etiqueta es pequeña, plana y flexible de modo que se apegue fácilmente a superficies curvadas.

La estrategia de backscatter empleada por sistemas pasivos RFID impone graves restricciones a la modulación. Los sistemas de banda 900 MHz emplean ahora en uso común una forma de codificación binaria ASK conocida como intervalo de pulso (PIE) En este esquema, cada periodo de bit comienza con un intervalo durante el cual el transportista está siempre encendido, y la diferencia entre un “0” y un “1” está representada por la fracción total del período de bits. Este esquema asegura que la etiqueta reciba suficiente poder para mantenerse energizada mientras responde. La señal de backscattered de la etiqueta al lector se modula normalmente utilizando uno de dos esquemas: “FM0” o modulación Miller. En estos esquemas los bits están representados por el número de cambios estatales durante un período de bits. FM0, por ejemplo, cero cambios en un período de bits indica un “1” mientras que un cambio en un periodo de tiempo indica un “0”.

Los índices de datos en RFID pasivos suelen estar entre 10 y 100 kb/s. El incentivo para altas tasas de datos es reducir la longitud de las transmisiones, a fin de minimizar la contención del espectro. La gama para sistemas pasivos que operan en la banda 900 MHz es típicamente 10 metros con niveles de transmisión de lectores de algunas watts. También son comunes los sistemas HF-band (13.56 MHz en los EE.UU.) pasivos RFID, que tienen mucho más rango pero también tienen ventajas en algunos escenarios donde la propagación de banda UHF es problemática; esto incluye en particular etiquetas afianzadas a contenedores de líquido. Los sistemas RFID activos y pasivos también aparecen en bandas alrededor de 150 kHz, 2.4 GHz, y teniendo en el rango 3–10 GHz varias ventajas;

Las etiquetas RFID semipasivas son etiquetas RFID pasivas que también incluyen una batería, que se utiliza para implementar funciones que deben mantenerse incluso cuando la etiqueta no está dentro del rango de un lector, o para las cuales la potencia proporcionada por la señal del lector es inadecuada. Aplicaciones típicas incluyen etiquetas utilizadas como sensores para monitorear temperatura u otras condiciones ambientales.

14Las frecuencias exactas varían entre países.

La “app de asesino” para RFID es control de inventario; es decir, rastrear la ubicación de un gran número de artículos como productos en tiendas minoristas, instrumentos médicos y productos farmacéuticos en hospitales, etc. Los elementos fundamentales de un sistema RFID son etiquetas, que se adjuntan a los objetos de interés; y lectores, cuyos lugares son conocidos y pueden comunicarse inalámbricamente con las etiquetas. La comunicación es típicamente iniciada por el lector, que transmite una señal de radio que todas las etiquetas dentro del rango deben ser capaces de detectar. Esto se conoce como interrogatorio. En respuesta, las etiquetas transmiten una señal que incluye información que permite al lector identificar de forma única la etiqueta. B.6.text_en_clean:
B.6 Radio Frequency Identification (RFID)

RFID encompasses a broad class of technologies for determining the identity and (sometimes) the status of objects over ranges of 10s to 100s of meters. The “killer app” for RFID is inventory control; i.e., tracking the location of large numbers of items such as products in retail stores, medical instruments and pharmacy items in hospitals, and so on. The fundamental elements of an RFID system are tags, which are attached to the objects of interest; and readers, whose locations are known and are able to wirelessly communicate with the tags. The communication is typically initiated by the reader, which broadcasts a radio signal that all tags within range should be able to detect. This is referred to as interrogation. In response, the tags transmit a signal which includes information that allows the reader to uniquely identify the tag. Detection of a tag’s signal indicates that the associated object must within range of the reader.

Figure B.2: A tag used in a 900 MHz-band passive RFID system. This tag is about 10 cm × 1 cm. The IC is the small rectangular device located near the center of the tag. The antenna is essentially a resonant dipole which has been compressed in length using a combination of “meandering” and end loading. Trademark and ©ALIEN. Used under fair use.

RFID systems can be broadly categorized as active, passive, or semi-passive. In an active RFID system, the tags are battery-powered and the system operates more or less as a traditional half-duplex radio communications system. Active RFID systems typically operate in the lower UHF band (e.g., unlicensed spectrum around 430 MHz), which is tradeoff that accommodates the relatively small size of the tags, which can accommodate only small antennas. The principal drawbacks of active RFID systems pertain to the tags, which are too bulky and expensive for tracking large numbers of small objects. Therefore active RFID is used mainly for tracking relatively small numbers of large or valuable objects; e.g., shipping containers.

In a passive RFID system, the tag is powered by the received signal. When a signal is received, the power in the signal is converted to DC, used to power-up the electronics (typically a small IC), which in turn controls the response. Because the available power is extremely limited, passive tags typically do not actually transmit a response signal. Instead, the tag’s antenna is connected to a varying impedance under the control of the tag’s electronics. The tag’s antenna re-radiates the incident power with a magnitude and phase that is determined by the connected impedance. A common scheme employs two states: One state in which the antenna is severely mismatched, resulting in most of the incident signal being re-radiated; and another state in which the antenna is well-matched, resulting in relatively low re-radiation. Thus the response signal received by the reader is the “backscatter” from the tag, with the information from the tag represented as variation in the magnitude and/or phase of this backscatter. This strategy offers the huge advantage that passive RFID tags can be made very inexpensively and with nearly-negligible bulk. For example, Figure B.2 shows a passive RFID tag designed for the operation in the 900 MHz unlicensed band.14 The tag is small, flat, and flexible so that it is easily attached to curved surfaces.

The backscatter strategy employed by passive RFID systems imposes severe constraints on the modulation. The 900 MHz band systems now in common use employ a form of binary ASK known as pulse interval encoding (PIE). In this scheme, each bit period begins with an interval during which the carrier is always on, and the difference between a “0” and a “1” is represented by the total fraction of the bit period during which the carrier remains on. This scheme ensures that the tag receives enough power to remain energized while responding. The backscattered signal from tag to reader is typically modulated using one of two schemes: “FM0” or Miller modulation. In these schemes the bits are represented by the number of state changes during a bit period. In FM0, for example, zero changes in a bit period indicates a “1” whereas one change in a bit period indicates a “0”.

Data rates in passive RFID are typically in the range of 10s to 100s of kb/s. The incentive for high data rates is to reduce the length of transmissions, so as to minimize contention for spectrum. Range for passive systems operating in the 900 MHz band is typically 10s of meters with reader transmit levels of a few watts. Also common are HF-band (13.56 MHz in the U.S.) passive RFID systems, which have much shorter range but also have advantages in some scenarios where UHF-band propagation is problematic; this includes in particular tags affixed to containers of liquid. Active and passive RFID systems also appear in bands around 150 kHz, 2.4 GHz, and in the 3–10 GHz range; each having various advantages and disadvantages.

Semi-passive RFID tags are passive RFID tags that also include a battery, which is used to implement functions that must be maintained even when the tag is not within range of a reader, or for which the power provided by the reader’s signal is inadequate. Typical applications include tags used as sensors to monitor temperature or other environmental conditions.

14Exact frequencies vary between countries.

B.7 Sistemas globales de navegación por satélite (GNSS)

Un GNSS es un sistema de transmisores basados en satélites que se pueden utilizar para determinar la ubicación de un receptor con alta precisión. Como este libro está siendo escrito, dos sistemas tales – GPS y GLONASS – están totalmente operativos; ver abajo para más información sobre estos. Por lo menos otros dos sistemas son semi-operacionales y todavía en desarrollo: Estos son el sistema Galileo de la Unión Europea y el sistema Beidou de China.

Los cuatro sistemas dependen del mismo principio, conocido como el tiempo de llegada (TOA). La idea es que cada satélite contiene un reloj preciso y codifica el tiempo actual en su transmisión. Al recibir esta señal, el receptor puede utilizar esta información para determinar el tiempo de viaje del satélite al receptor, y posteriormente la distancia entre el satélite y el receptor. El receptor también conoce la ubicación del satélite en el momento de la transmisión, que limita las posibles ubicaciones del receptor a la superficie de una esfera que rodea al satélite. Repetir este proceso con menos otros tres satélites resulta en por lo menos tres esferas tales cuyas superficies se intersectan en un solo lugar; es decir, el del receptor. En la práctica hay muchos problemas que contribuyen a la incertidumbre en este proceso; sin embargo, los receptores comerciales modernos GNSS suelen ofrecer precisión de ubicación en el orden de tan sólo 10 metros o mejor.

El Sistema de Posicionamiento Global (GPS) de los Estados Unidos consiste en unos satélites 30, como que 8 o así siempre están a la vista de un receptor sobre la superficie de la Tierra. La banda de frecuencia GPS primaria está centrada en 1575.42 MHz, también conocida como la frecuencia “L1”. Se utiliza la polarización circular derecha. La señal principal transmitida en la frecuencia GPS L1 se conoce como la señal de coarse/Aquisición. La señal C/A es una DSSS BPSK señal que se transmite de cada satélite utilizando un código de propagación único; por lo tanto GPS usos CDMA para permitir que todos los satélites compartan el mismo espectro (véase el ejemplo) 6.9). Los datos transmitidos en la señal C/A son una 50 b/s “Mensaje de navegación” que contiene la información requerida por el receptor para determinar el tiempo absoluto y los lugares de los satélites. 50 b/s se distribuyen datos usando un 1023- secuencia de chips 1.023 millones de fichas por segundo; por lo tanto 20460 chips por bit. Esto facilita la estimación TOA a una precisión de no peor que un período de chip, que es alrededor de 1 μs, correspondiente a una distancia de aproximadamente 300 m. En la práctica la exactitud realizable es típicamente una pequeña fracción de un período de fichas, correspondiente a errores de tan solo 10 metros. Los satélites GPS transmiten una serie de señales adicionales, incluyendo señales con tasas de chip más altas para facilitar una mayor precisión de estimación TOA. La frecuencia L1 en particular contiene no sólo la señal C/A, sino una serie de señales adicionales CDMA que ocupan un ancho de banda total de aproximadamente 24 MHz.

La Federación de Rusia GLONASS el sistema utiliza un número similar de satélites y un conjunto similar de frecuencias. Restricting attention to the C/A signal, the principle diferencia is that the GLONASS La señal C/A se difunde en 511 miles de fichas por segundo, resultando en un ancho de banda de aproximadamente la mitad de la GPS C/A ancho de banda de señal. Además, cada satélite transmite en una frecuencia de centro única, y las frecuencias del centro son igualmente espaciadas por 562.5 kHz empezar a 1602 MHz. Así GLONASS es un sistema FDMA: La modulación DSSS se utiliza sólo para la distancia, y no es necesario para el acceso múltiple.

B.7.text_en_clean:
B.7 Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS)

A GNSS is a system of satellite-based transmitters which can be used to determine the location of a receiver with high accuracy. As this book is being written, two such systems – GPS and GLONASS – are fully operational; see below for more information on these. At least two other systems are semi-operational and still in development: These are European Union’s Galileo system and China’s Beidou system.

All four systems rely on the essentially the same principle, known as time of arrival (TOA) ranging. The idea is that each satellite contains an accurate clock and encodes the current time in its transmission. Upon the receipt of this signal, the receiver is able to use this information to determine the travel time from the satellite to the receiver, and subsequently the distance between the satellite and the receiver. The receiver also knows the location of the satellite at the time of transmission, which constrains the possible locations of the receiver to the surface of a sphere surrounding the satellite. Repeating this process with least three other satellites results in at least three such spheres whose surfaces intersect at one location; i.e., that of the receiver. In practice there are many issues that contribute uncertainty in this process; however modern commercial GNSS receivers routinely deliver location accuracy on the order of just 10s of meters or better.

The U.S. Global Positioning System (GPS) consists of about 30 satellites, such that 8 or so are always within view of a receiver on the surface of the Earth. The primary GPS frequency band is centered at 1575.42 MHz, also known as the “L1” frequency. Right-circular polarization is used. The primary signal transmitted on the GPS L1 frequency is known as the coarse/acquisition (C/A) signal. The C/A signal is a DSSS BPSK signal which is transmit from each satellite using a unique spreading code; thus GPS uses CDMA to allow all satellites to share the same spectrum (See Example 6.9). The data conveyed in the C/A signal is a 50 b/s “navigation message” that contains the information required by the receiver to determine absolute time and the locations of the satellites. The 50 b/s data is spread using a 1023-chip sequence at 1.023 million chips per second; thus 20460 chips per bit. This facilitates TOA estimation to an accuracy of no worse than one chip period, which is about 1 μs, corresponding to to a distance of about 300 m. In practice the realizable accuracy is typically a small fraction of a chip period, corresponding to ranging errors of just 10s of meters. GPS satellites transmit a number of additional signals, including signals with higher chip rates to facilitate higher TOA estimation accuracy. The L1 frequency in particular contains not only the C/A signal, but a number of additional CDMA signals occupying a total bandwidth of about 24 MHz.

The Russian Federation’s GLONASS system uses a similar number of satellites and a similar set of frequencies. Restricting attention to the C/A signal, the principle difference is that the GLONASS C/A signal is spread at 511 thousand chips per second, resulting in a bandwidth of about half the GPS C/A signal bandwidth. Also, each satellite transmits on a unique center frequency, and the center frequencies are equally spaced by 562.5 kHz beginning at 1602 MHz. Thus GLONASS is an FDMA system: The DSSS modulation is used only for ranging, and is not needed for multiple access.

B.8 Radar, Remote Sensing, and Radio Astronomy
Radar is the sensing, ranging, and characterization of obje cts by reflection or scattering of radio signals. Applicatio ns of
radar are well known; it suffices here to point out that radars are radio systems which have a great deal in common with
communications and navigation systems. The principal dist inction is that a radar is designed to detect it’s own
transmissions, as opposed to those of other transmitters. 15
Radio systems also find applications in geophysical remote s ensing and astronomy. In these applications, radio is used t o
measure the intensity, polarization, spectrum, or wavefor m of naturally-occurring radio emission, with the goal of le arning
something about the source or the intervening medium. The pr inciples of antennas and receivers described in this book
apply equally-well to these applications. An important con sideration is that most sources of natural radio emission ar e
extraordinarily weak in comparison to anthropogenic radio emission, and useful frequencies span the radio spectrum. T his
leads to considerable difficulty in managing the use of the ra dio spectrum, since frequencies which are useful for remote
sensing and radio astronomy overlap frequencies which are a llocated to communications, navigation, and radar systems . A
15Although not even this is quite true: In multistatic radar, the transmitter and receiver are in separate locations.

B.8 Radar, percepción remota y radioastronomía

Radar es la detección, el alcance y la caracterización de objetos por reflexión o dispersión de señales de radio. Las aplicaciones de radar son bien conocidas; basta aquí para señalar que los radares son sistemas de radio que tienen mucho en común con sistemas de comunicaciones y navegación. La principal distinción es que un radar está diseñado para detectar sus propias transmisiones, en lugar de las de otros transmisores.15

Los sistemas de radio también encuentran aplicaciones en teleobservación geofísica y astronomía. En estas aplicaciones, la radio se utiliza para medir la intensidad, polarización, espectro o forma onda de emisión radiológica naturalmente recurrente, con el objetivo de aprender algo sobre la fuente o el medio interveniente. Los principios de las antenas y receptores descritos en este libro aplican igualmente bien a estas aplicaciones. Una consideración importante es que la mayoría de las fuentes de emisión de radio natural son extraordinariamente débiles en comparación con las emisiones antropógenas de radio, y las frecuencias útiles abarcan el espectro radiofónico, lo que provoca considerable dificultad para gestionar el uso del espectro radioeléctrico, ya que las frecuencias que son útiles para la teleobservación y las frecuencia de superposición de radio astronomía que se asignan a los sistemas de comunicaciones, navegación y radar.

15Aunque ni siquiera esto es cierto: En el radar multiestático, el transmisor y receptor están en lugares separados.

Se recomienda la introducción a la teleobservación y la astronomía radio desde la perspectiva de la gestión del espectro y la coexistencia [55].

B.8.text_en_clean:
B.8 Radar, Remote Sensing, and Radio Astronomy

Radar is the sensing, ranging, and characterization of objects by reflection or scattering of radio signals. Applications of radar are well known; it suffices here to point out that radars are radio systems which have a great deal in common with communications and navigation systems. The principal distinction is that a radar is designed to detect it’s own transmissions, as opposed to those of other transmitters.15

Radio systems also find applications in geophysical remote sensing and astronomy. In these applications, radio is used to measure the intensity, polarization, spectrum, or waveform of naturally-occurring radio emission, with the goal of learning something about the source or the intervening medium. The principles of antennas and receivers described in this book apply equally-well to these applications. An important consideration is that most sources of natural radio emission are extraordinarily weak in comparison to anthropogenic radio emission, and useful frequencies span the radio spectrum. This leads to considerable difficulty in managing the use of the radio spectrum, since frequencies which are useful for remote sensing and radio astronomy overlap frequencies which are allocated to communications, navigation, and radar systems.
